Energy Information Administration — the Weekly Petroleum Status Report schedule

The standard release time is 10:30 a.m. Eastern on Wednesday, with exceptions listed by week. For the data for the week ending November 6, 2026, the alternate release date is Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. Eastern, the exception noted against the Veterans Day holiday.

Subjective
SOFX — Iran vows to keep its enriched uranium for a nuclear fleet

Mr. Rezaei said Tehran will not surrender any enriched uranium and wants it to fuel nuclear-powered ships and submarines. He told Al Mayadeen television that Tehran had informed Moscow the material would stay in the country: “We will not remove a single atom of enriched material from Iran.” He said Iran is designing nuclear-powered ships and submarines, and eventually small modular reactors, and said no negotiations with Washington were under way. The agency’s estimate puts the stockpile at about 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent at the time of the June 2025 strikes, with the surviving quantity unclear. Iranian media said the Guard had destroyed enemy navigation systems on Oman’s Didamar Island; three sources confirmed to Reuters that Iran struck navigation systems on the island, though they gave no damage assessment, and a senior Omani official told another outlet the aids had not been hit. Satellite imagery from the morning of November 10 showed thermal activity and no clear damage to the lighthouse or the masts. The account records 37 vessels attacked in and around the strait in October. Mr. Rezaei said Iran has given Washington seven conditions and is awaiting a clear response, and that the nuclear file will stay outside any talks until combat halts on all fronts, including Lebanon.

Subjective
Devdiscourse — “Not a single particle”: Mr. Rezaei rules out moving the stockpile abroad

Mr. Rezaei ruled out transferring the enriched material abroad, asserting that Tehran would retain its entire stockpile and use it for domestic purposes, in an interview with Al Mayadeen on Wednesday. “Not a single particle, however insignificant, of the enriched material will leave Iran.” He said Iran had told its Russian friends the material will remain inside Iran, for applications including nuclear-powered vessels and small modular reactor plants. He said Iran is not currently holding negotiations with the Americans, that the seven conditions have been presented and a clear response awaited—the initial response not sufficient—and that the strait will not reopen until the conditions are implemented. The account also records that Mr. Rezaei met President Putin at the Kremlin on November 5 and delivered a message from Ayatollah Khamenei.

Subjective
Asia Today — Iran denies talks as the strait stays shut

Mr. Rezaei said no negotiations are taking place between Tehran and Washington, rejecting suggestions that diplomacy to end the war is under way, and insisting the strait will remain closed until the United States meets Iran’s conditions. He said Iran had set out seven conditions and was still waiting for a clear and explicit answer, and that the conditions were set out in a June interim agreement whose full list Iran has not published. He ruled out sending the enriched uranium abroad, saying Tehran would not allow even a single particle to leave. The agency’s estimate puts the stockpile at 440.9 kilograms enriched to 60 percent when the nuclear facilities were attacked in June 2025, with the surviving quantity unclear. The strait has been effectively closed to normal commercial traffic since late February.

Subjective
Kashmir InFocus — Iran sets seven conditions for reopening the strait

Iran is linking the restoration of normal shipping through the strait to sanctions relief, the removal of the American naval blockade, the release of frozen assets and an end to fighting across the region. Speaker Ghalibaf, Tehran’s chief negotiator, said in an interview published November 11 that Iran had sent Washington a detailed response through Qatari mediation and was waiting for an official answer, and that the waterway will never return to its pre-war arrangements. Iranian officials have referred to seven conditions, but the complete text has not been publicly released; the demands listed are a reconstruction from officials’ statements, not a verbatim list. Reuters reported on November 11 that October was the busiest month for Gulf liquefied natural gas exports since the war began on February 28, and that Mr. Rezaei said Tehran would not allow any enriched material to leave the country.

Subjective
El Constitucional — Congress votes on the housing decrees after the strike, with the PNV as the key

The Permanent Deputation will vote this Thursday on the two housing decrees approved by the government. The vote comes on the eve of the campaign for the November 29 elections, with a different result expected for each text. The decree carrying most of the measures has the announced support of the PNV, decisive to reach 35 votes against 34 from the PP, Vox and Junts; the text allows certain tenants to request an extraordinary extension of up to two years. The second decree, establishing compensation for certain tenants when the owner communicates non-renewal, still does not have a majority, and the PNV has announced it will vote against it. The Deputation brings together 69 deputies and carries the chamber’s functions while the Cortes are dissolved.

Subjective
EuropeSays — Spain’s nationwide strike over rent: why Prime Minister Sánchez supports the protesters

The biggest unions called their first nationwide general strike together in 14 years on November 11, demanding affordable housing, higher wages and stronger public services, and Prime Minister Sánchez defended the strike and backed its demands. His government is trying to get two housing decrees through a vote on November 12, before the November 29 election. On October 2 the lower house rejected two government decrees on housing; the prime minister called an early election, and his cabinet approved revised versions on October 6, which went to the Permanent Deputation with the parliament dissolved. The wider package includes temporary extensions for eligible rental contracts, eviction protections for vulnerable people without alternative housing and measures to increase affordable supply; the separate decree changes how leases for a main home renew, rolling over for five or seven years after the minimum term, with compensation where the landlord declines renewal. The broader package appeared to have enough support, and the lease-renewal decree still lacked a majority.

Subjective
MyListingo — Spain today, November 12, 2026

Storm Charles and the aftermath of Wednesday’s general strike shaped the day, with transport, weather alerts and a housing vote in Congress all in play. The strike mobilized hundreds of thousands of people across Spain, even with heavy rain from Storm Charles in several areas, on Europa Press reporting. The consumption ministry estimates the rent extension would benefit five million people and let a tenant save €4,300. The Permanent Deputation debates the two housing decrees on Thursday; the account says the full chamber rejected them in late September, and that rejection led to the early election and to Wednesday’s strike. The housing decree is expected to pass by a single vote. Opposition leader Feijóo says he would repeal the housing decrees if he governs, calling them bad for tenants and for owners.

Subjective
Associated Press — the Alaska Senate results page

The wire’s results page for the Alaska Senate race carries the status too early to call, with an estimated 86.2 percent of the vote in. The candidates listed stand at Ms. Peltola 121,487 votes, Senator Sullivan 117,512, and Mr. Daniel Sullivan 4,100.

Subjective
Poliwave — the live Alaska results

The live page carries the Senate count at Ms. Peltola 121,487 votes, 48.9 percent, Senator Sullivan 117,512, 47.3 percent, and Mr. Daniel Sullivan Jr. 4,100, 1.6 percent—a lead of 3,975 votes. The page notes no new numbers from its feed since 11:17 p.m. Eastern, and carries an update stamp of 0427 GMT on November 12. No winner has been called. If no one passes 50 percent of the first choices, the state counts the voters’ next choices before naming a winner.

Subjective
Global 1 News — Alaska’s race uncalled: the other Mr. Sullivan’s 4,027 votes

Alaska’s Senate race is the last one in America, and at its center sit 4,027 ballots cast for a retired teacher from Petersburg who shares the incumbent’s name. Ms. Peltola leads Senator Sullivan by 4,250 first-choice votes on the count released Tuesday night, which added almost 25,000 ballots: Ms. Peltola 118,926, Senator Sullivan 114,676, Mr. Heikes 5,318 and Mr. Daniel Sullivan 4,027, with the wire estimating about 84 percent counted. Her lead was 2,517 on Monday and 636 at the close of Election Day. Ballots mailed from within the United States must be in by Friday, November 13; ballots from outside the country can arrive as late as November 18. The tabulation runs November 18, the Division declares its unofficial winners that day, and the target certification date is November 25.

Subjective
Democracy Docket — Ms. Peltola leads both Sullivans combined

Ms. Peltola’s count reached 118,926, 49 percent, compared with 114,676 for Senator Sullivan and 4,027 for the retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., on the latest wire counts in this account; she leads the incumbent by over 4,000 votes and both Sullivans combined by 223 votes. She stands one percentage point from the 50 percent threshold. About 84 percent of the votes have been tallied, with the next major release expected Friday. Litigation is ongoing in the Ninth Circuit, where voting rights groups on Monday called the suit embarrassing and indefensible.

Subjective
Zark News — Israel’s new parliament sworn in as Mr. Eisenkot faces a hard test

The new parliament was sworn in on Tuesday without a new government, after the election stripped Prime Minister Netanyahu of his majority but left his rivals no clear path either. The final count gave Mr. Netanyahu’s alliance 53 seats and Mr. Eisenkot’s partners 48. Mr. Eisenkot was tasked on Sunday with forming a government after securing the backing of 67 members, against 46 for Mr. Netanyahu; he has until December 6 to assemble a coalition, and can seek a two-week extension to December 20. His bloc chose Mr. Kahana as its candidate for speaker, to replace Mr. Ohana; 67 lawmakers signed the request to remove Mr. Ohana, and the vote on his replacement is scheduled for Tuesday, November 17.

entry.title: Mississippi Is Called for Mr. Colom, Nvidia Falls After Hours as Its Board Meets on Its Chief, and the Capitals Trade Fire on the Night After the Talks
entry.summary: The midnight file for Thursday, November 12, 2026: what Wednesday settled and what it left open. The Associated Press called Mississippi’s Senate race for Mr. Colom at 1758 ET, by 4,669 votes on the totals the wire published, and Senator Hyde-Smith conceded by telephone and on video within the hour; the Democratic caucus stands at 55, and Alaska’s race is the last Senate race in the country without a call, with Ms. Peltola ahead by 4,250 and the next count on Friday. Nvidia closed up 2.92 percent at $173.73 and then fell 8 to 9 percent after hours, after The Wall Street Journal reported that its board is preparing to oust Mr. Huang and The New York Times reported a relationship with an executive who reports to him; the board met late Wednesday and no decision, interim chief or company statement had been announced at midnight. Asian markets opened Thursday mixed, and the dollar stood at its highest since April of last year. The delegations left Abu Dhabi with the prisoner numbers carried to Thursday and the envoys bound for Moscow, and early Thursday the two capitals exchanged attacks: explosions were heard in Kyiv and Moscow’s mayor counted five drones downed. Tehran restated that no enriched material will leave the country and that the strait stays shut until its conditions are met. Spain’s strike ended with its size in dispute, and its housing decrees go to a vote on Thursday. Collected at 0000.
entry.content:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Mississippi Is Called for Mr. Colom, Nvidia Falls After Hours as Its Board Meets on Its Chief, and the Capitals Trade Fire on the Night After the Talks

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: the longest count in the country ended with a call at 1758 and a concession within the hour; the chip rally that closed the day gave it back after the bell on a board meeting about one man; the talks’ delegations flew home over a night of fire on both capitals; and Alaska kept the last Senate seat for another night.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Thursday, November 12, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 34, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Wednesday, and in Wednesday’s earlier editions, Nos. 33 and 32. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Wednesday Settled, What It Left Open

Wednesday settled its longest count, its holiday and its strike, and it left its newest crisis—a board meeting in California—undecided at midnight, and the desk files the day in that order. The Associated Press called Mississippi’s Senate race for Mr. Colom at 1758 ET, eight days after the vote, on a margin of 4,669 votes in the totals the wire published, and Senator Hyde-Smith conceded by telephone and on video within the hour; the Democratic caucus stands at 55, and Alaska is the last Senate race in the country without a call. Nvidia closed the regular session up 2.92 percent at $173.73, completing the reversal of Tuesday that the evening edition printed, and then fell 8 to 9 percent after hours, after The Wall Street Journal reported that its board is preparing to oust its chief executive, Mr. Huang, and The New York Times reported a relationship with an executive who reports to him; the board met late Wednesday, and at midnight no decision, no interim chief and no company statement had been announced. The delegations went home from Abu Dhabi with the prisoner numbers carried to Thursday and the envoys bound for Moscow, and in the first hours of Thursday the two capitals exchanged attacks—explosions heard in Kyiv, five drones counted down over the road to Moscow—in the wire account filed below. Tehran restated its two sentences on the day the president claimed a won war at Arlington: no enriched material leaves the country, and the strait stays shut until its conditions are met. Spain’s strike ended with its size in dispute and its housing decrees going to a vote on Thursday.

This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 34, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Wednesday, and in Wednesday’s earlier editions, Nos. 33 and 32. The wire’s Mississippi call came at 1758, as the evening watch was closing, and the evening edition—which printed both races uncalled—stands unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Count at Midnight: Mississippi Called at 1758, a Concession Within the Hour, and Alaska Alone

The count that began with 43 votes ended with a call and a concession, and both are Wednesday’s facts. The Associated Press called the race at 5:58 p.m. Eastern, in the wire account, the call account and the totals account filed below, which agree on the hour. NBC News and CNN’s decision desks projected the same winner separately, and Reuters reported that Senator Hyde-Smith had lost her re-election bid. The unofficial totals the accounts publish stand at 473,336 votes, 49.2 percent, for Mr. Colom, 468,667, 48.7 percent, for Senator Hyde-Smith, and 20,234, 2.1 percent, for the independent candidate, Mr. Pinkins—a margin of 4,669 votes out of nearly a million cast. The wire’s published explanation, carried in the explanation account filed below, says the decisive update came from Jackson County, which reported another 2,173 votes, and estimates fewer than 12,000 ballots still requiring county review. Less than an hour after the call, Senator Hyde-Smith conceded: she telephoned Mr. Colom, on his campaign’s account, and then posted a video captioned “Thank you, Mississippi,” saying, in the concession account filed below, “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters.”

What the call makes of the Senate is arithmetic. Mr. Colom’s is the Democrats’ eighth pickup of the midterms; the caucus that convenes on January 3 stands at 55, and Alaska decides whether it stands at 55 or 56. The man carries two firsts into the chamber, both on the record of the accounts filed below: he is Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, and the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate in 44 years; the senator he defeated is the senator who blocked his nomination to a federal judgeship in 2023, in the history account filed below. The result remains unofficial: counties submit certified results by Friday, November 13, and the state certifies on December 3, and Mississippi law carries no automatic recount. The margins the day printed on its way to the call—3,041 at the evening’s tally, 4,404 on Wednesday afternoon in one account, 4,645 on Wednesday night in another, and 4,585 in the at-call totals one program published—stand in the Cocked Hat against the wire’s 4,669.

Alaska is now the whole of the Senate file. Ms. Peltola leads Senator Sullivan by 4,250 first-choice votes—118,926, or 49 percent, to 114,676, or 47.2 percent—on Tuesday’s update, and no new count posted on Wednesday. One account puts 84 percent counted and about 40,000 ballots remaining; another puts the remainder at about 46,000. The next count is scheduled for Friday, November 13; if no candidate passes 50 percent of the first choices, the ranked-choice tabulation runs on November 18, and the target certification date is November 25. The legal file stands where the week left it: a judge dismissed the administration’s suit over certification, and the Justice Department appealed, in the count account filed below. In the House, the wire’s results page for Florida’s 27th District carries the status Called for Representative Salazar, 124,519 votes to Mr. Rodriguez’s 123,433 after the machine recount, in the results page filed below; the canvassing board certifies on Friday and the state on November 17, in the recount account filed below. More than a dozen House races stood too early to call at the evening. Settled: Mississippi, and the size of everything except Alaska and the House margin. Open: one seat, and the paperwork.

Nvidia at Midnight: The Close Reversed, the Evening Reversed Back, and a Board Out Late

The day’s largest movement in any file came after the bell, in a company whose earnings are not due until Tuesday. Nvidia closed the regular session at $173.73, up 2.92 percent on the figures the evening edition printed, as the instrument of the chip rally that reversed Tuesday whole. About an hour after the closing bell, The Wall Street Journal reported that the company’s board is preparing to oust its chief executive and co-founder, Mr. Huang; minutes earlier in the evening’s sequence, The New York Times reported that Mr. Huang had also had a relationship with a company executive who reports to him, identified in one account of the Times report as the vice president of health care. The shares fell about 8 percent in after-hours trading in the wire account and the futures account filed below, 8.6 percent to $158.76 by 1959 ET in the price account filed below, and more than 9 percent in the ouster account filed below; all three figures stand in the Cocked Hat. A second wire service, CBS News, citing two sources, also reported the board preparing to oust him, and the board was meeting late Wednesday to decide, on a source familiar with the matter in the Reuters account above. Bloomberg is reported to have said the company has been working with an outside firm to identify possible replacements and is considering a temporary chief. At midnight the file holds no decision, no interim appointment and no company statement: the running file’s last update before this edition closed, stamped 0043 GMT, records none announced, in the running account filed below. Mr. Huang remains the chief executive. The allegations in this file are allegations, printed as the accounts print them; no finding has been made by the board, by any committee or by any court.

The record the board is deciding on is a week old and is printed here once, in order. On Sunday Mr. Huang admitted a relationship with a woman whom American officials suspect of working with Chinese intelligence, in the pressure account filed below. On November 8 the board opened an independent investigation and retained a former federal prosecutor, Mr. Kim, and the firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead it. On Monday Bloomberg reported that the company’s general counsel had intervened in the Commerce Department’s investigation into Megaspeed, its largest Southeast Asian customer, asking whether American authorities were involved in the woman’s detention in Singapore. The stock fell 9.5 percent across Monday and Tuesday to $168.89. On Capitol Hill the pressure ran on its own track: Senator Cramer of North Dakota repeated his demand that Mr. Huang resign, calling his actions a national security risk; Representative Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, gave Mr. Huang until the end of Wednesday to answer a request for a closed-door briefing, with a subpoena likely if he did not agree; and a second committee is reported to be preparing one. The company reports its quarterly results on Tuesday, November 17. Settled: the close, the fall, and that the board met. Open: the decision, which is Thursday’s first fact.

Asia at Midnight: A Wobble at the Open, a Dollar at a High, and Thursday’s Witnesses Named

The first markets to price the board meeting were Asia’s, and their verdict at the open was a wobble and not a rout. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 opened up 226.52 points at 61,475.11, a fourth straight higher open, and turned lower shortly after; Seoul’s Kospi opened 0.2 percent higher and stood 0.21 percent lower at 0915 local time; Hong Kong’s Hang Seng opened down 194 points at 24,121, and Taiwan’s TAIEX opened down 76.69 points, in the opening account filed below. A later snapshot in the Reuters account above runs the same morning the other way—the Nikkei up 0.5 percent, the Kospi up 0.2 percent, Taiwanese shares up 0.5 percent, and the broad Asia-Pacific index outside Japan 0.1 percent lower, weighed down by Hong Kong—and a third account’s open figures sit between the two, in the market account filed below. The three snapshots are printed in the Cocked Hat as three readings of one choppy morning, not averaged. Japan’s corporate goods price index rose 7.1 percent year on year in October, above the 6.5 percent median forecast. Brent stood steady at about $92.46 a barrel in early Asia trade, against Wednesday’s settlement of $92.76.

The dollar carried the rate story while the bonds were shut. The dollar index stood at 102.87 in Asian trade, its highest level since April 9 of last year on the Reuters account’s dating, after rising 0.6 percent on Wednesday as traders repriced December. The pricing in the same account puts the quarter-point increase at 87.3 percent and the half-point at 12.7 percent for the December 9 meeting—against 13.2 percent for the half-point in Wednesday’s afternoon pricing and 15.3 percent on Tuesday, all printed in the Cocked Hat. Late American futures priced the Nvidia fall and nothing else: Nasdaq-100 futures fell nearly 1 percent in the futures account above and stood 0.46 percent lower at 2131 ET in a second account, with the S&P 500 e-minis down 0.4 percent and Dow futures fractionally higher. Thursday returns the session’s missing witnesses: the cash bond market reopens after the holiday, and the official crude inventory figures, held from Wednesday by the holiday, are due. Friday’s producer price report is the next inflation fact in the file. Settled: Wednesday’s close and the dollar’s level. Open: whether the chip rally survives its own largest company.

Abu Dhabi at Midnight: The Delegations Go Home, the Numbers Go to Thursday, and the Capitals Trade Fire

The talks’ first night at home produced paper from one delegation and fire from both armies. Mr. Umerov, who headed the Ukrainian delegation, published the delegation’s own closing account: two days of negotiations concluded, the main result an agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange, the negotiators returning to their capitals to finalize the details, in the closing account filed below. Mr. Kushner’s closing sentences in the same account stand beside it: there is currently no trust between the two sides, which he described as expected after such a conflict, and territorial issues were discussed and would be the most difficult to resolve. The numbers are Thursday’s work, as they were when the evening edition closed; the exchange is expected to exceed 2,000 prisoners in total on the Russian general’s figure of more than 1,000 a side, with the swap itself in two to three weeks, in the swap account filed below. The itinerary is unchanged: Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff meet President Putin in Moscow on Thursday, where they are expected to raise adding the European partners to the talks, and then fly to Dublin to meet President Zelenskyy.

The war’s own file added its night entry in the small hours. Russia and Ukraine exchanged attacks on each other’s capitals early on Thursday, in the Reuters account at the top of this report: explosions were heard in Kyiv in the early hours, a Reuters witness said, and it was not immediately clear whether the city had incurred damage; Moscow’s mayor, Mr. Sobyanin, said on Telegram that five drones heading for Moscow were downed, without additional details. Wednesday’s counts stand as the evening edition printed them—three killed and 11 injured in the daytime attack on the market in the Odesa region, seven wounded overnight in Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv, and the drone counts unreconciled between the ministry and the governor. The talks and the strikes proceeded on the same hours for two days in Abu Dhabi; on the first night after them, the strikes proceeded alone. Settled: the round is over, the exchange is agreed in principle, the delegations are home. Open: the numbers, the land, the ceasefire, and Europe’s chair—all of it now addressed to Moscow.

Iran at Midnight: No Speck Leaves, an Answer Sent by Way of Qatar, and the Strait Shut

Tehran spent the president’s holiday restating its position in three voices, and midnight collects the three without joining them. Mr. Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, said in interview excerpts released Wednesday that no enriched nuclear material will leave the country, that Tehran had communicated the decision to Moscow—which has offered to receive the material, and whose foreign ministry spokeswoman confirmed on Wednesday that the offer stands—and that reports of a recent meeting between Iranian and American representatives in Qatar were fabricated: no negotiations are currently taking place, in the Tehran account filed below. Speaker Ghalibaf, Tehran’s chief negotiator, said in an interview published the same day that Iran had sent Washington a detailed response through Qatari mediation and was waiting for an official answer, and that the waterway will never return to its pre-war arrangements, in the conditions account filed below. The two sentences—no channel, and an answer sent through one—stand in the file side by side, unreconciled by either speaker. The seven conditions themselves remain unpublished as a text; the demands the accounts list are sanctions relief, the release of frozen assets, the end of the American blockade of Iran’s ports and an end to the fighting across the region.

On the water, the day added claims and one reported attack, and no confirmation of either claim in the file. The Revolutionary Guard claimed on Wednesday that two more tankers struck naval mines and caught fire attempting to leave the strait by an unauthorized route under American fighter protection; a maritime operations centre had received a report on Tuesday evening of a tanker struck by a projectile, in the Tehran account above. Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing three sources, that Iranian forces had attacked navigation systems on Oman’s Didamar Island, in the strait account filed below. Against the whole file stands the president’s Arlington sentence of the same day—“We won”—and the desk prints the two records as it finds them: a war claimed won from an amphitheater, and a strait claimed shut until conditions are met, with both blockades standing and no agreement in the file. Settled: the positions, restated by every authorized voice on both sides. Open: the strait, the material, and the war’s end, whenever either capital dates it.

Spain at Midnight: The Strike Ends, the Count of It Does Not, and the Decrees Go to Thursday

Spain’s first general strike in 14 years ran its 24 hours and ended, and the argument the day leaves behind is about its size. The unions’ figure stands at four million workers; the employers’ confederation put average participation at about 5 percent, and Madrid’s regional government said 9 percent of its public employees joined—three figures measuring three different things, printed as they were given, in the strike account filed below. Barcelona’s march drew 400,000 in the housing activists’ count and 55,000 in the city’s. The Interior Ministry’s running totals at 1700 stood at 919 incidents and 52 arrests, against the 476 incidents and 40 arrests the midday accounts carried; the newspaper figures carried in the Madrid account filed below put more than 280 flight cancellations on the day and at least 42 arrests across several cities. The electricity figures divide by their bases: consumption up to 1100 ran 7.5 percent below the grid operator’s forecast for a day without the strike, on the wire service EFE’s figure, while demand between 1000 and 1100 fell by as much as 15.5 percent on the figures the strike-day account filed below carried. Madrid’s Metro ran 42 percent below the same peak a week earlier; Barcelona’s ran only at the commuting peaks.

The strike’s politics move to parliament on Thursday, on the government’s own scheduling. Prime Minister Sánchez defended the strike and backed its demands; his government brings two housing decrees to a vote on November 12, and a property portal’s reading of the smaller chamber, carried in the Madrid account above, gives the broader package enough support and the lease-renewal decree no majority yet. The official campaign for the November 29 election opens on Friday, November 13. The housing deficit that made the day stands at about 750,000 homes on the central bank’s figures, growing past a million by 2028. Settled: the strike happened, on a national scale no account disputes, and the election is 17 days out. Open: how large it was, and Thursday’s votes.

The Rest of the File: Mildenhall’s Count Clarified, a Name in Kraków, and Two Files That Did Not Move

At RAF Mildenhall the week’s dispersal acquired better figures without acquiring an explanation. The flight-tracking data carried in the dispersal account filed below counts nine KC-135R tankers and three CV-22B Ospreys departing on Monday, the tankers to Ramstein, Morón and Glasgow Prestwick and the Ospreys to RAF Lakenheath; a second account counted ten tankers on Monday, and the running account filed below counts two further tankers departing on Tuesday—at least 15 aircraft over the two days, in the repositioning account’s tally. The evening edition’s 13 stands inside the counters’ range rather than against it. The security posture at Mildenhall and Lakenheath stands at Force Protection Condition Charlie, the second-highest level. What no official has supplied, on any day of the file, is the threat’s nature: the European Command and the Air Forces in Europe declined specifics again on Tuesday, citing operational security and intelligence, and the reported connection to Iran remains attributed to the reporting, not to any official statement.

In Kraków, the city’s mourning ran its last day, and the file gained a name. The British victim of the six killed in the square has been identified in The Telegraph’s reporting as James Thomas Campbell, 32, a DJ from Prestwick in Ayrshire, in the identification account filed below. The same account carries the investigation’s published details—the computer research into serial killers, the locker inscription reported by the Polish outlet Onet, more than 500 rounds and four pistols found in the car, no note and no manifesto, a specialist taskforce appointed—and the standing position that the exact motivations are still to be determined. No forensic opinion on the nine victims has been published; the wider investigation into motive and assistance continues, with the justice minister’s thread of extremism and the prosecutors’ caution unjoined, as the midnight edition of November 11 printed them. In Jerusalem, no new published fact entered the file between the evening and midnight: Mr. Kahana’s speaker vote stands for November 17 at 1600, Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate runs to December 6, and the government is unformed. In Washington, the House held no votes on the holiday, and the eight articles rest in Mr. Jordan’s Judiciary Committee, where the evening edition left them. The desk fills none of the space where those findings will go.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Mississippi’s margin, 4,669 in the wire’s call and its published totals—473,336 to 468,667—against 4,645 in a Wednesday-night account, 4,585 in the at-call totals one program published (472,188 to 467,603), 4,404 on Wednesday afternoon in a third, and 3,041 in the evening’s afternoon tally: one winner, five margins, the call itself in every account at 1758. On Nvidia’s fall, about 8 percent after hours in the wire and futures accounts, 8.6 percent to $158.76 at 1959 ET in the price account, and more than 9 percent in a fourth. On Asia’s open, the Nikkei up 0.17 percent in one account’s open figures and up 0.5 percent in the wire’s later snapshot, having opened 226.52 points higher and turned lower in between; the Kospi down 0.068 percent at the open, down 0.21 percent at 0915 Seoul time, and up 0.2 percent in the later snapshot; the TAIEX down 0.24 percent at the open and up 0.5 percent later. On Brent, a settlement of $92.76 on Wednesday, $93.64 in Wednesday’s midday print, and about $92.46 in early Asia trade. On the December half-point, 12.7 percent in Thursday’s pricing against 13.2 percent on Wednesday afternoon, 15.3 percent on Tuesday and 11.5 percent on Wednesday morning. On Spain, four million strikers in the unions’ count against about 5 percent average participation in the employers’ and 9 percent of Madrid’s public employees in the regional government’s; 52 arrests and 919 incidents at 1700 against 40 and 476 at midday; a march of 400,000 in the activists’ count and 55,000 in the city’s. On Mildenhall, nine tankers in the flight data against ten in a second account for Monday, 13 in the evening edition’s count, and at least 15 departures across two days in the running tally. On Alaska’s remainder, about 40,000 ballots in one account, about 46,000 in another, and 637 votes of margin in a Wednesday-night account the afternoon tallies had already moved past. Against the triangle, the day’s single-valued facts are these: Mississippi was called for Mr. Colom at 1758 and conceded within the hour, and the caucus stands at 55 with Alaska alone uncalled; Nvidia closed higher and fell after hours on a board reported to be preparing its chief’s removal, and the board announced nothing by midnight; the Abu Dhabi delegations went home with the exchange agreed in principle and its numbers due Thursday, and the capitals exchanged fire in the night; Tehran restated that no enriched material leaves and the strait stays shut; Spain struck and stopped; and no threat was named at Mildenhall, no forensic finding published in Kraków, and no government formed in Jerusalem. Thursday holds Moscow, the numbers, Spain’s decree votes, the bond market’s return and the crude figures. The log turns.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 33 items.

Subjective
Associated Press, via NPR — Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi’s Senate race

The Associated Press called Mississippi’s Senate race for Mr. Colom on Wednesday, narrowly defeating Senator Hyde-Smith after more than a week of counting outstanding, absentee and affidavit ballots, in the closest Senate race in the country. Senator Hyde-Smith conceded in a video posted to social media shortly after the wire’s call on Wednesday. The account was published at 1804 ET and updated at 1931 ET.

Subjective
EURweb — Mr. Colom makes history: Mississippi elects its first Black senator since Reconstruction

After eight days of counting, Mr. Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, defeated Senator Hyde-Smith, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first Black person elected to the Senate from Mississippi by popular vote. With approximately 99 percent of the vote reported, Mr. Colom led 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent, a margin of roughly 4,700 votes. The account records that the senator he defeated is the senator who blocked his nomination to become a federal judge in 2023, and that his victory gives the Democrats their eighth Senate pickup of the midterms. The results remain unofficial pending certification.

Subjective
The Shade Room — Mr. Colom wins, Senator Hyde-Smith concedes

The Associated Press declared Mr. Colom the winner at 5:58 p.m. EST on Wednesday, November 11, by 4,669 votes, after he had led by 43 votes on the first night. Less than an hour after the call, Senator Hyde-Smith publicly conceded, captioning her video post “Thank you, Mississippi,” and saying she wanted to congratulate Mr. Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing the state.

Subjective
BiographyPoints — Mr. Colom wins Mississippi’s Senate race, defeating Senator Hyde-Smith

The Associated Press called the race at 5:58 p.m. Eastern on Wednesday after eight days of counting; NBC News and CNN’s decision desks separately projected Mr. Colom the winner, and Reuters reported that Senator Hyde-Smith had lost her re-election bid. The unofficial totals carried here stand at 473,336 votes, 49.2 percent, for Mr. Colom, 468,667, 48.7 percent, for Senator Hyde-Smith, and 20,234, 2.1 percent, for the independent candidate, Mr. Pinkins. The account says the decisive update came from Jackson County, and that counties must submit certified results by Friday, November 13.

Subjective
DINA News — Mr. Colom wins: the wire calls Mississippi as Senator Hyde-Smith concedes

The wire called the contest at 5:58 p.m. Eastern on Wednesday, and the later reported margin is 4,669 votes on totals of 473,336 to 468,667. The wire’s published explanation, carried here from the account that printed it, says the decisive update came from Jackson County, which reported another 2,173 votes, and estimated fewer than 12,000 ballots still requiring county review. The account distinguishes the call and the concession from certification, which remains a separate governmental step, due from the counties by November 13.

Subjective
NewsCubby — Mr. Colom wins Mississippi’s Senate seat as Senator Hyde-Smith concedes

Projections by CBS News and NBC News joined the wire’s call on Wednesday. The unofficial totals published by CBS News, citing the wire’s data, show Mr. Colom at 473,336 votes, 49.2 percent, Senator Hyde-Smith at 468,667, 48.7 percent, and Mr. Pinkins at 20,234, 2.1 percent; a second account put Mr. Colom’s Wednesday-night lead at 4,645, printed in the Cocked Hat. Senator Hyde-Smith’s concession is quoted: “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters.” A source close to Mr. Colom’s campaign said she called him to concede before releasing the video.

Subjective
Big Sarge — she asked Mississippi to count every vote; it did

An account of the slow count, built on the wire’s figures: by 1817 ET on Wednesday the wire had Mr. Colom’s lead at 4,669 votes, up from 2,990 that morning, and in Hinds County officials accepted 817 affidavit ballots, of which 703 went to Mr. Colom, while rejecting 1,609. Nothing is certified: counties finish Friday and the state makes it official on December 3. On Alaska, the account puts Ms. Peltola ahead by 4,250 with 84 percent counted and the final count due November 18, and records that a judge dismissed the administration’s suit over certification and the Justice Department appealed.

Subjective
The BRAD BLOG — the Democrats appear on track to win both remaining uncalled Senate seats

Both challengers are reported ahead and widening. In Mississippi, Mr. Colom’s advantage is put at 4,404 as of Wednesday afternoon, as the grace period for late-arriving ballots closed and the provisional ballots were counted. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola’s lead is put at 4,250, at 49 percent of the first choices; if she exceeds 50 percent there is no ranked-choice tally, and if she does not, the tabulation runs on November 18, with an estimated 46,000 ballots left to arrive or be tallied in this account.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate results in Mississippi and Alaska

As of Wednesday night in this account, both races remain undecided, with the Democrats assured of at least 54 seats in the Senate that convenes on January 3. The Mississippi margin is put at 1,138 votes with a few thousand provisional and mail ballots left, and the secretary of state’s Wednesday statement is quoted counting roughly 3,600 mail ballots still to be tallied and an unknown number of affidavit ballots. The Alaska margin is put at 637 votes in this account—figures the afternoon tallies have since moved past, printed here as the account states them.

Subjective
While You Slept, on YouTube — Alaska’s lead hits 4,250, with a Mississippi update pinned

The program’s pinned update, posted Wednesday evening, reports that the wire called Mississippi’s Senate race for Mr. Colom—472,188 to 467,603, about 99 percent in, when the call came in this account’s figures—and that Senator Hyde-Smith conceded, leaving Alaska the last uncalled Senate race and the Democratic caucus at 55 seats. The program’s Alaska file stands as the evening edition carried it: Ms. Peltola ahead by 4,250 on Tuesday’s update, about 40,000 ballots remaining, the next count on Friday, November 13, and the tabulation on November 18.

Subjective
Associated Press — election results: the House, District 27, Florida

The wire’s results page for Florida’s 27th District carries the race-call status Called: Representative Salazar, Republican, 124,519 votes, marked with the call, against Mr. Rodriguez, Democrat, 123,433 votes, with 216 of 219 precincts reporting and an estimated 99 percent of the vote in.

Subjective
The Miami Focal — Representative Salazar wins Florida’s 27th District by 1,086 votes after the recount; the canvassing board certifies Friday

Representative Salazar won re-election by 1,086 votes—124,519, or 50.22 percent, to Mr. Rodriguez’s 123,433, or 49.79 percent—after an automatic machine recount, the margin of 0.44 percentage points having triggered the recount under Florida law. Mr. Rodriguez conceded on Tuesday. The Miami-Dade canvassing board reconvenes Friday to make the result official; a manual recount would have been required at a margin of a quarter of a point or less, and at 0.44 percent the machine recount stands.

Subjective
Reuters — Asian stocks fragile, Nvidia plummets as the board decides its chief’s fate

Global stocks wobbled at the start of Asian trade on Thursday, and Nvidia’s shares slid more than 8 percent after the bell on news that its board may oust its longtime chief executive. The board was meeting late Wednesday to decide whether to oust Mr. Huang, a source familiar with the matter said, and The New York Times has also reported that Mr. Huang had a relationship with a company executive who reported to him. In the regional snapshot carried here, South Korea’s Kospi rose 0.2 percent, Taiwanese shares gained 0.5 percent, Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed 0.5 percent, and the broad Asia-Pacific index outside Japan was 0.1 percent lower, weighed down by Hong Kong. The dollar index stood steady in Asian trade at 102.87, its highest level since April 9 of last year, and the FedWatch pricing carried here puts a 25-basis-point December increase at 87.3 percent against 12.7 percent for the half-point move.

Subjective
MarketWatch, via Morningstar — Nasdaq futures fall as Nvidia sinks 8 percent after hours on the report the board may oust Mr. Huang

Stock futures traded lower late Wednesday. Nasdaq-100 futures fell nearly 1 percent on Wednesday evening after Nvidia’s shares dropped about 8 percent in after-hours trading, following the report in The Wall Street Journal that the chipmaker’s board was preparing to oust Mr. Huang. The Journal’s report came about an hour after Wednesday’s closing bell and followed the revelations of two relationships, including one with a woman American officials suspect of working with Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported earlier Wednesday that Mr. Huang also had a relationship with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Filed at 2012 ET.

Subjective
Daily Caller — report: Nvidia moves to oust its chief executive after a second relationship allegation

The Nvidia board is preparing to remove Mr. Huang as chief executive, The Wall Street Journal reported, and directors could gather as soon as Wednesday to decide his future. The board opened an independent investigation on November 8 and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to review the allegations. Nvidia’s shares dropped more than 9 percent in after-hours trading once the report broke, in this account’s figure, and the company carries no public succession plan. Several members of Congress have called on Mr. Huang to resign, and Senator Cramer repeated his demand on Wednesday.

Subjective
MacObserver — Nvidia’s stock sinks 8.6 percent after hours as Mr. Huang faces a reported ouster

Nvidia’s shares fell 8.6 percent in after-hours trading after The Wall Street Journal reported that the board is preparing to remove Mr. Huang. The stock closed the regular session at $173.73 and slid to $158.76 by 1959 ET, a drop of $14.97 a share, on the price data carried here. Nvidia has announced nothing; Mr. Huang is still the chief executive, and the company did not comment on the board meeting when Reuters asked. The Times report is identified here as naming the executive as Ms. Powell, the company’s vice president of health care. Bloomberg is reported to have said the company has been working with an outside firm to identify possible replacements.

Subjective
Gizmodo — Republicans threaten to subpoena Nvidia’s chief executive

Lawmakers are pressing Mr. Huang as details emerge about his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Senator Cramer of North Dakota told Politico on Tuesday that Mr. Huang’s actions amount to a national security risk, and at least one senator is calling for his resignation. Representative Moolenaar of Michigan, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, told Fox Business on Wednesday that Mr. Huang had until the end of the day to respond to a request for a closed-door briefing or suggest another date, and a subpoena is likely if he does not agree. The account records that Mr. Huang admitted on Sunday that he had had a relationship, that the company on Tuesday announced it had retained a former federal prosecutor, Mr. Kim, and the firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the independent investigation, and that Bloomberg reported on Monday that the company’s general counsel intervened in the Commerce Department’s investigation into Megaspeed, asking whether American authorities were involved in the detention in Singapore of the woman in the case.

Subjective
Trend Brief Today — Nvidia after the probe: the board preparing to oust him, shares sink after hours, and what to watch before the November 17 earnings

A running file on the Nvidia case. The stock fell 9.5 percent in the two sessions to Tuesday’s close of $168.89 after the board opened its investigation, closed Wednesday at $173.73, and fell about 8 to 9 percent after hours when the Journal reported the board preparing to oust Mr. Huang. In this file’s update at 0043 GMT on Thursday, the wire service CBS News, citing two sources, also reported that the board is preparing to oust Mr. Huang soon, directors were expected to meet on Wednesday night, and no decision, interim chief or company statement had been announced. The file also carries the House side: the China committee’s chairman gave Mr. Huang until the end of Wednesday to answer the briefing request, with a subpoena likely, and a second committee is reported to be preparing one.

Subjective
CNBC TV18, via TradingView — the Asian markets open, November 12

Asian markets opened mixed on Thursday, November 12, with little conviction, as investors weighed the turmoil at Nvidia. Japan’s Topix gained 0.51 percent and the Nikkei 225 added 0.17 percent; South Korea’s Kospi slipped 0.068 percent and Taiwan’s TAIEX lost 0.24 percent, while Hang Seng futures dropped 0.7 percent. In the chip supply chain, SK Hynix slid and Samsung Electronics surrendered part of its early gains. Brent crude remained steady at about $92.46 a barrel in early Asia trade. The movement’s trigger, in this account, came in late American trading as Nvidia’s shares tumbled about 9 percent.

Subjective
TradingView, carrying Kabutan, Yonhap and HKET — the Asia market open: the Hang Seng opens down 194 points, the Kospi turns lower after a higher start

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 opened Thursday at 61,475.11, up 226.52 points, rising for a fourth straight session, and the broader Topix opened at 3,943.52, up 14.13 points; the Nikkei turned lower shortly after the open. Japan’s corporate goods price index rose 7.1 percent year on year in October, above the 6.5 percent median forecast. Seoul’s Kospi opened 0.2 percent higher and turned negative, losing 11.32 points, or 0.21 percent, to 5,364.04 at 0915 local time. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng opened down 194 points at 24,121, Taiwan’s TAIEX opened down 76.69 points, and the mainland indexes opened mixed.

Subjective
Reuters — Russia and Ukraine exchange attacks on the capitals as the American envoys head for Moscow

Russia and Ukraine exchanged attacks on each other’s capitals early on Thursday, a day after the peace talks ended and as the American envoys were set to travel to Moscow to meet President Putin. Explosions were heard in the Ukrainian capital in the early hours of Thursday, a Reuters witness said; it was not immediately clear whether the city had incurred damage. Russia downed five drones that were heading for Moscow, Mayor Sobyanin said on Telegram, without additional details. The envoys are expected in Moscow to raise the question of adding European partners to the talks, and then to fly to Ireland to meet President Zelenskyy, who is due to attend a meeting of European leaders there.

Subjective
Qazinform — the Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi yield a prisoner exchange deal, key issues unresolved

Speaking at a briefing after the talks, Mr. Kushner said the sides had agreed on the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, with the numbers to be finalized on Thursday, and acknowledged that deep divisions persist, saying there is currently no trust between the two sides, which he described as expected after such a conflict; territorial issues were discussed and would be the most difficult to resolve. Mr. Umerov, who headed the Ukrainian delegation, wrote that the negotiators were returning to their capitals to finalize the details of the exchange: “We have concluded two days of negotiations in the United Arab Emirates. The main result is that we reached an agreement on a large-scale POW exchange. We are now working to finalise the details and further practical realisation.” Published at 0005 GMT on Thursday.

Subjective
The Daily Flare — Russia and Ukraine agree in principle to a prisoner swap expected to exceed 2,000

Ukraine and Russia confirmed an agreement in principle for a large-scale prisoner exchange, with exact numbers still to be finalized. A Russian general said the planned exchange could involve more than 1,000 prisoners from each side and take place within two or three weeks, which would put the total above 2,000. The two-day talks addressed security guarantees, occupied territory and Ukraine’s reconstruction and produced no major breakthrough on ending the war. The Wednesday session lasted just under two hours.

Subjective
Demokratis — Iran rejects the uranium transfer as the talks stall

Iran has ruled out transferring its enriched uranium to another country. On November 11, Mr. Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, reaffirmed the position; the broadcaster IRIB reported his declaration, and a Lebanese channel released excerpts from an interview scheduled for broadcast later Wednesday. He said Tehran had communicated its decision to Moscow, and he dismissed reports of a recent meeting between Iranian and American representatives in Qatar as fabricated, saying no negotiations were currently taking place between Tehran and Washington. The account also carries the Revolutionary Guard’s claim on Wednesday that two additional oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to leave the strait, and a maritime operations centre’s report from Tuesday evening of a tanker struck by a projectile in the waterway.

Subjective
Kashmir InFocus — Iran sets seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz

Tehran is linking the restoration of normal shipping through the strait to sanctions relief, the removal of the American naval blockade, the release of frozen assets and an end to fighting across the region. Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf, Tehran’s chief negotiator, said in an interview published on November 11 that Iran had sent Washington a detailed response through Qatari mediation and was waiting for an official answer, and he warned that the waterway would never return to its pre-war arrangements. The complete text of the seven conditions has not been publicly released. The account also records the Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman’s confirmation on November 11 that Moscow continues to offer to receive Iranian enriched uranium on Russian territory.

Subjective
CrossGlobalNews — Iran issues its conditions: the strait stays at the centre of the energy crisis

Tehran declared it would not restore unrestricted shipping through the strait until Washington meets its seven conditions, and the complete official text of the conditions has not been made public. On November 11 Reuters reported, citing three sources, that Iranian forces had attacked navigation systems on Oman’s Didamar Island that are used to support maritime traffic. The account carries the November 11 oil prints—Brent up about 2.35 percent at $93.64 a barrel and American crude at $87.73 in the midday print—and the spokeswoman’s statement in Moscow that Russia continues to offer to receive the uranium.

Subjective
Straits — the index of strait incidents and developments

An indexed archive of dispatches on the strait: military strikes, maritime incidents, declared closures and diplomatic developments, each entry linked to its originating outlet. The most recent entry indexed, at 0010 GMT on Thursday, November 12, carries the headline that Iran says the strait will remain closed until the leader of the revolution orders it opened. The day’s earlier entries carry the claim of an attack on navigation systems on Oman’s Didamar Island, Speaker Ghalibaf’s sentence that Iran will not reopen the strait until the United States meets the seven demands, and the Revolutionary Guard’s claim that two more tankers exploded in the strait.

Subjective
CNN — millions of Spaniards stage the first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housing

Four million workers took part in a general strike on Wednesday, the unions said, in protest against the housing affordability crisis, less than three weeks before a snap general election on November 29. It is the first general strike since 2012. Shops on Madrid’s Gran Via drew their shutters under a heavy police presence; turnout was strongest at the ports and the automobile plants; electricity demand fell by as much as 15.5 percent between 1000 and 1100 on the grid operator’s figures; and police reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents. The country’s housing deficit is put at about 750,000 homes, growing to more than a million by 2028 on the central bank’s figures.

Subjective
EuropeSays — Spain’s nationwide strike over rent: why the prime minister supports the protesters

Spain’s biggest unions called their first nationwide general strike together in 14 years on November 11, demanding affordable housing, higher wages and stronger public services, and Prime Minister Sánchez defended the strike and backed its demands. His government is trying to get two housing decrees through a vote on November 12, before Spaniards elect a new parliament on November 29; the official campaign begins November 13. The account carries the newspaper El País’s figures: tens of thousands on the streets in each of Madrid and Barcelona, more than 280 flight cancellations during the day and at least 42 arrests across several cities, and the wire service EFE’s figure that electricity consumption up to 1100 was 7.5 percent below the grid operator’s forecast for a day without the strike. A property portal reported on November 11 that the broader housing package appeared to have enough support in the smaller parliamentary body and that the lease-renewal decree still lacked a majority.

Subjective
Wrivid — Spain’s strike disrupts transport and factories over housing costs

A 24-hour general strike disrupted Spanish transport and factories on Wednesday. The two largest unions said four million workers took part; the employers’ confederation put average participation at about 5 percent, and Madrid’s regional government said 9 percent of its public employees joined—figures that measure different groups. Barcelona’s march drew competing estimates: housing activists counted 400,000 people, while the city put the crowd at 55,000. At 1700 the Interior Ministry reported 919 incidents and 52 arrests. Madrid Metro said peak-hour use was 42 percent below the same period a week earlier, and Barcelona’s Metro ran only during commuting peaks.

Subjective
ADS Advance — the Air Force disperses aircraft from RAF Mildenhall amid a fresh Iran threat

The Air Force moved a number of aircraft away from RAF Mildenhall following a reported new threat from Iran, with heightened security at other American-operated bases in Britain. Flight-tracking data showed nine KC-135R Stratotanker aircraft of the 100th Air Refueling Wing, along with three CV-22B Osprey tiltrotors of the special operations wing, departing Mildenhall during the late afternoon and evening of November 9. Most of the tankers transferred to Ramstein in Germany or Morón in southern Spain, one diverted to Glasgow Prestwick, and the three Ospreys went to nearby RAF Lakenheath. The security posture at both bases was raised to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the second-highest level, and neither the Air Force nor the British Ministry of Defence has publicly confirmed the specific intelligence behind the measures.

Subjective
The War Zone — Air Force aircraft continue to reposition away from RAF Mildenhall amid reports of Iranian threats

The departure of the tankers from Mildenhall continued on Tuesday: two further tankers of the 100th Air Refueling Wing departed in the afternoon, after the ten tankers and three Ospreys that left on Monday in this account’s running count—at least 15 aircraft over the two days. The White House referred questions on Tuesday morning to the European Command, which declined to offer specifics about the movements or the increased security measures, in a statement nearly identical to Monday’s; the Air Forces in Europe also declined to provide details, citing operational security, and said it would be inappropriate to comment on matters of intelligence.

Subjective
The Telegraph, carried in a collected account — a Scottish DJ identified as a Kraków shooting victim

The British victim of the shooting in Poland has been identified by The Telegraph as James Thomas Campbell, a DJ from Scotland: Mr. Campbell, 32, from Prestwick in Ayrshire, was one of six people shot dead in Kraków. The account carries the investigation’s published details: searches of the gunman’s computer showed research into serial killers including Breivik, Manson and Kaczynski in the weeks before the attack; officers found an inscription on his work locker that appears to glorify Elliot Rodger, on sources cited by the Polish outlet Onet; police found more than 500 rounds of ammunition and four pistols in his car; and no suicide note or manifesto was found at his home, with the exact motivations still to be determined. A specialist taskforce has been set up in Kraków to investigate.

entry.title: Abu Dhabi Closes With Prisoners and No Ceasefire, Wall Street Buys Back the Chips, and the President Claims a Won War at Arlington
entry.summary: The evening file for Wednesday, November 11, 2026: the day’s developments whole, and the first considered responses from every side. The two days of talks in Abu Dhabi closed with a large prisoner exchange agreed in principle—the biggest humanitarian release, in Mr. Kushner’s words, the numbers to be finalized Thursday—and no ceasefire, no joint statement and no date for a next round; the envoys travel to Moscow on Thursday and then to Dublin, and the first considered responses divide between a humanitarian success and no clear step toward peace. Wall Street reversed Tuesday whole: the S&P 500 closed up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19, the Dow up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49, CoreWeave up 24.71 percent, and Brent settled up 1.39 percent at $92.76, on no cash bond trading for Veterans Day. At Arlington the president laid the wreath at 1100 and said of Iran, “We won,” that America did not start the war, and that the end is a question of timing and of a total victory, not a 93 percent victory; he put the American dead in the conflict at 18. The Hegseth articles rest in Mr. Jordan’s Judiciary Committee, and Mr. Jordan leads the House Republicans in the next Congress on the 106-to-73 vote. Neither Senate race was called; the afternoon tallies put Mr. Colom ahead by 3,041 in Mississippi and Ms. Peltola ahead by 4,250 in Alaska. In Spain four million workers struck over housing in the country’s first general strike in 14 years. Collected at 1800.
entry.content:
The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Abu Dhabi Closes With Prisoners and No Ceasefire, Wall Street Buys Back the Chips, and the President Claims a Won War at Arlington

The evening file: the day’s developments whole, and the first considered responses from every side. Abu Dhabi produced prisoners and no peace; the market took back Tuesday whole on one earnings report; the president used the holiday to claim a war already won; and both uncalled Senate races moved, without ending.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 33, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, and from Edition No. 32, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Evening in Brief

The day closed its talks, its market and its holiday, and it left its two counts, its one committee file and both of its wars exactly where the evening finds them: decided in form, open in substance, with the next step named and dated. The two days in Abu Dhabi ended with a large prisoner exchange agreed in principle and nothing else signed—no ceasefire, no joint statement, no date for a next round—and the process now travels: Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff meet President Putin in Moscow on Thursday and President Zelenskyy in Dublin after it, with the exchange numbers to be finalized the same day, in the wire account filed below. Wall Street reversed Tuesday whole: the S&P 500 closed up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19 and the Dow up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49, on one earnings report, with the bond market shut for the holiday and no cash rate to read the move against, in the closing account filed below. At Arlington the president laid the wreath at 1100 and then defended the Iran war from the amphitheater: America did not start it, Iran has waged war on America since 1979, the United States won, and what remains is the timing of a total victory, in the Arlington account filed below. The eight articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in a Judiciary Committee chaired by the man the House Republicans elected their leader for the next Congress on the same day as the referral. Neither Senate race was called: the afternoon tallies moved both Democratic challengers further ahead, to 3,041 in Mississippi and 4,250 in Alaska. In Spain, four million workers struck over housing in the first general strike in 14 years.
