Abu Dhabi, Whole: Under Two Hours, an Exchange in Principle, and the File Packed for Moscow

The talks are over, and their whole announced product is a prisoner exchange. Wednesday’s session ran just under two hours, against four hours on Tuesday, and closed with the agreement Mr. Kushner stated in one sentence: “One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow.” Mr. Medinsky, for Russia, and Mr. Umerov, for Kyiv, both confirmed the planned exchange, Mr. Medinsky with the qualification that the agreement is in principle, in the wire account above. On the size, the file still holds ranges and not a figure: more than 1,000 a side in the Russian general’s account, 1,000 to 1,500 in the plans President Zelenskyy announced, and an exchange in two to three weeks in General Zorin’s account, all carried at midday and unamended at 1800. No ceasefire was agreed. No joint statement was published. No date for a next round was announced. Foreign Minister Lavrov rejected the European demands for a ceasefire framework on the margins, and Mr. Kushner said no agreement could be reached until the territorial dispute was settled.

The first considered responses arrived in the afternoon, and they divide on what the two days were. The assessment filed below calls the exchange a success and good news for Ukraine, and in the same pages calls the ending predictable: no breakthrough, and no apparent progress on the ceasefire that remains Kyiv’s priority while, in one analyst’s words, Ukrainians endure another dark and cold winter. Washington is reported to have floated security guarantees modeled on the alliance’s Article 5, with the warning beside it that President Putin would likely seek additional territorial cessions in exchange. A negotiator found a little bit of flexibility in private conversations and gave no specifics. The conclusion printed is plain: none of this suggests that a clear step toward peace was made. The principals’ own registers stand apart from the assessment and from each other. Mr. Medinsky said the meeting helped the two capitals edge closer to peace; the Kremlin’s adviser, Mr. Ushakov, called the talks substantive and quite useful; President Zelenskyy wrote that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy; and Mr. Kushner wrote that the exchange will reunite families, build trust and create momentum toward peace, all in the wire account above.

Europe’s seat is the file’s standing disagreement, and Wednesday sharpened it rather than settling it. The European governments, the European Union and the alliance were in the capital and did not attend the three-way sessions, after Moscow objected; Kyiv’s delegation was to meet them separately on Wednesday. Kremlin spokesman Peskov said European representatives could eventually join but that their current statements show no desire to contribute to movement toward peace, and that Moscow complains Europe finances and supplies Ukraine’s weapons. Mr. Kushner said one goal of the Moscow meeting is to get the Europeans added to the talks, and Mr. Arakhamia, for Kyiv, said the next talks should be multilateral rather than trilateral, in the comparison account filed below. The itinerary is the next fact in the file: Moscow on Thursday, November 12, then Dublin and President Zelenskyy. Settled: the talks ended, the exchange is agreed in principle, the numbers are Thursday’s work. Open: the land, the ceasefire, and Europe’s chair.

The War, Whole: The Talks Closed Over a Day of Strikes in Both Directions

The fighting ran through the closing session for a second day, and the evening file carries one new count the midday file did not hold. A daytime attack on a market in the southern Odesa region killed three people and injured 11, and residential buildings were damaged, on the regional administration’s figures in the wire account above. The overnight counts stand as the midday edition printed them, unreconciled: Russia struck the Zaporizhzhia region and Kharkiv overnight, wounding seven civilians; Russia’s Defense Ministry counted 627 Ukrainian drones downed overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, against the governor’s earlier count of 92 over the Leningrad region, with a fire at the port of Ust-Luga injuring three workers. The industry figure stands unamended: Ukrainian attacks since late October have disrupted about 30 percent of Russia’s refining capacity. One smaller file entered the record in the afternoon: a 49-year-old Indonesian man is in Ukrainian custody after, on his account carried in the wire report, he signed what he believed was a construction contract in Moscow and was taken to the fighting in the Zaporizhzhia region without training; his embassy is seeking access, and neither government commented. The talks and the strikes proceeded on the same hours for two days; neither file mentions the other.

The Close, Whole: Tuesday Reversed on One Earnings Report, With No Bonds to Read It Against

Wall Street’s verdict on the day was given at the close, and it was a reversal, not a repair. The S&P 500 closed up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49, in the closing account above and the closing table filed below, which agree to the figure. A second closing table filed below runs the same session higher—the Nasdaq up 2.06 percent at 25,583.42 and the S&P 500 up 1.4 percent at 7,626.55, with the Dow lower than the first table at 52,337.86—and both tables stand in the Cocked Hat; the desk does not average them. The instrument behind the move was the same earnings report that lifted the morning: CoreWeave closed up 24.71 percent at $60.77, on quarterly revenue of $3.66 billion against a $3.56 billion consensus and a raised outlook, having said it would become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028, and Nvidia closed up 2.92 percent at $173.73 after two days of losses that took about $430 billion from its value. The technology index stood up nearly 4 percent in the afternoon, on track for its largest daily gain since August 4, and the volatility index fell for a fourth straight session, to 17.63 in the afternoon from 18.48 at midday.

The rally was not a rate story, and the file says so in its own figures. Traders fully price an increase of at least a quarter point in December, with the half-point move at 13.2 percent in the afternoon pricing—against 11.5 percent in the morning figures, 10 percent in the overnight print and 15.3 percent in a Tuesday instrument, all printed in the Cocked Hat. Governor Waller’s stated test stands met by Tuesday’s core print of 0.3 percent, and the committee’s decision stands untaken. The session ran, as the holiday required, without its second witness: the cash bond market stood closed for Veterans Day and reopens Thursday, and the official crude inventory figures, due Wednesday, come Thursday for the same reason. Oil closed the day’s other sentence upward. Brent settled up 1.39 percent at $92.76 and American crude up 0.57 percent at $86.53, in the closing account above, after a midday print at $93.64 on the sentence from Tehran that no enriched nuclear material will leave the country, in the wire account filed below; the morning’s prints ran from $92.01 to $92.81. Gold futures fell 0.93 percent, and the spot price stood below $4,000 in an afternoon reading. Friday’s producer price report is the next inflation fact in the file. Settled: the close, the earnings, and that December brings an increase on every pricing in the file. Open: 25 or 50, and whether the chip rally holds a second day.

Arlington, Whole: A Wreath at 1100, and a Won War Claimed From the Amphitheater

The capital’s holiday ran on its printed schedule, and the evening file now holds the text the midday file could only schedule. The president and the first lady took part in the wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100, and the remarks followed in the Memorial Amphitheater at the 73rd annual National Veterans Day Observance, with the vice president, the secretary of veterans affairs and Secretary Hegseth among those attending. The president’s address was a tribute built around named veterans—a survivor of the 1983 Beirut barracks bombing, in which 241 service members were killed; a 103-year-old veteran of the Bulge whose battalion was among the first into Dachau; a medevac pilot credited with 1,874 combat missions; a Green Beret who returned to combat after 27 surgeries—and a defense of the Iran war ran through the whole of it, in the Arlington account above.

The war sentences, as the accounts filed below quote them, are these. “America did not start a war with Iran. Iran has been waging war on America since 1979.” “We won. It’s just a question of when we want to end it.” “We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93 percent victory. It’s going to be total.” The president put the American dead in the conflict at 18, said the campaign began seven months ago with only a few weeks of intense fighting, said Iran would need 25 years to rebuild what was destroyed, and gave no date for an end. He praised Secretary Hegseth from the platform the day after the referral vote—“He’s done a fantastic job, and he loves you, and he protects you”—and he renewed the arch: “Soon, we’re going to dedicate a magnificent, triumphal arch to our veterans,” who have, in his words, been waiting for it for 200 years, in the second Arlington account filed below. One warning stood in the speech without a name attached: the country will not be allowed to be hurt by what he called a horrible ideology, and everyone knows what he means. On veterans’ services the president’s figures and his own proclamation’s figures do not match, and both stand in the Cocked Hat: a backlog cut by 71 percent and nearly 100,000 homeless veterans housed, in the speech as the Arlington account carries it, against a cut of more than 70 percent and nearly 52,000 housed in the proclamation filed at midday.

One exchange in the afternoon file belongs to the election as much as to the holiday. The president said the vice president was largely correct in blaming the Iran war for the party’s defeat, and the vice president’s post is quoted beside it: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night”—with the president’s eldest son backing the assessment, in the account filed below. The desk prints the agreement as the day’s political fact: the war’s authors and its critics in the president’s own house now give the same cause for the midterm result, and differ on what follows from it. Tehran’s standing sentences stand unamended beside the speech: no negotiations with the Americans are under way, no enriched material leaves the country, and the two blockades—Iran’s of the strait, America’s of Iran’s ports—both stand. No agreement on reopening the strait exists. The desk’s own record of the day stands in the Special Report filed this morning outside the watches.

Washington, Whole: The Articles Rest With the Leader’s Committee, and the Senate Picks Its Own

The impeachment file produced no new vote on Wednesday, and its state at 1800 is the state the midnight edition settled, with one alignment the day made visible. The eight articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in the Judiciary Committee after Tuesday’s referral vote of 211 to 204. The committee’s chairman, Representative Jordan of Ohio, is the man the House Republicans elected, the same day, as their minority leader for the 120th Congress, by 106 to 73 over Mr. Scalise, in the leadership account filed below. Mr. Jordan’s sentence for the next two years is on the record: when the Democrats provide more government, the Republicans will provide more freedom; and his stated purpose, in the accounts filed below, is to regain the majority. The expected chairman of the same committee in the next Congress, Representative Raskin, has said his party is sober about impeachment, and Leader Jeffries has indicated the Democrats will reassess when they take the majority on January 3, when this Congress’s articles expire and new ones would be required, in the fallout account filed below. Eleven Democrats were absent from Tuesday’s vote; Mr. Massie was the only Republican against the referral. The House scheduled no votes on the holiday. Across the Capitol, the Senate Republicans re-elected Senator Thune as their leader on Tuesday and chose Senator Moreno to lead the committee for the 2028 cycle, and one senator’s arithmetic entered the file: Senator Justice of West Virginia said his party can forget about winning back the Senate in 2028 after losing at least seven seats, in the 2028 account filed below. Settled: the referral, both leaderships, and the chairman’s double office. Open: January.

The Count at Evening: Both Challengers Wider Ahead, Neither Race Called

For a tenth day neither Senate race was called, and Wednesday’s part in both files is at last arithmetic and not only administration. In Mississippi, Mr. Colom led Senator Hyde-Smith by 3,041 votes—49.11 percent to 48.79 percent, with the independent candidate at 2.1 percent and about 98 percent counted—in the tally account filed below, up from about 2,607 in the last tally this paper printed. A second account puts the lead at 3,176 as of Tuesday night, as the grace period for late ballots closed and the provisional ballots were counted, in the count account filed below; a third account, printed in the Cocked Hat, still carries 1,138. The machinery stands as filed: about 14,200 provisional ballots processed with about 80 percent accepted, counties certifying by Friday, November 13, the state certifying December 3, and no automatic recount provision in Mississippi law, in the uncalled-races account filed below.

In Alaska, the afternoon tally moved the margin the midday file could only imply. Ms. Peltola led Senator Sullivan by 4,250 first-choice votes—118,926, or 49 percent, to 114,676, or 47.2 percent—up from 2,517 on Monday’s count, in the tally account and the count account above. An estimated 46,000 ballots remain to arrive or be tallied in one account. The rule that decides the calendar is unchanged: if Ms. Peltola passes 50 percent of the first choices there is no ranked-choice tabulation; if she does not, the tabulation runs on November 18, with the next count on November 13 and a target certification date of November 25. More than a dozen House races also remain too early to call, and the size of both majorities is therefore still undetermined a week after the vote. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide; the evening question is whether the majority stands at 54, 55 or 56. Settled: both margins widened, and both deadlines. Open: both seats.

The Rest of the File: A Strike in Spain, and Three Files That Did Not Move

The day’s largest event outside the American files was a strike. Four million workers took part in a general strike across Spain on Wednesday, the unions said, in protest against the housing crisis, less than three weeks before a snap general election on November 29; it is the country’s first general strike since 2012, in the Madrid account filed below. Shops on the Gran Via drew their shutters under a heavy police presence, turnout ran strongest at the ports and the automobile plants, electricity demand fell by as much as 15.5 percent in the late morning on the grid operator’s figures, and police reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents. The housing deficit stands at about 750,000 homes on the central bank’s figures, growing past a million by 2028. Two storms threatened the afternoon marches, and the demonstration in Cadiz was suspended. The prime minister’s stated purpose in calling the election—to turn the argument to housing and away from the corruption cases and the train crash in the file—is now the strike’s argument as well, and the vote is 18 days out.

Three files the desk carries produced no new published fact between midday and evening, and the evening records the absence as the fact. At RAF Mildenhall, the 13 American aircraft relocated on Monday on a threat no official has named stand relocated; the counts beneath the 13—ten tankers and three Ospreys in the flight-data accounts, 12 in total in another—stand unreconciled, the reported connection to Iran stands unattributed to any official statement, and no official has named the threat. In Jerusalem, the machinery named at midday stands: Mr. Kahana for speaker on November 17 at 1600, Mr. Folkman to chair the Arrangements Committee, the committee composition to the plenary on November 18, Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate running to December 6, and the government unformed. In Kraków, the city’s mourning ran its last day with no forensic finding published: the detailed opinions on the nine victims may take weeks, the proceedings against the dead suspect will be discontinued, and the wider investigation into motive and assistance continues, with the justice minister’s sentence on a strong thread of extremism standing beside the prosecutors’ position that motive remains unresolved, unjoined by them. The desk fills none of the space where those findings will go.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the close, two tables that agree to the figure—the S&P 500 up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19, the Dow up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49—against a second table’s Nasdaq up 2.06 percent at 25,583.42, S&P 500 up 1.4 percent at 7,626.55 and Dow at 52,337.86: one direction, two landfalls, the Dow’s two readings 149 points apart. On Brent, a settlement of $92.76 in the closing account against $92.81 in a morning account, $93.64 at 1204 in the wire print, and $92.01 to $92.53 across the early prints. On the December half-point, 13.2 percent in the afternoon pricing against 11.5 percent in the morning, 10 percent overnight and 15.3 percent on Tuesday. On the exchange, more than 1,000 a side in the Russian general’s account—his name spelled Zorin in the wire account and Sorin in one earlier account—1,000 to 1,500 in the president’s announced plans, the biggest release in the envoy’s, agreed in principle in a fourth. On the drones, 92 counted down over the Leningrad region in the governor’s first account, 150 over the St. Petersburg region and 627 in the whole country in the ministry’s count. On the veterans’ figures, a backlog cut of 71 percent and nearly 100,000 homeless veterans housed in the speech as one account carries it, against more than 70 percent and nearly 52,000 in the proclamation. On Mississippi, 3,041 ahead in the afternoon tally, 3,176 in a Tuesday-night account and 1,138 in a third account that the day has moved past. On Alaska, 4,250 ahead in the afternoon tally against the 637 one account still carries. On Mildenhall, 13 aircraft in the trackers’ count, ten tankers and three Ospreys in the flight-data accounts, 12 in total in another. Against the triangle, the evening’s single-valued facts are these: the Abu Dhabi talks ended with a prisoner exchange agreed in principle and no ceasefire, no joint statement and no next date, and the envoys travel Thursday; Wall Street closed higher on all three indexes on every table in the file, led by the chips, with the bond market shut; a wreath was laid at 1100 and the president claimed a won war and a total victory to come; the articles rest with Mr. Jordan’s committee and Mr. Jordan leads his party in the next Congress; both Senate challengers widened their leads and neither race was called; four million Spaniards struck; and no finding was published in Kraków, no government formed in Jerusalem, and no threat named at Mildenhall. The log proceeds to the midnight watch.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 24 items.

Subjective

Senate Republicans are reported to have re-elected Senator Thune as their leader on Tuesday and to have picked Senator Moreno to lead the committee for the 2028 cycle.

Subjective
political.org — Mr. Colom’s lead over Senator Hyde-Smith tops 3,000 votes in the uncalled Mississippi race

Mr. Colom led Senator Hyde-Smith by 3,041 votes in the latest tally carried here, with about 98 percent of ballots counted, and the race remains uncalled. Mr. Colom held 49.11 percent to the senator’s 48.79 percent, with the independent candidate at 2.1 percent. Counties must certify by Friday, November 13, and the state certifies on December 3. The account carries the Alaska figures on the same page: Ms. Peltola at 118,926 first-choice votes, or 49 percent, to Senator Sullivan’s 114,676, or 47.2 percent.

Subjective
The BRAD BLOG — the Democrats appear on track to win both remaining uncalled Senate seats

Both challengers are reported ahead and widening. In Mississippi, Mr. Colom’s advantage is put at 3,176 as of Tuesday night, as the grace period for late-arriving ballots closed and the provisional ballots were counted. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola’s lead is put at 4,250, at 49 percent of the first choices; if she exceeds 50 percent there is no ranked-choice tally, and if she does not, the tabulation begins on November 18, with an estimated 46,000 ballots left to arrive or be tallied in this account.

Subjective
Spectrum News — more than a dozen key races remain too early to call

The size of the majorities in both chambers remained undetermined a week after Election Day, with more than a dozen races still too early to call. The account carries the Mississippi deadlines—mail ballots received by Tuesday, certified county results due Friday, state certification December 3—and the secretary of state’s Monday figures of about 14,200 provisional ballots processed, about 80 percent accepted, and about 2,700 mail ballots not yet returned. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola led by about 2,500 votes on Tuesday afternoon in this account, with the ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18 if no candidate passes 50 percent and a target certification date of November 25.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate results in Mississippi and Alaska

As of Wednesday night in this account, both races remain undecided, with the Democrats assured of at least 54 seats in the Senate that convenes on January 3. The Mississippi margin is put at 1,138 votes with a few thousand provisional and mail ballots left, and the secretary of state’s Wednesday statement is quoted counting roughly 3,600 mail ballots still to be tallied and an unknown number of affidavit ballots. The Alaska margin is put at 637 votes in this account—figures the afternoon tallies filed above have since moved past, printed here as the account states them.

Subjective
CNN — millions of Spaniards stage the first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housing

Four million workers took part in a general strike on Wednesday, the unions said, in protest against the housing affordability crisis, less than three weeks before a snap general election on November 29. It is the first general strike since 2012. Shops on Madrid’s Gran Via drew their shutters under a heavy police presence; turnout was strongest at the ports and the automobile plants; electricity demand fell by as much as 15.5 percent between 1000 and 1100 on the grid operator’s figures; and police reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents. The country’s housing deficit is put at about 750,000 homes, growing to more than a million by 2028 on the central bank’s figures. Afternoon marches were threatened by two storms, and a demonstration in Cadiz was suspended.

entry.title: Abu Dhabi Ends With a Prisoner Exchange Agreed and the Land Untouched, the Chips Are Bought Back at Midday, and a Wreath Is Laid at Arlington
entry.summary: The midday file for Wednesday, November 11, 2026: the two days of talks in Abu Dhabi ended after a second session of less than two hours with a large prisoner exchange agreed—more than 1,000 a side in the Russian account, the numbers to be finalized Thursday—and no ceasefire, no joint statement and no date for a next round; the envoys travel to Moscow on Thursday and then to Dublin. Wall Street bought back the chips at the open: at 0949 the S&P 500 stood up 0.76 percent and the Nasdaq up 1.16 percent while the Dow lagged, CoreWeave rose 12.7 percent, and the bond market stood closed for Veterans Day. At Arlington the president and the first lady took part in the wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100, with the president’s remarks set for 1130. The Hegseth articles rest in a Judiciary Committee whose chairman, Mr. Jordan, was elected the House Republicans’ minority leader the same day, 106 to 73. Thirteen American aircraft stand moved out of RAF Mildenhall on a threat no official has named. Neither Senate race was called; Mississippi’s counties had filed paperwork, not new margins, and Alaska’s counted pile passed 245,000 ballots. Collected at 1200.
entry.content:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Abu Dhabi Ends With a Prisoner Exchange Agreed and the Land Untouched, the Chips Are Bought Back at Midday, and a Wreath Is Laid at Arlington

The news at midday: the week’s one negotiation produced its one agreement, on prisoners, and adjourned without a date; the market that sold the chips on Tuesday bought them back on Wednesday morning, in a session with no bond market to answer it; the capital kept a holiday—a wreath at 1100, remarks at 1130, no votes in the House—and the two Senate counts moved by paperwork and by pile, not by margin.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 32, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Edition No. 31, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Midday closed the Abu Dhabi file with an agreement on prisoners and nothing else signed, read a market buying back what it sold on Tuesday, and kept the capital’s holiday while the counts and the investigations ran on underneath it. The second day of the three-way talks ended after less than two hours with a large prisoner exchange agreed—the biggest humanitarian release, in Mr. Kushner’s words, with the numbers to be finalized on Thursday—in the Associated Press account and the closing account filed below; no ceasefire was agreed, no joint statement was published, and no date for a next round was announced. The envoys travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet President Putin and then to Dublin to meet President Zelenskyy. In New York, at 0949 the S&P 500 stood up 0.76 percent and the Nasdaq Composite up 1.16 percent on CoreWeave’s earnings and a chip rebound, while the Dow stood down 0.13 percent and the bond market stood closed for Veterans Day, in the Reuters morning account filed below. At Arlington National Cemetery the president and the first lady took part in the national wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100, and the president’s remarks followed at 1130, on the White House schedule filed below. The eight articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in the Judiciary Committee, whose chairman was elected the House Republicans’ leader for the next Congress on the same day as the referral. Thirteen American aircraft stand relocated out of RAF Mildenhall on a threat no official has publicly named. Neither Senate race was called.

Abu Dhabi at Noon: Under Two Hours, an Exchange Agreed, the Numbers Left for Thursday

The talks the overnight edition filed as entering their second day are, at noon, over, and their whole announced product is a prisoner exchange. Wednesday’s session wrapped up after less than two hours, against nearly four hours on Tuesday, in the TASS and Interfax reports carried in the day-two account filed below. Mr. Kushner’s sentence is the agreement’s text as published: “One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow.” The Russian delegation head, Mr. Medinsky, and Kyiv’s delegation head, Mr. Umerov, both confirmed the planned exchange. On the size, the accounts give ranges and not a figure: more than 1,000 prisoners on each side, in the Russian general’s account carried in the talks account filed below; between 1,000 and 1,500 in the plans President Zelenskyy announced; and an exchange in two to three weeks, in the TASS report carried in the wire account filed below. The exchange is to run under the facilitation of the International Committee of the Red Cross, in the closing assessment filed below. A date for the exchange itself has not been published by either side.

Everything else the two days were convened for stands where Tuesday left it, and the principals said so in their own registers. No ceasefire was agreed; Foreign Minister Lavrov, on the margins, rejected the European demands for a ceasefire framework, in the closing assessment above. Mr. Kushner said progress had been made on postwar security guarantees and that no agreement could be reached until the territorial dispute was settled, in the talks account above. Mr. Medinsky said the discussions centred on security guarantees for Ukraine and for Russia alike, and that his side had no contact with the European representatives present in the capital. Mr. Arakhamia, for Kyiv, said the Russian side had arrived with rigid positions and spoke of really big progress on other issues he could not detail, and of hope for a breakthrough by the end of the year. Europe’s seat remains the file’s standing disagreement: the European governments, the European Union and NATO were in Abu Dhabi consulting the Ukrainian delegation, and Mr. Umerov’s delegation was to meet them on Wednesday; Moscow opposed their presence at the table itself. The process now moves by airplane: Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff meet President Putin in Moscow on Thursday, November 12, and then fly to Dublin to meet President Zelenskyy, in the Associated Press account above; a European Political Community summit convenes in Dublin on November 12 in one account, and an informal summit of European Union heads of government is scheduled in Dublin on Friday, November 13, in another. No joint statement had been published at noon, and no date for a next round of talks has been announced.

The War at Noon: Seven Wounded in Two Cities, and a Drone Count That Will Not Sit Still

The fighting ran through the closing session, and the midday file carries the overnight exchange of strikes in the two capitals’ own counts, which do not agree. Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv overnight, wounding seven civilians and damaging property, in the Associated Press account above. On the other direction, Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to Governor Drozdenko, and that the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers, in the same account. The overnight edition carried the governor’s own earlier count of 92 drones shot down over the Leningrad region in the attack on the terminal and the refineries; the midday figures—627 in the ministry’s national count, 150 in the regional one—are printed beside it in the Cocked Hat, unreconciled. The industry figure the overnight edition carried stands unamended in the morning file: Ukrainian attacks since late October have disrupted about 30 percent of Russia’s refining capacity. The talks and the strikes proceeded on the same hours for a second day; neither file mentions the other.

The Markets’ Reading at Noon: The Chips Bought Back, the Dow Left Behind, No Bonds to Read

Wall Street’s midday reading reversed Tuesday’s in the technology shares and declined to reverse it anywhere else. At 0949 ET the S&P 500 rose 57.14 points, or 0.76 percent, to 7,578.07, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 288.47 points, or 1.16 percent, to 25,354.34, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 73.82 points, or 0.13 percent, to 52,162.06, in the Reuters morning account above. Six of the eleven S&P sectors stood positive, technology and energy leading; advancing issues led on the Nasdaq by 1.57 to 1 and ran about even on the New York Stock Exchange. The instrument behind the move was an earnings report: CoreWeave, the cloud firm whose results the morning accounts read as a test of the AI buildout’s returns, rose 12.7 percent after saying it would become profitable in the first half of 2028 on an adjusted basis; Nebius rose 12.5 percent and Applied Digital 5.2 percent beside it. Nvidia edged 2.4 percent higher after shedding about $430 billion in the last two sessions; the Philadelphia semiconductor index jumped 3 percent to a one-week high, with Marvell up 5.5 percent and Micron up 6.8 percent. The volatility index fell for a fourth straight session, to 18.48. The Anthropic terms filed Tuesday—825 million shares at $70 to $78, a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion—stood in the morning file as context, examined and unpriced until trading opens near November 19.

The session ran without its usual second witness, and the rate question it left open on Tuesday it left open again. The United States bond market is shut on Wednesday for Veterans Day, on the exchanges’ and the industry association’s calendars, in the holiday account filed below; the stock exchanges trade a full session, 0930 to 1600. With no cash Treasury trading, the morning’s only rate instrument was the futures pricing: traders see a December increase as a certainty, with an 11.5 percent chance of the half-point move, in the CME FedWatch figures carried in the Reuters morning account above—against 10 percent in the overnight futures print and 15.3 percent in a Tuesday instrument, all three printed in the Cocked Hat. Governor Waller’s stated test stands met by Tuesday’s core print of 0.3 percent, and the committee’s decision stands untaken. Oil, the session’s other witness, rose: Brent changed hands between $92.01 and $92.81 across the morning’s prints, up from Tuesday’s two-month lows, on the Hormuz file printed below.

Washington at Noon: A Wreath at 1100, Remarks at 1130, and a Committee Room Across Town

The capital’s official day was the holiday’s, and it ran on the printed schedule. Wednesday is Veterans Day, a federal holiday: the House has scheduled no votes, the Supreme Court is closed, and banks and federal offices are shut, in the Washington account filed below. The president and the first lady departed the White House for Arlington National Cemetery and took part in the 2026 National Veterans Day Wreath Laying Ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100, with the president’s Veterans Day remarks at 1130 in the Memorial Amphitheater, on the White House daily guidance carried in the schedule account filed below; live coverage of the ceremony ran through the morning, in the live account filed below. The observance is the 73rd annual National Veterans Day Observance; the vice president and the secretary of veterans affairs were among those attending, in the observance account filed below. The president’s proclamation, issued Tuesday and filed below, states the administration’s figures for the year: a record 3.1 million disability claims processed, the claims backlog cut by more than 70 percent, 47 new health care facilities opened, and nearly 52,000 homeless veterans housed, in the morning brief filed below; Secretary Collins, speaking Tuesday, put the backlog reduction at nearly 70 percent since January 2025, in the interview account filed below. The text of the president’s remarks is not in the midday file; the desk’s own record of the day stands in the Special Report filed this morning outside the watches. One piece of business from the cemetery’s neighbourhood stands in the file: nine members of the Kennedy family have joined the legal effort to block the president’s proposed 250-foot memorial arch near the cemetery, in the observance account above.

The impeachment file produced its morning-after fact across town: the committee that received the articles is chaired by the man the House Republicans chose, the same day, to lead them in the next Congress. The articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in the Judiciary Committee after Tuesday’s referral vote of 211 to 204; the committee is chaired by Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, in the referral account filed below. House Republicans elected Mr. Jordan their minority leader for the 120th Congress in a closed-door vote of 106 to 73 over Mr. Scalise, the Associated Press reported in the same account; Speaker Johnson is stepping down after the midterm losses, in the morning briefing filed below. Eleven Democrats were absent from Tuesday’s vote, in one account filed below; seven more votes against the referral would not have sunk it on the full count in any case, and the margin stands as cast. Leader Jeffries has indicated the Democrats will reassess the matter when they take the majority on January 3, when this Congress’s articles expire and new ones would be required. Settled: the referral, the chairman, and the leadership. Open: January.

England at Noon: Thirteen Aircraft Moved on a Threat No One Has Named

The week’s second security file is a movement, confirmed Tuesday and still unexplained at noon. The United States Air Force relocated aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England on Monday because of a threat, a United States official told the Associated Press; the official described the move as proactive rather than reactive and did not identify the threat’s source, in the Associated Press account filed below. The Military Air Tracking Alliance counted 13 aircraft departing for bases in Scotland, Spain and Germany—a combination of Osprey aircraft and midair refuelling tankers, some permanently based at Mildenhall and some there on rotation; the base hosts the 100th Air Refuelling Wing, the only permanent American refuelling wing in Europe. The counts beneath the 13 differ by observer and are printed in the Cocked Hat: ten KC-135 tankers identified in the flight-data accounts, three Ospreys moved to RAF Lakenheath in one account, twelve aircraft in total in another. The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the move, said the threat related to Iran, citing people familiar with the matter, and reported both Mildenhall and Lakenheath raised to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the second-highest level; a British paper’s understanding is that there was no direct or imminent threat to Mildenhall, in the relocation account filed below. The relocation follows the withdrawal of American bombers from RAF Fairford less than two months ago, while police investigated a suspected plot linked to Iran. The American command in Europe said coordinated measures are being taken to protect personnel and declined details. In a separate file the same morning, federal prosecutors have indicted three men accused of being Iran-backed operatives in connection with plots in Britain, in the morning briefing above. The desk prints the movement as confirmed, the threat as reported, and the connection between them as unestablished in any official statement in the file.

Iran and Hormuz at Noon: Oil Up on the Strait’s Count, and One New Sentence From Tehran

Neither capital moved on the Iran file in the morning; the strait’s traffic figures and one sentence from Tehran are the midday file’s whole addition. The sentence: Iran’s security chief said Tehran would not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country, carried in the Reuters morning account above as the occasion for part of oil’s rise. The figures: 37 vessels were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways during October, the highest monthly total since the war began, on the Washington Institute figures carried in the oil account filed below, and 10 attacks have been recorded so far in November. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a tanker struck by an unidentified projectile on Tuesday about 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman, the crew safe; Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said separately that two tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on an unauthorized route through the strait, a claim no other account in the file confirms. Brent rose through the morning on the accumulation—$92.01 a barrel at one print, $92.53 at another, $92.81 in the account that puts the rise at 1.4 percent—recovering from the two-month lows touched Tuesday, when the same barrel settled at $91.49. Preliminary industry data put American crude inventories up about 9 million barrels in the week ended November 6, and the Energy Information Administration expects Brent to average about $100 in November and December if the supply constraints persist, in the markets account filed below. The standing sentences stand: Secretary Rubio’s, that the blockade and sanctions make major combat unnecessary; Tehran’s, that no negotiations with the Americans are under way; and the Saudi East-West pipeline, struck Monday, kept flowing at about four million barrels a day in the last account in the file. No agreement on reopening the strait exists.

Jerusalem at Noon: The Committee Chairs Are Named, and the Week’s Work Is Assigned

Jerusalem’s midday addition is a set of names for the machinery that runs before a government exists. Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc has named incoming member Roy Folkman to chair the Arrangements Committee—the temporary committee that organizes a new Knesset’s work—and Liran Avishar Ben-Horin to chair the Finance Committee, beside Matan Kahana for speaker and Mr. Liberman for the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, in the appointments account and the comparison account filed below. The committee composition is to be discussed and finalized in the Arrangements Committee’s deliberations this week and submitted to the plenary for approval next Wednesday, November 18. The speaker vote stands set for Tuesday, November 17, at 1600, with the Arab lists’ announced votes putting Mr. Kahana ahead on the count published Tuesday: the prime minister’s bloc 53, Mr. Eisenkot’s coalition 48, the Arab parties 19, and 61 required. Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate runs 28 days from November 8, to December 6, with a possible 14-day extension. Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister. Settled: the chairs, the dates, the arithmetic as announced. Open: the government.

Kraków at Noon: The Mourning’s Last Day, and No Findings Published

Kraków’s file at noon is the overnight file, carried forward an hour: the instruments are running and nothing from them has been published. The examination of the suspect’s own body, expected separately on Tuesday, has produced no published finding in the morning file; the detailed forensic opinions on the nine victims may take weeks, in the investigation account filed below. The legal course stands as the prosecutors stated it: proceedings directed at the dead man personally will be discontinued—he died before charges could be presented or questioning held—while the wider investigation into motive, ideological influence and possible assistance continues, in the same account. The city’s mourning, declared by the mayor through November 11, runs its last day today; the two days of national mourning ran on November 8 and 9. Justice Minister Żurek’s sentence—a very strong thread of right-wing extremism, on the computer traces and the silencer found in the car—stands beside the prosecutors’ stated position that motive and influence remain unresolved, unjoined by them, as it stood at midnight. The desk files the absence of findings as the midday fact, and fills none of the space where findings will go.

The Count at Noon: Paperwork in Mississippi, a Larger Pile in Alaska

For a tenth day neither Senate race was called, and Wednesday’s part in both files, at noon, is administration rather than arithmetic. In Mississippi, the secretary of state’s office reported on Tuesday that 76 of the state’s 82 counties had submitted uncertified results and four counties had certified theirs, in the live results account filed below; all 82 counties must certify by Friday, November 13, and the secretary of state declares final results by December 3. The margin stands where Tuesday afternoon left it: Mr. Colom ahead of Senator Hyde-Smith by 2,607 votes out of 953,547 counted, in the Associated Press figures carried in the lead account filed below, and by about 2,700 in the running tally. Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. In Alaska, the counted pile grew without a new margin being published in the morning file: the latest tally in the live results account, stamped November 10, puts Ms. Peltola at 49 percent to Senator Sullivan’s 47.2 percent, with more than 245,000 ballots counted and 401 of the state’s 403 precincts reporting—against 218,641 ballots in the last count this paper printed, on which her lead stood at 2,517. The percentages imply a wider lead than 2,517; the account does not state the raw margin, and the desk does not compute one into print. Alaska’s next count is set for November 13 and its ranked-choice tabulation for November 18, if no candidate passes 50 percent. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the exchange, more than 1,000 a side in the Russian general’s account—his name spelled Sorin in one account and Zorin in another—between 1,000 and 1,500 in the president’s announced plans, the biggest release in the envoy’s, and agreed in principle in a fourth: one agreement, four sizes, the figure itself deferred to Thursday. On the drones, 92 counted down over the Leningrad region in the governor’s first account, 150 over the St. Petersburg region and 627 in the whole country in the ministry’s midday count. On the Dow’s morning change, a fall of 73.82 points to 52,162.06, which computes from a previous close of 52,235.88—four points above the closing table the midnight edition carried, and sixty-nine above the other; the S&P and Nasdaq changes compute exactly from the table the desk carried. On the December half-point, 10 percent in the overnight futures print, 11.5 percent in the morning FedWatch figures, and 15.3 percent in a Tuesday instrument. On Brent, $92.01, $92.53 and $92.81 across the morning’s prints. On Mildenhall, 13 aircraft in the trackers’ count, ten tankers and three Ospreys in the flight-data accounts, twelve in total in another. On Dublin, a European Political Community summit on November 12 in one account and an informal European Union summit on November 13 in another, with the envoys’ Zelenskyy meeting placed in the same city in both. Against the triangle, the midday’s single-valued facts are these: the Abu Dhabi talks ended with a prisoner exchange agreed and no ceasefire, no joint statement and no next date; the second session ran less than two hours; the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq rose at mid-morning while the Dow fell, and the bond market stood closed; a wreath was laid at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100; the articles rest with Mr. Jordan’s committee, and Mr. Jordan leads his party in the next Congress on a 106-to-73 vote; thirteen aircraft stand out of Mildenhall on an unnamed threat; Mississippi’s counties file toward a Friday certification; and no Senate race was called. The log proceeds to the evening.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 33 items.

Subjective
Associated Press, via WCMU — Russia and Ukraine agree to a large exchange of prisoners of war, officials say

Officials at the United States-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi said Wednesday that the sides have agreed a large exchange of prisoners of war. Mr. Kushner said the sides agreed to the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, with the numbers to be finalized tomorrow. Mr. Medinsky and Mr. Umerov confirmed the planned exchange. Mr. Kushner said he and Mr. Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet President Putin, then fly to Dublin to meet President Zelenskyy. The account also carries the overnight fighting: Russia struck the Zaporizhzhia region and Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians, and the Russian Defense Ministry said 627 Ukrainian drones were downed overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, with a fire at the port of Ust-Luga injuring three workers.

Subjective
EuropeSays — Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi end after less than two hours

The second day of the talks wrapped up after less than two hours, the TASS and Interfax agencies reported. Mr. Kushner spoke of some pretty tough discussions after almost eight months of not being together, and called the session a good first step. Mr. Medinsky said details of the number of prisoners and the procedure will be provided at a later date, and that the discussions centred on security guarantees for Ukraine and for Russia alike; his side had no contact with the European representatives present. Mr. Arakhamia expressed hope of a breakthrough by the end of the year. Earlier, President Zelenskyy had announced plans for the exchange of between 1,000 and 1,500 prisoners.

Subjective
Pollar — Russia, Ukraine agree prisoner swap after Abu Dhabi talks

The sides met for four hours on Tuesday and resumed on Wednesday. The only concrete result announced was a large prisoner exchange: a Russian lieutenant general said more than 1,000 prisoners on each side were to be exchanged, and Mr. Medinsky said mutual understanding had been reached on some issues. Mr. Kushner told reporters the talks had made progress on postwar security guarantees but that no agreement could be reached until the territorial dispute was settled. The envoys are due to meet President Putin in Moscow on Thursday, and an informal summit of European Union heads of state and government is scheduled in Dublin on Friday, November 13.

Subjective
Australian Associated Press — Russia and Ukraine agree to large prisoners of war swap

Russia and Ukraine have agreed a large exchange of prisoners of war, officials at the Abu Dhabi talks say. The swap may happen in the next two to three weeks, the TASS agency cited a Russian lieutenant-general as saying. The talks were largely about humanitarian issues, including possible prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country. The envoys plan to meet President Putin in Moscow and then President Zelenskyy in Dublin.

Subjective
Barbados Gazette — Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi end with prisoner exchange agreement

Two days of talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials, mediated by the United States, have yielded agreement on a prisoner exchange but failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war, which is nearing the five-year mark. Mr. Medinsky said both sides had agreed on a large-scale prisoner swap and that mutual understanding had been achieved on some issues. The TASS agency reported the exchange should happen in two to three weeks. Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff are then scheduled to fly to Dublin to meet President Zelenskyy and explore some of the ideas the talks produced.

Subjective
YallaYou — Abu Dhabi talks end day two with prisoner swap agreed

The second day of talks ended on Wednesday after just under two hours, according to a TASS correspondent at the venue; the first day ran about four and a half hours. Mr. Medinsky said in remarks broadcast on Russian television that the two sides had agreed on a large-scale prisoner exchange. A source close to the Ukrainian delegation told Interfax-Ukraine that an exchange of 1,000 for 1,000 or more had been agreed for the near future. Neither side has published a date. No joint statement had been published, and no date for a next round has been announced.

Subjective
The Leadsman — the Abu Dhabi closing: what two days in the UAE produced

The confirmed output of the two days is a commitment to a large-scale prisoner-of-war exchange in the near future, under International Committee of the Red Cross facilitation, with parameters to be agreed in a follow-on technical session. No ceasefire was agreed; Foreign Minister Lavrov, speaking on the margins of the talks, explicitly rejected European demands for a ceasefire framework. President Zelenskyy described the first day’s discussions as constructive and quite substantive and announced a joint position between Ukraine, the European Union and the United States. On November 12 the European Political Community Summit convenes in Dublin, the morning after the Abu Dhabi process concludes.

Subjective
The Daily Context — Russia, Ukraine and the United States hold Abu Dhabi talks

The two days of talks have ended with an agreement in principle on a large prisoner-of-war exchange but no ceasefire or territorial deal. Delegations from Russia, Ukraine and the United States met in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, the first trilateral round since February. Mr. Witkoff announced the meeting on November 2, and Kremlin spokesman Peskov told Interfax on November 7 that Russia’s delegation would again be led by Mr. Medinsky.

Subjective
Reuters, via Q101.9 — S&P 500, Nasdaq rise as CoreWeave results ease AI spending worries

The S&P 500 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbed on Wednesday after CoreWeave’s strong earnings calmed investor jitters about AI expenditure. At 0949 ET the Dow fell 73.82 points, or 0.13 percent, to 52,162.06, the S&P 500 rose 57.14 points, or 0.76 percent, to 7,578.07, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 288.47 points, or 1.16 percent, to 25,354.34. CoreWeave jumped 12.7 percent; Nvidia edged 2.4 percent higher after shedding about $430 billion in the last two sessions; the Philadelphia semiconductor index jumped 3 percent. The volatility index fell for a fourth straight session to 18.48. Traders see a December increase as a certainty, with an 11.5 percent chance of a half-point increase in the CME FedWatch figures. Oil prices climbed 1.8 percent after Iran’s security chief said Tehran would not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country. The United States bond market is shut on Wednesday for Veterans Day.

Subjective
Reuters, via WDSM — Wall Street set for higher open as CoreWeave results temper AI spending concerns

The main United States indexes were on track to open higher on Wednesday after CoreWeave’s strong earnings assuaged investor worries about AI expenditure. At 0826 ET, Dow futures rose 153 points, or 0.29 percent, S&P 500 futures were up 72.75 points, or 0.96 percent, and Nasdaq 100 futures gained 547.75 points, or 1.98 percent. Nvidia jumped 3.7 percent in premarket trading. Data storage firms Seagate Technology and Western Digital were among the top S&P 500 gainers, rising 9.5 percent and 8.6 percent. Investors also examined the terms set by Anthropic on Tuesday for its initial public offering, aiming at a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion.

Subjective
Summa Money — stock market today: futures rise as Nvidia recovers

United States stock futures rose on Wednesday as Nvidia and other chip stocks crept higher, investors shifted their bets on a Federal Reserve rate increase next month, and cryptocurrencies fell. CoreWeave shares popped 17 percent in premarket trading. It is a quiet day on the earnings and economic data front, with an update on mortgage rates coming later in the day. The account puts the S&P 500 up 9.5 percent year to date, ahead of the Dow Jones Industrial Average’s 8.5 percent advance and the Nasdaq Composite’s 7.5 percent rise.

Subjective
BigGo Finance — all three major indexes fall; Nvidia tumbles 5.5 percent as Anthropic presses ahead with its offering

All three major United States stock indexes closed lower on Tuesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 52,231.89, down 0.30 percent; the Nasdaq Composite closed at 25,065.87, down 0.74 percent; and the S&P 500 closed at 7,520.93, down 0.38 percent. Nvidia fell 5.53 percent, the main drag on the semiconductor sector. The Bureau of Labor Statistics showed headline consumer prices rose 0.4 percent month on month in October, above the 0.3 percent expected, and core prices rose 0.3 percent, also above the expected 0.2 percent. Amid the swings, Anthropic still launched its roadshow and released updated filing materials, continuing to advance its closely watched initial public offering.

Subjective
northjersey.com — what is open and closed on Veterans Day 2026

Wednesday, November 11, is Veterans Day, a federal holiday that closes many government offices, banks and post offices. The United States stock market remains open for normal trading, with the New York Stock Exchange’s regular session running from 0930 to 1600 ET and Nasdaq also open, even as the bond market closes for the day. The bond market is expected to reopen Thursday, November 12.

Subjective
Reuters, via Maaal — oil rebounds as Hormuz shipping attacks blunt hopes for an Iran truce

Oil prices rose on Wednesday from the previous session’s two-month lows, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the war on Iran and concerns about attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent futures climbed $1.04, or 1.1 percent, to $92.53 a barrel at 0420 GMT; West Texas Intermediate rose 67 cents, or 0.8 percent, to $86.71. A tanker was struck northeast of Lima in Oman, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Tuesday. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a separate statement on Tuesday that two tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on the unauthorized route in the strait.

Subjective
OilMonster — oil rebounds 1.4 percent as Hormuz attacks persist

Brent rebounded 1.4 percent from a two-month low, to $92.81 a barrel, as continuing tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz offset hopes for a de-escalation; West Texas Intermediate gained 1.3 percent to $87.12. Reuters reported that 37 vessels were attacked in the strait and surrounding waterways during October, the highest monthly total since the conflict began, with another 10 attacks recorded so far in November. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported another tanker attack on November 10 about 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman; the vessel was struck by an unknown projectile and the crew was reported safe.

Subjective
TalkMarkets — oil prices rise again, but why are Iran peace hopes not enough?

Oil prices rebounded as tanker attacks near the Strait of Hormuz offset optimism over a potential United States–Iran peace deal. Brent crude climbed 1.1 percent to $92.53 a barrel by 0420 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate gained 0.8 percent to $86.71. According to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, 37 vessels were attacked around the strait and neighbouring waterways during October. Preliminary American Petroleum Institute data indicated United States crude inventories rose approximately 9 million barrels in the week ended November 6. The Energy Information Administration expects Brent spot prices to average around $100 a barrel during November and December, assuming Middle Eastern supply constraints persist.

Subjective
The White House — Veterans Day, 2026: a proclamation

The president’s proclamation of November 10, 2026: November 11 of each year is set aside as a legal public holiday to honor the nation’s veterans, and the president proclaims November 11, 2026, as Veterans Day, encouraging all Americans to reflect on the fearlessness and sacrifice of veterans through public ceremonies and private thoughts and prayers of gratitude, and calling on federal, state and local officials to display the flag of the United States and to participate in patriotic activities in their communities.

Subjective
Mace News, via TradingView — Wednesday White House schedule: the president and first lady visit Arlington National Cemetery

The daily guidance and press schedule for Wednesday, November 11, 2026: the president and the first lady depart the White House en route to Arlington National Cemetery and arrive there; at 1100 the president and the first lady participate in the 2026 National Veterans Day Wreath Laying Ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery; at 1130 the president delivers Veterans Day remarks at Arlington National Cemetery.

Subjective
political.org — the president to mark Veterans Day with a wreath-laying and remarks at Arlington National Cemetery

The president is scheduled to deliver remarks at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, to commemorate Veterans Day. Before the speech, the president and the first lady are set to take part in the national wreath-laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, with the vice president also expected to attend, and the secretary of veterans affairs expected to attend and speak. The event is the 73rd annual National Veterans Day Observance. The cemetery is near the site of the president’s proposed 250-foot memorial arch, which faces a legal challenge from members of the Kennedy family; nine Kennedy family members have asked a judge to block the plan.

Subjective
Washington Examiner — watch live: the president delivers Veterans Day remarks at Arlington National Cemetery

The president is set to deliver remarks at Arlington National Cemetery Wednesday at 1130 to commemorate Veterans Day. Before the speech, the president and the first lady will participate in the 2026 National Veterans Day Wreath Laying Ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Other Veterans Day events at the cemetery include music by the United States Coast Guard Band and the United States Air Force Singing Sergeants and a parade of colors, both open to the public.

Subjective
Diego Clarke, Substack — today in Washington, Wednesday, November 11, 2026

Wednesday is Veterans Day, a federal holiday. The president and the first lady take part in the national observance at Arlington National Cemetery, the Supreme Court is closed, and the House has scheduled no votes. The White House issued the Veterans Day, 2026 proclamation on Tuesday. Today’s public schedule lists executive time at 0800 Eastern, closed press, an in-town pool call at 0900, departure with the first lady for Arlington National Cemetery, participation in the wreath-laying ceremony at 1100, and Veterans Day remarks at 1130. November 11 is listed as a legal holiday on the Supreme Court’s hearing list; no arguments are scheduled today.

Subjective
Newsmax — Secretary Collins: Veterans Day honors freedom’s defenders

Secretary of Veterans Affairs Doug Collins told Newsmax on Tuesday that Americans must never forget that the nation’s military veterans are the reason they can vote, speak freely and enjoy the constitutional freedoms that define the United States. He said he will join the president and the vice president at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday for a wreath-laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and a remembrance event at the cemetery’s amphitheater. Secretary Collins said the VA benefits backlog has fallen nearly 70 percent since January 2025.

Subjective
World Brief Now — morning brief: Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner-swap deal; aircraft moved off RAF Mildenhall; the House shelves the Hegseth impeachment; the president at Arlington

The morning brief’s headlines: the Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner-swap deal; 13 United States aircraft moved off RAF Mildenhall; the House shelves the Hegseth impeachment; and the president and the first lady lead the National Veterans Day wreath-laying at Arlington. In the proclamation, the president said the VA processed a record 3.1 million disability claims this year, cut its claims backlog by more than 70 percent, opened 47 new health care facilities, and housed nearly 52,000 homeless veterans last year.

Subjective
NPR, via WEKU — the House effectively ends the Hegseth impeachment; three men accused of plotting attacks in Britain

The House has effectively killed Representative Massie’s effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth. The chamber voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment articles back to the House Judiciary Committee for review; the move circumvents any potential floor vote on the impeachment and virtually ensures it will not be addressed before the current Congress ends. Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio will be the new minority leader of the House; House Republicans voted to replace Speaker Johnson, who is stepping down after last week’s midterm losses. United States federal prosecutors have indicted three men accused of being Iran-backed operatives.

Subjective
Interbellum News — the House refers the Hegseth impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee

The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday, November 10, to send Representative Massie’s eight articles of impeachment against Secretary Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee instead of voting on the charges. Every Democrat and Mr. Massie, the only Republican, voted against the referral. The 119th Congress ends on January 3, and an impeachment resolution not adopted by then does not carry over into the 120th. Republicans set their own course the same day: House Republicans elected Mr. Jordan, who chairs the Judiciary Committee now holding the resolution, to lead them in the next Congress, choosing him over Mr. Scalise 106 to 73 in a secret ballot, the Associated Press reported.

Subjective
Michael R. Cronin — House Republicans block the Hegseth impeachment push as Mr. Jordan takes the helm amid midterm fallout

In a procedural vote late Tuesday, the House derailed an effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth, referring the eight articles to the Judiciary Committee by a 211-to-204 margin. Mr. Massie was the sole Republican to side against the referral. Eleven Democrats were absent, contributing to the outcome in a chamber still under Republican control until the new Congress is seated in January. Leader Jeffries indicated the issue is not closed, noting Democrats will reassess once they assume the majority. The same day, House Republicans selected Representative Jordan as their minority leader for the 120th Congress in a closed-door vote of 106 to 73 over Mr. Scalise.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Military.com — the Air Force evacuates aircraft from a base in England because of a threat, an official says

The United States Air Force has relocated aircraft from a base in eastern England because of a threat, a United States official told the Associated Press. The Military Air Tracking Alliance said it spotted 13 United States aircraft stationed at RAF Mildenhall departing for bases in Scotland, Spain and Germany. The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the evacuation, said the threat related to Iran. The relocation came less than two months after the Air Force withdrew its bombers from another base in Britain, RAF Fairford, as police investigated a suspected terror plot linked to Iran. Some of the aircraft were permanently based at Mildenhall and others were there on rotation, including Osprey aircraft and midair refuelling tankers; the base also raised its alert level. The decision to move the aircraft was proactive rather than reactive, the official said.

Subjective
World Daily Times, via Senior Newspaper — why the United States moved aircraft from RAF Mildenhall amid a reported Iran threat

The Air Force moved aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England on Monday, November 9, because of a threat, a United States official told the Associated Press; the official described the relocation as proactive rather than reactive, without identifying the threat’s source. The Military Air Tracking Alliance identified 13 departing aircraft. Flight-data analysis identified 10 KC-135 tankers leaving Mildenhall on Monday: four bound for Spangdahlem and one for Ramstein in Germany, four for Morón in Spain, and one for Glasgow Prestwick in Scotland. The published counts differ: the tracking alliance counted 13 departures and one service identified 10 tankers plus three Ospreys, while another described nine tankers and three Ospreys, a total of 12. The Wall Street Journal reported that both Mildenhall and Lakenheath had been raised to Force Protection Condition Charlie. The Telegraph reported its understanding that there was no direct or imminent threat to Mildenhall.

Subjective
The Military Report — the United States moves tankers and Ospreys from a British base after a threat

The Air Force moved aircraft out of RAF Mildenhall in England on Monday after receiving a threat, a United States official told the Associated Press. Flight trackers identified 13 aircraft departing for other bases in Europe, including aerial refuelling tankers and Ospreys. The official described the move as a precaution; some aircraft were stationed at Mildenhall and others were passing through, and they could return. The official did not identify the source or nature of the threat. The Wall Street Journal reported an Iranian connection, citing people familiar with the matter. The departures follow the withdrawal of American bombers from RAF Fairford amid an investigation into a suspected Iran-linked plot. Mildenhall houses the 100th Air Refueling Wing, the only permanently assigned United States aerial refuelling wing in Europe.

Subjective
MK Niralo — the Kraków suspect dies in hospital as the terrorism investigation continues

The 24-year-old suspected of carrying out the November 7 mass shooting in Kraków died in hospital at about 0430 on Monday, November 9, after three operations, having been shot by police on Saturday. Prosecutors are treating the public attack—six people killed in the square, and three relatives found dead at his home—as a suspected terrorist offence, while stressing that the motive, any ideological influence and possible assistance by others remain unresolved. Post-mortem examinations of all nine victims were completed on Monday; detailed forensic opinions may take weeks. An examination of the suspect’s body was expected separately on Tuesday. The National Prosecutor’s Office said evidence gathered so far points to the man as the person responsible for both the public shooting and the three deaths at the family home.

Subjective
USA Today — Democrats slightly ahead in the uncalled Senate races: live results

Democratic challengers are barely ahead of Republican incumbents in the two uncalled Senate elections in Mississippi and Alaska, but votes are still being counted. On November 10, the Mississippi Secretary of State’s office said 76 of the state’s 82 counties have submitted uncertified results, and four counties have certified their results; the counties have until Friday, November 13, to upload the results. In Alaska, the tally as of November 10 shows Ms. Peltola with 49 percent of the votes to Senator Sullivan’s 47.2 percent, with about 87.3 percent of ballots counted and more than 245,000 ballots counted, with 401 of the state’s 403 precincts reporting. Under the state’s ranked-choice system, a candidate must get more than 50 percent of the vote to win, and the ranked-choice tally would not start until November 18.

Subjective
CNBC figures, via Suara Garut — Mr. Colom maintains a narrow lead in the Mississippi Senate race

Democratic candidate Scott Colom maintained a narrow advantage over incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, in a contest that could end a Republican winning streak dating back to 1982. According to Associated Press figures reported by CNBC, Mr. Colom led Ms. Hyde-Smith by 2,607 votes out of 953,547 ballots counted as of 1630 ET on November 10. Mississippi’s certification deadline is November 13, and the secretary of state must declare the final results by December 3. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola led Senator Sullivan by 2,517 votes, with 218,641 ballots counted and an estimated 76 percent of the vote reported in the earlier update.

Subjective
Fact — the Eisenkot bloc finalizes key Knesset roles, Matan Kahana for speaker

Mr. Eisenkot has reached an agreement with four opposition leaders on candidates for senior positions in the 26th Knesset, as he begins efforts to form the country’s next government. Under the agreement, former minister Matan Kahana has been named as the bloc’s candidate for Knesset speaker. Roy Folkman has been selected to chair the Knesset’s Arrangements Committee, while former defence minister Avigdor Liberman is the candidate to head the Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee. The Arrangements Committee will discuss the composition of the Knesset’s committees during its deliberations this week; the proposed composition will then be submitted to the Knesset plenary for approval next Wednesday. Mr. Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government.

entry.title: Veterans Day and Armistice Day: What November 11 Marks, and How the World Keeps It
entry.summary: On November 11, 1918, an armistice signed before dawn in a railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne stopped the fighting on the Western Front at 11:00 in the morning. This report follows what the day became: the two minutes of silence and the corn poppy—Papaver rhoeas, not the opium poppy; the American renaming that Kurt Vonnegut called the loss of a sacred day; the German day of mourning kept on a different date entirely; the Polish independence day that shares the date; and the several separate days on which the world marks the end of the Second World War—because there is no single one.
entry.content:
Special Report

Veterans Day · Armistice Day · Remembrance

Objective

Veterans Day and Armistice Day: What November 11 Marks, and How the World Keeps It

On November 11, 1918, an armistice signed before dawn in a railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne stopped the fighting on the Western Front at 11:00 in the morning. This report follows what the day became: the two minutes of silence and the corn poppy—Papaver rhoeas, not the opium poppy; the American renaming that Kurt Vonnegut called the loss of a sacred day; the German day of mourning kept on a different date entirely; the Polish independence day that shares the date; and the several separate days on which the world marks the end of the Second World War—because there is no single one.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0720 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

The File in Brief

The eleventh hour is an arithmetic fact, not a poem. The armistice document signed at Compiègne is headed “signed at 5 o’clock A.M. (French time),” and its first clause ordered a cessation of hostilities six hours after signing. Five plus six is eleven. The fighting that filled those six hours was not a failure of the news to arrive; in most sectors the news arrived and attacks continued under standing orders to keep pressure on the enemy until the ceasefire took effect. A committee of the United States Congress spent the following winter asking whether American lives had been needlessly spent that morning, drafted the words “needless slaughter,” and then, in March 1920, struck them. Men were still being killed in the war’s final minutes: a Canadian private, George Lawrence Price, died at 10:58 by the record his comrades carved; an American private, Henry Gunther, at 10:59 by one National Archives account and 10:58 by another. The desk prints the ranges, because the sources do.

The day was invented quickly and argued about immediately. Within a year the silence had been improvised in Cape Town, proposed in print in London, carried through a South African statesman’s letter to the King’s private secretary, and proclaimed by George V for the whole Empire. The flower that came with it is a botanical point this report states plainly because it is widely gotten wrong: the Flanders poppy of remembrance is the corn poppy, Papaver rhoeas. The opium poppy is a different species, Papaver somniferum. The two are cousins, not the same plant, and the distinction is the whole of the symbol’s history—the corn poppy is the weed that colonized the churned chalk of the battlefields because its seeds can wait in disturbed soil for decades.

The date does not mean one thing. In the United States, November 11 began as Armistice Day, a day the 1938 statute said was “to be dedicated to the cause of world peace,” and became Veterans Day in 1954, honoring the living veterans of all wars. Kurt Vonnegut, born on the day in 1922 and a prisoner of war in Dresden in 1945, wrote the dissent that is still quoted: “Armistice Day was sacred. Veterans’ Day is not.” In France it is a public holiday for the dead of all France’s wars. In Poland it is Independence Day, marking a state reborn the same morning. In Germany it is nothing at all: the German national day of mourning, Volkstrauertag, falls this year on Sunday, November 15, and Germany’s first national day for veterans—created by the Bundestag in 2024, first observed June 15, 2025—is deliberately not a holiday and deliberately not in November. Russia left the war eight months before Compiègne and keeps its First World War dead on August 1; its great day is May 9. And the question this report was asked—what is the World War II day?—has no single answer, because the second war ended in pieces: May 8 in most of Europe, May 9 in Moscow, August 15 in Britain, September 2 in the United States, September 3 in China and, since 2020, in Russia too.

1. The Eleventh Hour

The German delegation crossed the lines on the night of November 7–8, 1918, and was given seventy-two hours. It was headed by Matthias Erzberger, a Centre Party politician and Secretary of State, with Count Alfred von Oberndorff of the Foreign Ministry, Major-General Detlof von Winterfeldt for the army and Captain Ernst Vanselow for the navy. The convoy crossed the front in five cars on the evening of November 7 and was driven for some ten hours through the devastated north of France to Foch’s private train, standing in a siding in the Forest of Compiègne at Rethondes. The carriage was dining car No. 2419D of the Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits. Marshal Ferdinand Foch, the Allied commander-in-chief, appeared in person only twice in the three days—at the opening, and at the signing. Admiral Rosslyn Wemyss, the British First Sea Lord, was the second Allied signatory. The coldness was policy. Erzberger asked for an immediate ceasefire while the terms were considered; in Joseph Persico’s widely quoted reconstruction he pleaded, “For God’s sake, Monsieur le Maréchal, do not wait for those seventy-two hours. Stop the hostilities this very day.” Foch refused. The desk labels that sentence as reported dialogue from a secondary history; no stenographic transcript was located.

The terms were a dismantling.
