The pricing accounts filed below put a December increase at 95.6 percent in one instrument and near 99 percent in another; they agree on the direction and differ on the figure, and both figures stand in the Cocked Hat.

Washington, Whole: Twenty-Five Minutes at the Pentagon, and a Vote Taken Up but Not Read Out

Secretary Hegseth answered the articles in public, by name, and without conceding any of them. In his first Pentagon press conference since May, he said no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached in 250 years for carrying out lawful military operations, and that the effort is about policy disagreements and not high crimes, in the Reuters account filed below. The other accounts carry the sharper words: a farce and a stunt, and “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage,” in the Washington account filed below. Vice President Vance, in a post before the vote, posed the question whether the secretary had committed impeachable crimes and answered, “obviously not,” in the live account filed below. House Democratic Leader Jeffries has said he will vote to impeach. The articles are unchanged since Monday: three charging the Iran campaign under the War Powers Resolution, and the rest covering the school strike at Minab, the vessel strikes, Venezuela, Yemen, and the alleged retaliation against Senator Kelly. They are allegations in a charging document, found by no court.

The evening’s business was the procedural motion, and at 1800 the file holds the motion, not its result. Representative Massie posted that the House votes today: first on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, such as a motion to refer it to committee, and, if that effort is overcome, on to debate and a vote on the articles, in the vote account and the procedure account filed below. The schedule put the first and last votes at 1730. One account filed before the vote says that if the motion to refer fails, the House would likely set a vote on the articles themselves for November 11, and that Mr. Massie would request separate votes on each article. A simple majority impeaches in the House; conviction requires two-thirds of the Senate. The prediction accounts filed below price impeachment by December 31 at 79 percent on two exchanges; a price is not a vote, and the desk prints it as a price. No tally, no outcome, and no statement from either leader after a vote is in the evening file, and the desk does not supply one. The log proceeds to the midnight watch for the result.

The Close: A Partial Retraction of Monday, Priced in Full

Wall Street’s reading of the day was given at the close, and it was a giving-back, not a rout. The S&P 500 closed down 0.38 percent at 7,520.93, the Nasdaq Composite down 0.74 percent at 25,065.88, the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.30 percent at 52,231.89, and the Russell 2000 down 0.68 percent, in the closing account and the closing table filed below; the indexes closed well above their session lows, having fallen as much as 1.7 percent on the Nasdaq in early afternoon. The ten-year Treasury yield finished at 4.983 percent, up 11.9 basis points, after touching 5.03 percent in the day. Nvidia closed down 5.47 percent at $168.89, the second straight fall, and the technology sector was the worst of the eleven sectors. Gold fell about 2 percent in the accounts filed below; the figures differ by instrument and hour and stand in the Cocked Hat. One closing summary filed below runs the day larger—the S&P 500 down 0.99 percent and the Nasdaq 100 down 1.50 percent—on a different index and a different hour; the desk prints the disagreement rather than averaging it.

Oil finished the sentence the morning began. Brent for January settlement declined 1.2 percent to settle at $91.49 a barrel, after falling as much as 3.7 percent in the day and trading below ninety dollars for the first time since late August, at $89.88 in one intraday account; West Texas Intermediate declined 0.9 percent to settle at $86.04, in the settlement account and the oil account filed below. The benchmark that settled at $92.57 on Monday is down about $30 since the midterm elections on the accounts’ tally, on the cause they have named throughout: a president holding off further strikes on Iran. Beside the close, the day’s second large document held: Anthropic’s amended filing offers 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78, raising up to $64.35 billion, with a separate $26 billion private placement beside it and trading expected on the Nasdaq under ANT near November 19, in the filing accounts filed below. The valuation figures differ by definition—$1.404 trillion fully diluted against about $968 billion at the midpoint on the filing’s post-offering share count—and stand as a difference of definition in the Cocked Hat.

Abu Dhabi, Whole: About Four Hours, the Subjects Named, and the Land Carried to Wednesday

The first day of the three-way talks is a closed day with an open result. The delegations concluded the first day on Tuesday after nearly four hours in the Associated Press account, and after four and a half hours including a break of about forty minutes in a second account, in the wire account and the duration account filed below; the desk prints both durations. The Russian delegation is led by Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky, the Ukrainian by Rustem Umerov, and the American by Messrs. Witkoff and Kushner. President Zelensky, briefed by his team, said the sides discussed humanitarian measures, prisoner-of-war releases, security guarantees and de-escalation, in the first-day account filed below. Secretary Rubio, speaking in Paris after the first day, described the talks as “very productive” and said, “Obviously, there is still a lot of work to be done. This is not something that can be resolved in the next 24 hours.” No agreement, joint statement, or separate statement followed the first day in the wire accounts. One partisan account filed below calls the day a collapse and reports President Zelensky rejecting any exchange of Donbas territory; no delegation’s public statement in the file confirms a collapse, and the desk prints the claim as that account’s claim, beside the wire record of a day adjourned to Wednesday morning, November 11. The fighting did not pause while the delegations talked, in the same account’s closing line, and no account in the file reports that it did.

Paris, Whole: Europe at the Table, and an Ask for Interceptors

The G7’s second day in Paris closed with the transatlantic sentence spoken by the American, and a material ask spoken by the guest. Secretary Rubio dismissed concerns of a rift over the Ukraine negotiations: “I don’t think there’s a difference. I think we have the same interest in mind,” and, “Europe’s at the table. They’re with us,” adding that Washington thinks the trilateral should eventually include the European partners, in the Paris account filed below. Germany’s sentence stands from the morning: Europe belongs at this table, and no fundamental change to Europe’s security architecture is necessary. The Kremlin’s stands against both: the negotiations remain trilateral. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said after talks with Secretary Rubio on the sidelines that he had urged Washington to accelerate interceptor deliveries as Russia targets the power grid ahead of winter, and that Ukraine remained prepared to discuss de-escalatory measures including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure, with the Black Sea proposals conveyed through intermediaries including Turkey, Egypt and India, in the Reuters account filed below. France had indicated the meeting might produce no joint statement; none is in the evening file, and the desk files its absence as an absence.

Jerusalem, Whole: Sixty-Seven Signatures, a Date Set, and Two Speeches

Jerusalem supplied the day’s only dated decision. The 26th Knesset was sworn in on Tuesday. The opposition named Matan Kahana of Yashar as its candidate for speaker, to replace Amir Ohana of Likud, and Avigdor Liberman to head the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, in the candidate account filed below. In the fuller account filed below, the request to replace the speaker carried the signatures of 67 lawmakers—above the 61 required—and Speaker Ohana scheduled the vote for Tuesday, November 17, at 1600; the same account carries President Herzog’s plea that leaders “extend a hand to make concessions, even between rivals,” and the opening bills of Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc, for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023 attack, a limit on a prime minister’s time in office, and a repeal of the judicial overhaul, in the swearing-in account filed below. A second account records the two principals trading attacks at the ceremony—Prime Minister Netanyahu using the occasion against the government his rival is trying to form, and Mr. Eisenkot answering within the hour—in the ceremony account filed below. Mr. Ohana took the oath and holds the chair until the vote. Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate, given November 8, runs 28 days with a possible 14-day extension; Mr. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister. One figure still disagrees with itself: 46 first-time members in Tuesday’s candidate account against 47 in the overnight file. Both stand in the Cocked Hat.

Kraków, Whole: Thirteen in Hospital, a Computer Examined, and No Finding Stated

Kraków’s Tuesday file is a hospital count and an instrument, not a conclusion. Thirteen of the fifteen injured remained in Kraków hospitals on Tuesday, the regional governor said in the account filed below; one patient was discharged on Monday and an Austrian patient was transferred to Austria. The autopsies of the nine victims, begun Monday and expected to take about two days, had produced no published findings by collection time. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek told Radio Kraków on Tuesday that investigators had accessed the gunman’s computer and found evidence of visits to websites about Anders Breivik, in the Tuesday account filed below. The minister’s statement is a statement about a computer; it is not a finding of motive. The prosecutors’ standing limit stands beside it: they have no findings that would let them state responsibly that the gunman was inspired by any particular ideology. Both sentences are in the file, and the desk prints both, in the mourning account filed below and in the Tuesday account. The city’s mourning runs through tomorrow, November 11. The wounded counts that have disagreed since Saturday—15 in the governor’s hospital count, 16 and 17 in earlier printings that include the gunman or the first day’s tally—stand in the Cocked Hat, unresolved.

Iran, Whole: No New Sentence, and a Settlement as the Market’s Translation

Neither capital added a sentence to the Iran file on Tuesday, and the file at evening is Monday’s, with one price changed underneath it. The president’s position stands: fresh strikes held off for now after appeals from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait; the naval blockade kept in place; the war described by the president on Monday as militarily “effectively over” and his forces as locked and loaded, in the pause account and the effectively-over account filed below. Tehran’s two registers stand: negotiate with dignity, from its president; imaginary talks and the seven conditions, from its security council secretary. Secretary Rubio’s sentence stands against both: no progress, and the demands not realistic. The one unconfirmed enrichment report in the morning file remains unconfirmed by either government at evening. Brent’s settlement at $91.49, after a trade below ninety, is the day’s movement in this file, and it is financial, not verbal. What the two capitals agree on remains what they agreed on at midnight: the blockade exists. It is imposed in one account and demanded lifted in the other, and it stood all day.

The Count, Whole: Mississippi’s Deadline Day Ends, Alaska’s Batch Still Out

For a seventh day neither Senate race was called, and Tuesday moved both files by deadline and by one afternoon figure, not by a call. In Mississippi, Tuesday was the last day for mail ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive and for affidavit voters to cure their identification. The afternoon tally in the account filed below, as of 1455 ET, put Mr. Colom ahead by about 2,700 votes, at 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent with 99 percent counted in that account’s tally, in the clarity account filed below; the Associated Press estimate carried in this paper stands at about 97 percent counted and a margin of 2,574 in its last raw posting, and the two completeness figures stand unreconciled in the Cocked Hat. About 3,600 mail ballots were outstanding under the secretary of state’s November 4 statement. Counties certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. In Alaska, Monday’s count stands as the last posted count at evening: Ms. Peltola 106,321 to Mr. Sullivan 103,804, a margin of 2,517 first-choice votes, up from 637, in the widening account and the Juneau account filed below. The Tuesday batch—tens of thousands of early, absentee and questioned ballots, expected in the state’s afternoon, which is Washington’s night—had not posted in the file at 1800 ET, and one account expects it Tuesday night. The senator and the president have questioned the count on the ground that a second candidate named Daniel Sullivan drew 3,651 votes, more than the margin; the challenger’s campaign answers that the count is the system working as designed. No candidate is near 50 percent of first choices, and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18, with certification targeted for November 25. Sixteen congressional races in all remain uncalled in the account filed below, fourteen of them in the House. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide, and Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Abu Dhabi’s duration, nearly four hours in the wire account against four and a half including a break in a second. On Abu Dhabi’s character, a productive first day in the secretary’s word and an adjournment without agreement in the wire record, against a collapse in one partisan account that no delegation’s statement confirms. On the December increase, 95.6 percent in one pricing instrument, near 99 percent in another, and better than 80 percent before the print in a third—three instruments, one direction. On the close, one summary’s S&P 500 down 0.99 percent on a later hour and a different measure, against the closing table’s 0.38 percent. On gold, down 1.82 percent in futures in one account and 2.7 percent in an exchange-traded print in another. On Anthropic, $1.404 trillion fully diluted against about $968 billion at the midpoint on the post-offering count: a difference of definition. On Jerusalem’s new members, 46 against 47. On Mississippi’s completeness, 99 percent in the afternoon tally against about 97 percent in the wire estimate. On Kraków’s wounded, 15, 16 and 17 across the week’s printings. On the Hegseth vote, a schedule, two leaders’ stated intentions, and a 79 percent market price—and no tally in the file. Against the triangle, the evening’s single-valued facts are these: prices rose 0.4 percent and core prices 0.3 percent in October, a tenth hot on both measures; Governor Waller’s stated condition was met by the core print; Wall Street closed lower on all four indexes and Brent settled at $91.49 after trading below ninety; Secretary Hegseth spoke and conceded nothing; Abu Dhabi’s first day ended without an announced agreement and resumes Wednesday; 67 lawmakers signed to replace Speaker Ohana and the vote is set for November 17; thirteen of Kraków’s injured remain in hospital; and no Senate race and no impeachment article was decided in the file by 1800. The log proceeds to the midnight watch.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 36 items.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — a hot October inflation report rattles markets

United States consumer prices increased more than expected in October, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent after advancing 0.6 percent in September; economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent. Core prices rose 0.3 percent, against a forecast of 0.2 percent. Year-over-year readings were not published because last year’s shutdown prevented collection of October 2025 data; annual inflation was 3.7 percent in September.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — consumer inflation slows to 0.4 percent in October as energy pressures ease

The Consumer Price Index increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Core inflation was unchanged at 0.3 percent, the same rate as September and August. Energy prices increased 0.7 percent, sharply slower than September’s 5.2 percent rise; food prices rose 0.5 percent. No annual rate was published, because comparable October 2025 data were unavailable following the lapse in appropriations.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine, carrying Reuters — Governor Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in December

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday he would support raising short-term borrowing costs next month even if the data showed inflation cooled, and would consider an upsized half-point increase if the picture worsened. If core consumer prices rise 0.3 percent or more from September, a 50-basis-point hike should be considered at the December meeting, he said, adding that hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk.

Subjective
BigGo Finance — Governor Waller signals a December rate hike, 50 basis points if needed

Governor Waller said publicly on November 10 in London that he supports a December rate hike and drew a data threshold for its size: if the October core CPI gain remained around 0.3 percent or higher, he would support a 50-basis-point increase. Markets reacted swiftly: Nasdaq 100 futures fell, spot gold’s intraday decline widened to about 1 percent, and the dollar strengthened. The account carries CME FedWatch at 95.6 percent for a 25-basis-point December increase.

Subjective
Investopedia — stocks fall, Treasury yields jump as rate-hike concerns mount after the hot inflation report

Stocks closed lower Tuesday, though well above their session lows, following an inflation report that reinforced expectations the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates again soon. The Nasdaq Composite shed 0.7 percent after falling as much as 1.7 percent in early-afternoon trading, while the Dow and the S&P 500 finished down 0.3 and 0.4 percent. The ten-year Treasury yield was at 4.98 percent, down from an intraday high of 5.03 percent. Nvidia dropped 5.5 percent to pace Dow decliners.

Subjective
VistaP Global — stock market today, November 10, 2026

United States stocks closed lower Tuesday as a hotter-than-expected inflation report and rising Treasury yields complicated the outlook for interest rates and technology valuations. The closing table: the S&P 500 at 7,520.93, down 29.01 points or 0.38 percent; the Dow at 52,231.89, down 0.30 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 25,065.88, down 0.74 percent; the Russell 2000 down 0.68 percent. The ten-year yield finished at 4.983 percent, up 11.9 basis points.

Subjective
MarketOne — the closing bell, November 10, 2026

Stocks slid across the board as a hotter-than-expected inflation print collided with a hawkish Fed and sent chip stocks and growth names into retreat. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 percent, the Nasdaq-heavy QQQ dropped 0.9 percent, and small caps gave back 0.8 percent. Long bonds fell 1.3 percent on the day and gold fell 2.7 percent as a stronger dollar overwhelmed any safe-haven demand. Intel closed down 2.7 percent. CoreWeave reports after the close.

Subjective
XTB — daily summary: the CPI reading hits markets

Higher-than-forecast United States inflation—core CPI plus 0.3 percent on the month, headline plus 0.4 percent—sparked a hawkish reaction from Fed officials, and Wall Street came under strong selling pressure following the release. The summary’s figures, at its 2047 print: the S&P 500 falls 0.99 percent, the Nasdaq 100 falls 1.50 percent, and the Dow Jones falls 0.70 percent.

Subjective
Rigzone, carrying Bloomberg — oil prices retreat as peace hopes grow

Brent crude fell, briefly slumping below $90 a barrel, as technical factors helped deepen a selloff driven by expectations of further de-escalation in the Iran war. The global benchmark settled below $92 after declining as much as 3.7 percent on Tuesday: Brent for January settlement declined 1.2 percent to settle at $91.49 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate for December delivery declined 0.9 percent to settle at $86.04 a barrel in New York.

Subjective
OilPrice.com — oil falls to its lowest level since August

Brent crude briefly fell below $90 a barrel as hopes of diplomatic breakthroughs in Iran and Ukraine accelerated the oil market selloff. Crude prices have plunged by almost $30 a barrel since the United States midterm elections. The administration reiterated its reluctance to engage in new military strikes against Iran.

Subjective
TechCrunch — Anthropic sets an IPO price range of $70 to $78 a share

Anthropic, in an updated prospectus filed Tuesday, will offer 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 a share, reaching an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The offering would raise $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion. Trading is expected on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

Subjective
TronWeekly — Anthropic’s offering: $64.4 billion, 825 million shares at $70 to $78

Anthropic offered 825 million Class A shares at $70.00 to $78.00 apiece in its initial public offering on November 10, 2026: 801,351,354 shares offered by the company and 23,648,646 by shareholders, with an underwriters’ option for up to 123,750,000 more. Seven strategic partners have committed to a separate private placement of $26 billion at the IPO price. At the $74 midpoint, estimated net proceeds from the primary shares and the placement come to $84.6 billion.

Subjective
Reuters — the Pentagon chief calls moves to impeach him a farce that will fail

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday called moves to impeach him over abuse of power in the Iran war a farce that would fail. He made the comment at a news conference a day after Representative Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against him, in his first Pentagon news conference since May. In a post on X, Mr. Massie said the House would hold a first vote on Tuesday on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, and that if that effort is overcome, the House will proceed to a real debate and a vote on the articles.

Subjective
USA Today — Secretary Hegseth defends himself against impeachment: it is a farce

Facing a looming impeachment vote, the Pentagon chief dug in at a news conference on November 10. “What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle,” he said. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it.” The news conference lasted roughly 25 minutes and ended after he took a handful of questions. The House was planning to vote on whether to move forward later on November 10.

Subjective
USA Today — why the Pentagon chief is facing impeachment, and what happens next

The impeachment fight begins in the evening on November 10, when the House is slated to hold its first vote on the effort led by Representative Massie. House leaders are set to hold a procedural vote that could set aside the resolution, essentially killing it. If that motion fails, the House would likely set a vote on the articles for November 11, and Mr. Massie indicated he would request separate votes on each article. Any articles that pass on a simple majority go to the Senate, where conviction requires two-thirds.

Subjective
political.org — Secretary Hegseth calls the impeachment effort a farce and political spectacle as the House vote looms

Defense Secretary Hegseth on Tuesday denounced the impeachment effort led by Representative Massie, calling it a farce and political spectacle ahead of a House vote expected later in the day. The chamber is expected to take up the resolution Tuesday evening, but will likely first hold a procedural vote to table it. Before Democrats take control in January, impeachment would need at least three Republican votes if all Democrats vote yes, depending on absences; Senate removal would require more than a dozen Republicans.

Subjective
Reason — Representative Massie introduces articles of impeachment against Secretary Hegseth

Representative Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Hegseth on Monday. The resolution alleges three charges for illegally waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution; one for ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties; one for overseeing extrajudicial killings in strikes on alleged drug boats; one for suppressing free speech in connection with the effort to punish Senator Kelly; one for the capture of Venezuela’s president without congressional authorization; and one for illegally waging war against Yemen. Democrats are likely to side with Mr. Massie, and as few as three Republican defections or absences could allow the charges to advance.

Subjective
Action Network — the Hegseth impeachment odds tracker

Representative Massie filed eight articles of impeachment against Secretary Hegseth on Monday, and the fight is shaping prediction-market prices. Polymarket prices Hegseth impeached by December 31, 2026 at 79 percent; Kalshi prices impeached by January 1, 2027 at 79 percent; prices as of November 10, 2026. Today’s House vote is not a straight impeachment vote: lawmakers first decide whether to send the resolution to committee or table it outright.

Subjective
Live Updates, via Substack — Secretary Hegseth blames policy disagreements for the impeachment push

A live file on the impeachment day. The House clerk is reading the charges against Secretary Hegseth. Vice President Vance backed the secretary in a post on X ahead of the expected procedural vote, posing the question whether he had committed impeachable crimes and answering, “obviously not.” House Democratic Leader Jeffries has said he will vote to impeach. If the House impeaches before January 3, the approved articles can carry over to the next Congress; if the resolution is still pending then, it expires.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Military.com — Russia and Ukraine hold nearly four hours of United States-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi

Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington made another push to end the war. The two-day session in Abu Dhabi is the first such meeting since February and will focus on establishing future security guarantees, the White House said. The first day of talks concluded after nearly four hours, the RIA Novosti account said. They are expected to resume Wednesday, according to the press office of the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine.

Subjective
The Europe Today — Abu Dhabi talks: Russia, the United States and Ukraine end a four-and-a-half-hour first round

The Russian, American and Ukrainian delegations concluded the first day of the trilateral Abu Dhabi talks on Tuesday after four and a half hours of negotiations, including a break of about forty minutes. Contacts are expected to continue on November 11. The Russian delegation is led by Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky, the Ukrainian side by Rustem Umerov, and the United States is represented by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The Kremlin spokesman said ahead of the meeting that the talks would focus on security guarantees.

Subjective
YallaYou — Abu Dhabi talks: the first day ends after nearly four hours

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the United States ended the first day of their talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday after nearly four hours at the table. The session continues on Wednesday. It is the first three-way meeting since February. Ukrainian President Zelensky, briefed by his team, outlined the subjects discussed; Secretary Rubio, speaking in Paris, described the talks as very productive and said there is still a lot of work to be done and the matter cannot be resolved in the next 24 hours. Nothing has been announced, and no joint statement followed the first day.

Subjective
RussiaTruth, Substack — day one collapses in Abu Dhabi

The first round of trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi on November 10, 2026 has ended in deadlock, in this account’s reading. President Zelensky issued a public statement rejecting any exchange of Donbas territory for peace and dismissing any security framework short of full NATO membership, while Moscow refused an interim ceasefire. The account reports Ukrainian military sources saying orders have been issued concerning the bridges across the Dnieper River, and Russian forces closing near Sumy. Nothing emerging from Abu Dhabi suggests a diplomatic breakthrough is possible on November 11, in the account’s judgment.

Subjective
Reuters — Ukraine urges the United States to speed up interceptor deliveries as Russia targets the power grid

Ukraine’s foreign minister said he had urged Secretary Rubio on Tuesday to accelerate interceptor deliveries as Russia ramps up attacks on energy infrastructure as winter approaches. Speaking after talks with Secretary Rubio on the sidelines of the G7 meeting in Paris, Minister Sybiha said he had pressed Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow even as diplomatic efforts took place in Abu Dhabi. Ukraine remained prepared to discuss de-escalatory measures, including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure, with Black Sea proposals conveyed through intermediaries including Turkey, Egypt and India.

Subjective
DevDiscourse — “Europe’s at the table”: Secretary Rubio reaffirms transatlantic unity on Ukraine

Secretary Rubio, speaking during the G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris, dismissed concerns over a rift with European allies regarding the Ukraine negotiations, while asserting that Washington will escalate economic pressure on Tehran rather than yield to demands for reparations. “I don’t think there’s a difference. I think we have the same interest in mind,” he said. “There’s always this concern in Europe that they’re going to be left out… Well, Europe’s at the table. They’re with us.” German Foreign Minister Wadephul stressed that any post-conflict security architecture must involve Europe directly.

Subjective
The Insight International — the opposition picks Matan Kahana to replace the prime minister’s ally as Knesset speaker

Israel’s opposition bloc on Tuesday chose former minister Matan Kahana as its candidate for Knesset speaker, in a bid to take control of parliament from Prime Minister Netanyahu’s allies while it tries to form a government. Kahana, of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, would replace Amir Ohana of Likud. The announcement came hours before the 26th Knesset was due to be sworn in. Forty-six of its 120 members are serving for the first time. At least 61 lawmakers must sign a request or vote to replace the speaker; Speaker Ohana has said he will not hold the vote on inauguration day but will schedule it within the following week.

Subjective
Silent Dossier — the Knesset sworn in: can the prime minister stop the coalition?

Israel’s 26th Knesset was sworn in at Jerusalem on Tuesday, November 10. Speaker Ohana said he had scheduled the vote on his replacement for Tuesday, November 17 at 4 p.m., after 67 lawmakers signed a request to remove him. Opening the session, President Herzog asked party leaders to extend a hand to make concessions, even between rivals. The Eisenkot bloc announced bills for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023 attack, a limit on a prime minister’s time in office, and a repeal of the judicial overhaul, and filed the request, signed by 67 lawmakers, to replace Speaker Ohana with Matan Kahana.

Subjective
The Insight International — the prime minister and Mr. Eisenkot trade attacks as the new Knesset is sworn in

Israel’s 26th Knesset was sworn in on Tuesday, and caretaker Prime Minister Netanyahu used the ceremony to attack the government his rival Gadi Eisenkot is trying to form. Mr. Eisenkot, a former army chief, was given the mandate to form a government on Sunday. The opposition submitted the signatures of more than 61 lawmakers on Tuesday to replace Speaker Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, with Yashar’s Matan Kahana. Speaker Ohana has said he will schedule a vote within a week.

Subjective
The Gauge — the Kraków gunman dies in hospital; Tuesday update

The gunman who killed six people in Kraków’s Main Market Square died in hospital on Monday morning, Polish police said; six people were killed in the square and investigators are also examining three family deaths. Tuesday update: thirteen of the fifteen people injured remained in Kraków hospitals on Tuesday, the regional governor said; one patient was discharged on Monday and an Austrian patient was transferred to Austria. Justice Minister Żurek told Radio Kraków on Tuesday that investigators had accessed the gunman’s computer and found evidence of visits to websites about Anders Breivik.

Subjective
Brussels Signal — the Kraków gunman dies in hospital as Poland mourns the victims

The man behind the shooting in the historic centre of Kraków has died in hospital, police said. The 24-year-old died at about 4:30 a.m. on November 9 after at least three operations. Shortly after 3 p.m. on November 7, the gunman drove onto the Main Market Square and opened fire on passers-by; four women and two men were killed. Four of the dead were Polish, one was a British man and another an Austrian woman. Police later found the bodies of the gunman’s father, mother and sister at the family flat. Prosecutor Stasielak said autopsies on all nine victims would begin on November 9 and could take about two days. President Nawrocki declared two days of national mourning for November 8 and 9; Kraków’s mayor extended the city’s mourning until November 11.

Subjective
AnewZ — the president pauses Iran strikes and keeps the Hormuz blockade

President Trump said on Monday he would hold off on new military strikes against Iran for now, after appeals from Persian Gulf countries, but would keep the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz in place. “The United States of America is fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made, and we don’t think there’s going to be any reason to use it,” he told reporters. He named Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait. Under Iran’s proposal, the United States would end its blockade and lift some sanctions and stop its bombing campaign, while Tehran would end its own blockade of the strait. Iranian media said the United States struck Qeshm island late on Sunday night.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — the president says the Iran war is effectively over and signals no immediate strikes

President Trump on Monday told reporters he believes the war in Iran “militarily is effectively over,” in a surprise visit to the White House briefing room after meeting Qatar’s prime minister. “Iran militarily is effectively over,” he said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo.” He added that Iran has been “decapitated,” that there was “positive momentum” toward ending the war, and that American forces remain ready to resume strikes; the United States had identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes.

Subjective
USA Today — why clarity in the Mississippi Senate election could come by week’s end

Mississippi challenger Scott Colom was narrowly leading incumbent Senator Hyde-Smith as of 2:55 p.m. ET on November 10, with a margin of about 2,700 votes in a race with almost 1 million votes, or 99 percent of the total vote counted, according to results from USA Today. About 3,600 mail-in ballots, legally permitted to arrive by November 10 if postmarked by Election Day, were still outstanding under the secretary of state’s November 4 statement. All 82 counties must certify their results by November 13. In Alaska, as of 3 p.m. ET, Ms. Peltola was leading Senator Sullivan by a little more than 2,500 voters, with about 78 percent of the votes counted.

Subjective
Fox News — Ms. Peltola widens her narrow Alaska Senate lead over Senator Sullivan as counting continues

Alaska’s still too-close-to-call Senate race is expected to deliver another batch of ballot results Tuesday night after Monday’s ballot drop expanded Ms. Peltola’s lead over Senator Sullivan to 2,517 first-choice votes: 106,321 at 48.6 percent to 103,804 at 47.5 percent, with Gerald Heikes at 2.2 percent and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 1.7 percent, or 3,651 votes. Roughly 75 to 76 percent of the expected vote is in. The campaign said Ms. Peltola won Monday’s votes by a margin of 68 to 30. Official ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18, with certification set for November 25.

Subjective
Juneau Empire — Ms. Peltola extends her lead over Senator Sullivan as ballot-counting continues

Ms. Peltola extended her lead over Senator Sullivan in an updated vote total published Monday by the Alaska Division of Elections: as of 4 p.m. she led by 2,517 votes out of 219,342 cast, after the division added 4,947 counted ballots on Monday. With 48.5 percent of first-choice votes, she is coming closer to the threshold needed to win without the runoff. A much larger batch is expected on Tuesday, including absentee and early votes received in the days immediately before Election Day, withheld while officials cross-checked poll registers to prevent double voting; the Tuesday update could be decisive for more than the Senate race.

Subjective
New York Post — why it is taking so long to count the Election Day results, and when the 16 uncalled races should be known

A week after the polls closed, 16 congressional races remain without a winner, held up by recounts, late-arriving mail, ranked-choice arithmetic and provisional ballots. Democrats have secured 254 House seats to Republicans’ 163 and at least 54 seats in the Senate, according to the Associated Press. Fourteen House races and two Senate races remain. In Mississippi, the incumbent trails by less than half a point; in Alaska, by about one point. The Alaska Division of Elections is expected to add tens of thousands of ballots to the tally Tuesday and aims to certify results November 25.

entry.title: Inflation Runs Hot at 0.4 Percent, Hegseth Calls the Charges a Farce, and Abu Dhabi\u2019s First Day Ends Without a Breakthrough
entry.summary: The midday file for Tuesday, November 10, 2026: October consumer prices rose 0.4 percent on the month and core prices 0.3 percent for a third straight month, both a tenth above the consensus the overnight edition carried, with no annual rate published because the 2025 shutdown left no October 2025 index; Governor Waller’s stated test for considering a half-point December increase—core at 0.3 percent or higher—was met by the print. Secretary Hegseth, in his first Pentagon press conference since May, called the eight impeachment articles a farce, a stunt and sabotage, and the House takes its first procedural vote Tuesday evening, two days earlier than the midnight file expected. Wall Street opened lower, Brent broke below ninety dollars for the first time since August, and the Anthropic filing steadied technology by mid-morning. In Abu Dhabi the first day ended after nearly four hours with no breakthrough announced; in Paris the G7 closed its second day with Ukraine’s foreign minister in the room and no joint statement in the file; in Jerusalem the opposition named Matan Kahana for speaker as the 26th Knesset opened and Speaker Ohana took the oath and the chair. Neither Senate race was called and no new count figure was published by noon. Collected at 1200.
entry.content:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Inflation Runs Hot at 0.4 Percent, Hegseth Calls the Charges a Farce, and Abu Dhabi’s First Day Ends Without a Breakthrough

The news at midday: the morning’s one scheduled number came in a tenth hotter than the morning expected it, on both measures; the morning’s one scheduled witness answered his accusers for twenty-five minutes and the vote on him moved up a day; the market that rose on Monday gave back part of the rise at the open and then steadied on a filing; and the two tables the week opened—Abu Dhabi and Paris—produced a duration, a seating plan and no agreement by noon.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Tuesday, November 10, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 28, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Edition No. 27, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Midday corrected the morning on the number, on the vote, and on the speaker, and it left every negotiation and every count exactly where the night left them. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put October’s consumer prices up 0.4 percent on the month and core prices up 0.3 percent, in the Reuters account filed below; the overnight edition carried a consensus of 0.3 and 0.2, and the correction is a tenth on each measure, stated in the section below. At the Pentagon, Secretary Hegseth held his first press conference since May and called Representative Massie’s eight articles a farce, a stunt and sabotage, in the Washington account filed below; Mr. Massie answered that the House votes today, on a procedural motion first, with votes expected at 1730—not Wednesday, as the midnight file had it. In New York the three main indexes opened lower, the ten-year yield stood near 4.99 percent, and Brent crude traded below ninety dollars for the first time since August, before the Anthropic filing, printed below, steadied the technology shares by mid-morning. In Abu Dhabi the first day of the three-way talks ended after nearly four hours and resumes Wednesday, with no breakthrough announced. In Jerusalem the opposition named its candidate for speaker, Matan Kahana of Yashar, and the 26th Knesset opened in the afternoon with Speaker Ohana taking the oath and the chair. Neither Senate race was called by noon, and no new figure for either was published in the morning.

The Correction at Noon: The Number Came In a Tenth Hot on Both Measures

The day’s first official statement was a number, and the number corrects the consensus this paper printed at 0400. The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said in its release; core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as they did in September and in August—a third straight month at that rate, in the bureau’s figures as carried and the release account filed below. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent on the headline and 0.2 percent on the core. The overnight edition carried that consensus; the print is a tenth above it on both measures, and the desk files the correction at the head of the edition, where corrections belong. Inside the index: energy rose 0.7 percent, against 5.2 percent in September, with gasoline up 1.0 percent against 9.1 percent; food rose 0.5 percent, with food at home up 0.4 percent; shelter rose 0.3 percent and accounted for more than 30 percent of the monthly increase; real average hourly earnings were unchanged on the month. No annual rate was published, for the reason the overnight edition gave: the bureau collected no October 2025 data during last year’s lapse in appropriations, so there is no October-to-October comparison to print. September’s annual rate, 3.7 percent, remains a September figure. The next report, covering November, is scheduled for December 10—one day after the Federal Reserve meeting this report now feeds.

The print met, exactly, the test a governor of the Federal Reserve had set for it four and a half hours before it landed. Governor Christopher Waller, speaking in London in remarks published at 0900 GMT, said he was leaning toward supporting a 25-basis-point increase at the December 8–9 meeting even if October improved on September, and that if core prices rose around 0.3 percent or higher, a 50-basis-point increase should be considered, because hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk, in the London account and the remarks account filed below. Core printed 0.3 percent. The governor’s condition is therefore met on his own stated terms; the committee’s decision is not his alone and has not been taken. The market’s pricing moved in the same direction before and after the release: traders priced an almost 99 percent chance of a December increase in one account filed below, fully priced two quarter-point increases by March in another, and had priced better than 80 percent for December before the print. The accounts differ on the instrument and the hour; they agree on the direction, and the desk prints the agreement and the differing figures in the Cocked Hat.

Washington at Noon: Twenty-Five Minutes at the Pentagon, a Vote at 1730

Secretary Hegseth answered the articles the way the articles were filed—in public, by name, and without conceding any of them. In his first Pentagon press conference since May—six months in the Associated Press count, 180 days in the count this paper has carried—the secretary said no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached in 250 years for carrying out lawful military operations, that the effort is about policy disagreements and not high crimes, and that his accuser is a rogue lawmaker, in the Associated Press account filed below. The other accounts carry the same sentences in his sharper words: a farce and a stunt, in the Reuters account; “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage,” in the briefing account; and, on the troops, that anyone coming for the warriors would have to come through him, in the Pentagon account filed below. On the record he defends, he cited Operation Epic Fury’s more than 13,000 targets struck and the destruction of Iran’s navy and of more than 80 percent of its nuclear industrial base; those are the secretary’s figures, printed as his. The conference lasted roughly 25 minutes and took a handful of questions. The articles themselves are unchanged since Monday: three charging the Iran campaign under the War Powers Resolution, and the rest covering the school strike at Minab, the vessel strikes, Venezuela, Yemen, and the alleged retaliation against Senator Kelly. They are allegations in a charging document, found by no court.

The second correction of the day is the House’s clock. The midnight edition carried House leaders as having until Wednesday to table, refer or vote. On Tuesday morning Representative Massie posted that the House votes today: the first vote is on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, such as a motion to refer it to committee, and if that effort is overcome the House proceeds to debate and a vote on the articles, in the schedule account and the Reuters account filed below. The daily schedule Mr. Massie shared puts the House in at 1000 for morning hour and at noon for legislative business, with the first and last votes expected at 1730. At noon the procedural motion stands listed and unvoted. A simple majority impeaches in the House; conviction and removal would require two-thirds of the Senate, where Republicans hold 53 seats in the accounts filed below. Whatever Tuesday evening decides, the accounts agree the effort returns in January if it fails now, when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

The Markets’ Reading at Noon: A Hotter Print, a Lower Open, and Oil Below Ninety

Wall Street’s reading of the morning was given at the open, and it was a partial retraction of Monday, not a reversal of it. The Dow fell 226.5 points, or 0.43 percent, at the open to 52,163.21; the S&P 500 fell 36.8 points, or 0.49 percent, to 7,513.09; and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 205.7 points, or 0.81 percent, to 25,047.448, in the Reuters snapshot filed below. A second snapshot at 0948 ran a touch lower on all three—the Dow down 0.47 percent, the S&P 500 down 0.58 percent, the Nasdaq down 0.70 percent—with the ten-year Treasury yield at 4.988 percent, up from Monday’s close of 4.862 percent, in the early-session account filed below. Nvidia fell 2.6 percent in one opening account and 1.6 percent in a pre-open account; the chip shares that led Monday’s rise gave back part of it. Europe, which had risen into the number—the FTSE 100 up 0.5 percent at London’s midday, the CAC 40 up 1.2 percent and the DAX up 1.3 percent, in the London midday account filed below—pared its gains after it. Oil completed the morning’s sentence: Brent fell more than 3 percent and traded below ninety dollars a barrel for the first time since late August, at $89.88 in one account, with West Texas Intermediate down more than 2 percent to below $85, in the global markets account filed below. The same barrel that settled at $92.57 on Monday has now fallen through two round numbers in two days, on the same cause the accounts have named throughout: a president holding off further strikes on Iran.

By mid-morning the fall had steadied, and the steadying had a name. Both Nasdaq indexes erased their opening losses and traded into positive territory as attention shifted to Anthropic’s planned listing, before backing off to stand near unchanged, in the rebound account filed below. The filing behind the move is the morning’s second large document. Anthropic, in an updated prospectus filed Tuesday, will offer 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 a share, raising $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion, at a valuation of up to $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis, in the filing account filed below; the Reuters accounts put the non-diluted value at about $1 trillion to $1.02 trillion, the difference being the treatment of options and restricted stock, in the Reuters account and the exclusive account filed below. A separate $26 billion private placement with cornerstone investors including Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices stands beside the offering. The terms filed Tuesday are lower than the terms briefly circulated to bankers on Monday night and retracted—about 867 million shares at up to $80—and lower than the $2 trillion discussed earlier in the year, against a May private valuation of $965 billion. Run-rate revenue stood at $81 billion at the end of October. Trading is expected on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT near November 19. On the morning the print argued for dearer money, the largest test of the AI boom priced itself anyway, at a lower price than it first asked.

Abu Dhabi at Noon: Four Hours, a Framework Proposed, and the Land Left for Wednesday

The talks the overnight edition filed as open are, at noon, adjourned for the day, and the day produced a duration and a method and no result. The first day concluded after nearly four hours, the RIA Novosti account said, and the talks are expected to resume Wednesday, according to the press office of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, in the Associated Press account filed below. The day’s order is on the record: it began with a meeting of the Ukrainian team, the American envoys and representatives of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission, and then moved to the trilateral format with Russia. Mr. Kushner, opening, said the United States wanted to draw lessons from previous efforts and develop a new structure, and Washington is pressing a new European security framework, in the framework account filed below. One account citing an American official puts day one on policing a future ceasefire, with territory waiting until day two, and reports the same official saying both sides had privately shown some flexibility over a possible swap of territory, in the running-order account filed below. That flexibility rests on one unnamed official’s briefing and is printed as such. The stated positions have not moved in public, and no breakthrough has been announced by any delegation. The desk files four hours, a framework proposed, and the land question carried to Wednesday.

Paris at Noon: The Second Day, Ukraine’s Minister in the Room, No Statement in the File

The G7’s two days in Paris ran out at midday with the argument it opened with, now spoken by the guest as well as the hosts. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, joined Tuesday’s session on Ukraine—air defence, economic pressure, Black Sea navigation—having said before departing, “No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” in the Paris account filed below. Germany’s sentence stands: Europe belongs at this table, and no fundamental change to Europe’s security architecture is necessary, right or appropriate—an answer, in substance, to the framework Mr. Kushner proposed in Abu Dhabi the same morning. France’s stands: Europeans will participate in the Abu Dhabi discussions. The Kremlin’s stands against both: the negotiations remain trilateral. The Abu Dhabi lists at noon agree with the Kremlin on the main table and with France on the rooms around it. The second session took up instability in the Middle East, with the European ministers warning against renewed American strikes on Iran and arguing for restoring normal shipping through Hormuz, in the ministers account filed below. Canada announced fresh sanctions on Russia on Monday. France had indicated the meeting might produce no joint statement; at noon none is in the file, and the desk files its absence as an absence, not as a rupture.

Jerusalem at Noon: A Candidate Named, an Oath Taken, and the Chair Held for Now

Jerusalem supplied the day’s third correction: the unnamed speaker of the overnight file has a name. The opposition bloc on Tuesday chose former minister Matan Kahana of Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party as its candidate for speaker, to replace Amir Ohana of Likud, in the candidate account filed below. The naming settles the question the mandate carried from Sunday—who, if the chair changes hands—and leaves the other two open: at least 61 members must sign or vote for a replacement, Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc stands at 48, and Mr. Ohana has said he will not hold the vote on inauguration day but will schedule it within the following week on a valid request. The ceremony itself ran on its printed schedule: a plaza ceremony at 1520 Jerusalem time and the plenary at 1600, which is 0900 in Washington. In the opening broadcast account, President Herzog addressed the session, called on lawmakers to debate with respect, and invited Speaker Ohana to take the oath before handing him the chair; Mr. Ohana pledged, Psalm 122 was recited, and the roll-call pledges of the 120 members proceeded under his chairmanship, with one warning issued to a member over an interruption, in the opening account filed below. The account itself cautions that the broadcast segments reviewed do not establish that all 120 oaths were completed, and the desk prints the caution with the fact. Mr. Ohana’s assumption of the chair for the opening is a step in the ceremony, not the outcome of the speaker question; Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister, and the mandate runs to December 6. One figure in the file disagrees with itself: the overnight edition carried 47 first-time members, and Tuesday’s candidate account carries 46. The desk prints both in the Cocked Hat and settles neither.

Iran at Noon: No New Sentence, and a Barrel Below Ninety as the Market’s Translation

Neither capital added a sentence to the Iran file in the morning, and the file at noon is the standing one, with one price changed underneath it. The president’s position stands as Monday’s: fresh strikes held off for now after appeals from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait; the naval blockade and Operation Iron Gate kept in place; forces locked and loaded if the position changes, in the Reuters account and the pause account filed below. Tehran’s two registers stand: negotiate with dignity, from its president; imaginary talks and the seven conditions, from its security council secretary. Secretary Rubio’s sentence stands against both: no progress, and the demands not realistic. One unconfirmed report in the morning file says, on unnamed sources, that the United States is prepared to let Iran keep enriching uranium at 3.67 percent and that Tehran is willing to accept that limit; neither government has confirmed it, and the desk files it as one unconfirmed report, not as a term. The movement in the file is financial, not verbal: Brent’s fall below ninety dollars is the market’s translation of the pause. What the two capitals agree on remains what they agreed on at midnight: the blockade exists. It is imposed in one account and demanded lifted in the other, and it stood all morning.

Kraków at Noon: The Autopsies’ Second Day, and No Findings Published

Kraków’s file at noon is an instrument running, not a result. The autopsies of the nine victims, begun Monday, were expected to take about two days, which puts their completion at about today; no findings from them had been published by noon, and the desk does not fill the space where findings will go. The standing facts are Monday’s: the suspect died at about 0430 on Monday after at least three operations; the case against the dead man will in time be closed while the investigation around him—whether he acted alone or was inspired, the phones, computers and 11 firearms under analysis—continues; and the prosecutors’ limit stands, that they have no findings that would let them state responsibly that he was inspired by any particular ideology. The interior ministry’s review of gun licensing, announced after police data showed more than 50,000 new licences issued in 2025, is the file’s one new policy instrument; both the gunman and his father held permits. The city’s own mourning runs through tomorrow, November 11. The wounded stand at 15 in hospital in the governor’s count, against 17 in the prosecutors’ earlier count; the disagreement is carried in the Cocked Hat, as it has been since Monday.

The Count at Noon: Both Deadlines Fall Today, and No New Figure by Noon

For a sixth day neither Senate race was called, and the morning published no new figure for either race; Tuesday’s part in both files is deadlines, not numbers, until the counts run. Alaska’s next scheduled count falls today, carrying early votes cast October 30 to November 2, absentee and questioned ballots, on a race standing in the last state posting at Mary Peltola 102,962 to Dan Sullivan 102,325—a margin of 637 first-choice votes, with no candidate near 50 percent and the ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18. A running results account updated Tuesday carries the same race in rounder figures as of November 9—Ms. Peltola at 48.6 percent to Mr. Sullivan’s 47.5 percent, more than 220,000 ballots counted and about 78.5 percent of ballots in, in the running account filed below; the percentages and the raw posting are two printings of one standing count, not two counts. Mississippi’s deadlines fall today: mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive and affidavit voters must cure their identification, on a race standing at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on about 97 percent counted in the Associated Press estimate; the same running account carries Mississippi in percentages as 49.1 to 48.8 with 99 percent counted, a figure the desk cannot reconcile with the 97 percent estimate and prints as a disagreement in the Cocked Hat, in the delay account filed below. Counties certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. Alaska’s count, when it posts, will move in the state’s afternoon, which is Washington’s evening; the midday file therefore closes the count where the night left it, with both of its named days arrived and neither of its numbers yet moved. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the December increase, almost 99 percent in one pricing account, fully priced by March in another, and better than 80 percent before the print in a third—three instruments, one direction. On Anthropic, $1.404 trillion fully diluted against about $1.02 trillion not diluted: a difference of definition, printed as one. On the open, the Reuters snapshot and the 0948 snapshot differing by tenths on all three indexes, as snapshots an hour apart will. On Abu Dhabi’s flexibility, one unnamed official’s briefing against every delegation’s public silence. On the enrichment report, one unconfirmed account against no confirmation from either capital. On Jerusalem’s new members, 47 in the overnight file and 46 in Tuesday’s candidate account. On Mississippi’s completeness, about 97 percent in the wire estimate and 99 percent in the running account, irreconcilable at noon. On Kraków’s wounded, 15 in the governor’s hospital count against 17 in the prosecutors’ earlier count. Against the triangle, the midday’s single-valued facts are these: prices rose 0.4 percent and core prices 0.3 percent in October, a tenth hot on both measures against the consensus, with no annual rate in existence; Governor Waller’s stated condition for considering a half-point increase was met by the core print; Secretary Hegseth spoke for about 25 minutes and conceded nothing; the House’s first vote on his articles is set for Tuesday evening; Brent traded below ninety dollars; Anthropic filed at $70 to $78; Abu Dhabi’s first day ran nearly four hours and produced no announced breakthrough; Matan Kahana is the opposition’s candidate for speaker and Amir Ohana holds the chair; and no Senate race was called. The log proceeds to the evening.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 35 items.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — a hot October inflation report rattles markets

United States consumer prices increased more than expected in October, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent last month after advancing 0.6 percent in September; economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent. Core prices rose 0.3 percent, against a forecast of 0.2 percent. The bureau did not publish year-over-year readings because last year’s shutdown prevented collection of October 2025 data; annual inflation was 3.7 percent in September. Governor Waller, the account notes, had said the central bank ought to raise borrowing costs in December even if inflation cooled.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — consumer inflation slows to 0.4 percent in October as energy pressures ease

The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Core inflation was unchanged at 0.3 percent, the same rate as September and August. Energy prices increased 0.7 percent, sharply slower than September’s 5.2 percent rise; food prices rose 0.5 percent after remaining unchanged in September. No annual rate was published, because comparable October 2025 data were unavailable following the lapse in appropriations.

Subjective
USA Today — inflation slowed in October, but annual data is missing after the shutdown

Consumer prices climbed 0.4 percent in October, down from 0.6 percent in September and higher than forecasters expected; the Cleveland Fed’s nowcast had projected 0.24 percent. Core inflation rose 0.3 percent. The report is the last look at consumer prices the Federal Reserve will get before its December meeting, and one economist quoted says it most likely seals a rate increase to close the year. The account carries the gasoline figures: regular gasoline up 34 percent and diesel up 64 percent since February 28, on AAA data, with the national average at $3.98 on November 10.

Subjective
SHRM — inflation continued to rise in October

The consumer price index increased 0.4 percent in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on November 10, higher than the 0.3 percent economists expected. Shelter rose 0.3 percent and accounted for more than 30 percent of the monthly increase; food increased 0.5 percent, with food at home up 0.4 percent and food away from home up 0.5 percent; energy increased 0.7 percent after jumping 5.2 percent in September. Real average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October.

Subjective
Zacks — pre-markets drop on warmer CPI numbers

Pre-market futures swung lower ahead of the opening bell on October consumer prices of plus 0.4 percent on the month, 20 basis points below September’s 0.6 percent and 10 above consensus; core came in at plus 0.3 percent, also 10 hotter than expected. Bond yields climbed with the numbers: 4.936 percent on the ten-year, 4.627 percent on the two-year and 5.292 percent on the thirty-year, in the account’s prints. The small-business optimism index for October ticked down to 97.8.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine, carrying Reuters — Governor Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in December

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday he would support raising short-term borrowing costs next month even if the data showed inflation cooled, and would consider an upsized half-point increase if the picture worsened. If core consumer prices rise 0.3 percent or more from September, a 50-basis-point hike should be considered at the December meeting, he said, adding that hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk. Markets, the account says, had priced in about an 85 percent chance of a December increase to a 4.00 to 4.25 percent range.

Subjective
American Banker — Governor Waller calls for raising interest rates 25 basis points, at least

Governor Waller, in prepared remarks delivered in London on Tuesday morning, said he anticipates supporting a rate increase at the December meeting even if the consumer price print improves, and that if October’s monthly reading comes in at or above September’s level a 50-basis-point increase should be considered. The account’s key insight is that one of the Board’s leading monetary experts is committed to a December increase and could support a half-point move. He cited concern at the breadth of price increases, including core goods and core market-based services excluding housing.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Military.com — Secretary Hegseth says the impeachment push is about policy disagreements, not high crimes

WASHINGTON (AP): Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dug in for a fight on Tuesday against his potential impeachment, telling reporters a rogue lawmaker is targeting him over policy disagreements and not the high crimes the founders intended. In the 250 years of the republic, no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations, he said. The briefing was his first from the Pentagon in six months. Representative Massie, who lost his primary to a president-backed opponent, filed the resolution on Monday; it focuses largely on the Iran war and includes Yemen and Venezuela.

Subjective
USA Today — Secretary Hegseth defends himself against impeachment: it is a farce

Facing a looming impeachment vote, the Pentagon chief dug in at a news conference on November 10. “What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle,” he said. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it.” The news conference lasted roughly 25 minutes and ended after he took a handful of questions, mostly from reporters representing conservative media outlets, in the account’s description. The House was planning to vote on whether to move forward later on November 10.

Subjective
Reuters — the Pentagon chief calls moves to impeach him a farce that will fail

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday called moves to impeach him over abuse of power in the Iran war a farce that would fail. He made the comment at a news conference a day after Representative Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against him, in his first Pentagon news conference since May. In a post on X, Mr. Massie said the House would hold a first vote on Tuesday on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, and that if that effort is overcome, the House will proceed to a real debate and a vote on the articles.

Subjective
New York Post — Secretary Hegseth rips the impeachment effort in his first press conference since May

The secretary went on a fiery tirade on Tuesday against Representative Massie over his bid to impeach him, accusing the rogue legislator of sabotage: “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage.” He insisted he has done nothing worthy of being just the third cabinet official in history to be impeached. The articles announced Monday include three charges over the war in Iran, one on the operation to capture Venezuela’s leader, one on attacks against the Houthis in Yemen, one on ignoring laws aimed at minimizing civilian casualties, one for extrajudicial killings on alleged drug boats, and one for free-speech violations against Senator Kelly.

Subjective
Defense News — Secretary Hegseth denounces the farce impeachment in his first briefing since May

The secretary vehemently defended himself on Tuesday against impending impeachment proceedings, listing military successes in his first Pentagon press briefing in over six months. The conference lasted fewer than 25 minutes and he answered few questions. The articles, he said, are partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize the military. He painted himself as a champion for the troops, saying that if they want to come for the warriors, they will have to come through him. He praised Operation Epic Fury, claiming Iran’s navy and more than 80 percent of its nuclear industrial base were destroyed. Speaker Johnson will decide if lawmakers vote on each article individually or all eight as a whole, the account says.

Subjective
Military.com — Secretary Hegseth claims an Iran victory in the press conference as the war and impeachment fight continue

The secretary defended the administration’s military campaigns on Tuesday morning, declaring the president had kicked their teeth in in Iran and promising that anyone pursuing American service members would have to come through him. He celebrated Operation Epic Fury as a historic victory, citing more than 13,000 targets struck, extensive damage to Iran’s military infrastructure and destruction of much of its nuclear industrial capacity. The account notes the resolution seeks to impeach him as a civilian cabinet secretary and does not charge service members, and that the allegations concern his responsibility, including three articles alleging violations of the War Powers Resolution.

Subjective
ANI, via APNA MA TV — “Today the House will vote,” Representative Massie says

Representative Thomas Massie said on Tuesday the House of Representatives would vote on his impeachment resolution against Secretary Hegseth, with an initial procedural vote expected to determine whether it proceeds to debate and a vote on the articles. The first vote would concern a procedural motion aimed at blocking the resolution, including a possible motion to refer it to committee. The daily legislative schedule for Tuesday, November 10 listed the procedural motion among the day’s business; the House was due at 10 a.m. for morning hour and at noon for legislative business, with the first and last votes expected at 5:30 p.m.

Subjective
Reuters, via DevDiscourse — a defiant Secretary Hegseth blasts the impeachment effort ahead of the House vote

The secretary on Tuesday blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce that would embolden adversaries, as the House scheduled a procedural vote for late Tuesday that will test support for the impeachment. Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with the president’s Republicans still controlling the House until the new Congress takes over on January 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, the account says, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats.

Subjective
Associated Press, via WNCW — Russia and Ukraine hold nearly four hours of United States-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi

ABU DHABI: three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the Emirates, the first such meeting since February, in a two-day session focused on security guarantees. The first day of talks concluded after nearly four hours, RIA Novosti said; they are expected to resume Wednesday, according to the press office of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service. Mr. Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the American envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission, before the trilateral format.

Subjective
National Daily — the United States pushes a new European security framework as the talks begin in Abu Dhabi

United States-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine began in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, with Washington pushing for a new European security framework aimed at ending the war and preventing future conflicts. Opening the negotiations, Mr. Kushner said the United States wanted to develop a new framework by examining previous diplomatic arrangements and identifying what had worked and failed. Ukraine’s delegation, led by Mr. Umerov, began the day with discussions involving American representatives and European officials before moving into the trilateral format with Russia. The talks take place amid continued military operations, with both countries reporting overnight drone and missile attacks.

Subjective
Il Politico — Abu Dhabi peace talks: security guarantees before territory

The round runs Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10 and 11, the first since February, when talks in Geneva broke up without a deal on land. Day one is about policing a future ceasefire and the shape of security once the guns fall silent; territory waits until day two, according to Bloomberg citing an American official. The same official told Reuters both sides had privately shown some flexibility over a possible swap of territory, and that any deal on land would come at the very end, once everything else is settled. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov insisted the talks are trilateral, full stop.

Subjective
Grenada Chronicle — “Europe belongs at this table,” Germany tells the United States before the Ukraine talks

European foreign ministers told Secretary Rubio that Europe must have a say in any deal to end the war, on Monday in Paris at the G7 meeting. “It is certainly neither necessary, nor right, nor appropriate to make a fundamental change” to Europe’s security architecture, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said after talks with Mr. Rubio; “Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe, only with Europe.” The two-day Paris meeting ends Tuesday and overlaps the Abu Dhabi talks. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, is set to join a session on Ukraine on Tuesday; “No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” he said before departing. Iran is expected to feature prominently in Tuesday’s discussions.

Subjective
Europe Says — G7 ministers press Secretary Rubio on Iran and Ukraine at the Paris talks

PARIS: G7 top diplomats began a two-day meeting in Paris on Monday, with European foreign ministers set to press Secretary Rubio to ensure any settlement in the war with Russia is fair to Ukraine and to steer clear of any new escalation with Iran. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Europeans would be represented at the Abu Dhabi talks, with France also participating. European ministers warned against renewed American military strikes and advocated instead for the restoration of normal commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. On the sidelines, Canada announced fresh sanctions on Russia on Monday.

Subjective
Reuters, via DevDiscourse — Wall Street opens lower after October’s hot inflation print

Wall Street’s main indexes opened lower on Tuesday after hotter-than-expected inflation data for October threatened to pause a two-day rebound in technology shares and revive the selling pressure of last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 226.5 points, or 0.43 percent, at the open to 52,163.21. The S&P 500 fell 36.8 points, or 0.49 percent, to 7,513.09, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 205.7 points, or 0.81 percent, to 25,047.448.

Subjective
JBizNews — stocks open lower after the October inflation report as bond yields jump

Stocks opened lower on Tuesday as Treasury yields rose after the October inflation report, cutting into Monday’s rally. The Dow was down 0.47 percent at 52,144.30 in a quote stamped 9:48 a.m. Eastern; the S&P 500 was down 0.58 percent at 7,506.25 and the Nasdaq Composite down 0.70 percent at 25,076.221 at the same stamp. The ten-year Treasury yield stood at 4.988 percent, up from the previous close of 4.862 percent. These are early-session snapshots, not closing prices, the account notes. Chip shares were mixed as the market pulled back.

Subjective
Reuters, via DevDiscourse — stocks cut gains, the dollar and yields rise as the CPI cements December rate-hike bets

United States stocks were set for a lower open and European shares pared gains after a hotter-than-anticipated inflation reading bolstered the case for a December increase. Traders are now fully pricing two 25-basis-point increases by March, with the first expected in December, on data compiled by LSEG; the two-year yield rose 14 basis points to 4.69 percent. Brent crude futures fell over 3.2 percent, dipping below the ninety-dollar mark for the first time since late August. Earnings due this week from technology companies including CoreWeave will be another test for markets, the account says.

Subjective
InvestingLive — stocks rebounding despite the higher-than-expected CPI

United States stocks opened on the defensive after the stronger-than-expected report pushed Treasury yields higher, but the tone changed as attention shifted to reports about Anthropic’s planned listing.
