Orazio Petito was named as the Chi Phi chapter president “at the time.” On October 20, 2026, all parties stipulated to discontinue the claims against him with prejudice, the stipulation signed October 19 as NYSCEF Document No. 82. Reporting by ABC states he was mistakenly identified as chapter president at the time of the incident. He was never accused of participating in the alleged assault; his role in the complaint was supervisory, responsibility for the house and members. His attorney, Eric Bernstein: “My client deserved to be released from this case. They had the wrong guy, and justice was served as far as Mr. Petito was concerned.” The discontinuance is verified; the misidentification account is documented. Any account still listing Petito as a current defendant is out of date.

The institutional defendants’ responses are on the record, and they are not interchangeable. Cornell’s statements are at Sections 5 and 7. Chi Phi’s national organization made two distinct statements, which this report does not merge: on September 24, 2026, to CBS News, that the allegations are “deeply concerning”; “Anyone who reports sexual violence deserves to be heard and treated with compassion, dignity, and respect. Chi Phi unequivocally condemns sexual violence… We cannot discuss the specific allegations during pending litigation”; and around October 1, through Interim Executive Director Trey Robb, the account of the chapter’s removal vote and the national expulsion, with “These actions went beyond anything the law or Cornell University required of us” and “Chi Phi condemns sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse in the strongest possible terms.” No separate statement by the local Xi Chapter or Chapter House Association was found. Tri Delta’s on-record position, stated on behalf of the Alpha Beta Chapter, is: “Tri Delta does not comment on pending litigation,” and “As an organization, we are committed to supporting women and victims of sexual violence.” The organization did not respond to the Cornell Daily Sun’s request at filing, and no separate statement by the Alpha Beta House Corporation was found. Moonies denies serving Doe while underage: in its statement to the Sun, her claim of being served at Moonies is “completely inaccurate.” The bar’s position, as reported: the October 19 event was a private Tri Delta function, about 9 to 11 p.m., with about 185 guests; underage guests’ hands were marked, wristbands went only to guests 21 or older, and “no alcohol was served to guests who had marks on their hands.” The bar has moved to dismiss, and told Fox News Doe later worked for the company, in February–March 2025, and did not then say she had been served or intoxicated at Moonies. Giuffra responded that Moonies is “a minor player in the case” and the claims against it are limited, while standing by the allegation that she was served. The service question itself is contested and unresolved.

7. The Reopening: A Governor Displaces a District Attorney, and a Special Prosecutor Takes the Case

The sequence is eight dated steps. First, September 28, 2026: Van Houten reopened the case in the same press statement that defended the 2024 decision; his office had begun conversations with Doe and her attorneys, assigned a senior sex-crimes prosecutor, and planned to present the case to a Tompkins County grand jury; he stated that neither Doe nor her attorneys had contacted his office in the intervening two years and that he reached out to them after the lawsuit. Second, the same day, Attorney General Letitia James posted on her official X account, linking the Times’ reopening story, a text verified word for word: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.” Third, September 29: before acting on the prosecution itself, the governor called for an outside-counsel review of the local handling; Cornell agreed the same day. Fourth, October 1: Governor Hochul signed Executive Order No. 64—“Last night, I signed an executive order,” per her October 2 remarks—issued under Executive Law §63(2), appointing James as special prosecutor and expressly superseding the Tompkins County district attorney in the matter. Section 63(2) provides that when the governor so requires, the attorney general manages the specified criminal proceedings and the district attorney exercises only such powers as the attorney general requires. The order’s operative language, read in full, is to “displace and supersede” the district attorney; its recitals state that the district attorney declined charges “without speaking to Jane Doe” and that Doe’s statement as transmitted “reportedly omitted key portions”—the governor’s stated factual predicates, printed here as recitals, not as this report’s findings. Fifth, October 2, at a news conference: Hochul said Doe “had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable and then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her… That is why I’m invoking the power conferred to me as the Governor of the State of New York to enlist Attorney General James as an independent special prosecutor in this case.” She criticized the campus police for the omission of the “100% confident” statement and the district attorney for deciding without interviewing Doe or requesting the full transcript, and said she had lost confidence in the local handling. James announced an “active criminal investigation”: “Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly, that they will be seen and heard.” At the same conference Hochul said at one point that Doe was gang raped “by five men,” where seven are alleged; NPR noted the discrepancy, and no explanation is in the record; it is filed at Section 11. Sixth, October 2: Van Houten’s response, supporting the appointment and pledging full cooperation, at Section 4. Seventh, a policy rider on October 2: Hochul attacked the voluntary-intoxication limit in New York law—“If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape, period. I support closing this loophole and will work with the New York State Legislature to accomplish this.” Cornell publicly supported the law-change effort. The statute and the bill are filed at Section 10.

The appointment is challenged in two courts, and both challenges are pending. The first is Lopes v. Hochul and James, Index No. 911974-26, filed in Albany County Supreme Court on October 7, 2026, by Gillio Lopes through attorney Andrew Miltenberg of Nesenoff & Miltenberg LLP. Justice James R. Farrell signed the order to show cause on October 9; the State responded October 22 through Assistant Attorney General Kaitlin Vigars; and the hearing was held October 29, 2026, in Monticello, Sullivan County—which is why reporting variously placed the case in Albany County, its filing, and Sullivan County, its hearing. At the hearing Farrell pressed both sides and made no bench ruling; joinder papers from the other accused were due November 5. Miltenberg’s stated grounds: James’s September 28 post and other public statements show she has prejudged the matter. His framing: “My issue is not political, and it is not personal… Several days before her appointment, Letitia James made some comments on X, and those comments are such that I think it’s fair to look at them and say it appears that the person making those comments [is] biased”; “It’s OK to offer compassion and be empathetic to survivors… I do not believe she can be fair. Had she made a statement that was empathetic or compassionate towards a victim, that’s fine. I don’t think that person can become a neutral investigator or prosecutor.” He says the defence welcomes an investigation, just not one run by James. For the governor and the attorney general, Vigars argued the bias claim is premature, that no charges have been filed, and that the appointment is lawful. On November 5, Diego Sarabia, Scott Kretzschmar, Scott Norris, and Winston Lee joined the petition, so five of the seven men—Lopes plus four—are parties to the effort; Matthew Ingalls and Johnathan Newell did not join, and reporting states they lack representation in the civil case and did not respond to Lopes’s attorneys. Some headlines phrase this as “four of the accused joined the bid,” counting the four who joined the original petitioner; both phrasings describe the same five-man participation, and this report uses the five. The second challenge is separate: an attorney for Winston Lee filed a motion in Tompkins County Supreme Court seeking to prevent James from participating in any grand jury proceeding in the case; reporting on November 6–7 stated a decision is expected November 13, 2026. As of November 9 both challenges are pending, no ruling has issued on either, and James remains special prosecutor. A third track is not a court challenge: on October 9, 2026, the National Legal and Policy Center filed a bar and grievance complaint against James arising from the same statements, a professional-conduct complaint, documented as such.

The investigation has a named leader, no deadline, and one printed conflict about her authority. On November 4, 2026, James announced that Jacqueline Kelly will lead the investigation as outside counsel. Kelly is a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner, which she joined in 2025, a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York, and the first chief of that office’s Civil Rights Unit in the criminal division; she oversaw the prosecution of Sean “Diddy” Combs, and the Peter Nygård and Dr. Robert Cruciani cases. She is a Cornell graduate. Her team is drawn from the attorney general’s office and her firm. The authority conflict, printed as found: CNN’s November 4 account describes Kelly as holding “decision-making authority,” while the attorney general’s own primary release states that her team “will report to OAG.” The two characterizations differ on where final authority sits; the record does not resolve the difference. James’s statement pledged an investigation “guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law.” The attorney general’s office has set no deadline. Context noted by the Associated Press: the two-year limitations period for misdemeanors arising from October 2024 has run; New York sets no limitations period for the most serious sex offenses. James was re-elected attorney general on November 3, 2026, the day before the Kelly announcement.

Cornell’s independent review is constituted, scoped, and silent so far. It was announced October 6, 2026, by a newly formed Special Committee of the Board of Trustees, chaired by Board Chair Anne Meinig Smalling, and Sally Yates—partner at King & Spalding, former deputy attorney general and acting attorney general—was retained to lead it. Its scope, in Cornell’s statement: a comprehensive review of how Cornell prevents and responds to sexual harassment, assault, and related misconduct—report intake and investigation; student support; hearings, discipline, and appeals; the campus police role and coordination with law enforcement and prosecutors; campus safety reporting; Greek and student-organization oversight; and the Board’s own oversight—including a detailed review of the university’s response to the Jane Doe allegations and whether Cornell followed its policies. Its benchmarks are Title IX, the Clery Act, the VAWA Campus SaVE Act, New York law, and best practices. The review has full independence and reports to the Special Committee. The Board has said it intends to share the review’s “results and recommendations”; it has not committed to publishing the full report. No timeline has been announced, and there are no findings as of November 9, 2026.

8. The Leadership Crisis: No Confidence, a City Moratorium, and the Policy Changes

The Faculty Senate’s resolution is one sentence, and it is printed whole. “Resolved: That the Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.” It passed on November 6, 2026, 75 yes, 50 no, 5 abstentions, 5 non-votes—verified; Cornell’s own November 6 statement frames the same result as 55.6 percent in favor, 37 percent against, 7.4 percent abstaining or not voting, of 135 senators excluding Weill Cornell Medicine. The path: posted October 7; debated October 14 and October 28, when the Senate voted 76–48 against postponing the ballot until the Yates review ends; electronic voting ran from October 29 or 30 to November 6. Its lead sponsor was Paul Ortiz of the ILR School, a labor historian, with 13 faculty cosponsors per the Ithaca Voice. The resolution is non-binding, names the “central administration” rather than President Kotlikoff personally, and does not call for any resignation; only the Board of Trustees can remove the president. Per Cornell’s AAUP chapter, it is the first no-confidence resolution in the Faculty Senate’s history—its “56-year history,” per USA Today. Before the vote: at the closed October 14 session Kotlikoff acknowledged he had not read the Cornell police report, on audio obtained by the Associated Press; in an October 13 Times interview he said he had never followed up on Doe or on the criminal investigation; his public silence on the case lasted more than two weeks after the lawsuit. Dean of Faculty Chris Schaffer opposed the resolution, writing that it “falls short” because it does not spell out the administration’s specific failures. The Board’s response came the same day, within hours, from Chair Smalling: “Today’s Faculty Senate vote reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable… The Board of Trustees remains confident that President Kotlikoff and his administration are the right leaders to thoughtfully and comprehensively address the serious problem of sexual assault on our campus… The Board fully supports President Kotlikoff and his administration.” Since the vote: Kotlikoff has told the Times he has “no intention” of resigning; AAUP chapter president David Bateman asked the Board to “affirm the Faculty Senate’s vote”; the full Board’s next scheduled meeting is January 30, and its executive committee meets by Zoom on December 3 and can exercise most Board powers between meetings. No leadership change has occurred. One posture note completes the record: Reuters reported on November 6 that Kotlikoff had not yet responded to the vote itself and has 30 days to respond in writing; no formal post-vote statement by him was located through November 9, and his “no intention” remark attends the vote coverage rather than answering the result.

The president’s own statements, and one disputed remark, are filed separately from the vote. In a video statement on the weekend of October 3–4, 2026, Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing,” said they raise questions about the investigations conducted, and welcomed an independent review. In an October 13 letter to the community: “I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community.” He also apologized in his State of the University address, per the Cornell Daily Sun of October 19. The disputed remark: Doe, in a letter to faculty leaders transmitted through counsel, said her sorority president told her Kotlikoff had asked why she waited until the following month to report; Doe said the account left her feeling “unsupported and disbelieved.” Cornell disputes the characterization: it says Kotlikoff was asking why bystanders had not reported what they knew. The conflict is printed, not resolved.

Public pressure ran on a dated calendar of its own. A demonstration at Ho Plaza on October 5, 2026, as protests began. Faculty joined students at a rally on October 6–7 with signs reading “Justice for every Jane Doe” and “Cornell admin betrays survivors resign now.” A seven-hour sit-in on October 7, roughly 80 students at the Toni Morrison dining hall; students also hosted a town hall, and administrators, pressed at a webinar, confirmed two accused students remained enrolled. On October 13, hundreds of students, faculty, and Ithaca residents rallied on the Ithaca Commons, chanting “To Jane Doe, we stand with you” and “To Cornell: We are watching”; Cornell declined to comment on the rally. On October 16, protesters demonstrated outside the Board of Trustees’ meeting in Ithaca. Solidarity actions were reported at other campuses during the same weeks. Doe’s counsel welcomed the faculty vote: “We are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus.”

The City of Ithaca acted against the university, then let its act lapse with demands attached. Mayor Robert Cantelmo called for a moratorium in a September 28, 2026 statement expressing concern over the university’s response. On October 7, 2026, the Common Council voted 9–1 to adopt a temporary moratorium; its text is a primary document, verified. The city would issue no new permits to Cornell and affiliated organizations, including Greek organizations, under specified code chapters—including chapter 132 assemblies and parades, §132-7 special events, and noise permits, the provision with practical effect on parties; First Amendment-protected protests and assemblies remained permitted; and the Council “calls upon Cornell to hand over investigations of violent crimes and sex offenses to the Ithaca Police Department.” The moratorium was effective immediately and, absent further action, expired November 5, 2026. The Council session included a confrontation after a commentator who has publicly sought to name Jane Doe was not called among public commenters; this report does not name her, and it does not name him in connection with that effort. The lapse rests on a single local source and is graded accordingly: 607 News Now reported that on November 5, 2026, Mayor Cantelmo announced the city would allow the moratorium to lapse “for the time being,” coupled with three city demands—a permanent handover of sex-crime investigations to the Ithaca Police Department or another government agency; an independent investigation with a public accounting, which Cornell has agreed to; and Cornell’s advocacy on the voluntary-intoxication loophole, which Cornell has also agreed to—and the mayor reserved the threat of reviving the moratorium.

Cornell’s policy changes since September 2026 are announced, dated, and in one place stated two ways. Announced October 13, 2026, in the president’s letter: all parties and social events at Interfraternity Council houses suspended through the end of the 2026–27 academic year, covering more than twenty IFC fraternities, under a “zero tolerance” rule by which a violating chapter faces immediate emergency suspension; Kotlikoff: “These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.” New York State Police criminal investigators, independent of Cornell and trauma-informed, to have a role in campus sexual-assault investigations. A new case manager in the Office of Civil Rights to help complainants navigate the process. Expanded survivor advocacy and prevention programming and funding, including funding for alternatives to Greek parties, and a commitment to confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use. The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression sent an “urgent” letter criticizing the party ban. Formalized October 29, 2026, in a Cornell–State Police agreement, Cornell’s statement a primary document: effective immediately, a survivor who elects to pursue criminal charges may choose whether State Police or Cornell Police serve as the designated investigatory agency; State Police cases are independent from Cornell, which will assist as requested; the agreement runs during the Yates review and does not change a survivor’s autonomy over engaging law enforcement. Governor Hochul’s announcement framed the default as referral to State Police unless the survivor requests otherwise, and noted survivors may also choose Ithaca Police or the Tompkins County Sheriff, per Reuters. The two official framings—a survivor’s choice, and a default referral—are printed as issued. Earlier measures stand behind these: Cornell’s Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault was launched in February 2025 and issued its final report in March 2026; the Student Assembly has taken up a transparency-and-accountability resolution, SA R15 of 2026–27, pending in Cornell’s governance process; and Cornell’s 2025 campus survey, cited in October coverage, found 15 percent of respondents reported nonconsensual sexual contact since entering Cornell, including 35 percent of undergraduate women.

9. Both Sides, in Their Own Documented Form

Doe’s allegations are the complaint’s, at Sections 2 and 6; her own words are two statements, and they are printed whole. To the Cornell Daily Sun, September 18, 2026: “What happened to me was horrific and deeply disturbing. Almost two years later, I still carry the weight of its impact every day and night… I was deeply disappointed by the lack of support I received from the student community… that pain was compounded by being criticized and ostracized at a time when I needed compassion, support and care the most.” To CNN, September 28, 2026: “What I experienced from those who raped me in the fraternity was the worst experience of my life. I was brutalized and it injured me physically but perhaps more importantly, emotionally… It will haunt me and be part of me the rest of my life.” Her counsel’s institutional-negligence argument runs: Cornell knew or should have known of drug use at Chi Phi and of sexual-violence risk in Greek life and failed to supervise, warn, or protect; Cornell Health failed her on October 22, at Section 3; the criminal process failed her, the six-page summary omitting her “100 percent” statement while she was, per counsel, left believing an investigation continued—“I think she was misled”; Giuffra at filing, to CNN: “It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint… she was not contacted by investigators from the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors.” He has also alleged that when her parents sought a tuition refund or leave for her to heal, Cornell said “you have to stay in school,” leaving her on campus seeing the men regularly—counsel’s account, claimed, with no Cornell response to this specific claim found. The Title IX sanctions “did not reflect the severity of the charges,” and the “anemic response led her to conclude that the only avenue for justice was to file a lawsuit,” Giuffra to The Independent. “Her dreams were destroyed by a group of men who sought to abuse and humiliate her.” On the group chat: “Based on the group chat evidence, it was obvious that the complaint warranted an investigation and criminal charges against the involved abusers,” and Doe never received a callback from the campus police after reporting. On Doe’s own early texts, at Section 3: Giuffra told CBS News they reflect “classic symptoms of delayed recognition,” “a textbook response to sexual assault”—the plaintiff side’s answer to the consent reading of those messages. Giuffra has also said more than seven fraternity members may have been involved, and that the district attorney failed in 2024 to subpoena evidence he considers crucial, on BBC Newshour as reported. Doe’s stated aim, per Giuffra to AFP on November 6: she “wants her lawsuit to transform how Cornell and other US universities deal with sexual assault.” The accountability demands from her supporters, as documented: criminal charges via the special prosecutor; administrative resignations, on protest signage and from some faculty; affirmation of the no-confidence vote, from the AAUP; transfer of sex-crime investigations away from the campus police, from the Ithaca Common Council; and Greek-life restrictions, from the city moratorium and Cornell’s own party suspension.

The harassment record around the plaintiff is documented and belongs in this section because it is part of her side’s circumstances. On October 5, 2026, Doe received a text containing three gun emojis, and callers demanded she drop the lawsuit. On the night of October 6, 2026, a caller falsely reported a man had shot his mother and was turning the gun on his sister at Doe’s family home—a swatting call: the first officer stopped a car backing out of the driveway carrying Doe’s boyfriend and brother; her boyfriend was thrown to the ground, and officers pointed guns at her father; the caller rang again claiming an AR-15 while officers were inside. Police and the FBI are investigating, per Giuffra. Doe taped paper over the home’s windows the next day. Giuffra told BBC Newshour that both he and Doe have received death threats—one caller to his office: “drop the case, or I’m going to kill your wife,” per AFP—and Doe has received hundreds of harassing calls. At least three women wrongly identified online as Doe have been threatened, per Giuffra. The October 9 sealing order at Section 6 followed from this environment. All of it is documented through CNN’s police-report reporting, AFP, and The New Yorker.

The accused men’s position is uniform in its denial and divided in its details, and one count inside it does not settle. All seven deny wrongdoing; none has been charged. Per the Times’ review of the investigative records, four acknowledged sexual contact with Doe that they say was consensual; the others denied participating; their accounts to investigators “differed and frequently contradicted one another.” CNN’s account likewise gives four. Le Monde, on October 6, 2026, reports five admitted intercourse as consensual. The public record does not settle whether the difference is a counting choice—contact versus intercourse, or a fifth man’s partial account—and both figures are printed. In Cornell’s process the men’s position was that Doe consented and that they were themselves heavily intoxicated. Individually, as reported from the investigative record: Lee and Lopes each told investigators that Doe initiated contact with them, and Lee acknowledged snorting ketamine off her body. These are the men’s statements to investigators as reported, printed as their accounts, not as findings. Scott Kretzschmar, through counsel Jeremy Saland: “Scott never sexually assaulted or even touched the plaintiff in any way. Period.” Saland says a hair-follicle test showed no ketamine in Kretzschmar’s system, that Doe and her lawyer had the result before the suit was filed, and that he “was never accused of, nor found responsible for, rape.” Saland concedes his client “participated in a group chat whose content was ugly and reprehensible, and he regrets it,” but argues chat activity does not prove sexual assault. The follicle test was taken roughly ninety days after the night—the plaintiff counsel’s timing point, made in court correspondence; the test result itself is a defence claim, not independently verified, and it is filed at Section 11 with its timing attached. Giuffra’s October 14 court letter attributes to Saland the characterization of Doe’s claims as a “money grab,” attributed here as Giuffra’s characterization. Scott Norris, through counsel, released a statement denying participation in any sexual assault; he admits he engaged with the pictures in the group chat but says he did not physically participate and did not enter the room where the alleged assault occurred. Gillio Lopes, through Miltenberg: the complaint’s account as to Lopes is “not true.” Miltenberg’s core merits argument: “I understand that perceptions shift and memories shift after a period of time, but her initial statements, her initial texts, her initial testimony with respect to the police, all was very clear about how she viewed this situation”—the contemporaneous record, on the defence’s reading, contradicts the 2026 lawsuit. He has argued publicly that the publicly named defendants “deserve a meaningful opportunity to respond”: “The irony of Mr. Giuffra’s letter to the court is that it was he who invited media scrutiny, aggressively promoting Jane Doe’s narrative across television, print, and online media… Now that he dislikes the defense’s response, he is complaining to the judge.” Diego Sarabia, through Hacker Murphy LLP, “categorically denies” the allegations; his dismissal motion and the rejected restraint application are at Section 6. Winston Lee’s position is the recorded November 7, 2024 call at Section 3: he disputed knowing anything improper was occurring and attributed the room’s traffic to an unlocked door at a crowded party.

One accused man’s counter-allegation is in the record, with no finding on it. In a February 2025 email to Cornell’s Title IX investigator, obtained by ABC News, Matthew Ingalls claimed he was sexually assaulted that night: “After all, you received information that I was sodomized by her while I was incapacitated back in November and you never once thought to alert me of my rights under these procedures as a survivor of this assault? The very fact that I had to bring this to your attention now in February confirms my worst fears: that this process is rife with gender discrimination.” He accused the university of “entrapment” and suggested he would file his own complaint against Doe. Giuffra responded, in Us Weekly on October 7, 2026, characterizing the claim as an attempt to escape accountability. The panel nonetheless found Ingalls responsible for sexual assault and expelled him. No finding on his counter-allegation appears in the public record the desk reviewed. The due-process argument, as made by the defence side, stands as follows: the Title IX proceeding ran on a preponderance standard with hearings by Zoom; Kretzschmar’s court challenge called the process “fundamentally unfair,” a court dismissed it, and the appeal is pending; defence counsel argue the criminal standard—beyond a reasonable doubt, on a record whose centerpiece signed statement describes consent—cannot be met on these facts, and that the special-prosecutor appointment followed public pressure rather than new evidence. Van Houten’s own formulation of the evidence-first position is at Section 4. These are the defence side’s arguments, recorded as such; this report does not adopt them, and it does not adopt the other side’s either.

10. The Standards: Three Forums, Three Burdens, and the Statute the Case Turns On

Three forums have handled this case or will, under three standards, and the divergence of their outcomes is a function of those standards and their different records. In the criminal forum, a grand jury decides probable cause to indict and a trial jury decides guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; no charges have been filed, and the special prosecutor’s investigation is open. In Cornell’s discipline, a three-member panel decided under Policy 6.4 by a preponderance of the evidence—more likely than not; that proceeding completed in 2025, its outcomes are at Section 5, and one respondent’s court challenge was dismissed with an appeal pending. In the civil forum, a jury, demanded, would decide by a preponderance at trial; at the current CPLR 3211 stage, the complaint’s allegations are taken as true for motion purposes, and the case is in early motion practice. Every serious account of the case makes this point, the Associated Press’s October 14, 2026 Title IX explainer among them. This report states the divergence; it does not resolve it.

The criminal question turns on a definition, and the definition is printed from the statute. Penal Law §130.00(6): “mentally incapacitated” means rendered temporarily incapable of appraising or controlling one’s conduct by a narcotic or intoxicating substance “administered to him without his consent,” or by another act committed without consent. Section 130.00(7): “physically helpless” means unconscious or otherwise physically unable to communicate unwillingness to act. Section 130.05(2)–(3): lack of consent results from, among other things, forcible compulsion, or incapacity to consent, including being mentally incapacitated or physically helpless; for specified offenses it also results from clearly expressed non-consent that a reasonable person in the actor’s position would understand. The consequence, as documented in legal commentary and the governor’s October 2 statement: voluntary intoxication, without more, does not satisfy the “mentally incapacitated” definition, because the substance must have been administered without consent. That is the analytical core of Van Houten’s 2024 decision and of the reform debate. A bill first introduced by then-Senator Biaggi in 2019 would add voluntary-intoxication incapacity with a knowledge element; it passed the New York Senate in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024, and 2025 and never received an Assembly vote. The current vehicle is S10632 (Fernandez) and A101 (Dinowitz): it passed the Senate on June 4, 2026, no Assembly floor vote is recorded, and it is not law as of November 9, 2026; the governor’s October 2 pledge stands behind it. Two further provisions belong to the landscape. The “Rape Is Rape” Act, effective September 1, 2024—six weeks before the night at issue—brought vaginal, oral, and anal contact under the rape rubric, repealing and folding in the former criminal-sexual-act provisions, so any charging analysis of October 2024 conduct proceeds under the post-September 2024 numbering. And §130.10(1) provides an affirmative defense in prosecutions premised on incapacity: that the defendant did not know of the facts or conditions responsible for the victim’s incapacity. The defense is statutory and would be for the defence to prove; no defendant here has been charged, so it is an element of the legal landscape, not a live pleading.

The limitations record is printed with its open question left open. On the civil side, CPLR 213-c gives claims premised on specified sex offenses a twenty-year limitations window and expressly provides that no criminal charge or conviction is required; it is the provision Sarabia’s motion argues does not reach the narrower conduct alleged against him. CPLR 215(8)’s extension, by contrast, is contingent on a criminal action having been commenced, which has not occurred as of November 9, 2026; it is not established here. The Adult Survivors Act, CPLR 214-j, revived only claims already time-barred as of its 2022 effective date; it is not clearly applicable to October 2024 conduct, and Doe’s suit does not appear to rest on it. On the criminal side, under CPL 30.10, first-degree rape carries no limitations period, other felonies default to five years, and misdemeanors to two years—the two-year misdemeanor period for October 2024 conduct has run. Whether §30.10(2)(a-1)’s twenty-year period or the five-year default governs §130.30(4)–(6) conduct after the 2024 renumbering was not found on the sources the desk retrieved; this report does not assert an answer. The procedural instrument of the reopening, Executive Law §63(2), and its precedent use in Executive Order 147, are at Section 7.

11. What Is Not True, or Not Established: The Corrected Claims

The desk closes the record the way it audited it: with the circulated claims that the record does not support, corrected one by one. First, “they only had to write essays.” The viral version of the sanctions story—that the seven men were punished with essay-writing—is not supported by the record. What the record shows: reflection papers were components of sanction packages that also included two expulsions, two suspensions of two years and three semesters with probation, a three-year campus bar, no-contact orders, and required education, on the Times’ discipline summaries at Section 5. The complaint’s narrower claim—that suspended students were offered essays “to mitigate their conduct”—is expressly denied by Cornell. Both the viral claim and the complaint’s version stand in this file only with Cornell’s denial attached. Second, the wrongful identifications, which are documented harms to uninvolved people. A Chi Phi alumnus who had graduated before October 2024 was named in a TikTok video purporting to list the chat’s members, viewed more than two million times and built from an outdated roster; the roster was then posted by a website that described it as a “verified” roster of 57 men. His name, photograph, employer, home address, and field of study were published; his employer received anonymous messages and placed him on paid leave, demanding proof he had never been in the chat. After a cease-and-desist from defamation counsel, the site’s operator removed his name; counsel has contacted the operator about roughly ten other graduates listed who were never in the chat. The site no longer uses the word “verified” and currently names 42 men; the reporting outlet could not verify any of the roster’s names, and the roster claims are not verified. An active-duty Marine Corps sergeant named Matthew Ingalls, who never attended Cornell and has no connection to the case, was mistakenly served with the lawsuit after Doe’s attorneys attached his upstate New York address to the court docket; his family received threats—the event that prompted the October 9 sealing order. At least three women misidentified online as Jane Doe were threatened. Public attempts to name Doe continued through the fall, including at the October 7 Common Council meeting. This report reproduces no purported identity for her. Third, the Petito misidentification, at Section 6: the complaint named the wrong man as chapter president, corrected by stipulated discontinuance with prejudice; any account still listing him as a defendant is out of date. Fourth, the governor’s “five men”: at the October 2 news conference Governor Hochul said Doe was gang raped “by five men,” where seven are alleged; NPR noted the discrepancy at the time, and no correction or explanation appears in the record the desk found. It is printed here because the figure has circulated. Fifth, “Ithaca police are investigating”: the complaint initially stated it; the Ithaca Police Department states it never received a report and learned of the case from the media. The lead criminal investigator in 2024 was the campus police; since October 1, 2026, the investigation belongs to the attorney general as special prosecutor.

Sixth, the separate lawsuit, stated as what it is and what it is not. A 2023 Tompkins County filing by two undergraduate plaintiffs alleges a fellow student, named in New York Focus reporting, sexually assaulted them in 2018 and 2021, and that Cornell’s Title IX office failed to act despite complaints; the filing states “at least five-ten others” were allegedly abused by the same student. It was brought under the Adult Survivors Act, survived motions to dismiss, and is scheduled for trial in 2027. Cornell declined comment; the accused denied the allegations. It was first reported by New York Focus on November 9, 2026, the day this file was prepared, and covered the same day by the New York Post as “up to 10 students.” Available reporting describes a previously unreported 2023 case, not a newly unsealed one; the “unsealed” characterization is not found as phrased. And no response from any SUNY authority to that lawsuit was found: Cornell is a private university, searches for any SUNY-system statement returned nothing, and no SUNY role in either case is documented. Seventh, the Kretzschmar hair-follicle claim, at Section 9: the negative ketamine result is a defence claim, the test administered roughly ninety days after the night, a timing limitation noted by the plaintiff’s counsel in court correspondence; it has not been independently verified and does not, by itself, establish anything about Doe’s ingestion or consent. It is printed only as a claim with its timing attached. Eighth, “the judge rejected Sarabia’s dismissal motion on October 25”: a blog and tabloid-derived item claims Justice Perry-Bond rejected the motion on October 25, 2026; it is not verified and is contradicted by the docket posture—the motion was filed October 23 with a November 16, 2026 return date, and the Associated Press reported contemporaneously that Doe’s counsel had not yet responded. As of November 9 the motion is pending, and any account reporting a decision is, on this record, wrong. Ninth, the smaller numerical tensions, printed as ranges where they appear: Title IX interview counts of 48 against more than 50; hearing descriptions of 12 days against at least 12 hearings, settled by the litigation record to May 2–29, 2025; Lopes’s suspension at three semesters against his counsel’s “one-year”; and the lawsuit’s filing at September 14, the summons date, against September 16, the filing stamp. None is material to any outcome. One dating correction to the desk’s own early notes: the BBC explainer “What we know…” is dated September 30, 2026, by Nardine Saad; citations to it in this file follow that date.

12. The Open Record: What Remains Open

Eleven threads stand open, each with its next date or its stated absence of one. First, November 13, 2026: the expected decision on the Tompkins County motion to bar Attorney General James from any grand jury proceeding in the case, brought for Winston Lee. Second, the Article 78-style challenge to the James appointment, Lopes v. Hochul and James, heard October 29, 2026 in Monticello: ruling pending before Justice Farrell, with five of the seven men as parties. Third, the Kelly investigation: a grand jury presentation is possible, the attorney general’s office has set no deadline, misdemeanor limitations have run, and felony sex-offense exposure carries no limitations period on the most serious offenses. Fourth, the civil case: Sarabia’s motion is returnable November 16, 2026, Moonies’ motion is pending, discovery is to follow, the Doe defendants—Faculty, Alumni, and Executive Board—are unidentified in the public record, and a merits ruling is distant. Fifth, Kretzschmar’s appeal of the dismissal of his challenge to Cornell, in the Appellate Division, Third Department: pending. Sixth, the Yates review: no timeline; the Board has committed to sharing “results and recommendations,” not necessarily the full report. Seventh, the Ithaca moratorium: lapsed November 5, 2026 “for the time being,” with three city demands outstanding and revival expressly threatened; watch for revival if the demands stall. Eighth, Cornell governance: the Board’s executive committee meets December 3, the full Board on January 30, the AAUP is pressing the Board to affirm the Senate vote, the president’s written response to the vote is due within thirty days of November 6, and he has said he will not resign. Ninth, Albany: the voluntary-intoxication reform bill, S10632 and A101, Senate-passed on June 4, 2026, with no Assembly floor vote recorded, now carrying a gubernatorial pledge. Tenth, the 2023 Adult Survivors Act case: trial scheduled for 2027, its interaction with the Yates review’s scope untested. Eleventh, Student Assembly resolution SA R15: pending in Cornell’s governance process.

13. The Contradictions Ledger: Where the Record Does Not Agree with Itself

The desk closes the file the way the record leaves it: with its disagreements printed, not resolved. First and central, the complaint against the signed statement: the 2026 complaint alleges coerced ketamine, incapacitation, and gang rape over hours; the district attorney’s summary of the statement Doe signed in November 2024 describes voluntary, conscious, consensual participation, refusals honored, and states that when she said stop, the conduct stopped. Both documents exist; no public record reconciles them; and the signed statement itself retained non-consent language—“felt like coercion,” “pretty incapacitated”—so the dispute is over the omitted rape characterization, not over an empty page. Second, the transcript’s transmission: Cornell’s FAQ says the statement and a Snapchat screenshot were shared with the district attorney; Van Houten says his office was never provided with an image of a Snapchat group titled “Chi Phi Actives,” and that the transcript was “news to me” in 2026; Cornell’s first formulation was that campus police shared “all investigatory information.” Whether the transcript was offered and declined or never transmitted is unknown. Third, Sarabia’s sanction: a three-year campus bar imposed, on the Times and Sun summaries of Cornell’s discipline records, against the president’s September 29, 2026 statement that the graduated man left “before any sanction could be imposed.” Fourth, Kelly’s authority: “decision-making authority” in CNN’s account of her appointment, against the attorney general’s own release, in which her team “will report to OAG.” Fifth, the consensual-contact count: four of the men acknowledged sexual contact they say was consensual, in the Times’ and CNN’s readings of the investigative records, against five in Le Monde’s account; the record does not settle whether the difference is a counting choice. Sixth, the campus police alert’s date: October 25 in the alert as reproduced, against October 19–20 in the complaint, the district attorney’s statement, and every other account; no source reconciles it, and this file does not assume it an error. Seventh, the State Police referral framing: a survivor’s choice of investigating agency in Cornell’s October 29 statement, against a default referral to State Police unless the survivor requests otherwise in the governor’s announcement; both are official, and both are printed as issued. Eighth, the disputed remark: Doe’s account, through her sorority president and counsel, that the president asked why she waited to report, against Cornell’s account that he asked why bystanders had not reported. Ninth, the proceeding’s own dates: Cornell’s formal Title IX complaint of November 22, 2024, revised in January and March 2025, beside the January 14, 2025 investigation-opening date in the civil complaint and CNN’s timeline; both documented, neither harmonized here. Tenth and last, the count of the accused in the governor’s own words: “five men” at the October 2 news conference, against seven alleged in every filing; NPR noted it at the time and no explanation followed. The final paragraph of the report is the first paragraph’s restatement, as the form requires: a student alleges she was drugged and assaulted by seven fraternity members on a night in October 2024; the sworn statement she signed that November, on the prosecutor’s reading, alleges none of it, while the transcript of her interview says she was raped with 100 percent confidence; the university expelled two men and sanctioned five more under its own standard; a court has ruled on nothing of substance; the governor removed the prosecutor who declined, and the prosecutor who replaced him is herself challenged in two courts; the faculty has no confidence in the administration and the board has complete confidence in it; and the criminal question the case began with stands exactly where the record leaves it—open, under investigation, and uncharged.

The File, Clipped

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Twenty items.

Subjective
Tompkins County District Attorney—press statement of Matthew Van Houten, September 28, 2026 (primary, read in full)

The case’s hinge document: the fullest statement of the 2024 declination, the §130.05 analysis, the summary of the signed six-page statement, and, in the same instrument, the announcement of the reopening, the senior prosecutor assigned, and the grand jury planned. The report follows its quotations exactly.

Subjective
Jane Doe v. Cornell University, Inc., et al.—summons and complaint, New York County Index No. 161704/2026 (primary; the redacted complaint refiled as NYSCEF Doc. No. 71; Sarabia’s motion to dismiss, Doc. No. 90; the Petito discontinuance, Doc. No. 82; the restraint-order decision, Doc. No. 69)

The pleading of record: 101 pages, more than 590 paragraphs, the defendant list as verified from the summons, the ten causes of action, and the motion practice through November 9. The complaint’s narrative is filed in the report at the grade ALLEGED, as a pleading requires.

Subjective
Governor Kathy Hochul—Executive Order No. 64 (October 1, 2026), Executive Law §63(2), and the news-conference transcript of October 2, 2026 (governor.ny.gov; primary)

The displacement instrument and its spoken defense: the “displace and supersede” language, the recitals on the omitted statement, the criticism of the campus police and the district attorney, the voluntary-intoxication pledge, and the “five men” figure the report prints as a discrepancy.

Subjective
Attorney General Letitia James—the post of September 28, 2026; the October 2, 2026 announcement of an active criminal investigation; the November 4, 2026 release appointing Jacqueline Kelly

The special prosecutor’s own paper trail: the words the recusal challenge is built on, the investigation’s opening, and the appointment release whose “will report to OAG” the report prints against CNN’s “decision-making authority.”

Subjective
Cornell University—statements of September 21 and 28, October 2, 6, 13, and 29, and November 6, 2026, and the university’s FAQ

The institution’s record in its own hand: the process defended and FERPA cited, the sanctions in aggregate and the essay claim denied, the support for a special prosecutor and for changing the rape law, the Yates review’s scope, the State Police agreement, and the FAQ whose Snapchat sentence stands in the contradictions ledger.

Subjective
Cornell Faculty Senate—the no-confidence resolution and the Senate’s resolution record (primary text)

One sentence, printed whole in the report, with its path: posted October 7, debated twice, the postponement refused 76–48, and the ballot of November 6—75 to 50, 5 abstentions, 5 non-votes—and the Board of Trustees’ same-day answer.

Subjective
City of Ithaca—Common Council moratorium resolution, October 7, 2026 (primary), and 607 News Now on the November 5 lapse

The city’s instrument entire: the permit chapters suspended, the First Amendment carve-out, and the call to hand sex-crime investigations to the Ithaca Police Department; and the single local source for the lapse “for the time being,” graded as one source requires.

Subjective
CBS News—the interview-transcript reporting and the text exchanges, including the October 21, 2024 apology exchange in full

The outlet that obtained the approximately 120-page transcript and the complete apology thread the report quotes entire. Its documents reporting is one of three legs under every transcript quotation in the file.

Subjective
The New York Times—the October 1, 2026 investigation; the disciplinary summaries (October 3, 2026); the text-messages interactive, “Read the Text Messages at the Center of the Cornell Rape Inquiry” (no November 7 dateline located; surfaced in a push notification logged November 8, 2026, 22:54 UTC; contents verified through reproductions)

The fullest single newspaper file: the Title IX documents, the outcomes man by man under Cornell’s caveat, the records showing the district attorney’s office declining further evidence, and the thread presentation whose dating this report declines to fix beyond what the record shows.

Subjective
CNN—the case timeline and document reporting, including the November 4, 2026 Kelly appointment account

The chronology against which the file’s dates were checked, the campus-police records requests of November 15, 2024, the October webinar at which administrators confirmed two men’s enrollment, and the appointment account whose authority characterization conflicts with the attorney general’s release.

Subjective
ABC News—the Title IX records and the recorded calls of November 7, 2024

The intake phrase—“raped by 8-10 men”—that the signed statement omits; the recorded Lee call; the anonymous-tip reporting on the alleged silence meeting; and Ingalls’s February 2025 counter-allegation email, obtained and published here first among the file’s sources.

Subjective
The New Yorker—Jessica Winter, October 1, 2026, and the October 15, 2026 account of the wrongful identifications

The magazine’s case file and its doxing account: the alumnus named from an outdated roster, the employer’s paid leave, the cease-and-desist, and the roster that could not be verified—filed in the report as documented harm to an uninvolved man.

Subjective
BBC—the explainer “What we know…” (September 30, 2026, Nardine Saad) and BBC Newshour interviews

The British file: the case summarized for a foreign reader as of September 30, 2026—the date this report restores against its own early notes—and the Newshour interviews carrying counsel’s subpoena criticism and the death-threat account.

Subjective
The Associated Press, Reuters, and USA Today—the wires’ case reporting, including the October 14, 2026 Title IX explainer and the November 6, 2026 no-confidence coverage

The neutral instruments: the standards explainer the report’s Section 10 rests beside, the joinder count of November 5 verified, the president’s closed-session admission on the unread police report, and the post-vote posture reporting.

Subjective
NPR, NBC News, The Washington Post, and Le Monde—case reporting, October–November 2026

Four further instruments, each load-bearing somewhere in the file: the signed statement’s retained non-consent content, the district attorney on the declined interviews, the chapter’s removal vote in its fullest telling, and the five-man consensual-contact count the ledger prints against four.

Subjective
The Cornell Daily Sun—the first report of the lawsuit (September 18, 2026), the discipline corroboration (October 5, 2026), and the campus record throughout

The student paper of record: Doe’s first public statement at filing, the outcomes corroborated against the Times, the Moonies statement, the district attorney’s Snapchat sentence as reported, and the moratorium’s Ithaca proceedings.

Subjective
The court records of the collateral cases—John Doe v. Cornell University, Index No. EF2026-0292 (dismissed September 23, 2026; 2026 NY Slip Op 26172), and Lopes v. Hochul and James, Index No. 911974-26 (heard October 29, 2026)

Primary dockets: the Article 78 file that unsealed the panel decision and fixed the proceeding’s true dates—the formal complaint of November 22, 2024, the hearings of May 2–29, 2025, the 99-page report and the 1,732-page transcript—and the recusal proceeding as filed, answered, and heard.

Subjective
New York statutes—Penal Law §§130.00, 130.05, 130.10; CPL 30.10; CPLR 213-c, 215(3) and (8), 214-j; Education Law §6440; Executive Law §§63(2) and 296; and the pending bill S10632 / A101 (primary texts)

The law of the file, quoted rather than paraphrased where it decides something: the without-consent element inside “mentally incapacitated,” the affirmative defense, the twenty-year civil window and its limits, and a Senate-passed bill awaiting an Assembly vote since June 4, 2026.

Subjective
Chi Phi Fraternity, Inc.—the statements of September 24, 2026 and, through Interim Executive Director Trey Robb, of about October 1, 2026; and Delta Delta Delta’s stated position

The Greek organizations in their own words: the condemnation and the litigation silence held in one statement, the removal vote and permanent expulsion in the other, and Tri Delta’s two sentences—no comment on pending litigation, and a commitment to supporting women and victims of sexual violence.

Subjective
New York Focus—Sammy Sussman’s report of the 2023 Adult Survivors Act case, November 9, 2026, and the New York Post’s same-day coverage

The separate lawsuit as it actually stands in the record: a 2023 filing, previously unreported rather than newly unsealed, “at least five-ten others” in its own words, trial in 2027—and no SUNY response anywhere in it, filed in the report as a correction.

entry.title: Russell Brand Convicted and Sentenced: The Charges, the Verdicts, the Judge’s Reasons, and What Remains Open
entry.summary: Russell Brand was sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on November 9, 2026, to 10 years and 6 months in prison: convicted by a jury on November 5 of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women, offences from 2004 to 2009, and acquitted on three further counts. The desk files the complete record: the seven counts one by one with their verdicts and terms, the judge’s sentencing remarks in his own words, the dated timeline from 1999 to the sentencing, the prosecution case, the defence case, Brand’s own statements at each stage, the reaction of the police, the prosecutors, the broadcasters and the complainants, and the record that remains open: two further police files with the prosecutors, and a New York civil case that proceeds toward trial.
entry.content:
Special Report

The Case File—Charges, Verdicts, Sentence, and the Open Record

Objective

Russell Brand Convicted and Sentenced: The Charges, the Verdicts, the Judge’s Reasons, and What Remains Open — Special Report

A jury at Southwark Crown Court convicted Russell Brand on Thursday, November 5, 2026, of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women, for offences committed between 2004 and 2009, and acquitted him on three further counts; on Monday, November 9, Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced him to 10 years and 6 months in prison. The sentence is built of a nine-year term for the rape—in which, the judge found, a sexual act that began with consent continued after the condom was removed and after two loud requests to stop—and an eighteen-month term for the three assaults, running after it. The judge’s remarks name the offender a sexual predator, record that his status protected him until journalists published the allegations in 2023, and set out, count by count, what raised the sentence and what lowered it, including the aggravating factors he refused to find. Around the verdict stand the record that produced it: a media investigation in September 2023, four police interviews, charges in two tranches in 2025, a trial the official releases call four weeks and other reporting calls three, the prosecution’s case and the defence’s, the defendant’s own statements at every stage since 2023, and the reaction of the police, the prosecutors, two broadcasters, a government, and the four women whose impact statements closed the file. Two parts of the record remain open: files on two further women are with the Crown Prosecution Service, and a civil case in New York proceeds toward trial. The desk files the whole record, attributed and graded, in that order.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1245 ET, Monday, November 9, 2026.

The File in Brief

The case ended, in its criminal part, on a Monday afternoon in a London courtroom. Russell Brand, 51, of Oxfordshire, stood in Southwark Crown Court on November 9, 2026, and Mr Justice Joel Bennathan sentenced him to 10 years and 6 months in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women, the offences committed between 2004 and 2009, when Brand was becoming one of the most famous entertainers in Britain. The jury of eight men and four women that convicted him on Thursday, November 5, after deliberations reported at about eight and a half hours, returned unanimous verdicts, the Metropolitan Police state, and acquitted him on three further counts: a rape alleged in Bournemouth in 1999, an attempted indecent assault alleged at a London television workplace in 2001, and an oral rape alleged against the same complainant as one of the assaults of conviction. Brand was refused bail after the verdicts and spent the intervening days, including the weekend, at HMP Wandsworth. He will serve two-thirds of the sentence in custody before release on licence, and he is subject for life to the notification requirements of the Sexual Offences Act 2003—the sex offenders’ register. The judge’s opening finding is the sentence’s frame: “About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous. You were clever and, in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.”

The four convictions, in the judge’s findings, are these. In July 2004, at a party, Brand was told a woman wished to meet him and grabbed her breasts—“a clear and blatant sexual assault,” nine months. In 2004–2005, at a London radio station, in front of members of his entourage, he grabbed a newsreader’s face, kissed her, pinned her to a wall, groped her breasts and buttocks, and grabbed at her clothing—eighteen months, reduced from two years for totality. In the spring of 2009, at his home, with a 21-year-old fan he had met after his Hammersmith Apollo show: a sexual encounter that began consensually, with a condom at her insistence, became the rape of the indictment when, the jury found, he turned her over, removed the condom, penetrated her anally, and continued through two loud requests to stop—nine years, the top of the guideline range, raised there for the condom’s removal and its consequences and reduced by a year for mitigation. In late 2009, a woman working for a major television company, pressed into massaging him during the recording of an advertisement for a DVD of his work, felt his face placed in her lap and his breath on her through her clothes, and was then insulted—eight months, and the count of which the judge said: “Count 7 shows yet again your staggering arrogance.” The three assault terms run concurrently with each other and consecutively to the rape term, which is how four convictions become 10 years and 6 months.

The road to the courtroom ran through a newsroom. No charge in this case predates publication. On Saturday, September 16, 2023, The Times, The Sunday Times, and Channel 4’s Dispatches published a joint investigation, “Russell Brand: In Plain Sight,” carrying allegations from four women concerning 2006–2013; those four women are not the six complainants of this trial, a distinction the trial judge recorded and the Crown Prosecution Service confirms in substance: the trial complainants came forward after the broadcast. The Metropolitan Police investigated from September 2023, interviewing Brand under caution four times; the CPS authorised the first five charges on April 4, 2025, and two further charges on December 23, 2025. Brand pleaded not guilty to all seven counts, stood trial at Southwark from October 2026—the official releases call it a four-week trial; other reporting, including The Times’ main sentencing report, calls it three weeks, and the desk prints the conflict rather than a compromise—gave evidence for about four hours, and was convicted on four counts and acquitted on three. His defence, before the trial, during it, and in mitigation after it, never varied in substance: a promiscuous past, acknowledged in his own words as “beyond reckless philandering and idiocy,” and consent, in his account, “non-negotiable.” The judge found that account, in material parts, to be lies told to the jury, and said so in the remarks.

What the sentence is not is also on the record. The judge disregarded the media investigation’s allegations in sentencing, disregarded the acquitted counts entirely—“you have been acquitted of offences against two other women. Your sentence does not reflect those allegations in any way”—and rejected four of the prosecution’s aggravating submissions, including the submission that his fame was itself an aggravating factor. He found no sound evidential basis to conclude that Brand presents a future danger, and stated that a dangerousness finding would have made the sentence significantly longer. Mitigation he accepted—seventeen years without a further offence, addiction-recovery work a witness called particularly impressive, and the impact on Brand’s children—he confined to the single year taken off the rape term. No appeal filing, and no statement of intention to appeal, was found in the record as of the evening of November 9; commentators note a 28-day window to seek permission. Two further matters remain open and are filed in Section 9: a Metropolitan Police investigation of rape allegations by two further women, interviewed and filed with the CPS, on which no charging decision has been announced, and a civil case in a New York court, filed in November 2023 over an alleged assault on a film set in 2010, which a judge allowed to proceed toward trial on or about November 3, 2026. The sections that follow file the counts, the sentence’s arithmetic and reasoning, the timeline, the two cases argued, the defendant’s statements, the reaction, the open record, and the disagreements the record carries, each at the grade its instrument earns.

1. The Outcome: Conviction on Four Counts, Sentence of Ten Years and Six Months

The verdicts came on Thursday, November 5, 2026, and the sentence on Monday, November 9, both at Southwark Crown Court in London. Russell Brand, born June 4, 1975—the Metropolitan Police charge sheet gives the date of birth as 04.06.75—and of Oxfordshire, was convicted by a jury of eight men and four women of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women, offences committed between 2004 and 2009. The deliberations are reported at about eight and a half hours; one summary says more than eight hours over two days, and the desk files the majority figure with the variant noted. The police state the verdicts were unanimous. He was acquitted on three further counts, detailed in Section 2. Refused bail—the reason is reported in two formulations, flight risk in one account and his considerable resources in another, printed here as the two sourced versions they are—he was remanded to HMP Wandsworth, and the judge warned of a significant custodial term.

The sentence, passed in the afternoon of November 9 after a morning of impact statements and submissions, is 10 years and 6 months. Its composition is stated in Section 3. Time already served in custody counts toward it. Brand will serve two-thirds of the sentence in custody, then be released on licence and liable to recall; in the arithmetic of the remarks, two-thirds of 10 years and 6 months is seven years in custody before that release, subject to the time already served. He is indefinitely subject to the notification requirements of the Sexual Offences Act 2003—the register, for life. No pre-sentence report was ordered. Court reporting records that Brand showed no visible reaction to the sentence, and that he told his wife, “We’ll be okay,” as he was taken down, while she mouthed, “I love you, I’ll be OK”; his father, Ron Brand, told reporters outside court after sentencing that his son was the “victim,” and had earlier told the BBC he was shocked and devastated by the verdict.

The judge’s frame for the whole proceeding is set out in his first findings, and the desk prints them as he made them. “Your status protected you until 2023 when journalists collected and published the allegations against you.” And, at the end of the findings on the counts, the sentence’s general principle: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts when sexual predators such as you act without their consent.” Before passing sentence, the judge paused, in his words, “to pay tribute to the determination and bravery of all the women whose evidence I have been recounting,” and recorded that the complainants’ being confronted as liars was a consequence of the defence Brand instructed: “That was all done because of you, and your instructions.” He also commended the police investigation: “The police are sometimes criticised for their investigation of offences of this type. I have seen nothing to suggest criticism is appropriate here.”

2. The Charge Sheet: Seven Counts, Six Women, and the Verdict on Each

Seven counts were tried, against six women, for alleged offences from 1999 to 2009. All complainants have lifelong anonymity under UK law; the judge’s remarks open by recording the statutory prohibition on identifying them, and this report names none. The desk files the counts by their numbers in the indictment and the sentencing remarks, because the numbering matters to the sentence; it notes for the reader that press accounts also label the women by numbers of their own—“Woman 3,” “Woman 4,” and so on—which do not map consistently onto the counts, and it does not use those labels. The facts of the convicted counts are stated as the judge found them in the remarks; the facts of the acquitted counts are stated as the allegations were reported, the verdict having resolved them in the defendant’s favour.

Count 1, rape, 1999, Bournemouth: not guilty. The allegation was that Brand raped a woman he met at a cabaret event on the fringes of the Labour Party annual conference, in a hotel room. He was not yet famous. The jury acquitted.

Count 2, attempted indecent assault, 2001, London: not guilty. An MTV worker alleged that Brand dragged or grabbed her toward a men’s toilet at her workplace. The count was originally charged as indecent assault and amended; one detailed report states that the judge directed the change to attempted indecent assault on evidential grounds, and reputable UK reporting records the charge in its amended form at trial. The jury acquitted.

Count 3, sexual assault, July 2004: guilty, nine months. At a party for a mutual acquaintance—the venue and the complainant’s employer are named in some press accounts and not in the remarks, and the desk follows the remarks—Brand was told that a woman wished to meet him, and grabbed her breasts. The judge: “you committed a clear and blatant sexual assault.” The term, nine months, was set above the guideline range for its category, the judge said, “because of the level of harm that was caused.”

Count 4, rape, 2004: not guilty. The allegation was of oral rape in a toilet at a Soho bar, in a later encounter in the same period, against the same complainant as count 3. The jury acquitted; the judge, in sentencing, recorded the acquittal in terms: the jury had acquitted him “of a later attack on the same woman.”

Count 5, sexual assault, 2004–2005: guilty, eighteen months. The complainant was a newsreader at a London radio station—the station is named Choice FM in police-derived reporting and Capital Radio in other accounts, a conflict the desk leaves standing, as it leaves the year standing at 2004–2005, the sources dividing between the two. In front of members of his entourage, the judge found, Brand grabbed her face, kissed her, pinned her to a wall, groped her breasts and buttocks, and grabbed at her clothing. The term was reduced from two years to reflect the principle of totality; the judge cited “the degree of planning and the breach of the victim’s personal space in front of your entourage.”

Count 6, rape, spring 2009: guilty, nine years. The complainant was 21; Brand was 33. She was a fan who met him after his show at the Hammersmith Apollo. After earlier consensual sexual activity, at his home some days later—the home’s neighbourhood is given as Hampstead in some secondary coverage; it is not stated in the remarks or confirmed in the top-tier reports the desk reviewed, and it is not filed here as fact—vaginal sex began consensually, with a condom because she insisted on one. The jury found that he then turned her over, removed the condom, and anally penetrated her; that she twice asked loudly for him to stop; and the judge recorded her evidence that he continued and said, “I want you to feel my cum.” Brand had stored her number in his phone under “T” for “tart”; she was made to try to clean the soiled bed. The judge: “This was a grave offence committed with a complete disregard for the victim’s autonomy or feelings.” The sentence’s reasoning on this count is filed in Section 3.

Count 7, sexual assault, late 2009: guilty, eight months. The complainant worked for a major television company—reported as Channel 4—and was helping to produce the recording of an advertisement for a DVD of Brand’s work. An associate told her Brand would not continue unless she massaged him; during the massage, the judge found, Brand placed his face in her lap so that she felt his breath on her vagina through her clothes, and then insulted her. The judge: “Count 7 shows yet again your staggering arrogance”—explained in the remarks as that “you thought so little of the impact on the victim even of such public humiliation.” The term reflects, in the judge’s words, that “the abuse of power and trust is clear.”

3. The Sentence: How Ten Years and Six Months Is Built, and What Moved It

The total is an addition, and the remarks show the working. The rape, count 6, drew nine years. The three sexual assaults drew nine months, eighteen months, and eight months, running concurrently with each other—so that the longest of them, the eighteen months of count 5, is the effective assault term—and consecutively to the rape term, because, the judge held, consecutive structuring was required: “there was a series of serious offences against different women, over a period of years.” Nine years and eighteen months make the 10 years and 6 months of the headline. Time in custody since the verdict counts toward the whole.

On the rape, the judge placed the offence in Sentencing Council category 2B—starting point eight years, range seven to nine for a single offence—and raised it to the top of the range for two culpability factors: the removal of the condom, and ejaculation, with the consequential fear of HIV infection “in the days when HIV was a common and terrifying fear.” He then reduced the term by one year for mitigation, to nine years. The prosecution had sought a higher categorisation, category 1, with a starting point of twelve years and a range of ten to fifteen, and terms of one to four years on each assault count; the court did not adopt it.

The aggravating factors the judge rejected are part of the reasoning, and the desk files them with the same prominence as those he accepted. He rejected the prosecution’s submissions that on count 7 Brand acted with others; that his celebrity amounted to an abuse of trust; that fame was an overarching aggravating factor—“I do not regard your use of your fame and celebrity as a separate overarching aggravating factor”; and that the complainants on counts 3 and 6 were particularly vulnerable. His summary of the point is factual rather than rhetorical: “the common feature of all of these cases was his success and fame.”

The mitigation he accepted he also bounded. The record before him showed no significant previous convictions—the prosecution noted a cannabis possession conviction from 1995—seventeen years since the last offence, good work in addiction recovery, on which a statement by Dean Osgood was, in the judge’s words, “particularly impressive,” and his children: “the impact on your children is something of which you should be ashamed and which has played a part in my decision.” The judge expressly confined the good-character discount to the one year taken off the rape term, and he gave his reason in the defendant’s own evidence: “When you gave evidence, you maintained that you never touched any woman in a sexual way without her consent and so, in effect, that each of the women who gave evidence was lying. We now know that was one of a series of lies you told this jury. Those lies were not just about the offences themselves but about your drug consumption and your lifestyle.”

Two express limits close the reasoning. The judge did not find a sound evidential basis to conclude that Brand presents a future danger, and stated the consequence in terms: “Had I done so, the sentence would have been significantly longer.” And he excluded from the sentence everything outside the four convictions: “The court has disregarded anything said in the documentary or other media reports,” and, of the acquittals, the sentence “does not reflect those allegations in any way.” A note on the documentary source of this section: the sentencing remarks are quoted here from the full text as published in court reporting and reproduced in full by Media Mole; the official text on the judiciary’s website was not located in the desk’s search, and every passage quoted is corroborated by direct quotation in the reporting of The Times, The Guardian, and the wire services on November 9. If the official publication appears, it replaces the reproduction as the citation of record.

4. The Timeline: From a Bournemouth Hotel Room in 1999 to the Sentence in 2026

1999 to 2009: the allegations. 1999, the Bournemouth allegation of count 1, at the Labour Party conference period (acquitted). 2001, the London workplace allegation of count 2 (acquitted). July 2004, the assault of count 3, and in the same period the allegation of count 4 (acquitted). 2004–2005, the radio-station assault of count 5, the year within that range unresolved in the sources. Spring 2009, the rape of count 6, at Brand’s home days after the Hammersmith Apollo meeting. Late 2009, the assault of count 7, at the DVD advertisement recording.

2023: publication, then investigation. On Saturday, September 16, 2023, The Times, The Sunday Times, and Channel 4’s Dispatches published and aired “Russell Brand: In Plain Sight.” Brand had pre-empted publication with a video denying the allegations, filed in Section 7. The Metropolitan Police investigation that followed—named in reporting as Operation Actinolite, under the Central Specialist Crime Command—is reported to have taken evidence from more than 100 witnesses and thousands of documents. Brand was interviewed under caution four times: reporting gives precise dates for two of the interviews, December 14, 2023, and January 17, 2024, in each of which he read prepared statements, with footage released by the police after the verdict; the fourth interview took place in July 2025, before the further charges were authorised.

2025–2026: charges, pleas, trial. On Friday, April 4, 2025, the CPS authorised the first five charges—one rape, one oral rape, two sexual assaults, one indecent assault; 1999–2005; four women. Brand appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on May 2, 2025, and was granted bail; on May 30, 2025, at Southwark Crown Court, he pleaded not guilty to all five. On December 23, 2025, the CPS authorised two further charges—one rape, one sexual assault; two further women; 2009 incidents—bringing the indictment to seven counts and six women. He answered the further charges at Westminster Magistrates’ Court in January 2026, by video link, and pleaded not guilty to them at Southwark on February 24, 2026.
