Prosecutors charged Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. Judge Otazú also ordered former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo held in pretrial detention. Prosecutors have charged 27 people in total in connection with the Ueno case, and President Alliana has begun naming a new cabinet.

Subjective
NewsCubby — the Japan earthquake injures at least 22; more shaking is possible

The Associated Press reported at least 22 injuries from Sunday’s earthquake beneath western Shizuoka, while an updated Jiji Press account gave 21. Aichi’s second official report, with a 3:30 p.m. Sunday cutoff, recorded 19 injured within the prefecture, including one serious injury. The Japan Meteorological Agency’s event bulletin places the source beneath western Shizuoka, within the Philippine Sea plate; the United States Geological Survey identifies its reviewed location as 10 kilometres northwest of Hamakita, with an origin time of 16:04:35 UTC on November 7, which is 1:04 a.m. Sunday in Japan. The agencies’ magnitude estimates, 5.7 and 5.5, are separate estimates for the same earthquake. The agency’s advice calls for attention to further strong shaking for about a week, particularly during the first two or three days.

Subjective
Reuters — oil falls as Trump says new Iran attacks are unlikely

PERTH, November 9: oil prices fell at Monday’s open after President Donald Trump said he was highly unlikely to order new Iran attacks while talks to end the conflict make progress, despite both nations’ reports of attacks on ships in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Brent was down 84 cents, or 0.85 percent, to $97.48 a barrel by 0138 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate fell 32 cents, or 0.35 percent, to $90.51 a barrel. The fall reversed minor gains made on Friday’s settlement as the market assessed the possibility of further United States strikes on Iran, although Brent fell 17 percent last week, the steepest weekly drop since the start of the COVID pandemic on LSEG data dating back to 1988. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump told CNN in a phone interview. “The answer is, highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary.”

Subjective
Reuters, via BusinessToday — Asian stocks steady as Middle East jitters recede

Asian markets and United States equity futures made a steady start on Monday, November 9, wobbling into positive territory after a wild week where doubts about demand for computer chips sent tech-heavy markets in Asia into some of their steepest falls in years. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 0.8 percent after sliding 4.6 percent last week. Japan’s Nikkei index added 2.5 percent while Korean shares made small gains. Taiwan’s benchmark rose about 2.5 percent after notching its heaviest weekly drop for two decades last week, when fears about AI profitability and infrastructure demand turned into a rout following wins by Democrats at the United States midterm polls.

Subjective
CoinEdition — Asia market recap: Asian stocks recover from the midterm-driven tech rout while the Nvidia inquiry weighs on sentiment

Asian equities rose on Monday as a bounce on Wall Street helped the region recover part of last week’s heavy losses, although an inquiry at Nvidia kept investors wary. Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed 3.45 percent and the broader Topix opened 2.82 percent higher. Taiwan’s Taiex jumped 5.33 percent, South Korea’s Kospi added 1.68 percent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged up 0.19 percent, and MSCI’s index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan gained 0.8 percent, recovering part of last week’s 4.6 percent drop. The rebound follows a Friday in which the Kospi tumbled about 9 percent, the Nikkei lost roughly 6 percent and the Hang Seng fell more than 1 percent. Nvidia’s board launched an independent probe into its chief executive, the account reports.

entry.title: A Fourth Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, Khor Mor Goes Dark, and the Count Still Waits
entry.summary: The midnight file for Monday, November 9, 2026: what Sunday settled and what it left open. At Al-Ayyat the dead settled at seven and the chief prosecutor's late count put the injured at 125, with no cause stated. In Kraków the six of the square were named by age and nationality, the square reopened, and the joining of the square to the house remained a spokesman's 'highly likely.' In Hormuz an Iranian Navy statement raised the day's claimed tanker fires to four, a maritime account tentatively named one vessel, and Reuters could confirm none of them; a drone halted Iraq's Khor Mor gas field and took 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts off the Kurdistan grid, with no claim of responsibility. Gadi Eisenkot published four conditions and no coalition exists; the Senate count stayed frozen at Friday's figures, Mississippi at 2,574 votes and Alaska at 637; and oil fell at Monday's open after the president said fresh attacks on Iran were highly unlikely while talks progress. Collected at 0000.
entry.content:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

A Fourth Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, Khor Mor Goes Dark, and the Count Still Waits

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: Sunday settled the toll at Al-Ayyat at seven dead, settled the hurt in central Japan at 22 in the prefectures’ own division, named the six of the Kraków square and reopened it, and put a price on Monday—oil down at the open. It left open everything with a deadline: a fourth tanker claimed in Hormuz and none confirmed, a gas field dark in Iraqi Kurdistan with no one claiming the drone, a mandate in Jerusalem exercised in conditions and not yet in a coalition, a Senate count frozen since Friday, and the Abu Dhabi table, enlarged on Sunday, still two days from sitting.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Monday, November 9, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 22, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Sunday, and in Sunday’s earlier editions, Nos. 19 and 21, and its special reports. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Sunday Settled, What It Left Open

Sunday settled counts, names and a price, and it left causes, claims and coalitions open, and the desk files the day in that order. At Al-Ayyat the dead settled at seven in every later account, and the injured reached their last Sunday figure late in the day, when the chief prosecutor’s office put them at at least 125, in the updated running account filed below; no authority has stated a cause. In Kraków the six killed in the Main Market Square stand named by age and nationality, the square reopened late Sunday, and the joining of the square to the three dead at the suspect’s home stands at a prosecutor’s spokesman’s “highly likely,” in Reuters’ evening account filed below. In the Strait of Hormuz the claims grew after the evening edition closed: an Iranian Navy statement raised the day’s tally of tankers said to have struck mines to four, in the Navy’s account filed below, and no tanker fire of Sunday has been confirmed by a party that did not claim it. In Iraq a drone halted the Khor Mor gas field and took 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts off the Kurdistan grid, with no casualties in the first assessment and no claim of responsibility. In Jerusalem Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate produced four conditions and the week’s meetings, and no coalition. In the United States the Senate count posted nothing new for a second day. And at Monday’s open in Perth, oil fell, in Reuters’ market file filed below. Monday holds the handovers and the meetings; Tuesday holds the talks and the deadlines. That is the day whole, as it stands at midnight.

Al-Ayyat at Midnight: Seven Dead, 125 Injured in the Late Count, and No Cause

The railway file closed Sunday with its numbers at their highest and its central question unanswered. The Health Ministry’s staircase ran four dead and 88 injured, then seven dead and 112 injured, and late Sunday the chief prosecutor’s office put the injured at at least 125, with more than 70 of them discharged after treatment, in the Associated Press account filed below. Prosecutors who inspected the site said the Giza-to-Fayoum train, No. 134, hit the last carriage of the Cairo-to-Aswan train, No. 2010, which was stationary on the same track between Kafr Ammar and Raqqa stations; a conductor was among the dead, and the dead have not been named. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered a prompt investigation and accountability for anyone found negligent. No cause has been stated by the railway authority, the prosecutors or the ministry. Settled: the place, the two trains, the seven dead. Open: the 125 against the 112 and 114 also printed under official names during the day, and the cause, which the investigation now owns.

Kraków at Midnight: The Square Reopened, the Six Named, the Joining Still a Spokesman’s Word

Poland’s second day of mourning is Monday, and Sunday ended with the case in its legal shape and its human shape both on the record. The six of the square are counted by age and nationality: a 51-year-old Austrian woman, a 32-year-old British man, three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man of about 50. Prosecutors have opened the investigation as a terrorist offence covering two acts, the six murders in the square and the three murders at the home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, and are preparing six murder charges that could rise to nine. The spokesman Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the same person carried out both; highly likely remains an assessment, not a finding, and the suspect, in critical condition and not yet formally arrested or questioned, has answered nothing. The wounded stand at 16 in Reuters’ evening count, including the two officers and the gunman, and at 15 in other accounts; the three at home stand at 52, 51 and 21 in the evening brief and at 53, 52 and 20 in the prosecutors’ account, and the desk prints both triangles. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński declined on Sunday to withdraw his Saturday reading of the attacker’s views, and the opposition’s demand that he produce its basis stands unanswered. The square reopened late Sunday. National mourning runs through Monday.

Hormuz at Midnight: A Fourth Tanker Claimed, One Tentative Name, and Qeshm Unsettled

The strait’s tally grew by one after the evening edition closed, and its confirmation count did not grow at all. The Iranian Navy said a further tanker struck a mine in the eastern strait before noon on Sunday, its identification systems off in a prohibited area, and called it the fourth tanker to hit mines on Sunday; the Guards’ Navy’s own statement of the day counts three, exploded and on fire along an unauthorized route. The two statements are both Iranian, they differ by one ship, and the desk prints both. Against the claims stand the day’s firmer items, none joined to the tally by any authority: the Emirates’ rescue of 22 crew from a burning cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman, and the American disabling of the M/V Huda on Saturday, explained by Central Command. One name has been offered for one ship, and it is offered as tentative: open-source analysts identify the tanker that caught fire off Khasab, its crew evacuated and firefighting tugs alongside, as the Navig8 Messi, in the maritime account filed below. No owner, flag authority or coast guard has confirmed that identification. On Qeshm the record also disagrees with itself: the Tasnim agency reported two missiles struck the island, Iranian state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes and suggested the explosions might be related to Iranian military activity, and Reuters, in its Sunday file filed below, said it was not able to confirm any of the reported strikes. Three projectiles reported launched from Sirik toward vessels stand likewise unconfirmed, with no hit established.

Khor Mor at Midnight: 2,800 Megawatts Gone, and No Claim

The evening’s one confirmed interruption became, by midnight, the region’s largest measured fact. A single drone hit a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank at the Khor Mor gas field in Sulaymaniyah province on Sunday night; production halted, the fire was still raging in the first reports, and crews were ordered into shelters. The Kurdistan electricity ministry put the generation lost at 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts, gas supply was suspended to power plants in Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, and accounts put more than 70 percent of the region without power, with hospitals and water stations given priority and hydroelectric stations called on. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said an initial assessment found no casualties, and Baghdad directed a joint investigative committee, in the accounts filed below. The region’s ministries called the attack a terrorist attack in a joint statement. No group has claimed it, one reporter at the scene could not say whether the projectile was a drone or a rocket, and a security source’s claim about its launch place is unconfirmed. Settled: the field is stopped and the megawatts are counted. Open: the hand, the damage, and the restart.

Riyadh and Sanaa at Midnight: The Launchers Destroyed, the Toll Standing at 33

The Saudi–Yemen ledger did not move in its figures on Sunday night, and its two sides stand as far apart at midnight as at noon. The coalition said it destroyed two ballistic-missile launchers in Saada that it said were used in Sunday’s attack on Riyadh, after intercepting three ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles. The Energy Ministry’s account of the Aramco Tower stands: damage from falling debris, no casualties. The Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree’s claims stand against it: the financial district and King Khalid International Airport targeted, in operations the movement counts at four in one account and six in another, and a tally of coalition attacks over 24 hours that stands at 91 in one file and 105 in another. The Sanaa figure did not move: at least 33 killed, among them eight women and thirteen children, and 39 wounded, in the Houthi-run health ministry’s count for Saturday’s strikes on homes at al-Shariyah, east of the capital, which Saudi Arabia’s Center for International Communication said it was investigating. Every figure in this paragraph has its owner attached; none has been verified by a party that did not issue it.

Komyshuvakha at Midnight: 55 Dead, and the Missing at 45 or About 50

Ukraine’s file closed Sunday on a disagreement of five names. The toll of Monday’s bombing of the former school and the shelter at Komyshuvakha stands at at least 55 dead in every Sunday account, and Sunday’s drone strike on the rescue crews there injured no one and damaged specialized equipment, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. The missing do not agree: the military intelligence agency HUR lists around 50 people still missing, and the acting head of the regional military administration, Mykhailo Semikin, put the figure at 45 on Sunday afternoon, in the Associated Press account filed below. Many bodies recovered have not been identified and DNA analysis continues. HUR said Saturday it had identified some of the Russian service members it says took part in the first strike; Russia’s differing account of its operations around Komyshuvakha stands in the earlier files, and no Russian statement on Sunday’s drone strike was taken in. The accounts of both attacks rest on Ukrainian officials and the Associated Press’s reporting; no party that did not issue them has verified the toll.

Jerusalem at Midnight: Four Conditions Published, the Meetings Set, No Coalition

The mandate’s first day ended where it began: 48 seats in hand, 61 required, 28 days running. Mr. Eisenkot’s four conditions for joining his government stand as he published them: acceptance of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, the values of the Declaration of Independence upheld, universal military, national or civilian service supported, and Hamas recognised as a terrorist organisation. His challenge to Likud and Religious Zionism, to back a government under him if they stand by their calls for unity, drew no answer taken in on Sunday. The contest underneath the arithmetic is the conscription question, and its positions are all on the record: Mr. Liberman prepared to make painful compromises, including on the conscription law, to build 61 without the Arab lists; the commentator Amit Segal’s assessment that the price of such an arrangement is that the ultra-Orthodox would not be drafted; the Democrats’ chairman Yair Golan’s position that the ultra-Orthodox must be drafted; and Mr. Bennett’s party’s statement that its silence is not consent. Mr. Eisenkot was expected to meet Mr. Bennett on Sunday evening and Mr. Liberman on Monday; no outcome of the Bennett meeting was taken in by midnight. The Joint List said it was willing to help end Mr. Netanyahu’s tenure without demanding a place in the government, and had not yet been asked to commit its votes. On Tuesday the new Knesset is scheduled to convene.

Abu Dhabi at Midnight: Europe’s Chairs Claimed, the G7 in Paris on Monday, the Table on Tuesday

The talks have not begun, and everything about them that changed on Sunday was shape, not substance. France’s foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Europeans will be well represented in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday and that France will take part, that he will not personally sit at the table, and that Paris has not yet named its representative, in Reuters’ Paris file filed below. Russia’s delegation is reported led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky; the accounts of Ukraine’s delegation differ among themselves in the files taken in, and the desk prints no lead name as settled. Russia has suggested there would be no place for European representatives at the table; France says this time they will participate; both statements stand. The G7 foreign ministers meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday, with air defence and energy support for Ukraine on the agenda in the accounts taken in. The American president predicted a “very big” deal extending beyond Ukraine; Mr. Barrot said he did not know what the president had in mind. No agenda, draft or text has been published by any side.

Washington at Midnight: Miller Takes the Office on Monday, and the Answers Are In

The handover announced Friday takes effect at the start of the new day, and Sunday supplied the last of the considered answers to it. Stephen Miller, 41, deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, becomes chief of staff on Monday, November 9; Susie Wiles, whose resignation the president received Thursday night and whose last day was Friday, moves to the Trump Political Operation. The president’s words stand in the record: “Stephen’s been with me since the beginning. He gets it.” The opposition’s answers now stand in two voices: Senator Chuck Schumer’s, that the president “has learned nothing from his historic defeat,” and, on Sunday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’s, on ABC’s “This Week,” that his party will not work with Mr. Miller, in the Sunday account filed below. From the president’s own party, Representative Marlin Stutzman’s dissent stands as filed at evening. The Federal Register published nothing on Saturday or Sunday. Settled: the sequence and the date. Open: what the new chief of staff does with the office, which no statement yet describes.

Asunción at Midnight: 27 Charged, the Repayments Counted Two Ways, and No Ruling

Paraguay’s file ended its first weekend with the detention standing, the charges widened, and the money counted in two currencies of account. At least 27 people face charges in the Ueno case, including the bank’s lead shareholder Miguel Vazquez; former President Santiago Peña and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo are held in pretrial detention, Mr. Peña at the Presidential Escort Regiment, each of his two charges carrying up to ten years on the prosecutor’s statement. He declined to testify Saturday, maintains a plea of not guilty through his lawyer Ricardo Preda, and is presumed innocent; no court has ruled on any part of the case. On the repayments, the figures differ in their basis and the desk prints both: the central bank’s reporting, carried in the accounts filed below, puts about $160 million paid to nearly 1.2 million savers, while a second accounting of the guarantee fund puts the same 1.2 million savers at 994.6 billion guaraníes, equivalent to $153.5 million, as of November 6. Ueno administered around $850 million in public money, including state pension funds; how much of it can be recovered is not established. President Pedro Alliana is naming a new cabinet to serve through 2028.

The Count at Midnight: Frozen at Friday’s Figures, and the Estimates Still Apart

For a second day the count posted nothing, and midnight is the hour to say plainly what that means: the last votes counted in either Senate race were counted by Friday evening. Mississippi stands at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on 953,314 counted, the tally stamped 5:02 p.m. Friday. Alaska stands at Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan by 637 first-choice votes, 48.2 percent to 47.9, on a count posted Wednesday. The estimates of what remains in Mississippi run from about 3,139 mail ballots outstanding on Friday’s count to the state Republican chairman’s 23,000 to 25,000 affidavit or mail ballots, with a tracker’s roughly 30,498 ballots left in its own model; the desk prints the three with their owners. The calendar is the settled part: in Mississippi, mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive, and affidavit voters must cure missing identification, by 5 p.m. Tuesday, November 10; counties certify by November 13; state law provides no recount for this race, and a plurality wins. In Alaska the next count is expected Monday or Tuesday, absentee ballots arrive through November 18, and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for that day if no candidate clears 50 percent. The Associated Press ledgers stand at 54 Democrats to 44 Republicans in the Senate and 252 to 161 in the House, with 22 House races uncalled, Colorado’s 4th among them. Neither Senate race has been called, on the sixth day after the election.

Shizuoka at Midnight: The Hurt Settled at 22, and the Agency Meets on Monday

Central Japan’s file is the day’s one clean settling. The afternoon official division stood at midnight: 19 injured in Aichi Prefecture, one of them serious, and three minor injuries in Shizuoka, 22 in all, between a morning figure of 15 and a printed 24 that no later official account carried forward. The earthquake stands as filed: magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency and 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, at 1:04 a.m. local time Sunday beneath western Shizuoka at about 40 kilometres’ depth, upper 5 on the Japanese scale in Chita, no tsunami threat and no deaths. One later account gives 21 injured in an updated Jiji Press count against the Associated Press’s 22, and the desk notes it without moving its figure, in the correction file filed below. The agency lowered its landslide-warning thresholds for the hardest-shaken municipalities of Aichi, kept its guidance of caution for about a week with the risk highest in the next two to three days, and is to investigate the quake further at a meeting on Monday, the television accounts report. A separate magnitude 4.3 tremor in the Kumamoto area on Sunday produced no reports of serious damage.

The Markets’ Reading: Oil Fell at Monday’s Open

The weekend’s claims met their first price in the small hours, and the price went down. Oil fell at Monday’s open in Perth after the president said fresh American attacks on Iran were “highly unlikely” if negotiations continued to advance, Reuters reported: Brent down 64 cents, or 0.64 percent, to $97.67 a barrel, briefly down more than a dollar, and West Texas Intermediate down 35 cents to $90.51, against Friday’s settlements of $98.32 and $90.83. An earlier print in the same opening, at 0138 GMT, carried Brent at $97.48, down 84 cents; the two prints are an hour’s movement, not a disagreement. Asian shares opened higher in the early accounts, Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 up about 3 percent in the first Monday trading after its 5.96 percent fall on Friday. The reading the desk files is narrow: at the first price after a weekend of claimed tanker fires, a halted gas field and debris in Riyadh, the market paid more weight to a president’s sentence about talks than to any claim out of the strait. What the American and European sessions do with the same file on Monday is not yet in the record.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point, and Sunday’s triangles are these. On Al-Ayyat, the dead agree at seven and the injured stand at 125 in the prosecutor’s late count against 112 and 114 printed under official names during the day; the cause is stated by no one. On Kraków, the wounded stand at 15 or 16, the three at home at two sets of ages, the joining of the two scenes at a spokesman’s “highly likely,” and the minister’s reading as a hypothesis defended and challenged, with the man who could answer it silent in hospital. On Hormuz, the Guards count three burning tankers and the Navy counts a fourth, Reuters confirms none, one name is offered tentatively by analysts and by no authority, and Qeshm is a missile strike in one Iranian account and unconfirmed military activity in another. On Khor Mor, the halt and the megawatts are confirmed by the ministries that lost them, and the hand is claimed by no one. On the missing at Komyshuvakha, the agencies of the same government stand at 45 and about 50. On Jerusalem, a mandate has conditions and meetings and no coalition. On Asunción, the repayments are $160 million in one accounting and $153.5 million in another, on the same 1.2 million savers. On the count, the margins are Friday’s and Wednesday’s, and the estimates of what remains run tenfold apart. The log turns with Monday’s handovers in Washington and meetings in Jerusalem and Paris, and Tuesday’s talks in Abu Dhabi and deadlines in Mississippi and Alaska. The desk files the day settled where it settled, and open where it stands open.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 30 items.

The running account, updated at 20:57 UTC on Sunday: the chief prosecutor’s office said late Sunday that seven people were killed and at least 125 injured, the toll given by the Health Ministry; its earlier updates carried seven killed and 114 injured, and before that four killed and 88 injured. Investigators at the site found the Giza-to-Fayoum train had hit the last carriage of the Cairo-to-Aswan train, stationary on the same track. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered a swift investigation and accountability for anyone found negligent. No cause was given on Sunday.

Subjective

Seven people were killed and at least 125 others injured when two trains collided in the Al-Ayyat district of Giza province, about 32 miles south of Cairo, the chief prosecutor’s office said in a statement late Sunday. The Health Ministry said more than 70 of the injured had been discharged after treatment. The crash occurred when a train travelling to Fayoum crashed into the rear of a train heading to Aswan; an inspection indicated the Aswan train’s last carriage was stationary on the same track. The president ordered a prompt investigation.

Subjective
AfroNews — Egypt: seven killed in the train collision

Egypt’s Health Ministry said seven people died and 112 were injured in Sunday’s train collision at Al-Ayyat in Giza governorate, and 45 of the injured had been discharged. Prosecutors later gave a provisional estimate of seven dead and 114 injured, saying the count continued. After inspecting the site and hearing witnesses, prosecutors said the front of the Giza-to-Fayoum train hit the rear of the Cairo-to-Aswan service, which had stopped on the tracks; both trains were travelling in the same direction. President al-Sisi ordered an urgent inquiry and accountability, and Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir visited. The cause remained unestablished.

Subjective
Reuters — Poland mourns the victims of the Kraków mass shooting as security fears grow

KRAKOW, Nov 8: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday and police bolstered security after six people were killed in the southern city’s historic main square. Sixteen people were wounded in addition to those killed, including two police officers and the suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish man who remained in critical condition in hospital. One of the dead was a British citizen and another Austrian; five foreign nationals, from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia, were among the wounded. Prosecutor’s office spokesperson Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the killings in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski and Kraków were carried out by the same person, and that the three bodies at the home had gunshot wounds, with firearms and a significant quantity of ammunition recovered. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński’s Saturday reading drew a demand from PiS deputy head Przemysław Czarnek for explanations; on Sunday the minister told TVN24 he was not retracting his statements. The square and surrounding streets reopened late Sunday; the hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s was suspended for twelve hours, the first time since 1939, PAP reported; and the two wounded officers have regained consciousness.

Subjective
Le Monde — Poland in shock after the Kraków mass shooting

Poland woke up on Sunday, November 8: on Saturday at 3 p.m. in Kraków a man opened fire with an automatic weapon from his car, killing six people and wounding 15 others around the market square in the historic centre, and was arrested a few streets away after a shootout of about 20 minutes. Police identified him as Michał O., a 24-year-old Polish national with no criminal record, from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski; that evening police found the bodies of his parents and sister in the family apartment. Initial findings did not clarify his motives but revealed a young man with radical ideas, in Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński’s account; on Sunday morning prosecutors announced an investigation into an act of terrorism; two days of national mourning, Sunday and Monday, run with flags at half-staff.

Subjective
European Interest — the prosecutor’s office launches its investigation into the Kraków attack

Spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk of the Małopolska Branch of the National Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime and Corruption announced the start of an investigation into the Kraków attack, classified under terrorist offences and covering two acts: the murder of six people with a firearm in the square, with attempted murder of others including police officers, and the murder of the three people in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. The bodies at home are given as a father aged 53, a mother aged 52 and a sister aged 20. Both acts carry the potential penalty of life imprisonment. The suspect has not yet been formally arrested because of his medical condition, though he remains under constant surveillance, and preliminary findings indicate he possessed a firearms permit.

Subjective
Press TV — the Guards’ Navy: three oil tankers engulfed in flames in the Strait of Hormuz

The Islamic Revolution Guards Corps Navy says three oil tankers exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after violating Iran’s regulations on maritime traffic, in incidents starting in the early hours of Sunday along an unauthorized shipping route, with the tankers’ navigation and identification systems switched off. The statement attributes the burning to the “mischief” of the American army. Less than a day earlier the Guards’ Navy said two tankers attempting the strait via unauthorized routes had struck naval mines and caught fire, one east of the waterway and one within it. Southern routes near Omani waters are declared unauthorized and mined; safe passage is confined to designated northern corridors requiring prior authorization.

Subjective
Press TV — the Iranian Navy: another tanker set ablaze after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz

The Iranian Navy says a tanker caught fire after striking a mine in the eastern Strait of Hormuz before noon on Sunday, having switched off its identification systems and sailed through a prohibited area. It was, the statement says, the fourth oil tanker to hit mines in the waterway on Sunday. In a separate statement the Guards’ Navy reported three tankers struck by mines and on fire on Sunday. The Navy warned the strait would remain closed to vessels violating Iranian regulations until all threats had been removed.

Subjective
The Maritime Executive — a tanker burns after a strike in the Strait of Hormuz

On Saturday at least two tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, including one that caught fire about eight nautical miles off Khasab, on Oman’s Musandam Peninsula; its crew was evacuated, no injuries were reported, and at least two firefighting tugs were working the blaze. Open-source analysts have tentatively identified that vessel as the Navig8 Messi, a products tanker chartered to ADNOC L&S, hit once previously in August and since repaired. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency received a second report of a tanker hit by a projectile during an outbound transit, its crew safe and no environmental impact reported. On Saturday American forces also targeted and disabled the vessel Huda.

Iranian media suggested explosions in southern Iran on Saturday evening were related to Iranian military activities rather than American strikes, while both sides reported shipping hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory following blasts heard in several areas, including on Qeshm Island; the Tasnim agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm, with no official information on possible damage. The United States said its air force had disabled a vessel in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday evening. Iran said two vessels had hit mines and a third had caught fire. Reuters was not able to confirm any of the reported strikes. The Saudi Energy Ministry said an Aramco administrative building in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries or fatalities.

Reuters — production suspended at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field after the drone attack

Nov 8: production was halted on Sunday at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field, one of the largest in the Kurdistan region, after a drone attack hit the field. Two sources in the region’s electricity ministry said production was suspended after a single drone strike hit the LPG storage tank, causing a fire that was still raging. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the attack did not result in casualties, based on an initial assessment. A joint statement by the region’s natural resources and electricity ministries described the attack as a “terrorist attack.” Some 2.8 gigawatts of power generation in the Kurdistan region was lost, the electricity ministry said. A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield caused a fire at the facility and cut power to the region, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials, and the Sunday night attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power. Al Jazeera’s fact-checking agency Sanad verified footage of smoke and flames rising from the vicinity of the gasfield in Sulaimaniyah governorate. An attack on the Khor Mor gas field in Chamchamal district late on Sunday started a large fire and halted production at the Kurdistan Region’s biggest source of power plant fuel, local officials and security sources said. This afternoon President Herzog officially gave Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form a government; he has 28 days, plus 14 more if he requests them and Herzog grants the extension, and if he fails the mandate will go to Prime Minister Netanyahu. The Levant Files — the Sunday live file, closed: Iran talks remain open as the drone attack halts Iraqi gas production

The live file for Sunday, November 8, closed with its headline standing: Iran talks remain open as the drone attack halts Iraqi gas production. In its closing entries: a drone attack halted production at the Khor Mor gas field, cutting gas supplies to five power stations, and Iraq’s prime minister said an initial assessment found no casualties; Baghdad said it was discussing an American request to close all but two crossings with Iran. On Hormuz, the Guards’ Navy attributed two tanker fires to mines and the Fars agency reported a third; Reuters could not independently verify the incidents, and the Emirates’ rescue of 22 crew from a burning cargo ship remains unlinked to the Iranian reports. On Jerusalem, President Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot 28 days to try to form a government; after receiving the mandate Eisenkot set four conditions for joining it, and he was expected to meet Naftali Bennett on Sunday evening and Avigdor Liberman on Monday.

Subjective
USA Today — Trump names Stephen Miller the new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles

WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said top aide Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, beginning November 9, while Wiles moves to the president’s political operation. Miller, 41, has been deputy chief of staff for policy and the president’s homeland security adviser. Wiles gave the president her resignation on Thursday night, and Friday was her last day in the post. The president’s words on his choice: “Stephen’s been with me since the beginning. He gets it.” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer’s verdict, carried in the account’s headline, is that the president “has learned nothing from his historic defeat.”

Subjective
USA Today — Jeffries says Democrats will not work with Trump’s new chief of staff

Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said his party will not work with Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff, during an appearance on ABC’s “This Week” on November 8. Miller was tapped on November 6 to replace Susie Wiles and steps into the role on November 9. The account also carries Jeffries saying an impeachment of the defense secretary has Democratic support.

Subjective
TrenderHQ — the Ueno Bank collapse: why one bank’s failure triggered a political crisis in Paraguay

When regulators took over Ueno Bank in early November 2026, nearly half the country was locked out of its accounts, and within days the Senate had removed the president. Ueno served about 3 million people, roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adults, and held about $800 million of public money; the central bank calls it an isolated case, not a wider banking collapse. The Senate removed President Santiago Peña on November 6, and a judge ordered him held before trial on November 7; he denies wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty, and each of his two charges could carry up to ten years. The government rushed through a law to pay savers back, beginning with small accounts of up to 10 million guaraníes; the central bank reports paying about $160 million to more than 1.2 million depositors so far, and the deposit insurance fully covers 97 percent of Ueno’s customers. Six Ueno executives were ordered held, with 27 people charged in total. No one has been convicted, and it is not yet clear how much of the public money can be recovered.

Subjective
Edge Consultancy — Paraguay pays 1.2 million Ueno Bank savers as the former president is detained

Paraguay’s guarantee fund had paid 1.2 million Ueno Bank savers by November 6, payments totalling 994.6 billion guaraníes, equivalent to $153.5 million. Prosecutors charged 27 people linked to Ueno and related companies on November 4 over loans and overdrafts to associated firms in 2025 and 2026, with outstanding balances of $167.0 million and 343.2 billion guaraníes—equivalent together to $219.9 million—whose recovery prosecutors say may be compromised; these are allegations at the investigative stage, not established losses. Prosecutors charged Peña and former central bank president Carlos Carvallo on November 7 over alleged irregularities in the placement of public and pension money at Ueno and in its supervision. A judge ordered both men into pretrial detention on November 7, Peña at a military facility. He denies wrongdoing.

Subjective
Senate Watch, on YouTube — Senate update, November 8: what changed in Mississippi, Alaska and the leadership fights

The Sunday roundup: neither uncalled Senate race has been called by the Associated Press. Mississippi: the Democrat Scott Colom leads the Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by 2,574 votes, 49.1 percent to 48.8, with about 97 percent counted, in the AP count posted Friday evening, November 6; about 3,139 mail ballots were outstanding as of Friday and count if they arrive by Tuesday, November 10, affidavit ballots are still being reviewed, and estimates of how many remain vary; counties must certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no recount process. Alaska: the Democrat Mary Peltola leads the Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 637 first-choice votes with about 74 percent counted, in a count posted Wednesday, November 4; the next count is expected November 9 or 10, and a ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18 if no one tops 50 percent. The AP ledger stands at 54 Democrats to 44 Republicans.

Subjective
Still Counting — Mississippi and Alaska, updated November 8 at 8:37 p.m. Central

Mississippi, updated at 8:37 p.m. Central on November 8: about 97 percent of the expected vote is counted, 953,314 ballots, with roughly 30,498 left; Scott Colom stands at 467,930 votes and 49.1 percent. Alaska: about 74 percent counted, 213,733 ballots, with roughly 74,706 left; Mary Peltola stands at 102,962 first-choice votes and 48.2 percent. The page’s projected final margins are its own model’s, printed as projections and not as counts.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — a strong earthquake shakes central Japan, injuring at least 22

A strong earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday, shattering store windows and leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media. The Japan Meteorological Agency put the quake’s magnitude at 5.7, while the United States Geological Survey reported it at 5.5. The quake struck at 1:04 a.m. beneath western Shizuoka Prefecture at about 40 kilometres’ depth, and the meteorological agency warned people to brace for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially the next two to three days.

Subjective
NewsCubby — the Japan earthquake injures at least 22; more shaking is possible

The Associated Press reported at least 22 injuries from Sunday’s earthquake beneath western Shizuoka, while an updated Jiji Press account gave 21. Aichi’s second official report, with a 3:30 p.m. Sunday cutoff, recorded 19 injured within the prefecture, including one serious injury; Hamamatsu’s 3 p.m. municipal report recorded one injury within the city. The Japan Meteorological Agency’s advice calls for attention to further strong shaking for about a week, particularly during the first two or three days. The two agencies’ magnitudes, 5.7 and 5.5, are separate estimates for the same earthquake.

Subjective
Reuters — oil falls on the open as Trump says fresh Iran attacks are ‘unlikely’

PERTH, Nov 9: oil prices fell at Monday’s open after President Donald Trump said he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progress, even as both countries reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Brent was down 64 cents, or 0.64 percent, to $97.67 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate fell 35 cents, or 0.40 percent, to $90.51; Brent briefly fell over $1 a barrel. The president had hinted at renewing major attacks on Iran after last week’s midterm elections, but there has been no sign of a large-scale American military operation. Iran has said it would respond by striking American and Israeli targets.

entry.title: Genocide and Conquest: The Definition, the Intent Test, and Where the Courts Drew the Line
entry.summary: Genocide has a precise legal definition: coined by Raphael Lemkin in 1944, set in the 1948 Convention as five acts committed with intent to destroy a protected group in whole or in part. Conquest, the older word, carries no legal test. The desk files the coinage, the Convention, the older record of conquest the word was carried back to, the retrospective applications, the determinations, and the judgments where courts drew the line, closing in a four-column ledger.
entry.content:
Special Report

The Definition File — Coinage, Convention, and the Courts

Objective

Genocide and Conquest: The Definition, the Intent Test, and Where the Courts Drew the Line

“Genocide” is a word with a birth certificate: coined in print in 1944, defined by treaty in 1948 as five acts committed with intent to destroy a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group, in whole or in part, as such, and applied by courts only where that intent is proven to the standard the International Court of Justice set—the only reasonable inference from the record. “Conquest” is the older word: it names the transfer of peoples and territory by force, and it carries no legal test at all. The desk files the coinage, the Convention, the older record the word was carried back to, and the judgments, in that order.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 2000 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026.

The File in Brief

The word is younger than the practice it names, and the record keeps the two apart. Raphael Lemkin, a Polish jurist, coined “genocide” in his 1944 book Axis Rule in Occupied Europe, joining the Greek genos (race, tribe) to the Latin -cide (killing), and defined it as “the destruction of a nation or of an ethnic group”—a coordinated plan against the essential foundations of a group’s life, of which mass killing is one instrument among several. The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide on December 9, 1948; it entered into force on January 12, 1951. Article I declares the crime punishable “whether committed in time of peace or in time of war.” Article II lists five acts—killing, serious bodily or mental harm, conditions of life calculated to destroy, measures to prevent births, forcible transfer of children—and attaches all five to a single mental element: intent to destroy the group, in whole or in part, as such. The courts call that element dolus specialis, specific intent, and the International Court of Justice ruled in 2015 that it is “the essential characteristic of genocide, which distinguishes it from other crimes.” On that test the adjudicated record is narrow. The Rwanda tribunal’s 1998 judgment in Akayesu was the first genocide conviction by an international court. The Cambodia tribunal convicted the Khmer Rouge leaders Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan of genocide in 2018, for the Vietnamese and, in Nuon Chea’s case, the Cham. The International Court of Justice in 2007 found that the July 1995 killings at Srebrenica—more than 7,000 Bosniak men and boys—were genocide, and found Serbia in breach of its duty to prevent them; the same judgment declined to find genocide across the wider Bosnian war. In 2015 the Court dismissed both Croatia’s claim against Serbia and Serbia’s counter-claim, holding in each direction that the material acts were established and the specific intent was unproven: the campaigns aimed at forced displacement, the record’s word, and displacement stands outside the Article II list. Executive governments apply the word on a different instrument: the United States has issued eight formal genocide determinations since 1993, the eighth being Secretary of State Antony Blinken’s March 21, 2022 determination on the Rohingya, and President Joseph Biden’s April 12, 2022 statement calling Russia’s war in Ukraine genocide was a presidential characterization that no formal determination followed. The word’s spread through print is measurable: Google Books data assembled by the historian Dominik Schaller show decided rises in the second half of the 1960s and in the 1990s, and “genocide” has appeared in books more often than “massacre” since the late 1990s. The older record, the centuries of conquest the word now gets carried back to, was written in a different vocabulary: Thucydides records Athens killing the men of military age it captured on Melos in 416 BC, enslaving the women and children, and settling 500 colonists on the island, and no word in his account corresponds to the 1944 coinage. The desk files the coinage and the Convention first, the older record second, the retrospective application third, and the courts’ line last, closing in a four-column ledger.

1. The Coinage: A Word With a Birth Certificate

Raphael Lemkin put the word into print in November 1944. Axis Rule in Occupied Europe: Laws of Occupation, Analysis of Government, Proposals for Redress, published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, is a compilation of the occupation law of Axis Europe, and its ninth chapter, titled “Genocide,” opens with the coinage: “New conceptions require new terms. By ‘genocide’ we mean the destruction of a nation or of an ethnic group. This new word, coined by the author to denote an old practice in its modern development, is made from the ancient Greek word genos (race, tribe) and the Latin cide (killing), thus corresponding in its formation to such words as tyrannicide, homicide, infanticide, etc.” Lemkin’s own biography sits inside the book’s occasion: he was a Polish lawyer of Jewish descent who had fled Poland in 1939, and 49 members of his family were killed in the Holocaust.

Lemkin’s definition ran wider than killing, and he said so in the same passage. “Generally speaking, genocide does not necessarily mean the immediate destruction of a nation, except when accomplished by mass killings of all members of a nation. It is intended rather to signify a coordinated plan of different actions aiming at the destruction of essential foundations of the life of national groups, with the aim of annihilating the groups themselves.” The chapter then works through the fields in which such a plan operates—political, social, cultural, economic, biological, physical, religious, and moral—and states the aim in terms of substitution as well as destruction: the oppressor’s own national pattern imposed on the emptied ground. The object of the crime, in Lemkin’s construction, is the group as an entity; the acts fall on individuals as members of the group.

The word entered a courtroom document within a year, as description rather than as charge. The indictment of the major German war criminals at Nuremberg, filed October 18, 1945, charges under Count Three, war crimes, that the defendants “conducted deliberate and systematic genocide, viz., the extermination of racial and national groups, against the civilian populations of certain occupied territories in order to destroy particular races and classes of people and national, racial or religious groups, particularly Jews, Poles and Gypsies and others.” The Charter of the International Military Tribunal, the instrument that defined the tribunal’s charges, contains no such word; genocide appears in the indictment as a term for conduct charged under the existing counts. On December 11, 1946, the General Assembly’s Resolution 96 (I) affirmed genocide as a crime under international law, and the drafting of a convention followed. The sequence is the file’s spine: a scholar’s coinage in 1944, a prosecutor’s descriptive use in 1945, an Assembly affirmation in 1946, a treaty definition in 1948.

2. The Convention: Five Acts, Four Groups, One Intent

The treaty text is short, and its architecture is exact. Article I: “The Contracting Parties confirm that genocide, whether committed in time of peace or in time of war, is a crime under international law which they undertake to prevent and to punish.” Article II defines the crime as any of five acts “committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such”: (a) killing members of the group; (b) causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; (c) deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part; (d) imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group; (e) forcibly transferring children of the group to another group. Article III makes punishable the crime itself and, beside it, conspiracy to commit genocide, direct and public incitement, attempt, and complicity. The Convention’s preamble records that “at all periods of history genocide has inflicted great losses on humanity”—the treaty’s own acknowledgment that the practice predates the word. Article IX sends disputes between states over the Convention’s interpretation and application to the International Court of Justice, the door through which every state-versus-state case in this file arrived.

Four features of the definition govern everything the courts have done with it. First, the protected list is closed: national, ethnical, racial, and religious groups. Political groups stand outside it; the destruction of a political class, however complete, is charged under other law. Second, three of the five acts involve no killing: serious mental harm, birth prevention, and child transfer can each complete the crime. Third, the acts carry the crime only when joined to the intent to destroy the group as such; the same killing, committed with the intent to expel, to punish, or to win ground, is a different offense in the Convention’s scheme. Fourth, Article I severs the crime from war in the treaty’s first sentence: the crime exists in peacetime on the same terms as in wartime, and war crimes law, which attaches to armed conflict, has no corresponding clause. The Convention entered into force on January 12, 1951, ninety days after the twentieth ratification, and its definition was carried nearly verbatim into the statutes of the Rwanda and Yugoslavia tribunals, the Cambodia chambers, and the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court.

The intent element is where cases are won and lost, and the courts have priced it high. In its judgment of February 3, 2015, in Croatia v. Serbia, the International Court of Justice stated the doctrine at paragraph 132: the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such” is “the essential characteristic of genocide, which distinguishes it from other crimes,” a dolus specialis, a specific intent, which must be present in addition to the intent required for each individual act. Where intent is to be inferred from a pattern of conduct, the Court’s standing test, applied in both the 2007 and 2015 judgments, requires that the genocidal intent be the only reasonable inference the pattern supports. Discriminatory intent—targeting members of a group for abuse, expulsion, or killing as enemies—does not by itself satisfy the test; the inference must run to destruction of the group, in whole or in part, as an end. Every judgment in section 6 of this report turns on that paragraph and that test.

3. The Older Record: Conquest Before the Word

The ancient record describes the outcomes in the vocabulary of war and victory, and the outcomes themselves need no translation. Thucydides, in Book V of his History of the Peloponnesian War, records the Athenian expedition against the island of Melos in 416 BC: a neutral Dorian island that refused submission to the Athenian alliance. His account gives the negotiation as the Melian Dialogue, in which the Athenian envoys state the operating rule in the open—right is in question between equals in power; the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must—and then gives the result in one sentence: the Melians surrendered at discretion, the Athenians put to death all the grown men they had taken, sold the women and children for slaves, and sent out 500 colonists to settle the place themselves. The passage is the classical world’s own description of a conquest that ended a people’s civic existence on its island. Thucydides files it as war.

Carthage supplies the largest ancient specimen, and its numbers come with their instruments attached. The Yale historian Ben Kiernan’s study “The First Genocide: Carthage, 146 BC,” published in Diogenes in 2004, assembles the ancient accounts: Cato the Censor’s standing close to his Senate speeches from 153 BC, Delenda est Carthago—Carthage must be destroyed—which Kiernan identifies as possibly the first recorded incitement to genocide; the three-year siege; a population he puts at 200,000 to 400,000, of whom at least 150,000 perished; and the end in 146 BC, when Scipio Aemilianus razed the city and dispersed the 55,000 survivors, including 25,000 women, into slavery. Kiernan also records the limits of the file: the famous salting of the earth appears in no ancient source, and the earliest claim of it he traces dates to 1930. The ancient writers themselves—Polybius, an eyewitness attached to Scipio’s staff, and Appian, writing three centuries later—describe destruction, extermination of the city’s population in the fighting, and enslavement of the remnant, in the vocabulary available to them. The word applied to the event in Kiernan’s title dates from 1944.

Lemkin himself drew the line of descent, in a footnote. Chapter nine of Axis Rule cites, as classical examples of wars of extermination in which nations and groups were completely or almost completely destroyed, the destruction of Carthage in 146 BC and of Jerusalem by Titus, the religious wars of Islam and the Crusades, the massacres of the Albigenses and the Waldenses, and the siege of Magdeburg in the Thirty Years’ War, and adds the wholesale massacres in the wars of Genghis Khan and Tamerlane. His unfinished History of Genocide, planned in three volumes and left in manuscript at his death in 1959, assigned nine chapters to antiquity—among them Assyria, Carthage, Gaul, and the Celts—twelve to the Middle Ages, among them the Albigensians, the Mongols, the Moors, and medieval England, and forty-one to modern times. The retrospective application of the word, documented in section 4, begins with the word’s own inventor, and it begins as history rather than as law: Lemkin’s chapters judge the dead by a definition written in 1944, and no court has ever been asked to do the same, the Convention having no retroactive reach.

4. The Word Carried Backward: Retrospective Application

The scholarly application of “genocide” to conquests widened in steps, and the steps are datable. The word’s frequency in print, measured in the Google Books corpus of more than five million books and assembled by Dominik Schaller in Genocide Studies and Prevention in 2011, shows no single explosion: decided rises came in the second half of the 1960s—Schaller and the literature after him associate the rise with the fiftieth anniversary of the Armenian genocide in 1965, with the violence of post-independence Rwanda and Burundi, and with the Vietnam War and the American civil-rights movement—and again in the 1990s, with the field of genocide studies expanding rapidly after the Cold War’s end. Since the late 1990s the corpus has used “genocide” more often than “massacre.” The retrospective shelf grew with the frequency: David E. Stannard’s American Holocaust: Columbus and the Conquest of the New World (Oxford University Press, 1992) argued that within twenty-one years of Columbus’s first landing the island he renamed Hispaniola was effectively desolate, nearly 8,000,000 people killed, in Stannard’s accounting, by violence, disease, and despair; that historical demographers had found post-contact depopulation rates of 90 to 98 percent region by region, with an overall decline of about 95 percent as a working rule of thumb; and that the destruction of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas was “far and away, the most massive act of genocide in the history of the world.” The desk files Stannard’s numbers as his: the pre-contact population of Hispaniola is contested across a wide range in the demographic literature, and Stannard’s figures stand at the high end of it, a placement his appendix argues for directly.

States have also applied the word backward, and the instruments they use record the strain of doing so. In May 2021, after negotiations begun in 2015, Germany and Namibia initialled a joint declaration on the German colonial war of 1904 to 1908 in what is now Namibia, in which General Lothar von Trotha’s extermination order of October 2, 1904 stands at the head of a campaign in which, on the standard estimates, about 65,000 Herero—about 80 percent of the people—and about 10,000 Nama—about 50 percent—perished by killing, starvation, and the camps. The declaration’s operative sentence is written in the present tense looking back: the atrocities “culminated in events that, from today’s perspective, would be called genocide.” Germany coupled the acknowledgment to €1.1 billion over thirty years for reconstruction and development programs, and both governments framed the money as reconciliation; the declaration carries no legal duty of reparations, Germany’s stated ground being that the prohibition of genocide in international law postdates 1904 to 1908. Descendant organizations of the Herero and Nama rejected the declaration, on the record, for negotiating over their heads and for the exclusion of reparations. In the same year, 2021, the United States recognized the Armenian genocide of 1915 to 1916, a determination that arrived a century after the events and against the background of the Ottoman Empire’s wartime deportations and massacres. In each case the naming instrument is political—a declaration, a presidential statement—and in each case the namer states, or the record shows, that the legal category postdates the events it is carried back to.

5. Genocide Without War: The Crime Detached From Battle

Article I’s clause—in time of peace or in time of war—has a case record, and Cambodia is its center. On November 16, 2018, the Trial Chamber of the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia convicted Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan, the two surviving senior leaders of Democratic Kampuchea, of genocide, and sentenced both to life imprisonment, for crimes committed between April 17, 1975 and January 6, 1979. Both men were convicted of genocide against the Vietnamese ethnic, national, and racial group; Nuon Chea was convicted in addition of genocide against the Cham ethnic and religious group, on the basis of his superior responsibility. The convictions arose from a state’s campaign against groups inside its own territory and under its own administration—minorities marked out within a population the regime already ruled—and the same judgment’s structure displays the Convention’s boundary from the other side: the far larger killing of ethnic Khmers by the Khmer Rouge, the regime’s own national group destroyed in the hundreds of thousands as class and political enemies, was prosecuted in the case as crimes against humanity, because Article II’s closed list covers national, ethnical, racial, and religious groups and the Khmer victims were targeted as political and social categories. The largest part of one of the century’s largest killings stands outside the genocide counts of its own tribunal, on the text of the definition.

The first conviction under the Convention carries the same lesson in miniature. On September 2, 1998, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda convicted Jean-Paul Akayesu, the bourgmestre of Taba commune, on nine of fifteen counts, including genocide and direct and public incitement to commit genocide, and sentenced him to life imprisonment—the first genocide conviction by an international tribunal, fifty years after the Convention’s adoption. The judgment also held, for the first time in an international court, that rape and sexual violence can constitute acts of genocide when committed with the specific intent, under the Article II head of causing serious bodily or mental harm. The Rwanda killings of 1994 ran alongside a civil war, and the tribunal’s statute covered both; the genocide counts in the judgment attach to intent and to the protected group, and the war supplies setting rather than element. Article III completes the detachment: conspiracy and direct and public incitement are punishable as such, so the crime in law can be complete before any of the five acts occurs, in a radio studio as readily as on a battlefield.

6. War Without the Finding: The Intent Test Applied

The Bosnian case is the fullest worked example of a war passing through the test and emerging divided. Bosnia and Herzegovina sued Serbia and Montenegro under Article IX in 1993, alleging a campaign of genocide across the war of 1992 to 1995. In its judgment of February 26, 2007, the International Court of Justice concluded that the acts committed at Srebrenica in July 1995—the killing of more than 7,000 Bosniak men and boys by forces of the Republika Srpska—fell within Article II (a) and (b) and were committed with the specific intent to destroy in part the group of the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina as such, and were accordingly acts of genocide. The Court found that Serbia had neither committed that genocide nor been complicit in it, and it found Serbia in breach of the Article I obligation to prevent it, and of its obligations to cooperate with the Yugoslavia tribunal, including by failing to transfer Ratko Mladić. The wider campaign—killings, detention camps, and mass expulsion across Bosnia, documented in the same record—produced no genocide finding. One enclave in eleven days met the test; a three-year war around it did not, and the difference the Court recorded is the presence, at Srebrenica, of an intent it could name.

The Croatia case ran the instrument in both directions and it returned the same reading twice. Croatia claimed Serbia was responsible for genocide in the war of 1991 to 1995; Serbia counter-claimed over Operation Storm of August 1995, in which more than 200,000 Serbs fled or were expelled from the Krajina. On February 3, 2015, the Court rejected Croatia’s claim by fifteen votes to two and Serbia’s counter-claim unanimously, in a single judgment. For each claim the Court found the actus reus established—killings and serious harm within Article II’s list, committed by the other side’s forces—and the dolus specialis unproven: the conduct, on the evidence, aimed at the forced displacement of the population from territory, and displacement, however violent, is an aim the Convention’s list does not convert into destruction of the group. The judgment is the standing citation for the gap this report files: a war can satisfy the physical half of the definition at scale, on both sides, and satisfy the mental half on neither.

Darfur shows the same events passing through two different instruments and returning two different answers, six years apart. The United States ran its own instrument first: a State Department team interviewed 1,136 Darfurian refugees at nineteen locations in eastern Chad between July 12 and August 18, 2004, of whom 74 percent reported Sudanese military involvement in the attacks on their villages, and on September 9, 2004 Secretary of State Colin Powell told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that “genocide has been committed in Darfur and the Government of Sudan and the jinjaweed bear responsibility—and genocide may still be occurring”—the first invocation of the Convention by a sitting United States official for an ongoing crisis. The International Criminal Court’s instrument ran slower and under judicial standards: its first warrant for President Omar Al Bashir, March 4, 2009, charged war crimes and crimes against humanity and carried no genocide count, the Pre-Trial Chamber’s majority holding the genocidal intent not then established to its standard; after the Appeals Chamber ruled that standard too demanding for the warrant stage, a second warrant issued on July 12, 2010, adding three counts of genocide—by killing, by causing serious bodily or mental harm, and by deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to destroy—against the Fur, Masalit, and Zaghawa groups, on reasonable grounds to believe Al Bashir acted with the specific intent. Al Bashir was never surrendered to the Court and never tried. The executive determination of 2004 and the judicial warrant of 2010 name the same crime over the same ground; the six years between them are the distance between the two instruments’ standards of proof.

7. The Word in Present Wars: Determinations, Characterizations, and Provisional Measures

Governments now apply the word through a standing administrative practice, and the practice has a ledger. Secretary Blinken’s statement of March 21, 2022, at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, announcing his determination that members of the Burmese military committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya, counted the practice aloud: “Beyond the Holocaust, the United States has concluded that genocide was committed seven times. Today marks the eighth.” The seven, in the order the United States recognized them, were Bosnia, Rwanda, Iraq, Darfur, the territories ISIS held and the Yazidis it targeted, China and the Uyghurs, and Armenia. A determination is an executive act: it carries political and statutory consequences inside the issuing government and binds no court. Beside the ledger stands the looser instrument of characterization. On April 12, 2022, in Iowa, President Biden said of Russia’s war in Ukraine, “Yes, I called it genocide,” adding that it had become clearer that President Putin was “just trying to wipe out the idea of even being able to be Ukrainian,” and in the same exchange assigned the legal question elsewhere: “We’ll let the lawyers decide internationally whether or not it qualifies, but it sure seems that way to me.” No formal State Department genocide determination on Ukraine followed; the Department’s formal accusation of March 23, 2022 charged war crimes. Other governments divided on the word in public: President Emmanuel Macron of France declined to adopt it for Ukraine, describing Russian actions as war crimes. Russia’s own stated ground for its invasion included the claim that Ukraine was committing genocide in the Donbas, and Ukraine carried that claim to the International Court of Justice as the applicant: in its judgment on preliminary objections of February 2, 2024, the Court found jurisdiction to entertain Ukraine’s request for a declaration that there is no credible evidence Ukraine committed genocide in the Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, and found it lacked jurisdiction over Ukraine’s submissions on Russia’s use of force; by an order of December 5, 2025, the Court found Russia’s counter-claims in the case admissible, with pleadings now running into 2027. The word in that file has been claim, counter-claim, and stated cause of war, and the Court has so far ruled on which questions it may hear.

At the Court, the live genocide cases stand at the provisional stage, and the provisional stage has a precise meaning that the record states in its own terms. In The Gambia v. Myanmar, the Court’s unanimous order of January 23, 2020 found the rights The Gambia claimed for the Rohingya plausible, found a real and imminent risk of irreparable prejudice to them, and ordered Myanmar to take all measures within its power to prevent acts within Article II; the order decided nothing on the merits, which remain pending. In South Africa v. Israel, filed December 29, 2023, South Africa alleges that Israel’s campaign in Gaza breaches the Convention; Israel’s stated position, presented at the January 2024 hearings, is that the case presents a grossly distorted picture, that Israel is fighting Hamas in self-defense after the October 7, 2023 attack, and that the intent element of genocide is, in its counsel’s words, completely missing. The Court’s order of January 26, 2024 found at least some of the rights South Africa claimed plausible—including the right of Palestinians in Gaza to be protected from acts of genocide—and indicated provisional measures; further orders of March 28 and May 24, 2024, the last by thirteen votes to two, ordered Israel immediately to halt its military offensive in the Rafah Governorate and any other action there risking conditions of life capable of bringing about the group’s physical destruction in whole or in part. The Court has issued no finding that genocide occurred; its then-president, Judge Joan Donoghue, stated publicly in April 2024 that the Court decided the Palestinians had a plausible right to protection and did not decide that the claim of genocide was plausible. A separate United Nations body, the Human Rights Council’s Commission of Inquiry, concluded in September 2025 that genocide had been committed in Gaza, finding four of the five Article II acts and intent as the only reasonable inference; Israel rejects the Commission’s findings, and the Commission is an investigative body whose conclusions bind no court. Written pleadings in the Court case run to 2029. The desk files the three instruments at their own grades: a court’s provisional measures, which protect rights pending judgment; an inquiry’s conclusions, which persuade or fail to; and a merits judgment, which does not yet exist in the case.

8. The Two Categories, as the Record Defines Them

War and genocide, in the instruments this file has used, are defined on different axes, and the adjudicated record shows the overlap and the remainder on both sides. The laws of war attach to armed conflict: the Geneva Conventions of 1949 govern international and non-international armed conflict, and a war crime in the tribunal statutes requires conduct linked to such a conflict. The category is defined by the parties and the fighting. Genocide is defined by a target and an intent: a protected group, and the purpose of destroying it in whole or in part. Scale appears in neither definition as a threshold. The genocide finding of the modern record rests on eleven days and more than 7,000 victims at Srebrenica, because the intent was proven; the expulsion of more than 200,000 people in Operation Storm drew no such finding, because it was not. Of the three tribunal matters that have produced genocide convictions—Rwanda in 1998, Srebrenica in the Yugoslavia tribunal’s judgments, and Cambodia in 2018—two arose inside wars and one inside a regime’s administration of its own state. The executive ledger and the press usage run wider than the judicial record in every period the file covers, and the distance between the word as governments and newspapers use it and the word as courts apply it is the quantity the cases measure: identical in spelling, different in standard, and separated, in the instances documented here, by the single element of proven intent to destroy a group as such. The older word, conquest, belongs to neither axis: no treaty defines it, no court applies it, and its record—Melos emptied and recolonized, Carthage razed and its survivors enslaved, peoples transferred and territories annexed across the centuries the word governed—was written by its makers as victory and by its subjects as catastrophe, in vocabularies that predate the legal one by two thousand years and more.

9. The Ledger

The whole subject, sorted by the state of its evidence. The desk closes the file with the four-column accounting the report has applied throughout, to every side’s claims at the same grade. Verified: established by treaty text, adjudication, or the official record. Documented-but-small: real, proven, and bounded by its instrument. Claimed-but-unproven: asserted by named makers, awaiting or lacking adjudication. Disproven: tested by the instrument built to test it and failed.

VerifiedDocumented-but-smallClaimed-but-unprovenDisproven
“Genocide” was coined by Raphael Lemkin in Axis Rule in Occupied Europe (1944), from genos and -cide, defined as the destruction of a nation or ethnic group by a coordinated plan against the foundations of its life. The word’s first courtroom appearance is descriptive, in Count Three of the Nuremberg indictment (1945); the Charter contains no such charge. The Convention (adopted December 9, 1948; in force January 12, 1951) defines the crime as five acts against a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group, committed with intent to destroy it in whole or in part, as such, “in time of peace or in time of war.” Specific intent (dolus specialis) is “the essential characteristic of genocide” (ICJ, 2015, para. 132). Adjudicated: Akayesu (ICTR, 1998), the first international genocide conviction, rape held an act of genocide; Srebrenica a genocide (ICJ, 2007), Serbia in breach of the duty to prevent; the Cambodia convictions of 2018 (Vietnamese; Cham, Nuon Chea). The United States has made eight formal determinations, the Rohingya last (March 21, 2022). Thucydides records Melos: men of military age killed, women and children enslaved, 500 colonists settled (416 BC). The adjudicated set is small against the word’s usage: three tribunal matters have produced genocide convictions (Rwanda, the Yugoslavia cases over Srebrenica, Cambodia), and the International Court of Justice has found genocide established in one place, Srebrenica, across three state-versus-state judgments. Kiernan’s Carthage file is bounded by its sources: a population of 200,000 to 400,000, at least 150,000 dead, 55,000 enslaved—estimates built on Polybius and Appian. Germany’s Namibia acknowledgment is bounded by its own text: the word applied “from today’s perspective,” €1.1 billion as reconciliation, no legal reparations duty accepted. The United States’ Darfur determination rested on 1,136 refugee interviews in Chad. President Biden’s April 12, 2022 characterization of Russia’s war in Ukraine as genocide: a presidential statement, expressly left by its maker to “the lawyers,” with no formal determination following. Russia’s claim that Ukraine committed genocide in the Donbas, the stated ground of invasion: before the International Court of Justice as a request for a declaration that no credible evidence supports it, counter-claims admitted December 2025, undecided. South Africa’s allegation of genocide in Gaza: provisional measures granted on plausible rights, merits undecided, pleadings to 2029; the UN Commission of Inquiry’s September 2025 conclusion of genocide is an investigative finding, rejected by Israel, binding no court. Stannard’s Hispaniola figures—nearly 8,000,000 dead, 95 percent decline—are one historian’s high-end accounting in a contested demographic field. The claim that the International Court of Justice found genocide, or a plausible claim of genocide, in Gaza: the Court’s January 2024 order found claimed rights plausible and its then-president stated on the record that it did not decide the claim of genocide was plausible; no merits finding exists.
