Sullivan Jr. holding 3,600 votes, more than five times the margin. Against those standings, the desk notes a figure in circulation this morning: an explainer on the delays, republished Sunday, carries Mississippi’s margin as 1,138 votes—which was Wednesday night’s margin, in the explainer filed below. Both figures are true of their hours; only one is true of this one. A count is a dated instrument, and the desk dates it. The calendar around the standings is unchanged and triple-headed: on Tuesday, November 10, Mississippi’s mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive and its boards of commissioners complete the provisional count, and Alaska publishes its next update; Mississippi counties certify by November 13; Alaska’s absentee ballots arrive through November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is set, no candidate having cleared 50 percent. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with the two Senate races, the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, ahead by 3,172 votes in Friday’s figures, no newer figure taken in by noon. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. At noon on the fifth day, neither race has been called.

Shizuoka at 1200: The Count of the Hurt Settles Into a Range

Central Japan’s morning produced the day’s other correction file: not a new event, but a settling count. The earthquake itself stands as the overnight edition filed it: magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency, 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, at 1:04 a.m. local time beneath western Shizuoka Prefecture at a depth of about 40 kilometres, upper 5 on the Japanese intensity scale in Chita, Aichi—the strongest shaking in western Shizuoka in 107 years and in Aichi since 1997—with no tsunami threat and no deaths reported. The injured count rose through the morning and the accounts do not land on one figure. The Seoul account, drawing on the meteorological agency and NHK, counts 15 injured—12 in Aichi, hurt in falls and by blows to the head, and three in Shizuoka, in the morning file filed below. The wire account carried in India counts at least 22 injured, with shattered storefront windows and disrupted trains, in the second file below; local papers and broadcasters in the region have carried 24. The desk publishes the range, 15 to 24, and notes that the counts were taken at different hours of an assessment still under way. The agency’s standing guidance is the settled part: caution for about a week against tremors up to upper 5, the risk highest in the next two to three days, and its assessment that the quake’s pattern differs from, and is unlikely to lead to, the Nankai Trough megaquake.

The Markets’ Reading: Friday’s Settlements, One Festive Hour, and a Monday

There is no American or European session to report on a Sunday, so the desk reports the readings the weekend published. On the settlements, the Sunday accounts agree to the cent: Brent crude closed Friday at $98.32 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate at $90.83, in the Saudi Sunday-morning snapshot and in the Sunday markets newsletter, both filed below, the snapshot noting that Saudi markets open their week on Sunday with those Friday figures as the last confirmed settlements. On the week’s size, the accounts do not agree, and the disagreement is a matter of baselines: the newsletter measures Brent down about 17 percent from $117.64 at the end of the week before; this paper’s Saturday file measured the same barrel down 13.3 percent on the week from its own baseline, and a Sunday market table prints 12.7 percent for Brent and 11.9 for West Texas Intermediate. The settlements are the point; the percentages are the triangle, and the desk prints both. Underneath every measure sits the same fact the newsletter states plainly: expectations of de-escalation in the Iran conflict took the geopolitical premium out of the barrel during the week, and the tanker fires around the Gulf mean the supply risk has not disappeared—a sentence written before the Guards raised their tally to three this morning, and the first thing Monday’s open will reprice.

The one session the world did hold on Sunday was seventy minutes long and festive. India’s exchanges opened for the Diwali Muhurat session—pre-open at 2:05 p.m. in Mumbai, continuous trading from 2:20 to 3:30 p.m., 0350 to 0500 ET—marking Laxmi Pujan and the start of Samvat 2083, the Hindu financial new year. The session closed up: the Sensex rose 400 points to 81,406 and the Nifty crossed 25,100, with Tata Steel and Sun Pharma among the leading gainers, in the session’s account filed below. Regular Indian trading resumes Monday and closes again Tuesday for Diwali-Balipratipada. It is a ceremonial hour and the desk files it as one; its direction, on the day Poland mourned and the strait burned in claims, was up. The rest of the markets’ week is a calendar: Monday’s full reopening, Tuesday’s talks in Abu Dhabi and counting deadlines in two American states, and an oil price that ended Friday below a hundred dollars with a war premium half in and half out.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point. On Kraków, the triangle has three sides: the wounded at 15 in the square accounts and 16 in the prosecutors’; the suspect at 24 in the prosecutors’ and police accounts and 25 in others; his sister at 20 in the morning’s prosecutors’ account and 21 in the accounts the overnight edition filed. The desk publishes all three triangles and chooses in none of them; the settled facts are the investigation, the classification, and the nine dead. On Hormuz, the Guards say three tankers; no name, flag, crew, or independent confirmation attaches to any of the three, and the confirmed rescue and the explained disabling beside them are separate reports that no authority has joined. On Shizuoka, the injured stand between 15 and 24 by the hour of the count, and the magnitude stands at 5.7 by the agency that owns the scale and 5.5 by the American survey. On the count, the margins are unchanged and the figures in circulation are dated Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday; read with their dates, they do not conflict. On oil, the settlements agree and the weekly percentages do not, because their baselines do not. On Jerusalem, the mandate has changed hands and no government has been formed; both halves of that sentence are the news. On Asunción, the detention is a fact and the charges are allegations, and the presumption of innocence is printed with them. The edition closes at noon with the case opened, the mandate running, the table enlarged, the count standing, and everything of consequence in this file—the Abu Dhabi talks, the counting deadlines, the markets’ reopening—falling on the same Tuesday.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-four items.

Subjective
European Interest — the prosecutor’s office launches its investigation into the Kraków attack

Spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk of the Małopolska Branch of the National Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime and Corruption announced the start of an investigation into the Kraków attack, and Prosecutor General Waldemar Żurek emphasised that the division handles cases related to terrorist crimes. The Saturday attack was carried out by a 24-year-old man who drove into the Main Market Square and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 16, including two police officers; the prosecutor’s investigation, classified under terrorist offences, covers the murder of the six and the attempted murder of others including officers on duty, and a second act, the murder of three people in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. Both injured officers have regained consciousness; the three at home—a father of 53, a mother of 52, and a sister of 20—had bullet wounds, Sub-Inspector Andrzej Fijołek said, so it is likely they died of gunshot wounds; both acts carry the potential penalty of life imprisonment; and the suspect has not yet been formally arrested because of his medical condition, though he remains under constant surveillance.

Subjective
Augerton, carrying ABC News — Polish prosecutors open a formal terrorism investigation

Updated at 6:56 a.m. ET on November 8: Polish prosecutors opened an investigation Sunday into Saturday’s Kraków shooting and intend to treat it as a terrorist act, Prosecutor Tomasz Waszczuk told ABC News; they are preparing six murder charges, potentially rising to nine if investigators establish the gunman was responsible for the deaths of his parents and sister, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk said were found dead at home. Six people were killed in the attack and more than a dozen wounded, including two police officers; authorities said the attack was likely inspired by far-right ideology; police shot and arrested the suspected gunman, identified in this account as a 25-year-old Polish citizen; and Poland declared two days of mourning.

Subjective
Energy Radio — the Kraków shooting, the running account through Sunday morning

The running account, last updated at 9:40 a.m. UK time on Sunday: six people killed and fifteen injured after a gunman opened fire from a car in and around the Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon; at 9:30 a.m. UK time prosecutors in Kraków said Saturday’s attack will be classified as a terrorist offence, with spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk telling Polish television a formal investigation will be opened on Sunday; the 24-year-old suspect is still in hospital under constant guard and cannot yet be questioned or charged, which prosecutors say may not be possible for hours or days, and he could face life imprisonment; early findings suggest he held a firearms licence, and the investigation will look at how he obtained it, his background, his personal connections, and the events leading up to the attack; Waszczuk has confirmed the detained man is 24-year-old Michał O., according to Polish media, with prosecutors investigating alongside the Internal Security Agency and examining ideological and personal motives; two of Kraków’s carriage drivers are among the most seriously injured; hospitals have appealed for blood donors; bomb disposal experts found no explosives in the suspect’s car; and a Mass for the victims is set for 4 p.m. local time Sunday at St. Mary’s Basilica.

Subjective
Le Monde — Poland in shock after the Kraków mass shooting

Poland woke up on Sunday, November 8, as if thrust into a new era: on Saturday at 3 p.m. in Kraków a man opened fire with an automatic weapon from his car, killing six people and wounding 15 others around the market square in the historic centre, and was arrested a few streets away after a shootout of about 20 minutes. Police identified him as Michał O., a 24-year-old Polish national with no criminal record, from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, 140 kilometres northeast of Kraków; that evening police found the bodies of his parents and sister in the family apartment. Initial findings did not clarify his motives but revealed a young man with radical ideas, in Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński’s account; the Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime joined the investigation to examine media and social-media reports of possible links to radical groups; on Sunday morning prosecutors announced an investigation into an act of terrorism; two officers were wounded, one seriously; and two days of national mourning, Sunday and Monday, run with flags at half-staff, the first political answer expected at the November 11 national holiday.

Subjective
News Central — Poland mourns six killed in the Kraków shooting

Poland began a two-day national mourning period after the shooting in Kraków left six people dead and 15 injured; the Main Market Square remained cordoned off on Sunday as residents laid candles for the victims. Police confirmed a British national was among those killed, with citizens of Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal, and Russia among the injured, according to the PAP agency. Three bodies found at the suspect’s residence in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometres northeast of Kraków, were identified as his parents and sister—a 53-year-old man and two women aged 52 and 21. The suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish national, was shot and wounded by police and remains in critical condition in hospital. Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident as terrorism, although police had not established a motive. Police appealed for blood donations for the officer identified as Jakub Kulik, whom they commended for confronting the armed suspect without hesitation, and investigators quoted by Polish media said the suspect had no previous criminal record.

Subjective
The Levant Files — the Sunday live file: the mandate, the strait, and Riyadh

The live file for Sunday, November 8, updated at 5:34 p.m. Cyprus time: at 5:07 p.m. Cyprus time it heads an entry ‘Herzog Hands Eisenkot the Mandate to Form Israel’s Next Government’; at 2:39 p.m. Cyprus time it reported that the Revolutionary Guards Navy’s tally had risen to three tanker fires in the Strait of Hormuz, the third incident unverified, the ships’ identities unknown, and the United Arab Emirates’ rescue of 22 crew members from a burning cargo ship not yet linked to the tally, with a tanker fire reported off Khasab, Oman, likewise unlinked; the Guards’ spokesman Hossein Mohebbi dismissed Washington’s new Iron Gate task force and said Iran had taken steps to strengthen ties with its neighbours; on Saudi Arabia and Yemen, Qatar condemned the Houthi attacks citing two ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh and called for an immediate halt, Doha reaffirming support for Saudi measures, while the Saudi-led coalition’s Sunday-morning tally stood at five interceptions, the Energy Ministry reported limited debris damage to an Aramco office building and no casualties, and the authorities in Sanaa reported at least 33 killed in Saturday’s strikes near the capital.

Subjective
The Jewish Weekly — Eisenkot asked to form a government by Herzog

President Isaac Herzog’s decision to ask Gadi Eisenkot to form Israel’s next government marks a significant setback for Benjamin Netanyahu, whose existing alliance with Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich cannot simply resume governing on its previous terms, though the result is not yet a settled transfer of power, Israel having produced a parliamentary deadlock. Herzog announced that Eisenkot would receive the mandate on Sunday, November 8, following consultations in which 67 members recommended the Yashar leader against 46 backing Netanyahu, with United Torah Judaism’s seven recommending neither. Once formally entrusted, Eisenkot has 28 days to assemble a government, with a discretionary extension of up to 14; failure does not automatically return Israel to elections, since the president can give another member a further 28 days, and a 21-day parliamentary stage can follow. Eisenkot’s four-party change bloc holds 48 seats; the additional 19 recommendations came from the Arab-led parties.

Subjective
The American Quorum — Herzog chooses Eisenkot to try to form Israel’s next government

Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced Saturday that Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s principal rival, would receive the first opportunity to form a government after an election that left both blocs short of a majority; the formal handover was scheduled for Sunday, November 8, at 5 p.m. in Jerusalem, after which Eisenkot has 28 days to negotiate, with a possible extension of up to 14 days, and Netanyahu remains prime minister while the process proceeds. Herzog’s November 5 statement recorded recommendations for Eisenkot from factions representing 67 lawmakers against 46 for Netanyahu. A recommendation identifies the politician a faction wants to negotiate first; it is not a completed bargain over ministers, policy, or parliamentary support. The October 27 election gave Netanyahu’s bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset and the parties aligned against him, excluding the Arab lists, 48. Israel’s Basic Law establishes the 28-day period and permits extensions totalling no more than 14 days; receiving the mandate is an opportunity to negotiate, not an appointment as prime minister.

Subjective
IANS — Netanyahu faces a major setback as Herzog tasks Eisenkot with forming the government

Jerusalem, November 8: President Isaac Herzog has tasked opposition leader and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot with forming the country’s next government, dealing a significant setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to retain power after the October 27 election. Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, secured the backing of 67 lawmakers in consultations, compared with 46 who recommended Netanyahu; the formal handover was scheduled for Sunday, November 8, at 5 p.m. local time at the President’s Residence in Jerusalem, and Eisenkot will have 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. Sixty-one seats are required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. In this account’s breakdown, Eisenkot received support from 48 lawmakers of the Change Bloc, seven from the Arab party Ra’am, and 12 from the Joint List.

Subjective
India International Times — the Emirates rescue all 22 aboard a burning cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman

The United Arab Emirates Coast Guard rescued all 22 crew members from a cargo ship that caught fire in the Gulf of Oman, the UAE National Guard said Sunday; rescuers answered the crew’s distress call, evacuated everyone aboard, administered first aid, and handed the crew to the authorities, all 22 in stable condition, the vessel unidentified and the fire’s cause unstated. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said Sunday it had received a report that a tanker caught fire on Saturday about eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, and that its crew had been evacuated. In its statement on Saturday’s operation, United States Central Command identified its target as the St. Kitts and Nevis-flagged cargo ship M/V Huda. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said early Sunday that one oil tanker had struck mines east of the strait and a second had hit mines while crossing it, both with navigation and positioning systems switched off and both burning after the explosions; the navy named neither tanker, and its account could not be independently verified.

Subjective
Nation Press — 22 rescued as a cargo ship burns in the Sea of Oman

A cargo ship caught fire in the Sea of Oman on November 8 and the United Arab Emirates Coast Guard brought all 22 crew members to safety, the crew all of Arab nationality and in stable condition after first aid, according to the UAE National Guard, which did not disclose the fire’s cause or the damage. The navy of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said early Sunday that two oil tankers attempting an unauthorised route in the Strait of Hormuz caught fire after striking naval mines, one east of the strait and one crossing it, both with navigation and GPS systems off and both burning, and warned that any vessel cooperating with the American army and entering the unauthorised region would definitely hit naval mines, as reported by Xinhua. United States Central Command said its forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman after the crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times, a military aircraft firing precision munitions at the stern of the St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda after the crew was directed to abandon targeted spaces. The identities of the two tankers in the Guards’ account and their flags have not been officially confirmed.

Subjective
Press TV — the Guards warn they will hit harder if the United States attacks Iran’s vessels

November 8: the Revolutionary Guards warned the United States against attacking Iranian vessels in regional waters, vowing a harsher response to any such move. Spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebi said on Sunday that the war between Iran and the enemy continues on military and economic fronts; reacting to the American military’s newly announced plan to disrupt Iran’s land-based supply routes under its Iron Gate campaign, he said Washington can never achieve the type of economic blockade it is seeking, whatever form it takes. Central Command, which Iran has designated a terrorist organisation, announced on Saturday a new task force to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials; Admiral Brad Cooper said it would reinforce what he described as the success of the American naval blockade of Iran, the task force based in Tampa, Florida, coordinating with other agencies to block Iran’s land borders and Caspian Sea routes. On Sunday, three oil tankers exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after violating Iran’s maritime traffic regulations, in the same account.

Subjective
Crisis Zone — Task Force Iron Gate: Central Command targets Iran’s border routes

Published November 8 at 10:43 a.m.: United States Central Command announced Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday, November 7—a team of about 20 civilian and military personnel at headquarters in Tampa, Florida, whose formation Admiral Brad Cooper directed. A Central Command graphic, quoted by Türkiye Today, says the task force will monitor, detect, and disrupt any illicit movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s borders and the Caspian Sea, the graphic highlighting the borders with Türkiye, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, and Pakistan. Central Command named no crossings, methods, or legal authorities, so its early reach may run through sanctions, banks, and neighbouring capitals. On Sunday, Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi told the Fars agency that the Iron Gate plan is merely a wordplay, Reuters reported. Türkiye Today reported that Iran demands an end to the blockade before it reopens the Strait of Hormuz; no report links Iron Gate to the talks.

Subjective
Fana News, carrying QNA — Qatar strongly condemns the continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

Doha, November 8 (QNA): the State of Qatar condemned in the strongest terms the continued attacks by the Houthi group on several areas of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, most recently the targeting of the city of Riyadh with two ballistic missiles, describing the assaults as shameful, aggressive behaviour, an unacceptable disregard for civilian lives, a flagrant violation of Saudi sovereignty, and a clear breach of the rules of international law. In its Sunday statement the Foreign Ministry stressed Qatar’s categorical rejection of attacks targeting civilians and civilian objects, emphasised the urgent necessity of an immediate halt to these actions, and reaffirmed its support for Saudi measures to protect its security and sovereignty.

Subjective
Reuters — Europeans will join the Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, the French foreign minister says

Paris, November 8: Europeans will participate in talks on Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Sunday. “The Europeans will be well represented; France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these discussions,” Barrot told the radio station RTL. “I can’t tell you yet who will be representing France on this occasion, but France will certainly be there,” he added. American envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday that Washington would bring delegations from Ukraine and Russia together in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 to discuss ending Moscow’s war against Ukraine, post-war security agreements, and de-escalation.

Subjective
Arab News, via Europe Says — Zelensky says Russia is ramping up strikes to pressure Ukraine at the talks

Kyiv: President Volodymyr Zelensky on Saturday accused Russia of ramping up strikes across his country in order to pressure Ukraine and its allies at the American-brokered talks scheduled for next week. The latest barrage came ahead of another joint effort with partners to reinvigorate negotiations, he said: “By intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and our infrastructure at this very moment, Russia is trying to additionally lay the groundwork for putting pressure on Ukraine’s position and that of its partners.” Russia has continued to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure despite renewed diplomatic efforts, which will see American, Russian, and Ukrainian officials hold trilateral meetings in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. Zelensky had warned on Friday that more attacks on the energy sector and civilian infrastructure were imminent, and said on social media that Russia had launched 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones in a combined attack; Russia is preparing for the trilateral talks by launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, he said.

Subjective
Devdiscourse, carrying Reuters — a judge orders Paraguay’s ex-president Peña held before trial

Updated November 8: a Paraguayan judge on Saturday ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility while prosecutors investigate his ties to the digital lender Ueno, whose collapse has left millions of customers struggling to access their accounts. Judge Humberto Otazú ordered Peña, who has been charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain, held at the facility, saying detention was necessary to ensure he remained in the country while the case proceeded. The detention, a day after Peña’s removal from office, deepens a political and financial crisis that has prompted protests in Asunción, swept up senior officials, and led regulators to try to contain risks to the wider financial system. Peña’s attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists that Peña was pleading not guilty. Otazú also ordered former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo to pretrial detention in a holding centre, and Peña had arrived at the Attorney General’s Office earlier on Saturday to appear before prosecutors following his removal from power on Friday.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate results in Mississippi and Alaska

The explainer, republished on Sunday, November 8, sets out why the final two Senate contests remain uncalled: as it stands, the Democrats will usher in the 120th Congress on January 3 with a majority of at least 54 seats. In Mississippi the race between the incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, and Scott Colom proved tighter than expected, both holding about 49 percent with 96 percent of ballots counted; as of Wednesday night—the explainer’s own date—Colom was leading by 1,138 votes, with a few thousand provisional and mail-in absentee ballots left; Secretary of State Michael Watson counted roughly 3,600 mail-in ballots still to be tallied with an unknown number of affidavit ballots, and wrote that counties have 10 days from the election to submit certified results, which is November 13. In Alaska, Mary Peltola leads Dan Sullivan by 637 votes as of Wednesday night according to the Associated Press, nearly a quarter of the votes remain uncounted, the state’s ranked-choice system publishes its tabulation 15 days after the election, on November 18, and a second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher, has drawn more votes than the margin.

Subjective
Election Central — Alaska and Mississippi Senate race update: they are still counting votes

Four days after Election Day, two Senate races remain unresolved and remarkably close. In Mississippi, Scott Colom continues to hold a lead of roughly 2,500 votes over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the latest Associated Press count putting Colom at about 49.1 percent and Hyde-Smith at 48.8 with the independent Ty Pinkins just over 2 percent; all Election Day precincts have reported, the Associated Press estimated Friday afternoon that roughly 30,000 ballots could still be outstanding statewide, mail ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive through November 10, and counties have until November 13 to report certified totals including affidavit ballots. In Alaska, Mary Peltola leads Senator Dan Sullivan by only 637 votes in the latest AP count, 48.2 percent to 47.9, with roughly 74 percent of the expected vote reported; the remaining vote includes absentee ballots, ballots from remote communities, and votes from Alaskans living or serving overseas; the AP will continue to update as ballots are processed, state officials target November 18 for the ranked-choice tabulation if no candidate reaches a majority, and neither candidate is above 50 percent. A second candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has received about 3,600 first-choice votes, far more than the current margin.

Subjective
Seoul Economic Daily — the Japan quake rattles Shizuoka with its strongest shaking in 107 years

Western Shizuoka Prefecture recorded shaking of upper 5 on the Japanese intensity scale for the first time in 107 years, and Aichi its strongest in 29 years. According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, a magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck western Shizuoka at about 1:04 a.m. on the 8th, its focus at a depth of 40 kilometres, with no tsunami threat identified. Injuries were reported across the area: according to NHK and other broadcasters, at least 12 people in Aichi Prefecture were hurt after falling or striking their heads, and three more were injured in Shizuoka—15 in all. At an early-morning news conference the agency said caution was needed for about a week against quakes of up to upper 5 intensity, the likelihood of a large earthquake particularly high over the next two to three days, while it assessed the quake as unlikely to lead to the Nankai Trough megaquake Japan has long feared, and train services were disrupted.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — a strong earthquake shakes central Japan, injuring at least 22

A strong earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday, shattering store windows, causing people to flee buildings, and leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media. The Meteorological Agency put the quake’s magnitude at 5.7, while the United States Geological Survey reported it at magnitude 5.5. The quake struck at 1:04 a.m., about 40 kilometres below the surface in Shizuoka Prefecture; no tsunami warning was issued; authorities reported no deaths; the quake shattered storefront windows, knocked items off shelves, and caused transport disruption in parts of the country.

Subjective
Invest News Week, a LinkedIn newsletter — Nasdaq enters correction, Brent falls, American jobs surge

Issue No. 10, November 8, 2026: since last week, three signals changed rapidly, and oil delivered a dramatic reversal—Brent ended the week before at $117.64 a barrel and this Friday settled at $98.32, a fall of about 17 percent over the week, its steepest percentage fall since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, while West Texas Intermediate finished at $90.83, down around 13 percent for the week. Expectations of possible de-escalation in the Iran conflict removed part of the geopolitical premium, although tanker attacks around the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz mean supply risk has not disappeared. The newsletter’s other signals: the Nasdaq entered correction, American jobs surged, India’s market rallied 8.8 percent, and Korean chip exports jumped 259 percent.

Subjective
Saudi Moments — Saudi gold, oil, and riyal rates for November 8, 2026

The Sunday-morning market snapshot for November 8, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Saudi time: Brent crude at $98.32 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate at $90.83, both identified as Friday, November 6, American market close—the latest confirmed settlement prices available for Sunday’s Saudi market opening, not live Sunday quotes. Oil enters the new week below $100 following substantial volatility in international energy markets, and the day’s focus is Saudi markets beginning a new trading week as investors assess oil-price volatility, regional developments, and the outlook for business activity. Gold prices and Saudi riyal exchange rates for the day are carried in the same snapshot.

Subjective
The Daily Jagran — Muhurat trading 2026: the Sensex rises 400 points, the Nifty crosses 25,100

The Indian stock market opened with significant gains during the special Muhurat trading session on Sunday, November 8—the market ordinarily closed on Sundays, opened for Diwali, with trading from 2:20 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. Indian time marking the beginning of Samvat 2083. The session’s account, published at 4:28 p.m. Indian time, carries the Sensex up 400 points to 81,406 and the Nifty across 25,100, with Tata Steel and Sun Pharma among the top gainers. The exchanges conduct the annual session on Diwali for Laxmi Pujan; the Multi Commodity Exchange held its own Muhurat window in the same hours.

entry.title: Deportation in America: Visa Overstays, Removal Orders, and How the Law Actually Works
entry.summary: How deportation actually works in American law: unlawful presence as a civil matter, the notice-to-appear ladder, voluntary departure against the reentry bars, the overstay counts, the criminal-removal shares year by year, the exposure a long-settled resident carries, and what naturalization is in the statute. Filed cold, closing in a four-column ledger.
entry.content:
Special Report

The Removal File — Status, Process, and the Counts

Objective

Deportation in America: Visa Overstays, Removal Orders, and How the Law Actually Works

Deportation in the United States is an administrative process, not a criminal sentence: being present without status is a civil violation, while entering improperly and reentering after removal are federal crimes, and the system runs on that seam. Its caseload is majority non-criminal in the recent record—two-thirds of fiscal 2024 removals involved no criminal conviction or pending charge—its court backlog stands above three million cases, more than 1.4 million people carry final removal orders unenforced, and the statute that governs it, at the removability stage, asks nothing about whether the person removed is good. The desk files the law, the process, the counts, and the error file, in that order.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1115 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026.

The File in Brief

The desk has no position on immigration policy in this file, for or against, and this report is written from that position: the law, the process, and the counts, with every side’s claims tested by the same instrument. On the verified record: unlawful presence in the United States is a civil violation, not a crime; improper entry (8 U.S.C. §1325) and reentry after removal (§1326) are crimes; and removal itself is an administrative proceeding under the Immigration and Nationality Act, run through two statute lists—the grounds of inadmissibility at INA §212, applied to people seeking entry, and the grounds of deportability at INA §237, applied to people already admitted. The standard track runs from a notice to appear through master calendar and merits hearings before an immigration judge, with appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals, and three faster tracks run beside it: expedited removal at the border and, since January 2025, by designation nationwide; administrative removal for aggravated felons without a judge; and reinstatement of an old order without a new hearing. The consequences are tiered by how a person leaves: a removal order carries reentry bars of five, ten, or twenty years under INA §212(a)(9)(A), permanent for aggravated felons, while voluntary departure—taken before or after proceedings conclude, under different conditions—carries no removal-order bar, though the separate three- and ten-year unlawful-presence bars at §212(a)(9)(B) turn on time accrued, not on the manner of leaving. The counts: ICE removed 271,484 people in fiscal 2024, of whom 88,763, or 32.7 percent, had criminal convictions or pending charges; the no-criminal-history share of removals has risen every recent year, reaching roughly two-thirds in 2024 and higher in 2025 by independent reconstruction, and in ICE’s interior enforcement—arrests away from the border—the criminal share runs the other way, about 93 percent of interior removals in fiscal 2024. The overstay, not the border crossing, has been the larger source of new unauthorized residents since about 2007 by the Center for Migration Studies’ estimates: the Department of Homeland Security counted 538,548 suspected overstay events in fiscal 2024 against 46.7 million expected departures, a rate of 1.15 percent, with Mexico, Colombia, India, and Canada the largest counts and European visa-waiver states contributing about 61,000 suspected overstays against 1,540 European removals in the last full yearbook year. The system holding these cases is backlogged and exposed: 3,037,800 cases pending in immigration court at the end of September 2026 by TRAC’s count, an estimated 1.6 million people on ICE’s non-detained docket carrying final orders, 65,765 people in detention on a July 2026 count of whom 70.6 percent had no criminal conviction, and a resident population of lawful permanent residents whose exposure to the deportability grounds never expires—a conviction from the third year of a forty-year residence is chargeable in the thirty-seventh, because the statute carries no limitations period and only naturalization ends the exposure. The public, polled by Pew and Gallup in 2025, holds a model the statute does not contain—65 percent for a requirements-based path to stay, 97 percent of the selective majority for deporting the violent, 15 percent for deporting the employed—in the language of this report, a ripening doctrine whose only living statutory relative is cancellation of removal’s ten-year presence rule and whose ancestor, the 1986 legalization, has not been rerun; and the precarity the system manufactures is a priced commodity in adjudicated fact, from smuggling fees of $6,500 to $18,000 a person in the sentencing records, through the sanitation contractors’ child-labor judgments, the $14 million Signal verdict, and the $65.5 million au pair settlement, to the lawful tether of the H-1B and the 1.1-million-deep Indian green-card queue. The desk closes the file with the definitions the argument uses loosely—naturalization is a statutory process with stated requirements, not a ripening of residence into entitlement—and with the error file, in which the government’s own auditors have documented citizens arrested, detained, and removed, graded by the same instrument as every other claim in the report.

1. The Legal Architecture: A Civil System with Criminal Edges

Presence is civil; entry is criminal; the distinction organizes the whole system. A noncitizen who is present in the United States without lawful status commits no federal crime by being present. The Supreme Court stated the point in Arizona v. United States, 567 U.S. 387 (2012): “As a general rule, it is not a crime for a removable alien to remain present in the United States.” What the criminal code reaches is conduct at the border and after removal. Improper entry—crossing at an undesignated place, evading inspection, or entering on false documents—is a federal misdemeanor for a first offense under 8 U.S.C. §1325, punishable by up to six months, and a felony on repetition. Reentry after a removal order is a felony under §1326, punishable by up to two years, rising to ten years after removal following certain convictions and twenty years after an aggravated felony. Removal itself—the process the public vocabulary calls deportation—is neither: it is an administrative proceeding conducted by the executive branch, in which the respondent has the right to counsel at no expense to the government, no right to a jury, and a burden structure set by statute rather than by the criminal standard. Since the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, the proceeding has had one name: “removal,” which merged the old exclusion and deportation tracks into a single process under INA §240.

Two lists in the statute book decide who may enter and who must leave, and they are not the same list. INA §212(a) (8 U.S.C. §1182(a)) states the grounds of inadmissibility—the charges applied to a person seeking admission at a port of entry, applying for a visa, or, in specified circumstances, adjusting status or returning from travel. INA §237(a) (8 U.S.C. §1227(a)) states the grounds of deportability—the charges applied to a person who was admitted and is now alleged to have forfeited the admission. The deportability list, which is the operative one for residents, runs in classes: persons inadmissible at the time of entry or adjustment; persons present without admission or parole; persons who violated the conditions of their status, including failure to maintain student or exchange status; persons who fail to register a change of address; document fraud and false claims to citizenship; and the criminal classes at §237(a)(2)—crimes involving moral turpitude, aggravated felonies, high-speed flight, controlled-substance offenses, firearms offenses, and crimes of domestic violence, stalking, and child abuse or neglect. Which list governs a given person is a threshold litigation point in real cases, because the burdens differ: in deportability cases the government must prove alienage and the ground by clear and convincing evidence; in inadmissibility postures the applicant bears more of the burden. The architecture is therefore dual by design—one list for the door, one list for the house—and much of the case law in this field is argument about which list a particular life falls under.

The visa and the status are different instruments, and confusing them misreads the overstay problem. A visa is a travel document: it permits the holder to present at a port of entry during its validity window. Status is the authorization to remain, and its clock is set at admission, on the Form I-94 record, by the inspecting officer—typically six months for a B-2 visitor, the duration of a course for an F-1 student, a fixed term for a worker. A traveler may hold a visa valid for ten years and a status that expires in six months; overstaying the status is the violation, and the visa’s printed dates do not extend it. Three consequences follow in the statute. Under INA §222(g), the visa of a person who overstays is void automatically, by operation of law, and a future visa may be sought only in the home country absent exceptional circumstances. Unlawful presence begins accruing the day after the status expires (or the day after an immigration judge or the agency so finds), and it is the accrual, not the overstay itself, that arms the reentry bars in section 5 below. And the overstay converts the person’s posture from the deportability list to a hybrid: overstays are charged as present without admission or in violation of status, and if they later seek to adjust or reenter, the inadmissibility list—including its unlawful-presence bars—applies to them in full.

2. The Ladder: From Notice to Appear to the Plane

The standard track begins with a charging document and runs through a court that is not a court of the judiciary. Proceedings open when the Department of Homeland Security files a Notice to Appear (Form I-862) with the immigration court and serves it on the respondent, stating the charges from the two lists. The immigration courts belong to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, a component of the Department of Justice; their judges—557 of them by USAFacts’ 2026 count, down from a peak of 735 in fiscal 2024—are executive-branch adjudicators, and the department’s own prosecutors, ICE trial attorneys, argue the government’s side. The first hearing is the master calendar hearing: pleadings are taken, the respondent admits or denies the charges, counsel is sought—at the respondent’s expense; there is no appointed counsel in removal proceedings—and applications for relief are identified. The case then moves to an individual, or merits, hearing: testimony, evidence, cross-examination, and a decision from the bench or in writing. Either side may appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals within thirty days; a further petition for review lies to the federal circuit court, and removal is ordinarily stayed while a timely petition is litigated. When the Board’s order becomes administratively final and no stay is in force, the order is a final order of removal, and its execution passes to ICE.

The ladder has branch points, and every branch is a form of relief with statutory elements. An asylum application (INA §208) asks for protection on account of race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or particular social group, with a one-year filing deadline and statutory bars; withholding of removal (§241(b)(3)) and protection under the Convention Against Torture run beside it on a higher burden and confer no path to a green card. Cancellation of removal (§240A) is the long-resident’s branch: for a lawful permanent resident, seven years of continuous residence and no aggravated felony; for a non-resident, ten years of physical presence, good moral character, and exceptional and extremely unusual hardship to a qualifying citizen or resident relative, under an annual cap of 4,000 grants for the non-resident form. Adjustment of status (§245) converts the proceeding into a grant where an immigrant visa is immediately available and the applicant is admissible. Waivers—§212(h) for certain criminal and fraud grounds among them—excuse specified inadmissibility. A respondent who concedes removability and asks for none of this may instead ask the judge for voluntary departure, the branch treated in section 5. A respondent who does not appear receives an order in absentia under §240(b)(5), entered on proof of written notice; it may be rescinded on a motion to reopen for lack of notice or exceptional circumstances, and it carries the final order’s full consequences plus a ten-year bar on most relief. Each branch is charged, pled, and proven like a claim, because that is what it is: the ladder is not a conveyor but a decision tree, and the overwhelming majority of its traffic is resolved at the branches, not at the top.

Three faster tracks run beside the court track, and most removals never see a judge. Expedited removal (INA §235(b)(1)) authorizes a DHS officer, without a hearing, to order removed a person who arrives without documents or with fraudulent ones; the 1996 statute permits its application to persons already inside the country who cannot prove two years of continuous presence, and by designation it was long confined to ports of entry and the border zone before the designation was extended nationwide in January 2025—an expansion that has been litigated since, with the litigation continuing at filing. A person who expresses fear of return is routed to a credible-fear screening and, if the screening is passed, into the court track; a negative screening is reviewable by an immigration judge on request. Administrative removal (§238(b)) applies to non-residents convicted of an aggravated felony: the agency itself issues the order, with notice and a chance to rebut, and no immigration judge sits. Reinstatement (§241(a)(5)) applies to a person who reentered after a prior removal: the old order is reinstated on the agency’s finding of identity and the prior order, “not subject to being reopened or reviewed,” and the person may be removed on it directly. Stipulated orders, in which the respondent waives the hearing in writing, complete the set. The arithmetic of the system follows from the tracks: in any recent year the majority of formal removals are executed through the fast tracks at and near the border, while the court track—the ladder the public picture shows—carries the minority and accumulates the backlog recorded in section 12.

Between the final order and the plane stands an enforcement apparatus with its own queue. ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations directorate executes final orders. Its non-detained docket—persons in proceedings or under orders but not in custody—stood above 7.6 million at the end of fiscal 2024 by ICE’s annual report and at 7.3 million in February 2026 by the Congressional Research Service’s estimate, of whom an estimated 1.6 million carry final orders (the figure stood at 1,445,549 in November 2024). Persons under orders who are not detained report on orders of supervision—scheduled check-ins at field offices, in person or, increasingly since 2025, through reporting applications—and receive letters directing them to present for removal on a date, with travel documents requested from consulates in the interval; a passport or laissez-passer from the country of nationality is ordinarily required before a removal flight can be boarded, and uncooperative consulates are a standing mechanical bottleneck the statute answers with visa sanctions under INA §243(d), invoked against a rotating list of states. Persons who do not report are classified absconders and assigned to fugitive operations teams for arrest. Detention, where it is used, is civil custody in a network of county jails and contract facilities; the average daily population and the counts are filed in section 12. The ladder thus ends not in a single act but in a logistics chain—order, documents, custody or compliance, flight—each link of which has its own failure modes, which is why final orders outstanding are counted in the millions and removals in the hundreds of thousands.

3. Status Killers: What Voids a Life Built Here

For the lawful permanent resident, deportability is a defined list, and the list is mostly a criminal code annex. A green-card holder is removable under §237(a)(2) on conviction of: an aggravated felony, at any time after admission; one crime involving moral turpitude committed within five years of admission for which a sentence of one year or longer may be imposed, or two such crimes at any time not arising from a single scheme; a controlled-substance offense, with exactly one exception in the statute—a single offense of simple possession of thirty grams or less of marijuana; a firearms offense; or a crime of domestic violence, stalking, child abuse, neglect, or abandonment, or violation of a protection order. The aggravated-felony term, defined at §101(a)(43), is the broadest instrument in the book and the least matched to its name: it includes murder, rape, and drug trafficking, and also theft or burglary with a sentence imposed of one year—a suspended year counts, under §101(a)(48)(B)—fraud or deceit with a loss to the victim over $10,000, tax evasion, commercial bribery, obstruction of justice, failure to appear, and, since Sessions v. Dimaya, 584 U.S. 148 (2018) voided the residual clause, a “crime of violence” only as the elements of the offense define one. Non-criminal grounds run beside the convictions: the admitted smuggler of another person (including, on the inadmissibility side, one who helped a family member enter), the person who falsely claimed citizenship, the person who voted unlawfully, the person who failed to register an address change, and the resident who, by conduct, abandoned the residence itself—a surrender that can be found in long absences, a home and job established abroad, and is formalized on Form I-407. None of these grounds inquires into the person’s record of work, family, tax compliance, or service; those inquiries live entirely on the relief side of the ledger, in section 9 below.

A resident’s travel is itself a screening event, governed by a provision the frequent flyer rarely meets until it is read to him. Under §101(a)(13)(C), a returning permanent resident is ordinarily not treated as seeking admission—the doctrine that descends from Rosenberg v. Fleuti, 374 U.S. 449 (1963), codified and narrowed in 1996—unless one of six conditions holds: he abandoned or relinquished the status; he was absent more than 180 days; he engaged in illegal activity after departing; he left while in proceedings; he committed an offense listed at §212(a)(2); or he is attempting entry without inspection. If any condition holds, the return is processed as an application for admission, the inadmissibility list replaces the deportability list, and grounds that could not touch him at home—including the public-charge ground at §212(a)(4) and the health-related grounds—are in play at the airport. Parallel machinery reaches the nonimmigrant: under §221(i), a consular officer or the Secretary of State may revoke a visa at any time, in discretion, and the State Department’s practice of prudential revocation—revoking on notice of an arrest, effective on the holder’s next attempt to travel, often without notice until then—means a visa can die before its holder learns it has. Status, in short, is not a possession but a standing, renewed at every border crossing, every filing, and every arrest report that crosses the desk.

The drunk-driving case states the current law exactly, and it is the opposite of the common account. A single ordinary DUI conviction is, under current federal law, not a ground of deportability for a permanent resident, and not a ground of inadmissibility either. The Supreme Court held unanimously in Leocal v. Ashcroft, 543 U.S. 1 (2004), that a state DUI offense—there, one causing serious bodily injury, committed with criminal negligence—is not a “crime of violence,” because the offense does not require the active use of force; it therefore cannot be an aggravated felony, the ground that would make removal near-automatic. The Board of Immigration Appeals held in Matter of Lopez-Meza, 22 I&N Dec. 1188 (BIA 1999), that ordinary DUI is not a crime involving moral turpitude, because the offense as commonly defined carries no corrupt or fraudulent intent; the same decision found turpitude in the aggravated variant before it—driving under the influence while knowing one’s license was suspended or revoked—because the knowing violation of the licensing order supplied the element the plain offense lacks. The edges, where DUI does become fatal to status, are specific and printable: drugs in the offense move it into the controlled-substance ground, which has no de minimis exception for a DUI formulation; a child endangered in the car changes the CIMT and child-abuse analysis; injury and flight stack further offenses onto the plea; repeat convictions operate on the discretionary side—under Matter of Castillo-Perez, 27 I&N Dec. 664 (A.G. 2019), two or more DUI convictions raise a presumption against the good moral character that cancellation of removal and naturalization require; a DUI history routes visa applicants and returning residents into the health-related screening at §212(a)(1)(A)(iii), under which alcohol abuse associated with harmful behavior is a ground of inadmissibility administered through panel physicians; and the State Department prudentially revokes the nonimmigrant visa on the arrest itself, before any conviction. The legislative proposal to close the gap between the common account and the law is pending and is filed as pending: H.R. 875, the Jeremy and Angel Seay and Sergeant Brandon Mendoza Protect Our Communities from DUIs Act, would add DUI to both lists—a new inadmissibility ground at §212(a)(2)(J) reaching convictions and admissions alike, and a deportability ground at §237(a)(2)(G)—with no misdemeanor exception, no waiver, and no limit on the age of the conviction. It passed the House on June 26, 2025, by 246 to 160, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the next day, and no Senate action is recorded as of filing; a narrower companion aimed at undocumented drivers in fatal and serious-injury crashes was introduced in April 2026. As the law stands on the day of this report, the resident who drives drunk once has committed a crime the state will punish; he has not, by that act alone, forfeited the green card.

4. The Criminal Sequence: Jail First, Then the Airport

The sequence for the convicted runs in the order the public phrase reverses. A noncitizen arrested on a criminal charge is booked, and the booking fingerprints are shared with the Department of Homeland Security as a matter of automated routine. If ICE elects to act, it lodges a detainer (Form I-247A) asking the jail to notify the agency before release and to hold the person up to forty-eight hours beyond the release the criminal case has ordered. The criminal case proceeds first and on its own clock: plea or trial, then the sentence, served in full or as the court directs. Only at the end of that sequence—at release from criminal custody—does the detainer bite and the transfer to ICE custody occur. Removal proceedings, where a hearing is required, run after or, in detained practice, alongside the end of the sentence; for the aggravated felon the administrative track of section 2 substitutes. ICE’s own terminology for the pipeline is the Criminal Apprehension Program and its jail-based predecessors; the mechanical point the desk files is that the deportation facility is not an alternative to the jail in the convicted person’s itinerary. It is the last stop after the jail, and the share of removals drawn from this pipeline is a measured quantity, printed next.

The criminal share of removals is a series with a trend, and the trend runs against the frame in both directions. The desk prints the ICE series as the agency and its critics publish it, with the definitions attached, because the definitions move the number more than the operations do. In fiscal 2013, ICE’s own report counted 368,644 removals, of which 59 percent—216,810—were of persons previously convicted of a crime; of the 133,551 interior removals, 82 percent were convicted criminals. In fiscal 2015, the interior convicted share reached 91 percent while the overall convicted share held at 59 percent. In fiscal 2023, of 142,580 ICE removals, about 49 percent—69,902—involved criminal charges or convictions. In fiscal 2024, of 271,484 removals, 88,763—32.7 percent—had criminal histories, that category bundling convictions with pending charges; the interior cut of the same year inverts the headline: of 47,732 interior removals, 36,279 were of convicted persons and 8,028 of persons with pending charges—93 percent criminal-involved—while only 3,425 were of other immigration violators, because interior enforcement is fed by the jail pipeline and the fugitive docket, and the border fast tracks, which produce the bulk of the total, process recent entrants who carry no American criminal record to count. In fiscal 2025, independent reconstructions from ICE’s biweekly releases put total removals at about 320,000 to 329,000, and the Migration Policy Institute and others record the convicted share falling to the lowest of the modern series; the department’s separate public claim of 622,000 deportations since January 20, 2025, issued in December 2025, aggregates categories beyond ICE removals and is filed in the ledger as a claim whose methodology is not comparable to the series here. The detention snapshot agrees with the direction: of the people booked into ICE detention in November 2025, the Cato Institute’s analysis of ICE data counted 73 percent with no criminal conviction and 5 percent with a violent conviction. The “eighty percent non-criminal” figure that circulates in the argument matches no official series the desk could locate; the measured series runs from 41 percent non-convicted of all removals in fiscal 2013 to roughly two-thirds without conviction-or-charge in fiscal 2024, higher still in 2025—the direction of the claim is the direction of the record, at magnitudes the record states more precisely than the claim does.

5. Leaving: Voluntary Departure, Self-Deportation, and the Bars

American law prices departure by its form, and the price list is written in three subsections of §212(a)(9). A person removed under an order is inadmissible for five years if removed on arrival, ten years if removed after proceedings or having departed under an order, twenty years after a second or subsequent removal, and permanently if convicted of an aggravated felony—§212(a)(9)(A), with consent to reapply (Form I-212) the only door before the term runs. A person who accrued more than 180 days of unlawful presence and then departs—in any manner, including under a removal order or entirely unobserved—is barred for three years; more than a year of unlawful presence, ten years—§212(a)(9)(B), the departure itself being the trigger that arms the bar. A person who accrued an aggregate year of unlawful presence, or was removed, and then reenters or attempts reentry without admission is permanently inadmissible under §212(a)(9)(C), waivable only after ten years spent abroad. These bars stack: a long-term overstayer removed under an order ordinarily carries both the removal bar and the unlawful-presence bar, and each must expire or be waived on its own terms. Against this schedule stands the voluntary forms. Voluntary departure under §240B, granted by an immigration judge, is an order permitting departure at the person’s own expense by a set date in place of removal: requested before or at the master calendar stage, it may run up to 120 days and requires only removability conceded and ability to depart; requested after proceedings conclude, it is capped at sixty days and conditioned on good moral character, a clean recent record, a departure bond, and travel documents in hand—and in both forms, a person who departs on time carries no removal order, and therefore no §212(a)(9)(A) bar, while a person who accepts voluntary departure and does not leave is converted to a removal order by statute, fined, and barred from most relief for ten years. At the border itself, withdrawal of an application for admission and voluntary return dispose of arriving cases without orders at all. The framing that voluntary departure “preserves the ability to apply again” against removal’s forfeiture is therefore correct in structure and requires one filing correction: voluntary departure avoids the removal-order bars and the removal record, but it does not erase the unlawful-presence bars of §212(a)(9)(B), which turn on accrued time and are armed by any departure at all—the long-term overstayer who leaves voluntarily at year ten has preserved his channels and still serves the ten-year bar, absent a waiver.

“Self-deportation” is the policy name for inducing the voluntary forms at scale, and its 2025 instrument and its headline count grade differently. The instrument is documented: the CBP Home application, repurposed in 2025 to register intent to depart, with travel assistance and a $1,000 stipend offered to those who depart through it, inside a public campaign whose stated object is to make the voluntary forms the rational choice against the bars of the involuntary one. The count is a claim: the Department of Homeland Security announced in October 2025 that 1.6 million people had self-deported since January 20, 2025, and raised the figure to 1.9 million in December. The department has published no line-by-line methodology; reporting on the figure traces it to estimates of foreign-born population decline built from Current Population Survey data—the Center for Immigration Studies’ survey analysis, whose own authors describe it as a preliminary estimate from imperfect data—rather than to a count of departures. The counted instruments run orders of magnitude lower: the Deportation Data Project’s tabulation of the courts’ records shows 6,118 grants of voluntary departure between January 20 and July 29, 2025, and analysts put application-confirmed departures through CBP Home in the tens of thousands for the year. The desk files the mechanism as verified, the incentive as verified, and the million-scale count as claimed-but-unproven, in the ledger below—the same column, the reader will note, as the largest claims of the other side.

6. The Comparative Ledger: Windows Are the World Norm

Every state on the desk’s shelf grants the visitor a window and attaches consequences to outstaying it; the United States is unexceptional in kind and specific only in its numbers. The Schengen area—twenty-nine European states, including non-EU members Switzerland (a member since 2008), Norway, and Iceland—admits the visa-exempt short-stay visitor for ninety days in any 180-day period, and the clock is cumulative: it is a rolling window counted backward from each day of presence, so a departure does not reset it, and the traveler who has spent ninety days inside must spend ninety outside before the arithmetic admits him again; the popular border-hop reading of the rule is a misreading, and the strategy sometimes built on it—sitting out the clock in a nearby non-member state—works only where the waiting state is genuinely outside the area, as the United Kingdom and Ireland are, and fails where it is not, as Switzerland is not outside it. Overstay consequences inside the area include fines, recorded alerts, and entry bans that vary by state from months to years. Canada admits the ordinary visitor for up to six months as stamped or presumed at entry, extendable on application. Common grants elsewhere run thirty days (much of Southeast Asia’s visa-exempt practice), ninety days (Japan, Brazil, and the Schengen norm), and six months (the United Kingdom’s standard visitor, Canada, and the United States’ own B-2). Where clocks are per-entry rather than cumulative—in the thirty-day regimes—the visa run is a real institution, with its border towns and same-day return buses, and states that tire of it convert to cumulative counting or per-year caps, which is the direction of travel in the systems the desk examined. The structure is everywhere the same three parts: a window, an accounting, and a price for exceeding both.

Germany’s file is the desk’s exhibit of the accounting run as routine administration. A person who takes up residence registers the address with the municipal office—the Anmeldung, due within fourteen days of moving in, producing the registration certificate on which the rest of German administrative life depends: bank account, tax class, health insurance, the residence file itself. The non-European who stays beyond the Schengen short-stay window holds a residence permit, the Aufenthaltserlaubnis, issued for a stated purpose—work, study, family—by the local foreigners’ authority, time-limited, renewable on the purpose continuing, and ripening toward a settlement permit on years, language, and contributions. Nothing in the arrangement is ceremonial: it is a ledger of who is present, on what basis, until when, kept by clerks, and its premise—that presence in the territory is an accounted condition rather than a default—is the premise of every system in this section, including the American one. The desk files the comparison without a moral: the states differ in window length, in ripening rules, and in the price of the overage, and they do not differ in keeping the ledger.

7. The Overstay Category: The Larger Half of the Flow

The Department of Homeland Security counts the overstay every year, and the count is the largest single exhibit in this report. The Entry/Exit Overstay Report for fiscal 2024 records 46,657,108 expected departures of nonimmigrant visitors arriving by air and sea, and 538,548 overstay events—a total overstay rate of 1.15 percent—of which 482,954 were suspected in-country overstays at the report’s close, a figure that had fallen to 427,204 by February 2025 as late departures and status adjustments resolved. The largest national counts are Mexico (61,442), Colombia (28,409), India (27,585), and Canada (25,309, at a rate of only 0.27 percent of Canadian departures); the visa-waiver states’ suspected in-country rate is 0.43 percent, the non-waiver rate excluding Canada and Mexico 2.22 percent, and the student and exchange categories (F, M, J) run at 2.45 percent, while the highest rates belong to small programs—Myanmar at 43 percent, Suriname at 31, Haiti at 25—where a few thousand admissions produce the percentage. The category’s weight is in the accumulation: the Center for Migration Studies has estimated, in a series of studies running back a decade, that overstays have exceeded entries without inspection among new additions to the unauthorized population in every year since about 2007, reaching roughly three-fifths of new additions in peak years and about 40 percent of the newly unauthorized in fiscal 2023—which is to say, the characteristic modern entrant into unlawful status is a person who arrived inspected, with a visa, and stayed past the date on the I-94. The stock figures bound the flow: the Pew Research Center’s estimate puts the unauthorized population at about 14 million in 2023, a record, against about 11 million in the department’s own earlier series—estimates, both, built from census residuals, and filed as estimates wherever this report repeats them.

8. Exposure Over Time: The Resident’s Ledger of Tripwires

Consider the resident the system actually holds: admitted lawfully, employed for decades, remitting wages, raising citizen children—and carrying, for every day of those decades, the full deportability list of section 3. His exposure is not a mood but an inventory, and the desk files the inventory as he accumulates it. The moral-turpitude rules run on two clocks: one CIMT committed within five years of admission, on a charge carrying a possible year’s sentence, is a ground; two CIMTs not from a single scheme are a ground at any time. The aggravated-felony definition runs on sentence arithmetic: a theft or burglary plea with one year imposed—suspended in full, served not a day—is inside it, as is a fraud with $10,001 of loss and a drug offense that the charging statute calls trafficking at quantities the street calls personal. The controlled-substance ground admits one exception and one only, the single thirty-gram marijuana possession case. The domestic-violence ground, §237(a)(2)(E), reaches crimes against a protected person and violations of protection orders, and its definitions are litigated household by household. The false-claim ground—a claim to citizenship made for a purpose or benefit, on a driver’s license form or an I-9 as readily as at a naturalization interview—carries, on the inadmissibility side, a bar with no general waiver, relieved only by a narrow exception for the child of citizens who reasonably believed the claim. Unlawful voting is its own ground on both lists. Alien smuggling includes driving a relative across or paying his guide, subject to a discretionary family waiver on one list and not the other. The address-registration ground is rarely charged and entirely on the books. Abandonment can be found in the pattern of his trips home. And overlaying the whole inventory, the disposition of his case if charged depends on relief whose elements—good moral character above all—are themselves forfeited by entries in the same inventory. No single line is exotic; the exposure is the sum, carried without expiry.

The bar fight is the cleanest test of the inventory, and the desk runs it as the record runs it: the same night ends in three different countries of outcome depending on the charge, the plea, and the sentence. Simple assault—an ordinary fight, no weapon, no serious injury—is generally not a crime involving moral turpitude, because the offense requires no intent to steal, defraud, or commit an inherently base act; the immigration courts have found turpitude where the statute adds an aggravator: a weapon, intent to injure seriously, a protected victim. It is likewise not an aggravated felony as a “crime of violence” unless the offense is a felony under the elements clause of 18 U.S.C. §16 as preserved by Dimaya and the term of imprisonment imposed is at least one year—imposed, again, not served, the suspended year counting in full. The hinges are therefore clerical: whether the prosecutor charges the simple or the aggravated form; whether the plea is taken to assault, to disorderly conduct, to a theft count offered in substitution; whether the sentence negotiated is 364 days or 365—a distinction with no meaning in the criminal court’s own purposes and the whole meaning in the immigration court’s. A resident of forty years who pleads to a misdemeanor assault with a 364-day suspended sentence has ordinarily bought a criminal record and kept his residence; the same man, pleading to the same conduct on a differently drawn statute with a year imposed, has purchased an aggravated felony, mandatory detention, ineligibility for nearly all relief, and removal under the administrative track without a merits hearing on his equities. Between those two outcomes stands no finding about the man. There stands a charging document and a sentencing line.

Most charging documents are written in plea negotiations, and until 2010 the immigration consequences were not required to be in the room. In Padilla v. Kentucky, 559 U.S. 356 (2010), the Supreme Court held that the Sixth Amendment requires defense counsel to advise a noncitizen client when a plea carries a risk of deportation—precisely and personally where the statute makes the consequence clear, in general terms where it is not—because deportation is, in the Court’s words, a particularly severe penalty intimately related to the criminal process. Chaidez v. United States, 568 U.S. 342 (2013), confined the rule to cases after 2010, leaving the earlier decades’ pleas where they lie. The working system the two decisions describe is this: the criminal courts dispose of the overwhelming majority of their cases by plea; the plea’s immigration weight is fixed by category-matching between the statute of conviction and the federal lists, an exercise neither the prosecutor’s offer sheet nor the defendant’s intuition performs unaided; and the immigration-safe plea—the substituted count, the 364-day sentence—is a known technology, available where counsel on both sides know to ask for it and invisible where they do not. A large share of the conviction-based removals in section 4’s series originated in that room, on charges whose immigration valence nobody at the table had priced. The desk files this as the plea system’s operating description, supplied by the Supreme Court itself.

The time dimension completes the exposure: deportability has no statute of limitations. A conviction entered in the third year of a residence may be charged in the thirty-seventh, when it surfaces—in a naturalization fingerprint check, a travel screening, a later arrest’s booking referral—and the government’s delay is no defense in the proceeding. Lawful permanent residence does not ripen: there is no term of years after which the §237 list ceases to apply to the resident, no doctrine of repose in the deportability statute, and the resident’s protection is therefore never his longevity but only the absence of a chargeable event and the presence, if charged, of a relief whose character elements his record still satisfies. Exactly one event ends the exposure, and it is the subject of section 10: naturalization, after which the former resident is a citizen, removable no longer, and answerable to the immigration law only through the narrow door of denaturalization for fraud in the procurement itself. The exposure ledger and the definitions ledger are the same ledger read at two ends: between admission and oath, the resident carries the list; the oath is the only discharge the book provides.

9. Virtue Is Not a Defense: What the Statute Asks and What It Does Not

The grounds of removability in INA §237 contain no character credit. Read as a list—and section 3 above is the list—the grounds are categories of status and conduct: admitted or not, registered or not, convicted or not, of enumerated offenses, within enumerated periods. No subsection asks whether the respondent is industrious, charitable, devout, beloved, or the support of a household; no defense in the proceeding consists of being good. The statute’s character inquiry exists, but it is stationed elsewhere, and the placement is the point: “good moral character” is an element of benefits and relief—a condition of naturalization under §316(a), of cancellation of removal under §240A(b)(1), of post-conclusion voluntary departure under §240B(b)—where it operates as a gate the applicant must pass, defined in part by a disqualifier list at §101(f) that includes habitual drunkenness, certain convictions, and false testimony. Character, in the statute’s architecture, can qualify a person for mercy or for membership; it cannot excuse a status violation, because the violation is not charged as a failure of character. The removable saint and the removable felon stand in the same posture before §237, differentiated only by the relief each can reach—and the desk notes, as a matter of the same record, that the relief map is itself drawn in conduct: the felon’s aggravated felony closes doors the saint’s clean record leaves open. The system is not indifferent to virtue out of absent-mindedness. It is built so that virtue is currency in the relief market and legal tender nowhere else.

The public debate poses its version of the question through a hypothetical: a figure of universal charitable reputation—the standing example is Mother Teresa of Calcutta, Albanian-born, a citizen of India, founder of the Missionaries of Charity—entering the United States to do religious work without status. On the statute as written, she would be removable, because the grounds in section 3 would apply to her as to anyone, and her works would appear in her case only as equities in a discretionary request. The record files what the hypothetical leaves out. A dedicated lawful channel exists for exactly her case and has for generations: the R-1 nonimmigrant classification at §101(a)(15)(R) admits religious workers—ministers and persons in religious vocations, members of a denomination with a bona fide nonprofit religious organization in the United States, coming to work for it—for up to five years, and the EB-4 special-immigrant category admits religious workers to permanent residence. And the historical case itself ran through the law’s front door and past it: by Public Law 104-218, enacted October 1, 1996, Congress conferred honorary citizenship of the United States on her, making her one of eight persons so honored in the republic’s history and one of two—with Winston Churchill, in 1963—honored in her lifetime. The State Department’s own manual (8 FAM 306.1) records the honor’s legal content: honorary citizenship confers no special entry, travel, or immigration benefits, and its holder is not eligible for a United States passport. Which is to say, the republic’s highest civic compliment left its recipient’s immigration position exactly where the statute put it, and the honor and the removability coexisted in the same file without contradiction, because they answer different questions. The desk files the exhibit at that temperature: the removability grounds ask nothing about character; the channels exist; the actual case used them.

10. “Naturalization”: A Definitions Section

The word does one job in the statute and another in the argument, and the desk files both. In law, naturalization is the defined process by which a person not born a citizen becomes one, at INA §§310–347 (8 U.S.C. §§1421–1459).
