The election account of the local votes: more than forty measures across ten states, the opponents of data-center development successful in virtually all of them, Ohio carrying the most initiatives, some votes advisory rather than binding, and a single locality where the facilities prevailed. Ballotpedia’s complete count, forty-one measures and forty for tighter limits, is the figure the report prints.

Subjective
Inflect — site selection in 2026

An industry account of how sites are now chosen: the field splitting into hyperscale campuses of hundreds of megawatts and hyperlocal sites of one to twenty megawatts; deliverability defined as the overlap of entitled land, available power, and a community willing to partner; and demand pushing activity into secondary markets as primary markets fill.

entry.title: Tokyo Closes in a Bear Market, Brent Crosses a Hundred, and the Count Waits
entry.summary: The overnight file for November 6, 2026: Tokyo closes 6 percent lower in a bear market and Seoul closes 6 percent lower after a circuit breaker, Brent briefly crosses $100 on the tanker file, the president says he will soon decide on Iran, gold falls with the shares, and no race is called in the night. Collected at 0400.
entry.content:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Tokyo Closes in a Bear Market, Brent Crosses a Hundred, and the Count Waits

At 0400 the night’s work is finished in Asia and not begun in Washington. Tokyo and Seoul have closed about 6 percent lower, Brent has briefly crossed $100 a barrel on the tanker file and stands just under it, gold has fallen with the shares it usually shelters from, the president has said he will soon decide whether to resume all-out war in Iran, and no race was called in the night. Friday’s first American fact is set for 0830: the October payrolls report.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 9, the Midnight Watch, which carried Asia’s Friday session in its morning state. The closes printed here replace the morning figures; the midnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

No race was called in the night, in either chamber, in any state. The Senate stands where it has stood since Wednesday: 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled. The governorships stand at 28 for the Democrats, with Alaska and Kansas open. Colorado’s 4th District stands in its latest state with the Democrat ahead by 3,024 votes and the race uncalled. What moved in the night was not the count. It was the price of the election, taken a second time in Asia and closed there; the price of oil, carried back over $100 and held just under it; and the war, on which the president, meeting his national security team for the first time since the vote, said a decision is coming soon. The desk files those three in that order.

Asia Closes: Tokyo in a Bear Market, Seoul Off the Floor

Asia’s Friday session is closed, and the closes are the night’s largest settled fact. In Tokyo the Nikkei 225 closed down 3,666.99 points, or 6.00 percent—at 57,410.91 in the closing account carrying the market data filed below, at 57,434.70 in the Tokyo–Seoul closing account, and at 57,420.23 in the morning brief. The three figures differ in the last digits; the fall, the worst day since April 2025 per Dow Jones Newswires’ closing update, does not. The index had closed above 72,000 for the first time in late June; a close more than 20 percent below that record puts it in a bear market, and every closing account records it there. SoftBank Group fell more than 10 percent in the Dow Jones figures and 10.83 percent to 3,549 yen in the closing account; Kioxia fell 8.72 percent to 8,511 yen.

Seoul closed off its floor, after a halt and an emergency meeting. The Kospi fell more than 8 percent in the morning, to an intraday low of 4,911.28, broke below 5,000 for the first time since February 6, and triggered a Level 1 circuit breaker at 9:03 a.m. that halted trading for 20 minutes—the eleventh breaker of the year, per the Seoul closing account filed below. The government convened an emergency meeting to review market conditions, support buying followed, and the index closed down 324.11 points, or 6.02 percent, at 5,059.69; the closing account’s last figure is 5,059.65. Samsung Electronics closed down 6.35 percent at 188,700 won, and SK Hynix down 10.44 percent to 1,132,000 won. The Kosdaq closed down 5.03 percent at 644.27. Of the twenty largest stocks in Seoul, only Naver rose, up 2.87 percent. In Taipei the Taiex ended 4.5 percent lower, its largest daily fall since July, with TSMC down 4.7 percent; the Hang Seng Tech Index was 1.8 percent lower; Singapore’s Straits Times Index was 2.9 percent lower in the Dow Jones update’s last state. The reason the accounts give is the reason Thursday gave in New York: the Democratic victory, read as regulation and delay for the data-center buildout Asia supplies, priced into the same chip names on the next day’s date. No new American fact arrived in the night to change that reading, and none was needed.

The Futures, and the Test at 0830

The American futures spent the night in two directions, and the desk prints both states with their hours. In the early evening, carrying CNBC’s figures, the futures account filed below recorded S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 futures each down 0.4 percent and Dow futures down 201 points. In the early European hours, the later futures account recorded Dow futures down 0.85 percent at about 51,170, S&P 500 futures up 0.06 percent at about 7,390, and Nasdaq 100 futures up 0.90 percent at about 26,990. A bounce in the Nasdaq contracts and a fall in the Dow contracts is not a recovery and not a rout; it is a market waiting, and what it is waiting for is printed on the calendar. The October employment report is due at 0830 ET. The Dow Jones consensus stands at 59,000 jobs added, against 29,000 in September, with the unemployment rate expected to hold at 4.2 percent; the forecasts on the shelf run from about 55,000 to 65,000, and the private ADP report, already in, stands at 86,000 against 75,000 expected. The report is the first hard labor figure since the sell-off, and it lands in front of the Federal Reserve’s December 9 meeting, at which traders price the chance of a further 25-basis-point increase between 67 and about 70 percent in the files on the shelf.

Oil: Brent Crosses a Hundred, and Holds Just Under It

Brent crossed $100 in the morning trade in Asia and did not hold the round number. Reuters’ Beijing and Perth file records January Brent up $1.29, or 1.31 percent, at $99.58 a barrel as of 0504 GMT, briefly breaching $100 in morning trade, and West Texas Intermediate up 86 cents, or 0.95 percent, at $91.38. A later account, carrying CNBC’s figures at 0730 GMT, puts Brent at $99.90, up 1.67 percent, and West Texas Intermediate at $91.69. Thursday’s settlement stands beneath both: Brent at $98.29, up $3.67, and West Texas Intermediate at $90.52. The week’s bearing stands in the same files and does not move: both benchmarks remain on course for a fall of about 12 percent on the week, after Wednesday’s 8 percent fall on the election result. The rebound is two days old and is carried, in every account, by the same cargo: the tanker attacks in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and the finding, stated by ANZ’s senior commodity strategist in the files, that flows through the strait are running at under 60 percent of capacity. Against the rebound, JPMorgan’s estimate, carried in the oil account filed below, is that supply exceeded demand by 1.1 million barrels a day in September and by 1.4 million in October. Both facts are in the price at 0400: a strait at three-fifths flow, and a world producing more oil than it burns.

The Strait, and the Decision the President Says Is Coming

The tanker file did not grow in the night; the decision file did. The claims stand where the midnight edition left them: Iran reported three more tankers attacked in the strait on Thursday, on top of the Guards’ report of two tankers and a tugboat catching fire, and the British agency UKMTO’s count stands at at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday, at close to the record pace of October. No independent confirmation of the Thursday incidents appears in any file the desk took in the night. What the night added is the president, on the record, in the Oval Office on Thursday, after meeting his national security team on Iran for the first time since the elections. The account of the meeting, carrying Axios’s reporting filed below, records his words: “Now we will make a decision.” Asked whether to go further with strikes to ensure Iran’s nuclear program is dead and that “it will never happen again,” he said: “I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You’ll know soon enough.” The options before him are stated in the same account as three: new strikes, continued economic pressure, or a deal carrying significant concessions. Central Command is finalizing preparations to resume major combat operations and has received no new directive, per an American official in the account; a third carrier group, led by the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is due in Singapore on Friday for a port call and cannot reach the region before mid-November.

The mediation now has a printed shape, and Tehran’s answer to it was delivered in Moscow. The Qatari mediators’ draft, in the same account, runs on two days: on the first, the United States lifts its naval blockade and releases some of Iran’s frozen funds, and Iran invites the International Atomic Energy Agency to send inspectors to the bombed nuclear sites; on the second, the Strait of Hormuz reopens, and nuclear talks resume on Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, spent Thursday in calls with mediators from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, and Egypt. Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, spent it at the Kremlin, delivering a message from the supreme leader to President Putin, who stated his readiness to help end the war. Rezaei’s statement after the meeting is the night’s second fixed point: “We told Mr. Putin that we announced seven conditions to the Americans regarding diplomacy, and that until the Americans fulfill our seven conditions, neither the Strait of Hormuz will be opened nor will there be any negotiations.” A separate file records that Iran returned a copy of one nuclear proposal to the United States through the Qatari mediators on Thursday. No agreement was announced. The two tracks—a two-day draft in Doha and seven conditions in Moscow—are both on paper at 0400, and they do not describe the same distance.

The Count at 0400, and the Business of Friday

The count did not move in the night, and its latest states are printed for the record. The Associated Press Senate file in its latest state lists Alaska too early to call at 73.95 percent of precincts reporting and Mississippi too early to call at 99.83 percent. The margins underneath them stand as the earlier editions printed them: in Mississippi the Democrat, Scott Colom, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 1,138 votes in the Associated Press figures of November 5 and by 1,824 in Decision Desk HQ’s later figures, with other files running the lead from a few dozen votes to just over a thousand—a spread the desk prints rather than resolves; in Alaska the Democrat, Mary Peltola, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 626 to 637 first-choice votes, with a second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holding more votes than the margin. The dates govern: Mississippi’s affidavit identification is due November 10 and its counties certify by November 13, and the candidate with the most votes wins; Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18. In Colorado’s 4th District the wire’s latest state, carried in the state results file updated at 6:25 p.m. MST, puts the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 184,103 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 181,079—a margin of 3,024, with 96.89 percent of precincts reporting and the race uncalled. Weld County, the incumbent’s strongest, has finished its ordinary counting; what remains sits largely in counties the challenger is carrying, and the cure and overseas deadline is November 12.

Friday’s Washington business is a deadline, not a session. Candidates for the House Republican leadership elections must declare by noon today. The field as filed stands: Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek the minority leadership; Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan are declared for it; Majority Whip Tom Emmer seeks to remain whip and is challenged by August Pfluger; and the elections are set for Tuesday, November 10. On the other side of the chamber, Hakeem Jeffries has sought his colleagues’ support to become Speaker when the new Congress convenes on January 3. Congress itself returns Monday, November 9, to the lame-duck session, funded through December 11. None of that business was transacted in the night. It is filed here because Friday will transact the first of it before the Midday Watch collects.

Gold Falls With the Shares; Europe Waits to Open

Gold did the unusual thing in the night: it fell while the shares fell. Spot gold slipped 0.6 percent to $4,063.39 an ounce by 0248 GMT and December futures fell 1 percent to $4,072.90, per the gold account filed below; the Dow Jones closing update records precious metals swept up as investors sold positions to cover losses elsewhere. The metal had touched $4,146.63 on Thursday, a high of more than two weeks, and stands about 4 percent higher on the week even after the fall. Goldman Sachs on Thursday cut its end-of-2026 target by $500, to $4,150 an ounce from $4,650. Silver rose 0.3 percent to $51.91. The accounts give the same two reasons for gold’s fall as for oil’s rise: crude back toward $100 carries an inflation reading with it, and an inflation reading carries the expectation of higher American rates, which is the weather gold does not like. Europe, at 0400, has not opened. Its futures have: contracts on the EURO STOXX 50 were down 1 percent at 0652 GMT, with German contracts down 0.8 percent and British down 0.9 percent, per the Reuters account of the European open filed below. The STOXX 600 stands, in that account, up more than 1.3 percent on the week and just over 1 percent from a record high, carrying less of the AI trade than the indexes that fell in New York and Tokyo. Whether that shelter holds is the European session’s question, and it belongs to the Midday Watch.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Tokyo’s close: 57,410.91, 57,420.23, and 57,434.70 in three closing files, a spread of 24 points on a fall of 3,667—the level agreed, the last digits not. Second, the futures: down across the board in the early-evening account, split in the early-European account, Dow down and Nasdaq up—two states of one unsettled night, printed with their hours because the hour is the difference. Third, Mississippi: a Democratic lead of a few dozen votes in one file, 1,138 in the wire’s, 1,824 in the decision desk’s, each taken at a different stage of the same unfinished count. Fourth, Brent: $99.58 at 0504 GMT, $99.86 in an earlier overnight state, $99.90 at 0730 GMT, and $100 crossed briefly between them—one rising market read at four hours. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the night are single-valued: Asia is closed and down about 6 percent in Tokyo and Seoul; the Nikkei is in a bear market; Brent settled Thursday at $98.29 and trades just under $100; gold stands at about $4,063; no race was called; the president said a decision on Iran is coming soon and named no date; Tehran’s seven conditions stand unwithdrawn; and the payrolls report is due at 0830. The log proceeds to Friday.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-nine items.

Subjective
Dow Jones Newswires, via Morningstar — Asian equities tumble as the AI selloff deepens

Friday’s closes in the update timed 02:15 ET: the Kospi down as much as 8.8 percent in the session and finished 6.0 percent lower, with weekly losses of 12 percent; the Nikkei below 60,000 and closed 6.0 percent lower in its worst day since April 2025; the Taiex 4.5 percent lower; SK Hynix down over 10 percent, SoftBank down over 10 percent, TSMC down 4.7 percent; the Hang Seng Tech Index 1.8 percent lower; gold down 1 percent as positions were sold to cover losses; Brent up 1.7 percent and reclaiming $100 in its figures; and the ANZ analysts’ sentence that the reality of the situation hit home, with Iran still holding the Strait of Hormuz.

Subjective
Reuters, via EuropeSays — Asia stocks crumble after the AI rout

Filed from Singapore on November 6: Asia’s tech-heavy markets sank as fear of regulatory scrutiny and a slowdown in the AI build-out followed the steepest fall in American stocks since the tariff rout of a year and a half before; the Kospi down more than 8 percent with a 20-minute circuit-breaker halt and the Nikkei down 5 percent at the file’s hour; $3 trillion wiped off S&P 500 companies; the semiconductor index down 12.2 percent overnight and the Nasdaq 12 percent below its record close of a month before; and the Singapore and Sydney analysts’ readings of a shift in sentiment.

Subjective
TradingKey — the Kospi reclaims 5,000, Tokyo and Seoul pare their losses

The closing account: the Kospi down more than 8 percent intraday, below 5,000, with a 20-minute circuit breaker, then support buying from the National Pension Service and other institutions, closing down 6.02 percent at 5,059.65; Samsung Electronics down 6.35 percent at 188,700 won and SK Hynix down 10.44 percent at 1,132,000 won; the Nikkei gapped below 60,000 and closed down 5.96 percent at 57,434.70, with Kioxia down 8.72 percent at 8,511 yen and SoftBank down 10.83 percent at 3,549 yen.

Subjective
Seoul Economic Daily — the Kospi plunges 6.02 percent to close at 5,059.69

The close recorded in one line: the Kospi at 5,059.69, down 324.11 points, or 6.02 percent.

Subjective
Money Today — the Kospi closes above 5,000 after the breaker

The Seoul close in full: the Kospi at 5,059.69, down 6.02 percent, after a low of 4,911.28, the first intraday break of 5,000 since February 6; a Stage 1 circuit breaker at 9:03 a.m. halting trading for 20 minutes; the Kosdaq at 644.27, down 5.03 percent; Naver the only riser among the twenty largest stocks, up 2.87 percent; and the won closing its day session at 1,342.1 to the dollar in the same account.

Subjective
KuCoin News, carrying Huo Xing Finance — the Nikkei falls 6 percent into a bear market

The closing figures in one file: the Nikkei 225 down 3,666.99 points, or 6.00 percent, at 57,410.91, more than 20 percent below its June closing peak and in a technical bear market; the Kospi down 324.15 points, or 6.02 percent, at 5,059.65, after a morning fall of more than 8 percent, a break of 5,000, and its eleventh circuit breaker of the year; the South Korean government’s emergency market meeting, after which the decline narrowed; the Kosdaq down 5 percent; SK Hynix down over 10 percent and Samsung Electronics down 6.35 percent.

Subjective
Samuel & Co Trading — Asia catches the Nasdaq correction, the morning brief for November 6

The brief’s view: the Nikkei closed at 57,420.23, down 5.99 percent and into bear-market territory; the Kospi fell 5.41 percent to 5,092.38 in its figures after a worse open; American futures trying a mild bounce into Friday, with S&P futures near 7,388.50, Nasdaq 100 futures near 27,009, and Dow futures near 51,139 in the London morning; about $3 trillion wiped off S&P 500 firms on Thursday; and the payrolls report named as the dial that settles whether Thursday was a one-day fall or the start of a deeper unwind, with December hike odds at roughly 70 percent.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — the Nikkei plunges, the Kospi falls, in the morning state

The Asian session at midday, updated November 6 at 08:52: the Nikkei 5.7 percent lower at 57,576.63 by midday after a fall of more than 6 percent at the open; the Kospi down 7.4 percent to 4,985.99, with Samsung Electronics down 7.9 percent in the morning; Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 down 1.0 percent to 8,973.00; the Hang Seng down 0.7 percent to 24,630.03 and the Shanghai Composite down 1.3 percent to 3,642.10; and Nvidia named as the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 on Thursday.

Subjective
The Business Standard — the Democrats’ win spooks AI investors

The rout and its cause in one file: investors worried the party will use its gains in Congress and the state capitols to regulate and slow the AI build-out; the Nasdaq down 5.56 percent in its figures, its most dramatic fall in 19 months, two days after Democrats flipped seven Senate seats, gained at least 39 in the House, and picked up five governorships; and the Alaska and Mississippi races still uncalled, with the majority’s possible rise to 56–44 stated.

Subjective
Reuters, via 98.5 The River — oil set for a sharp weekly drop, supply concerns a floor

Beijing and Perth, November 6: January Brent up $1.29, or 1.31 percent, to $99.58 a barrel as of 0504 GMT, briefly breaching $100 in morning trade, and West Texas Intermediate up 86 cents, or 0.95 percent, to $91.38, both up for a second day; Brent on track to fall 12 percent on the week and West Texas Intermediate 12.1 percent; Wednesday’s 8 percent fall on the election result, and the rebound on the surge of tanker attacks on Wednesday and Thursday; Iran’s report of three more tankers attacked and UKMTO’s near-record pace; and the KCM analyst’s reading of a technical recovery over a problem that has not disappeared.

Subjective
FinanceFeeds — Brent at $99.90 on Friday morning

Updated November 6 at 07:30 GMT, carrying CNBC’s figures: Brent up 1.67 percent to $99.90 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate up 1.43 percent to $91.69; Brent still heading for a weekly loss of about 12 percent; the reference levels stated at $93.50 below and $103.60 above; Iran’s three more reported tanker attacks on Thursday and UKMTO’s near-record rate; flows through the strait at less than 60 percent of capacity in the ANZ strategist’s figure; and the October jobs report named as the day’s demand question.

Subjective
Invezz — Brent nears $100 despite a 12 percent weekly slump

November 6, 01:43: Brent up 1.31 percent to $99.58 at 0504 GMT after briefly crossing $100, and West Texas Intermediate up 0.95 percent to $91.38, with both benchmarks still on course for weekly losses of around 12 percent; tanker attacks near the strait keeping a risk premium in the price while hopes of an easing of the war pull the other way; flows through the strait below 60 percent of capacity in the ANZ estimate; and JPMorgan’s estimate that supply exceeded demand by 1.1 million barrels a day in September, widening to 1.4 million in October.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — crude gains amid fresh tanker attacks

Friday morning in the Indian market’s figures: January Brent at $99.83, up 1.57 percent, at 10:04 a.m., and December West Texas Intermediate at $91.73, up 1.34 percent, after Brent crossed $99; UKMTO’s reports of tanker attacks in the Gulf and the strait since Sunday; and the Revolutionary Guards’ report of two oil tankers and a tugboat catching fire in separate incidents in the strait.

Subjective
OilPrice — oil heads for a 12 percent weekly loss despite fresh tanker attacks

Brent at $99.42 and West Texas Intermediate at $91.242 at the file’s hour, both up from Thursday’s close on reports of fresh tanker attacks; both benchmarks down 12 percent since Monday on hopes the midterm result brings a swift end to the war; at least five vessel incidents in the Gulf since Sunday in the Reuters figures carried in the story; and shipments through the strait recovering while threats to commercial traffic persist.

Subjective
Axios, via Zot — the president says he will soon decide on resuming all-out war

The Thursday meeting and the diplomacy in one file: the president’s first meeting with his national security team on Iran since the elections, held as part of his weekly intelligence briefing; his words in the Oval Office—“Now we will make a decision,” and “I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You’ll know soon enough”; the three options of new strikes, economic pressure, or a deal with significant concessions; Central Command finalizing preparations without a new directive, and the USS Theodore Roosevelt due in Singapore on Friday, unable to reach the region before mid-November; the Qatari two-day draft—blockade lifted and frozen funds released and inspectors invited on the first day, the strait reopened and nuclear talks resumed on the second; Araghchi’s calls with six regional mediators; and Rezaei at the Kremlin, delivering the supreme leader’s message, stating the seven conditions to President Putin, and Putin’s readiness to help end the war.

Subjective
New York Post — the commander’s podcast, as the president weighs his next move

Iran reviewing American-backed proposals on its nuclear program, with at least three meetings on concrete proposals in the past week in Tehran and Doha through Qatari mediators, and Iran returning a copy of one nuclear proposal to the United States through the mediators on Thursday, per the Reuters reporting carried in the story; the president’s Oval Office sentence on destroying the rest of the country; the June memorandum that collapsed over shipping routes in the strait; the parliament speaker’s charge that the president is preparing the next phase of the war; and, in the same file, Central Command’s commander launching a podcast on Thursday with jokes about French fries and retiring to play basketball.

Subjective
Reuters, via The Business Standard — tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure

Dubai, November 5: Iran reported three more tankers damaged in the strait on Thursday; at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in UKMTO’s count, against 35 vessels hit in October, the most of any month of the war; Qatar’s statement that the United States and Iran are reviewing proposals to bridge their differences, with no breakthrough announced; the vice president’s blame of the war for the defeat and the president’s defense of it; the two unnamed sources’ statement that the president is planning to bomb Iran and held off for the midterms; and the four subjects of the peacemaking—the strait, the blockade, sanctions, and the nuclear program.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska too early to call at 73.95 percent of precincts reporting and Mississippi too early to call at 99.83 percent, and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
ASEAN Now, carrying the agencies — Alaska and Mississippi to decide the strength of the majority

Days after the vote, the two Senate races remain uncalled and will determine the size of the Democratic majority: in Mississippi, Colom leading Hyde-Smith by just over 1,000 votes with counting continuing, in a state the president carried by 20 points in 2024, and the lead narrowing in Decision Desk HQ’s figures at more than 95 percent counted; in Alaska, Peltola at 48.2 percent to Sullivan’s 47.9 with about 69 percent counted in the file’s figures, with the governorship and the ballot measure on the state’s primary and ranked-choice system also uncalled.

Subjective
The Business Standard — why Alaska and Mississippi have not been called

The Associated Press had not called either Senate race by Thursday. Mississippi: Colom leads Hyde-Smith by 1,138 votes, about 3,600 mail ballots outstanding, affidavit identification due by November 10, counties to certify by November 13, the most votes wins with no runoff, and no automatic recount. Alaska: Peltola leads Sullivan by 626 votes, mail accepted for 10 days domestic and 15 overseas, ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18, the certification suit dismissed November 1 with an appeal stated, and the governor’s race on the same schedule.

Subjective
Associated Press — Colorado’s 4th District

Laubacher 184,103, Boebert 181,079, with 96.89 percent of precincts reporting and an estimated 97.03 percent of the vote in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
Rocky Mountain Voice — Colorado, every race

The secretary of state’s figures, updated 6:25 p.m. MST on November 5: Democrats have won all four statewide constitutional offices and lead in seven of the eight congressional districts; in the 4th District, Laubacher at 184,103 votes, 48.75 percent, and Boebert at 181,079, 47.95 percent, a lead of 3,024 in a district redrawn to favor Republicans after the 2020 census; and races the Associated Press has not called marked pending, with results unofficial until certified.

Subjective
Wikipedia — the 2026 House Republican Conference leadership election

The election set for November 10, 2026, with representatives required to declare by November 6: Speaker Johnson declined for minority leader; Scalise and Jordan declared, from Louisiana’s 1st district and Ohio’s 4th; Whip Emmer seeking re-election and challenged by Pfluger of Texas’s 11th; Conference Chair McClain seeking re-election; and the campaign-arm chair’s race open after the incumbent lost his North Carolina seat.

Subjective
FXStreet — Dow futures fall, payrolls awaited

The futures in the early European hours on Friday: Dow futures down 0.85 percent at about 51,170, S&P 500 futures up 0.06 percent at about 7,390, and Nasdaq 100 futures up 0.90 percent at about 26,990—mixed after Thursday’s fall, the worst single-day drop since April 2025, on concern that Democrats could impose tighter regulation on the AI sector; and traders awaiting the Nonfarm Payrolls report for its bearing on the Federal Reserve’s December decision.

Subjective
CNBC, via Binance News — futures fall, payrolls awaited

Stock futures fell Thursday evening after the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.5 percent and closed more than 10 percent below its recent high, in correction territory: S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 futures each declined 0.4 percent, and Dow futures lost 201 points, or 0.4 percent; and traders awaited Friday’s October payrolls report, the Dow Jones consensus calling for 59,000 jobs added and an unemployment rate of 4.2 percent.

Subjective
Invezz — gold falls as Goldman cuts its forecast by $500

November 6, 00:50: spot gold down 0.6 percent to $4,063.39 an ounce by 02:48 GMT and December futures down 1 percent to $4,072.90, falling despite the Asian stock fall, as rising oil and expectations of further American rate increases weakened demand; gold still roughly 4 percent higher on the week, after reaching $4,146.63 on Thursday; Goldman Sachs cutting its end-2026 target by $500, to $4,150 from $4,650, on Thursday; and the October employment report named as the next test.

Subjective
TradingKey — gold falls below $4,100, payrolls in front of it

Gold down about 0.85 percent in the Asian session on Friday to near $4,050, after touching $4,147.06 on Thursday, its highest in more than two weeks, and closing below $4,100; October payrolls projected at 65,000 in the file’s survey, up from 29,000 in September, with unemployment expected steady at 4.2 percent; the CME FedWatch probability of a December hike at about 68.4 percent; and the levels stated at $4,030 and $4,000 below and $4,100 and $4,150 above.

Subjective
Reuters, via Devdiscourse — European shares set to fall as the rout gathers pace

Friday before the open: EURO STOXX 50 futures down 1 percent at 0652 GMT, with German contracts down 0.8 percent and British down 0.9 percent; $2.5 trillion wiped off the Nasdaq in the previous session in the file’s figure; the STOXX 600 up over 1.3 percent on the week and just over 1 percent from a record high, its smaller AI exposure stated as its shelter; and ASML, Infineon, Schneider Electric, and Siemens Energy named as likely to stay under pressure.

Subjective
Trading Economics — European stocks set for a negative open

November 6, 06:27: European markets set to open sharply lower as the global selloff widened, on concern over tighter AI regulation and a slowdown in data-center expansion after the Democratic victory; Euro Stoxx 50 and Stoxx 600 futures both down approximately 1 percent in premarket trading; the day’s European figures named—the British house price index, French trade, and Eurozone retail sales; earnings due from ENGIE, Daimler Truck, International Airlines Group, Amadeus IT, and Mediobanca; and Thursday’s European fall recorded in the same file, the Euro Stoxx 50 down 0.9 percent and the Stoxx 600 down 0.4 percent, with the technology sector down more than 4 percent and ASML down 7 percent.

entry.title: The Rally Is Gone and the Count Is Not Finished
entry.summary: The midnight file for November 6, 2026: at 0000 the Dow's fall and Brent's settlement are fixed, futures and Tokyo fall further in the evening, Iran's tanker claims grow to five, no Senate race is called for a second day, and Colorado's 3rd District has changed hands since the count was last printed whole. Edition No. 9, the Midnight Watch.
entry.content:
The Midterm Elections — The Last Entry of the Day

Objective

The Rally Is Gone and the Count Is Not Finished

The last entry of the day at 0000: Thursday’s closes are fixed and lower, the futures fall again in the evening, Tokyo opens its Friday in a slide that carries the Nikkei into a bear market, Brent trades back toward a hundred dollars on an expanded tanker file, and the count—two Senate seats, two governorships, and the last House races, Colorado’s among them—goes to Friday unfinished.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026—the midnight that begins this date and closes the day before it. This edition completes the log of November 5 begun in Edition No. 6, the Overnight Watch, continued in Edition No. 7, the Midday Watch, and carried whole in Edition No. 8, the Evening Watch, with The Second Reading filed outside the watches at 1912. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open—and in Colorado’s 3rd District they differ in the leader, not only in the margin.

What Thursday Settled

Thursday’s closes are fixed, and they are the day’s largest settled fact. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 1,833.06 points, or 3.44 percent, at 51,523.06, against a gain of 1,569.40 points on Wednesday. The S&P 500 closed down 4.36 percent at 7,353.73, its worst day since April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 5.52 percent at 24,315.00, in correction territory, 11.9 percent below its October 6 record close. The Nasdaq 100 closed down 6.36 percent at 26,629.81, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25 percent to 9,011.14, and the Russell 2000, in the evening futures account filed below, lost 4.5 percent. The volatility index closed at 28.09, up 69.1 percent, and the ten-year Treasury yield slipped about six basis points to roughly 4.84 percent. All three principal indexes closed below their levels of Tuesday, election day. The figures stand as the Evening Watch printed them, from the closing account; midnight adds nothing to them except the hours after them, which are filed below.

The day’s economic figures are also fixed, and they run the other way. Initial claims for unemployment benefits stand at 189,000 for the week ended October 31, down 6,000, the lowest reading since 1969, per Reuters’ report of the Labor Department’s releases; third-quarter productivity rose at a 3.6 percent annualized rate and unit labor costs fell 0.7 percent. In London, Bank Rate stands at 4 percent, raised from 3.75 percent by 8–1, per Reuters’ Bank of England file. Control of Congress and of the governorships stands settled as it stood on Wednesday: the Senate at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, the governorships at 28 for the Democrats, and the Democrats to organize the House in January. What Thursday added to the settled column was calls. The Associated Press called Colorado’s 5th District for the Democrat, Jessica Killin, in the afternoon. In the evening the wire called New York’s 17th District for the Democrat, Cait Conley, at 140,165 votes to the incumbent Republican Mike Lawler’s 128,292, per the district file—two days after Lawler called Conley himself to concede on election night, per the account of the networks’ confirmation filed below. The running live file recorded the evening’s other calls in sequence: Democrats flip Arizona’s 6th, Colorado’s 5th, Montana’s 1st, and North Carolina’s 9th Districts at 5:55 p.m. ET, and New York’s 17th at 6:44 p.m.

The Count at Midnight

No Senate race was called on Thursday, for the second full day, and the two open races end the day where the evening left them. The Associated Press Senate file in its latest state lists Alaska and Mississippi as too early to call, Mississippi at 99.83 percent of precincts reporting. The newest figures under the two races are Decision Desk HQ’s. In Mississippi, in the file’s update of 4:12 p.m. EST carried in the live results file filed below, the Democrat, Scott Colom, stands at 466,763 votes and the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, at 464,939—a lead of 1,824 votes, at the top of the range this paper printed during the day, with more than 95 percent of the estimated vote counted. In Alaska the same file carries the Democrat, Mary Peltola, at 102,962 first-choice votes and the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, at 102,325—a lead of 637. The dates that govern both races stand as filed: Mississippi’s affidavit identification is due November 10 and its counties certify by November 13, and the candidate with the most votes wins; Alaska takes domestic mail ballots until November 13 and overseas ballots until November 18, and its ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18.

The House count crept again in the evening, and the call desks end the day farther apart in arithmetic and in agreement on everything else. The Associated Press tracker’s latest state, as the Evening Watch printed it, shows 248 seats won by the Democrats and 13 more led, against 154 won and 20 led for the Republicans. The live results file’s check at 22:45 CET runs the called figure higher: 251 House seats called for the Democrats and 155 for the Republicans, with 29 still uncalled. Newsmax’s Thursday account runs it higher still, on a projection: the Associated Press projects the Democrats will win 252 seats, with 19 races still uncalled, 38 seats flipped, and the party’s highest House total since 2009; the Republicans, in the same account, flipped only one seat in a district unaffected by mid-decade redistricting, Maine’s 2nd. The three files were taken at different hours by different methods—seats won, seats called, seats projected—and the desk prints them as three bearings, not one number. The governorships stand at 28 for the Democrats with Alaska and Kansas open. Kansas stands where it stood: the Democrat, Cindy Holscher, ahead by 7,045 votes with all precincts reporting, the close-race audits ordered, the race uncalled.

Colorado, Corrected in the Open

Colorado’s 3rd District has changed hands since this paper last printed it whole, and the correction is the midnight file’s first duty. The Midnight Watch of November 5 and the editions that followed carried the Democrat, Dwayne Romero, leading the incumbent Republican, Jeff Hurd, by more than 2,200 votes, on the Colorado live file as it signed off on election night, when Romero did lead. The lead changed hands overnight, as the district’s remaining vote came in, and on Thursday it widened in the incumbent’s favor. The state results file, carrying the secretary of state’s figures and updated at 5:25 p.m. MST, puts Hurd at 162,669 votes, 49.31 percent, and Romero at 156,472, 47.43 percent—a margin of 6,197 votes. Decision Desk HQ’s file at 9:07 p.m. EST runs the same order slightly wider: Hurd 163,655, Romero 157,523, a margin of 6,132 in a count of 332,044 votes. The Associated Press district file carries the state’s figures and labels the race too early to call, at 96.73 percent of precincts reporting. The margin stands outside the half-percent threshold that would require a recount. The leader this paper printed on Wednesday was the leader of Wednesday’s count; the leader of Thursday’s count is Hurd, and the log records the change where it happened, in the open.

Colorado’s 4th District narrowed all day and ends it uncalled, with the incumbent’s strongest county finished counting. The state’s figures at 5:25 p.m. MST put the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 184,024 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 180,758—a margin of 3,266. Decision Desk HQ’s file at 9:56 p.m. EST puts the same pair at 184,624 and 181,555—a margin of 3,069, in a count of 378,685 votes, more than 95 percent of the expected vote. A later account of the state results, filed below, puts the lead at 2,376 votes and records the fact the remaining arithmetic turns on: Weld County, which gives Boebert her largest county lead, 20,074 votes to 13,572, has finished counting except for ballots with signature problems and ballots forwarded from other counties, and the ballots still out are concentrated in Douglas, Larimer, and Arapahoe counties, which Laubacher is carrying. The district’s own paper counts at least about 7,000 ballots remaining in the four most populous counties as of 5:30 p.m. and 474 ballots in Weld awaiting signature cures. Signature fixes and military and overseas ballots are due by 11:59 p.m. on November 12, and the counties finish tabulating on November 13. The Associated Press has not called the race.

After the Close: The Futures, Then Tokyo

The evening trade continued the day’s direction, at a slower speed, in two readings that do not match. The early-evening account, carrying CNBC’s figures, records S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq-100 futures each down 0.4 percent and Dow futures down 201 points, or 0.4 percent. The later account, in the same wire’s figures at a later hour, records S&P 500 futures down 0.8 percent, Nasdaq-100 futures down 1.3 percent, and Dow futures down 264 points, or 0.5 percent. Both accounts name the same subjects in front of the market: the October payrolls report, due Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET, and the concern, stated in the later account, that the Democratic victory could slow the pace of the data-center and artificial-intelligence buildout. No floor was reported in either account. The futures are a reading, not a close, and the desk files them as a reading.

By the hour Washington reached midnight, Tokyo was already in its Friday afternoon, and Friday there opened with the same selling, in larger size. The Nikkei 225, which had closed Thursday at 61,077.9 in the figures carried in the Tokyo–Seoul account filed below, gapped down at the open to 60,374.35 and fell 6.2 percent to 57,288.91. A second account of the Tokyo morning carries the fall deeper: an intraday low of 56,745.81, down 7 percent, and the index 5.7 percent lower at 57,579 at 11:18 a.m. in Tokyo. The index closed above 72,000 for the first time in late June; a fall of more than 20 percent from that record puts it in a bear market, and both accounts record it there. The names are the supply chain of the same buildout: Advantest down 12 percent, SoftBank Group down 11 percent, Kioxia down 11 percent, and Tokyo Electron down nearly 9 percent, in CNBC’s figures carried in the accounts. In Seoul the Kospi fell 8.55 percent to 4,923.47, below 5,000, and a Level 1 circuit breaker halted trading for twenty minutes; Samsung Electronics fell 10.07 percent to 181,200 won and SK Hynix fell 12.26 percent to 1,109,000 won. Taiwan’s Taiex fell more than 8 percent in its session before recovering part of the fall, and the Shanghai Composite stood down 1.1 percent and the Hang Seng down 0.60 percent in the Tokyo-morning snapshot. No new American fact arrived in the night to explain the Asian session. The explanation the accounts give is the one Thursday gave in New York: the election, read as a check on the buildout, priced a second time—this time on the other side of the Pacific, on the next day’s date.

Oil at Midnight: Brent Toward a Hundred Again

The settlement is fixed, and the evening trade carried Brent past it. Brent crude futures settled on Thursday up $3.67, or 3.88 percent, at $98.29 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate closed up $2.40 at $90.52, per Reuters’ New York file as the Evening Watch printed it. In the hours after the settlement, Reuters’ early-Friday file records Brent futures for January up $1.57, or 1.6 percent, at $99.86 a barrel as of 0222 GMT, and West Texas Intermediate up $1.10 at $91.62; the Tokyo-morning account carries an evening-session high of $99.62. The same Reuters file holds the week’s other bearing in the same paragraph: Brent remains on track to fall about 12 percent for the week, after the December contract’s expiry on October 30, and the rebound of Wednesday and Thursday is recorded as a rebound on the surge in tanker attacks in the Gulf and the strait. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz, in that file’s figure, run under 60 percent of capacity.

The tanker file grew on Thursday, in claims, and the claims are filed as claims. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, in their Operational Statement No. 21, said two tankers and a tugboat caught fire after using unauthorized routes through the strait—one tanker on a naval mine in the southern passage and a supertanker on fire in the eastern strait. Later on Thursday Iran’s regular navy reported three additional tanker incidents, vessels said to have struck naval mines in restricted waters east of the strait, per the account of the expanded claims filed below; the Iranian claims for Thursday thus stand at five tankers and a tugboat. Reuters’ Dubai file records the measured file beside them: at least five vessels have reported incidents since Sunday, according to the British maritime security agency UKMTO—about the pace of October, when the agency counted 35 vessels hit, the most of any month of the war—and a vessel was struck by two unidentified projectiles late on Wednesday, placed in the expanded account at about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash-Shamal in Qatar. No independent confirmation of the three additional Thursday incidents appears in any file the desk took in the evening. South Korea’s Defence Ministry said it will deploy maritime patrol aircraft and an explosive ordnance disposal team to waters near the strait, per the account of the strait’s week filed below, which records that South Korea sourced 70 percent of its oil from the Middle East in 2025 and that Iran has warned South Korea against the deployment. No agreement was announced on Thursday. The mediation stands where the midday and evening editions left it—Qatar’s efforts intensified, both governments reviewing proposals, Tehran’s conditions stated, per the mediation account—and Eurasia Group’s odds, carried at evening, stand unrevised at midnight: a deal at 10 percent, renewed American strikes at 60 percent, a continued standoff at 30 percent.

Washington at Midnight

The positions filed on Thursday stand unchanged at midnight, and the evening’s new paper is arithmetic. The president’s two halves—he will get along with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive, and he holds the power of the veto—stand as the Evening Watch printed them, with his answer on impeachment, “not even a little bit.” The incoming majority’s program stands as filed: affordability first, the Medicaid changes reversed, the lapsed health-insurance credits restored, and the funding bills used to limit the administration and the war. The evening account of what happens next, filed below, works the arithmetic both sides are working from: most legislation needs 60 votes to clear the Senate and then the president’s signature; overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers, 67 votes in the Senate, which the majority does not hold; the House can impeach by a simple majority and the Senate can remove only by the same 67; and the power that changes hands whole on January 3 is the Senate’s power to confirm or refuse the president’s nominees. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, on NPR’s Morning Edition on Thursday, stated the majority’s order in her own words, per the account of the interview filed below: lowering costs, restoring health care access, and ending the war in Iran; on the Medicaid restoration, “I dare him to veto that”; on impeachment, no commitment; and, on doing accountability and legislation together, “We can do both.”

The calendar the lame duck will run on is settled, and its first deadline is today. House Republicans’ candidates for their leadership elections must declare by today, Friday, November 6; the elections themselves are set for Tuesday, November 10, in both parties’ House conferences and in the Senate Republican conference, as the Evening Watch filed. Congress returns on Monday, November 9, for the lame-duck session. The government is funded through Friday, December 11, under the stopgap the president signed on September 2, Public Law 119-103, per the funding account filed below; twelve fiscal 2027 appropriations bills stand unfinished, the House having passed three and the Senate none in the accounting carried in the funding files, and the largest sticking point recorded is defense spending, against a request of about $1.5 trillion. Money for the war with Iran is recorded in the same files as the largest item on the outgoing majority’s wish list for the session. None of that business was transacted on Thursday. It is the work the log hands to the week that begins on Monday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the House at midnight: 248 seats won and 13 led in the Associated Press tracker’s latest state, 251 called in the live file’s evening check, and 252 projected with 19 uncalled in the Newsmax account—three methods, three hours, one chamber, and agreement on the outcome and on nothing smaller. Second, Colorado’s 4th: margins of 3,277 votes in the district paper’s 5:30 p.m. count, 3,266 in the state’s 5:25 p.m. figures, 3,069 in Decision Desk HQ’s 9:56 p.m. file, and 2,376 in the later state-results account—the leader the same in all four, the margin narrowing in all four, the race uncalled in all four. Third, the strait: five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in the British agency’s count, against five tankers and a tugboat claimed by Iran for Thursday alone—a count of reports and a count of claims, printed side by side because they are not the same kind of number. Fourth, Friday’s test arrives with a spread already on it: the October payrolls forecasts stand at about 55,000 in one survey, 59,000 in the Dow Jones consensus, and 65,000 in another, per the preview of the report filed below, against September’s 29,000 and an unemployment rate expected to hold at 4.2 percent—with the private ADP report, already in, at 86,000 jobs added against 75,000 expected. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the day are single-valued: no Senate race was called on Thursday; the Dow closed down 1,833.06 points and the Nasdaq Composite down 5.52 percent, in correction; Brent settled at $98.29; Bank Rate stands at 4 percent; jobless claims stand at 189,000; Colorado’s 3rd District is led by its Republican incumbent; and the payrolls report is due at 8:30 a.m. The count belongs to the clerks until November 13 in Colorado and Mississippi and November 18 in Alaska. The log proceeds to Friday.

What the Log Leaves Open

The last entry of the day closes with the open file, stated plainly. The October employment report, today at 8:30 a.m. ET, with a forecast spread of 55,000 to 65,000 jobs around a consensus of 59,000. The House leadership declarations, due today. The leadership elections and Mississippi’s affidavit deadline, on November 10. Colorado’s cure and overseas-ballot deadline at 11:59 p.m. on November 12, and its counties’ final tabulation and Mississippi’s certification on November 13. Nvidia’s earnings on November 17. Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation on November 18. The Federal Reserve’s last meeting of the year on December 9, at which traders, in the preview’s CME figures, price a 67 percent chance of a further 25-basis-point increase. The funding expiry on December 11. The Congress that convenes on January 3. Beneath the calendar, the same open questions the day began with: two Senate seats, two governorships, and between 19 and 29 House races, on the clerks’ schedules; the final size of a majority every file agrees on; and the end of the war, which no agreement announced on Thursday. Until those counts and that Congress settle them, they stand in the log as open. The day is filed. The log turns.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Thirty-one items.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska and Mississippi both too early to call—Mississippi at 99.83 percent of precincts reporting—and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
Votendi — the live results file, House and Senate

251 House seats called for Democrats and 155 for Republicans with 29 still uncalled, in the Associated Press results published by The Guardian in the file’s November 5 check; Decision Desk HQ’s Mississippi figures at 4:12 p.m. EST put Colom at 466,763 votes and Hyde-Smith at 464,939, a lead of 1,824, with more than 95 percent of the estimated vote counted; its Alaska figures put Peltola at 102,962 first-choice votes and Sullivan at 102,325, a lead of 637; and neither lead is a race call.

Subjective
LiveNewsWorld — the running file, evening entries

The file as last verified at 6:44 p.m. ET: at 5:55 p.m. Democrats flip Arizona’s 6th, Colorado’s 5th, Montana’s 1st, and North Carolina’s 9th Districts; at 6:44 p.m. Democrat Cait Conley flips New York’s 17th District, ousting Representative Mike Lawler; and the standing note that the Mississippi and Alaska Senate contests and the Kansas and Alaska governor races remain uncalled, with many House seats not yet projected.

Subjective
Newsmax — House Democrats surpass 250 seats

Democrats reach their highest House total since 2009: the Associated Press projects Democrats will win 252 seats, with 19 races still uncalled and 38 seats already flipped; the Republicans managed to flip only one seat in a district unaffected by mid-decade redistricting, Maine’s 2nd; and New York’s 17th is listed among the uncalled races at the file’s hour, with Lawler already conceded.

Subjective
Associated Press — House, District 17, New York

The district file in its latest state: the race called, Cait Conley at 140,165 votes and Mike Lawler at 128,292, with 87.48 percent of precincts reporting.

Subjective
The Regional Dispatch — the networks confirm Lawler’s Tuesday projection

NBC News projects Conley the winner on Thursday evening and CBS News projects it too, two days after Lawler called Conley to concede on election night; the count at 52.2 percent to 47.7 percent with 87.6 percent of the expected vote in and about 39,000 votes still out in NBC’s estimate; and the Westchester County scanner malfunction that held back part of the count on election day.

Subjective
Rocky Mountain Voice — Colorado, every race

The secretary of state’s figures, updated 5:25 p.m. MST: Democrats have won all four statewide constitutional offices and lead in seven of the eight congressional districts; in the 3rd District, Hurd at 162,669 votes, 49.31 percent, and Romero at 156,472, 47.43 percent, the lead changed hands overnight and the margin widened through the day; in the 4th, Laubacher at 184,024 and Boebert at 180,758, with one of the district’s 21 counties finished counting.

Subjective
Associated Press — House, District 3, Colorado

Hurd 162,669, Romero 156,472, with 96.73 percent of precincts reporting in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
Decision Desk HQ — Colorado’s 3rd District

The returns at 9:07 p.m. EST: Hurd at 163,655 votes, 49.29 percent, Romero at 157,523, 47.44 percent, and the Libertarian Robertson at 5,539, in a file of 332,044 votes. The race is uncalled in the file.

Subjective
Decision Desk HQ — Colorado’s 4th District

The returns at 9:56 p.m. EST: Laubacher at 184,624 votes, 48.75 percent, and Boebert at 181,555, 47.94 percent, in a file of 378,685 votes, more than 95 percent of the expected vote. The race is uncalled in the file.

Subjective
The Coloradoan — when the 4th District will be known

As of about 5:30 p.m. on November 5 the margin stands at 3,277 votes, Laubacher at 48.79 percent and Boebert at 47.92 percent; at least about 7,000 ballots remain to be counted in the four most populous counties in the district; Weld County’s clerk states the bulk of its ballots are counted, with 474 ballots needing signature cures and only military, overseas, and forwarded ballots left; and more counting may still be required on November 6.

Subjective
9NEWS Colorado, via Opera News — Boebert’s strongest county finished

Weld County’s clerk and recorder tells 9NEWS the county has finished counting votes in the 4th District except for ballots with signature problems and ballots forwarded from other counties; the latest state results put Laubacher’s lead at 2,376 votes; Boebert leads in Weld by 20,074 votes to 13,572; about 90 percent of the roughly 26,500 uncounted ballots sit in Douglas, Larimer, and Arapahoe counties, which Laubacher is carrying; and signature fixes and military and overseas ballots are due by 11:59 p.m. on November 12, with counties finishing tabulating on November 13.

Subjective
MarketSpeaker — the close, November 5

The closing levels: the Nasdaq 100 down 6.36 percent to 26,629.81, the Nasdaq Composite down 5.52 percent to 24,315.00, the S&P 500 down 4.36 percent to 7,353.73, and the Dow down 1,833.06 points to 51,523.06; the VIX at 28.09, up 69.1 percent; Nvidia down 9.3 percent, AMD down 17.3 percent, SanDisk down 22.3 percent; the ten-year yield down about six basis points to roughly 4.84 percent.

Subjective
Reuters, via Kitco — Wall Street slumps on chip losses

Qualcomm down 9 percent on the smartphone chip miss; the semiconductor index down 7.1 percent at its hour; IREN, Hut 8, and Applied Digital down between 6 and 11 percent; CoreWeave down 9.3 percent and Nebius down 13.4 percent; Dell down 10.5 percent; Tesla down 9.5 percent; the Swissquote analyst’s statement on scrutiny of the AI buildout; and Cleveland Fed President Hammack’s preference for a gradual rate-hike path.

Subjective
CNBC, via Binance News — futures fall, payrolls awaited

Stock futures fell Thursday evening after the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.5 percent and closed more than 10 percent below its recent high, in correction territory: S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 futures each declined 0.4 percent, and Dow futures lost 201 points, or 0.4 percent; and traders awaited Friday’s October payrolls report, the Dow Jones consensus calling for 59,000 jobs added and an unemployment rate of 4.2 percent.

Subjective
CNBC, via TradingView and Stocktwits — futures dip further after hours

Futures extending declines after hours as investors sold technology and chipmaker stocks on concern a Democratic win could derail the pace of the data-center and AI buildout: S&P 500 futures lost 0.8 percent, Nasdaq-100 futures slid 1.3 percent, and Dow futures shed 264 points, or 0.5 percent; the Russell 2000 lost 4.5 percent in the regular session; and retail sentiment on SPY, QQQ, and DIA was bearish.

Subjective
TradingKey — the Kospi breaker and the Nikkei slide

During Asian trading hours on November 6 the Kospi plunged 8.55 percent to 4,923.47, triggering a Level 1 circuit breaker that halted trading for 20 minutes and breaching the 5,000 level; Samsung Electronics tumbled 10.07 percent to 181,200 won and SK Hynix plunged 12.26 percent to 1,109,000 won; and the Nikkei 225 gapped down at the open to 60,374.35 points from a previous close of 61,077.9 and widened its decline to 6.2 percent, at 57,288.91, breaching 60,000.

Subjective
Upstox — Asian markets on Friday morning

The Nikkei 225 crashed 7 percent to an intraday low of 56,745.81 on Friday, against a previous close of 61,077.90, and stood 5.7 percent lower at 57,579 at 11:18 a.m. in Tokyo; the Kospi tumbled 8.7 percent to a low of 4,911.28 against a previous close of 5,383.80; the Shanghai Composite was down 1.1 percent at 3,649.47 and the Hang Seng down 0.60 percent at 24,649; Brent traded 1.35 percent higher at $99.63 a barrel after an evening-session high of $99.62; and October manufacturing activity in Japan eased to 53.3 from 54.1 in September.

Subjective
Reuters — oil set for a sharp weekly drop, supply concerns a floor

Brent crude futures for January rose $1.57, or 1.6 percent, to $99.86 a barrel as of 0222 GMT on Friday, and West Texas Intermediate futures climbed $1.10, or 1.22 percent, to $91.62; Brent is on track to drop by 12 percent this week after the December contract expired on October 30, and West Texas Intermediate by 12.1 percent; prices rebounded on the surge in tanker attacks on Wednesday and Thursday; overall flows through the Strait of Hormuz are under 60 percent of capacity; and Iran said on Thursday that three more tankers had been attacked in the strait.

Subjective
Reuters, via LSE — Brent settles up over $3 after tanker attacks

New York, November 5: Brent settled up $3.67, or 3.88 percent, at $98.29 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate closed up $2.40, or 2.72 percent, at $90.52, after both fell more than 8 percent on Wednesday; five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in the UKMTO count; Eurasia Group’s revised odds—a deal at 10 percent, renewed strikes at 60 percent, a standoff at 30 percent; the Saudi alerts at Yanbu and the Houthi claim at Dammam; and Foreign Minister Araghchi’s calls with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts.

Subjective
Reuters, via Jack 106.5 — tankers hit in Hormuz, pressure kept up

Dubai, November 5: Iran reported three more tankers damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday; attacks on tankers are still running close to a record pace, at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in the UKMTO count, against 35 vessels hit in October; the Revolutionary Guards said two tankers had struck naval mines and another had caught fire on Thursday; Parliament Speaker Qalibaf’s answer to the vice president is quoted; the supreme leader’s statement against submission is recorded; two unnamed sources state the president is still likely to order resumed hostilities; and peacemaking efforts revolve around the strait, the blockade, sanctions, and the nuclear program.

Subjective
Open Chronicle — five tankers reported damaged

The Revolutionary Guards initially reported two tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents overnight, one said to have struck a naval mine in the southern passage and a supertanker on fire in the eastern strait; Iran’s regular navy later reported three additional tanker incidents east of the strait; the UKMTO separately reported a vessel struck by two projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash-Shamal in Qatar; Brent climbed sharply by Thursday’s close; and the full circumstances could not be independently verified.

Subjective
UmmahAtlas — Project Freedom and the November 5 reports

The mission the president announced on Sunday to guide stranded ships through the strait, its pause while talks continued, and the blockade remaining in force; the United States military’s denial of the claim that a warship was hit near Jask; South Korea’s Defence Ministry announcing on November 5 that it will deploy maritime patrol aircraft and an explosive ordnance disposal team to waters near the strait, with South Korea sourcing 70 percent of its oil from the Middle East in 2025; Iran’s warning to South Korea against the deployment; and the Guards’ November 5 statement that two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire after crossing an unauthorized southern route, with two drones seized.

Subjective
AnewZ — tensions persist as Qatar pushes for a deal

Qatar’s mediation intensified; both governments reviewing the mediators’ proposals; the senior Iranian official’s statement that the sides remain far apart and that Tehran’s conditions must precede the strait’s reopening; the 36-hour expectation for responses, and the later statement that no fixed deadline exists.

Subjective
CNBC, via TradingView — 59,000 forecast for October payrolls

Economists expect nonfarm payrolls to increase by 59,000 in October, up from 29,000 in September, while the unemployment rate holds at 4.2 percent, in the Dow Jones consensus; the Bureau of Labor Statistics is scheduled to release the report Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET; payroll growth averaged 35,000 from January 2025 through September 2026, while the labor force contracted by 434,000 during that period.

Subjective
Archynewsy — what to expect from the October jobs report

The forecasts split between 55,000 and 65,000 jobs: the Dow Jones consensus at 59,000, Bloomberg-surveyed economists at 65,000, and the Kiplinger-cited forecasts at about 55,000, with unemployment unchanged at 4.2 percent; the ADP private report showed 86,000 jobs added in October, above the 75,000 expected; annual wage growth is forecast at 2.9 percent against September inflation of 3.7 percent, with paychecks losing ground to prices for a seventh straight month; and traders see a 67 percent chance of a 25-basis-point increase at the Federal Reserve’s December 9 meeting.

Subjective
Reuters, via 941 The Duke — jobless claims at 57-year lows

Initial claims down 6,000 to 189,000 for the week ended October 31, against a forecast of 196,000, matching the lowest reading since 1969; continuing claims at 1.718 million; third-quarter productivity up at a 3.6 percent annualized rate against a forecast of 2.8 percent; and the statement that the claims report has no bearing on Friday’s October employment report.

Subjective
Reuters — the Bank of England raises rates

Bank Rate raised to 4 percent from 3.75 percent by 8–1, Catherine Mann voting for 4.25 percent; inflation expected to reach about 5 percent in the middle of next year and to return to target in the third quarter of 2028; Governor Bailey’s statement that the increase is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict is resolved.

Subjective
WAMC, carrying NPR — Senator Gillibrand on the majority’s work

Senator Gillibrand on Morning Edition: Democrats would focus on lowering costs, restoring health care access, and ending the war in Iran; she challenges the president to veto bipartisan legislation restoring Medicaid coverage; asked about impeachment, she did not commit to pursuing it; and she proposes a ban on stock trading by members of Congress and senior administration officials, stating that the majority can do both accountability and legislation.

Subjective
The funding account — the stopgap and the lame duck

There is no shutdown on the calendar for 39 more days: the stopgap bill the president signed on September 2, Public Law 119-103, keeps every federal agency funded through Friday, December 11, 2026; Congress returns on Monday, November 9, to a lame-duck session; twelve full-year fiscal 2027 appropriations bills are still unfinished; the House Appropriations Committee has advanced all twelve draft bills; and the biggest sticking point is defense spending, with a request of about $1.5 trillion.

Subjective
The Miami Metropolis — what happens next, the veto pen

Florida stayed with the Republicans while the Democrats took both chambers; the incoming majority’s first statements, including the two-word message to the administration from the incoming Oversight ranking member, “Lawyer up”; the arithmetic that most legislation needs 60 Senate votes and the president’s signature, that overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers, and that a third impeachment could pass the House and would need 67 Senate votes to remove; and the Senate’s power to confirm or refuse cabinet secretaries, judges, and ambassadors from January 3.

entry.title: The Second Reading: The Chips Fall Twelve Percent and the Buildout Is Repriced
entry.summary: A special report from the desk, filed outside the watches: on Wednesday the market bought the midterm result; on Thursday it sold the same result. The Nasdaq fell 5.52 percent into correction, the semiconductor index fell 12.25 percent, and the ballot record on data centers reached the tape.
entry.content:
Special Report

The Markets File — The Second Reading of an Election

Objective

The Second Reading: The Chips Fall Twelve Percent and the Buildout Is Repriced

On Wednesday the market read the midterm results and bought. On Thursday it read them again and sold. The two closes, the ballot record underneath them, and the governments the voters chose, in one file, outside the watches.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1912 ET, Thursday, November 5, 2026. The day’s complete record—the count, the strait, the considered responses of every side—stands in Edition No. 8, the Evening Watch. This report stands the market story on its own.

The Two Closes

The same election was priced twice in two sessions, and the second price erased the first and went past it. On Wednesday, the first session after the midterms, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,569.40 points, or 3.0 percent, to 53,356.12; the S&P 500 rose 1.6 percent to 7,688.62; the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4 percent to 25,736.51. On Thursday the Dow fell 1,833.06 points to 51,523.06; the S&P 500 fell 4.36 percent to 7,353.73, its worst day since April 2025; the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52 percent to 24,315.00. All three indexes closed below their levels of Tuesday, election day, and the Nasdaq’s close stands 11.9 percent below its record close of October 6—inside correction territory, by the usual definition.

IndexWednesday, Nov. 4Thursday, Nov. 5
Dow Jones Industrial Average+1,569.40 (+3.0%) · 53,356.12−1,833.06 (−3.44%) · 51,523.06
S&P 500+1.6% · 7,688.62−4.36% · 7,353.73
Nasdaq Composite+1.4% · 25,736.51−5.52% · 24,315.00

No result changed between the two sessions. The ballots counted on Wednesday morning were the ballots counted on Thursday morning. What changed was the reading. Wednesday’s session priced the election as an event completed. Thursday’s session priced it as a program begun: a Congress of the other party, governors elected on stated intentions toward the data-center buildout, and a ballot record, assembled measure by measure across ten states, in which voters had answered the buildout directly. The desk states the sequence because the sequence is the fact: the votes were counted first, the governments changed second, and the capital was repriced third.

What Fell on Thursday

The selling was led by the companies that build the artificial-intelligence infrastructure, and it was the largest single-day destruction of market value on record. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25 percent to 9,011.14, its second-worst fall on record. SanDisk fell 22 percent; Advanced Micro Devices fell 17.26 percent; Micron and Marvell fell about 17 percent each; Broadcom fell 10.43 percent; Nvidia fell 9.26 percent to $181.60, erasing its gains for the year; Qualcomm fell 9.5 percent. Roughly $2.5 trillion of value left the Nasdaq Composite and roughly $2.9 trillion left the companies of the S&P 500, each a single-day record in the accounts filed; the seven largest technology companies lost about $1.04 trillion among them. The volatility index rose 69 percent to 28.18.

The falls were lopsided, and the lopsidedness is part of the record. The companies that own computing capacity fell far less than the companies that build it or finance it. Meta Platforms fell 3.4 percent. The neocloud companies, which borrow to build capacity and rent it out—CoreWeave and Nebius—fell between 10 and 17.6 percent; the data-center operators IREN, Hut 8, and Applied Digital fell between 6 and 11 percent; Tesla fell 11 percent. The market did not sell the use of the machines at the rate it sold the making of them.

The Ballot Record

On Tuesday, in ten states, the buildout itself was on the ballot, and the answers were recorded precinct by precinct. Forty-one local measures on data-center construction were put to voters in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, and Wisconsin. In the fullest tracker the desk can file—Ballotpedia’s, with results for all forty-one—forty went the way of tighter limits: bans adopted, moratoriums approved, rezoning refused, measures that would have eased construction rejected. The one exception was Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected an added review requirement for large industrial projects by 325 votes to 105. Some of the measures are binding law and some are advisory; the desk prints them as one record because the voters cast them as one.

The margins were not narrow. Kansas wrote its definitions into the questions—a high-impact facility is one drawing more than 10 megawatts of peak electricity or more than 100,000 gallons of water a day—and El Dorado adopted a ten-year ban by 71 to 29, Emporia a prohibition by 60 to 40, and Ottawa a ban on facilities above 25 megawatts by 69 to 31. In Alhambra, California, 82 percent voted to ban data centers from the city. In Joliet, Illinois, 79 percent answered no to an advisory question asking the city to approve them, and 88 percent of Morgan County, Illinois, backed restrictions. Ohio carried twenty-one of the forty-one measures, the most of any state: in Wilmington, rezoning for a data-center project was rejected by roughly four votes to one, and in Hubbard more than three-quarters approved a ban. Edgewater, Florida, voted that no new data centers be built there. An Ohio effort to place a constitutional amendment banning new construction on next year’s statewide ballot is under way. The record is not closed: Clarksville, Arkansas, decides data-center bond questions on December 1, and Mandan, North Dakota, votes on a ban covering facilities of 25 megawatts or more on December 15.

The Governments the Voters Chose

The partisan result is stated as the counts stand on Thursday evening. The Democrats will organize both chambers of the Congress that convenes on January 3. The Senate stands at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled and the Democratic candidate leading in each. The Associated Press House tracker in its latest state shows 248 seats won by the Democrats and 13 more led, against 154 won and 20 led for the Republicans. The governorships stand at 28 for the Democrats, with Alaska and Kansas open, and by Ballotpedia’s accounting the party will hold 21 state trifectas—the most it has held since 1992.

In the state where the buildout is concentrated, the governorship changed hands on the question. Texas holds the largest share of planned American data-center capacity. Its voters elected the Democrat, Gina Hinojosa, over the incumbent Republican governor, Greg Abbott, after she promised a moratorium on new data-center construction. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship after calling for a pause on new data centers. In Ohio, the state with twenty-one measures on its local ballots, the Democrat, Amy Acton, won the governorship. What the incoming Congress will do with the buildout has not been filed as legislation; what is on the record is the expectation, stated by the analysts quoted in the clippings below, of scrutiny of the construction program, and a bank’s estimate, carried in the morning file, that about 30 percent of the data-center additions expected in 2028 stand at risk from pauses.

What Did Not Happen, and What Comes Next

No collapse in demand for the technology was reported on Thursday, and no company at the center of the fall reported one. AMD fell 17.26 percent two days after guiding its results above expectations. Qualcomm’s Wednesday disappointment, the one company-specific result in the chain, was in smartphone chips and the rising cost of memory, a different ledger from the data centers. The day’s economic figures ran the other way: initial claims for unemployment benefits stood at 189,000, the lowest reading since 1969, as the Evening Watch filed. The reported trigger of the repricing was not an earnings statement. It was the election, read the second time.

The calendar ahead is fixed, and the desk prints it as the file’s last entry. Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET brings the October employment report. On November 10 the House parties hold their leadership elections and Mississippi’s affidavit identification falls due; Mississippi certifies on November 13. Nvidia reports on November 17. Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18. The Arkansas and North Dakota data-center votes follow on December 1 and December 15. The Congress whose scrutiny the market priced on Thursday convenes on January 3.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. The ballot record carries one. A Wednesday-morning tally counted thirty-eight of the forty-one measures decided, thirty-seven of them for limits. Ballotpedia’s tracker, complete at forty-one, counts forty for limits. A New York Post accounting counted at least fifty measures, forty-seven decided against the buildout. The tallies were taken at different hours, over different definitions of what counts as a data-center measure; they do not agree on the size of the record, and they agree on its direction—no tally on the shelf runs the other way. Against the triangle, the single-valued facts of this report are the two closes: on Wednesday the Dow rose 1,569.40 points; on Thursday it fell 1,833.06. The results did not change. The reading did. The log proceeds to the Midnight Watch.

The Clippings Filed With This Report

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this report stamped objective. Six items.

Subjective
Reuters — the tech rout and the retreat from the AI trade
